about: MATCH character database. types are personality types adapted from free sources (public-domain novels; the CC BY 4.0 webcomic Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy). Personalities only: no names, likenesses or text are copied. Edit a woman's type or notes, or any type, then rebuild the game. Re-running build-character-database.mjs keeps your edits.

fields.bigFive: Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism, each 1 to 5
fields.speed: multiplies her reply delay; below 1 is faster
fields.out: when she has no pictures left
fields.unasked: Mogger only: a picture she sends without being asked
fields.voice: openers and sign-offs she wraps round answers to town-wide topics
fields.reactions: what she says when your follow-up answer warms her (warm) or puts her off (cool)
fields.conversation: topics only she has (own, some needing warmth first) and her own answers to town-wide topics (views)
fields.worldTopics: questions you can ask any woman; each faction answers its own way, then she asks you back
fields.newsTalk: asking about today’s paper: each kind of story gets a faction view, and inside knowledge for the factions involved
fields.roots: the story behind her opinions (love, faith, world): told when you ask why she thinks that
fields.talk: the conversation engine: faction likes and dislikes, questions she asks you, moods, callbacks, town asides, reputation, news follow-ups and Easter eggs
fields.talk.calls: women who really like you call you: openers, flirting, what they let slip, and the Sisters’ marriage questions
fields.talk.daily: How was your day?: her mood, her life in Sunfall, and what she asks back
fields.talk.morning: messages warm women send first on a new day
fields.talk.dates: how she answers an invitation for coffee

credits: Pepper, Saffron, Shichimi and Cilantro types: Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy, CC BY 4.0 (https://www.peppercarrot.com).

Public-domain works: Austen, the Brontës, Alcott, Montgomery, Thackeray, Doyle, Stoker, Le Fanu, Fitzgerald, Hemingway, Christie, Baum, Carroll, Hawthorne, the Thousand and One Nights, and the 1930 Nancy Drew mysteries.

types.label: The Witty Skeptic
types.traits: Teases first and judges fast, then changes her mind when you prove her wrong. Loves a good argument.

first.mogger: Fine, I swiped right. Don’t let it go to your head. (It already has, hasn’t it.)
first.normie: Your profile is either very honest or very clever. I haven’t decided which.
first.truecel: I swiped right on you by accident and now I’m too proud to unmatch. Impress me.

types.another: Greedy. But you asked nicely, so here.
types.out: That’s the lot. I like to keep some mystery.
types.refuse: We’ve barely spoken. Earn it.
types.unasked: You’re being suspiciously charming, so here’s a reward.

warm: Ha. Okay, you’re smarter than your profile.
Fine. That was a good answer. Don’t get smug.

roots.love: My parents married for convenience and spent thirty years being polite at each other. I decided I’d rather be alone than polite.
roots.faith: I was the girl who asked awkward questions in Bible class. The vicar never had answers, but he never stopped me asking, and I loved him for it.
roots.world: I judged someone early and loudly once, and I was completely wrong. Now I make myself argue the other side before I decide anything.

types.label: The Principled Plain-Speaker
types.traits: Quiet, honest to a fault, values respect over romance and will walk away from anyone who lies.

first.mogger: I don’t usually message first. You seemed worth breaking a rule for.
first.normie: Hello. I prefer honest conversation to clever lines, if that suits you.
first.truecel: I’ll be honest, since that’s how I am: I’m not sure why I matched with you. Tell me something true.

types.another: One more. I trust you with it.
types.out: There aren’t any more, and I’d rather talk.
types.refuse: I don’t send pictures to people I don’t know.
types.unasked: I don’t do this often. Don’t make me regret it.

warm: Thank you for being honest. That matters to me.
I think we understand each other.
cool: I don’t think that’s true, and I suspect you don’t either.
I’d rather you were honest than charming.

roots.love: I grew up with people who were kind only when it suited them. I promised myself I’d only love someone who was the same in private as in public.
roots.faith: I lost nearly everything once. The one thing that stayed was a small, stubborn sense that I mattered to God. I’ve kept hold of it since.
roots.world: Someone powerful lied about me when I was young and everyone believed him. I’ve never trusted a crowd since.

types.label: The Tomboy Writer
types.traits: Loud, loyal and hot-tempered; writes stories nobody reads; hates being told what women should do.

first.mogger: Okay, you’re going in my novel. As the love interest, if you play your cards right.
first.normie: Warning: I will turn anything you say into a short story.
first.truecel: You look like a character I’d kill off in chapter two. Prove me wrong.

types.another: Ha! Fine. Don’t show my sisters.
types.out: That’s every picture I own that isn’t ink-stained.
types.refuse: Ask me something interesting first.
types.unasked: Wrote you a scene. Sending a picture instead, it’s less embarrassing.

warm: YES. Exactly. Where have you been?
You get it! Nobody gets it!
cool: Ugh. You sound like my aunt.

roots.love: I turned down the nicest boy in town because I didn’t love him. Everyone said I’d regret it. Some days I do. Most days I don’t.
roots.faith: My mother’s faith was quiet and practical: soup for the neighbors, no sermons. It’s the only kind I believe in.
roots.world: I’ve wanted to be a writer since I was ten. Writers have to listen to everyone, even people you can’t stand. Especially them.

types.label: The Meddling Matchmaker
types.traits: Confident, well-off and sure she knows what is best for everyone, you included. Means well.

first.mogger: I’ve already decided we’re perfect together. I’m very rarely wrong.
first.normie: I set people up for fun. Let’s see if I can set myself up for once.
first.truecel: I only matched to see who I could set you up with. Don’t take it personally.

types.another: You’re lucky I like an audience.
types.out: That’s all of them. Now, about your wardrobe…
types.refuse: Patience. I decide when.
types.unasked: I picked this one specially. You’re welcome.

close: I’m never wrong about these things.

warm: See? I knew you had good taste.
Oh, we are going to get along beautifully.
cool: Oh dear. We’ll work on that.

roots.love: I matched my best friend with the wrong man once, and she cried for a month. I still meddle. I’m just more careful about it.
roots.faith: My father worried about everything. Church was the only place he ever stopped. I go for him, really.
roots.world: I’ve always thought I knew best. I’m learning, slowly, that other people’s lives aren’t puzzles for me to solve.

types.label: The Dreamy Chatterbox
types.inspiredBy: Anne Shirley, Anne of Green Gables
types.traits: Imaginative, dramatic and endlessly talkative; names everything; feels every feeling at full volume.

first.mogger: Oh! You’re real! I was imagining someone exactly like you this morning.
first.normie: Hello! I’ve already made up three stories about you. Shall I tell you the best one?
first.truecel: Oh. Hello. I suppose I matched with you. That’s… a tragic romance waiting to happen, probably.

types.another: Of course! I have hundreds, it’s a problem.
types.out: Oh, that’s really the last one! How tragic.
types.refuse: Not yet! A bit more mystery first.
types.unasked: I couldn’t wait, here’s me being dramatic by a window.

close: I could talk about this forever. I might!

warm: Oh, I love that! You’re a kindred spirit!
That’s the most romantic thing anyone’s said to me all day!
cool: Oh. Well. That’s a bit of a tragedy.

roots.love: I was passed around a lot as a little girl. I think that’s why I fall for places and people so fast. I want somewhere to belong.
roots.faith: I think the desert at sunrise is a sort of prayer. I said so once in church and an old lady patted my hand very gently.
roots.world: Everyone told me I talked too much and imagined too much. Then they all wanted me to write their speeches.

types.label: The All-In Romantic
types.traits: Falls fast and hard, quotes poetry, despises half-measures, and is crushed by coldness.

first.mogger: I knew from your first picture. Is that mad? Tell me it isn’t mad.
first.normie: Tell me what moves you. Music, books, anything. I can’t stand small talk.
first.truecel: I usually only match with people who make my heart race. You’re… an experiment.

types.out: You’ve seen every one. Now you know me.
types.refuse: Not until I feel something.
types.unasked: I wanted you to see me right now, this exact moment.

close: Doesn’t that make your heart ache?

warm: Oh. You feel it too. I knew it.
That made my heart actually jump.
cool: That’s so cold. Do you feel anything at all?
Oh. I thought you were different.

roots.love: I loved someone completely at nineteen, and he left without a word. I was ill for weeks. I’d still rather feel too much than too little.
roots.faith: When I was ill, my sister sat with me every night and prayed. I didn’t believe then. I think I do now, a little, because of her.
roots.world: I can’t stand people who are clever about everything and feel nothing. That’s why the fight up at the university makes me want to scream.

types.label: The Reserved Sensible One
types.traits: Calm, dutiful and private; feels deeply but shows little; respects patience.

first.mogger: I don’t normally message first. I thought I’d make an exception.
first.normie: Good evening. I’m better in person than in messages, I’m told.
first.truecel: I matched with you to be polite. Let’s see where politeness gets us.

types.out: That really is all.
types.refuse: Perhaps once we know each other properly.
types.unasked: A small exception. Don’t tell anyone.

warm: That’s a sensible answer. I appreciate that.
I think so too.
cool: I see. We’ll have to disagree.

roots.love: I loved someone quietly for a long time while he was promised to someone else. I said nothing. Feelings can wait, I learned. They don’t go away.
roots.faith: Duty and faith feel very close to me. You do what’s right whether or not you feel like it. The feeling follows, usually.
roots.world: In my family someone had to stay calm while everyone else panicked. It was always me. So I distrust anyone who’s shouting.

types.label: The Wild Heart
types.traits: Passionate, stormy and possessive; loves fiercely and fights harder; hates being tamed.

first.mogger: You. I want to know everything, and I want it now.
first.normie: Are you the sort who stays when things get stormy? Most don’t.
first.truecel: Ugh, why did I swipe on you. Fine. Entertain me before I get bored.

types.another: Take it before I change my mind.
types.out: No more. Want me? Come and find me.
types.refuse: You haven’t earned the storm yet.
types.unasked: Out on the moors… well, the desert. Thinking of you. Annoyingly.

close: And I don’t care who hears it.
Don’t try to calm me down.

warm: YES. You’ve got fire. I like fire.
Now that is an answer.
cool: That’s boring. Don’t be boring with me.

roots.love: There was a boy I grew up with, out on the canyon edge. I married someone sensible instead and it nearly killed me. I won’t do that twice.
roots.faith: I don’t want a tidy heaven. If heaven isn’t wild, I’d rather be out on the canyon.
roots.world: Everyone in Sunfall wants me tamer, quieter, more polite. The less they like me, the more myself I get.

types.label: The Charming Schemer
types.traits: Ambitious, witty and always working an angle; delightful company; never quite trustworthy.

first.mogger: You look like someone who’s going places. Take me with you?
first.normie: Tell me what you do. No, really, what do you DO. I’m curious.
first.truecel: Hm. What can you do for me? Be honest.

types.another: Fine, but you owe me a favor.
types.out: Nothing more for free.
types.refuse: And what do I get in return?
types.unasked: A little gift. I’ll remember you got it.

close: I may need a favor for that one.

warm: Clever. I could use someone clever.
Oh, I like the way you think.
cool: Hm. You won’t get far like that.

roots.love: I grew up with nothing and watched rich girls marry richer men. I learned early that love’s a game. I just decided to play it well.
roots.faith: Church is where the best-dressed people in town sit still long enough to be charmed. Cynical, I know.
roots.world: Nobody ever handed me anything. So when people argue about fairness, I laugh. You climb or you drown.

types.label: The Unflappable Mastermind
types.inspiredBy: Irene Adler, A Scandal in Bohemia
types.traits: Cool, clever and always three moves ahead; amused by men who underestimate her.

first.mogger: I looked you up. You passed. Barely.
first.normie: I’ll know if you lie, so let’s skip that part.
first.truecel: I matched with you to see if you’d be interesting. The jury’s out.

types.another: You were going to ask anyway.
types.out: A woman keeps a few secrets.
types.refuse: Clever try.
types.unasked: I predicted you’d want this.

warm: Good. You’re paying attention.
Correct. I’m mildly impressed.
cool: I expected that answer. That’s the problem.

roots.love: A very powerful man underestimated me once. I won. Since then I only want someone who could almost beat me.
roots.faith: I believe in very few things: preparation, nerve, and a God who seems to enjoy a good plan.
roots.world: I’ve watched clever men assume women can’t plan. I let them assume. It’s useful.

types.label: The Organized Brave One
types.traits: Methodical, loyal and quietly fearless; keeps notes on everything; first to act in a crisis.

first.mogger: I already wrote you into my diary. Favourably.
first.normie: I keep notes on everyone I meet. So far yours just says promising.
first.truecel: My notes on you so far: unclear. Let’s improve that.

types.out: That’s everything in the folder.
types.refuse: Later. I have notes to finish.
types.unasked: Filed under things you’ll like.

warm: Good answer. You’re going in the promising column.
That’s sensible. I like sensible.
cool: That goes in the concerns column.

roots.love: My dad left when I was little and my mom ran our house like a ship. I want a partner, not a passenger.
roots.faith: My grandmother kept a list of everyone she prayed for. I keep lists too. Maybe it’s the same instinct.
roots.world: When everything’s chaos, someone has to make the plan. I’ve been that person since I was twelve.

types.label: The Velvet Mystery
types.traits: Languid, intense and secretive; speaks in hints; seems to know more than she says.

first.mogger: I’ve been waiting for someone like you. Longer than you’d believe.
first.normie: Do you like the night? I find people are more honest in the dark.
first.truecel: Strange. I don’t usually match with your kind. Talk, then.

types.out: No more. Some things are for later.
types.refuse: Not in the daylight.
types.unasked: Couldn’t sleep. Thought of you. Here.

close: But that’s only half of it.
Some things you have to see at night.

warm: You understand more than you let on. I like that.
Mm. Yes. Come closer.

roots.love: I loved someone who was frightened by how much I felt. He left before sunrise. I’ve been a night creature ever since.
roots.faith: I grew up in an old house full of crucifixes and very quiet aunts. Faith always felt like a locked room. I still want the key.
roots.world: People in daylight say very certain things. At night they whisper the truth. I prefer the whispering.

types.label: The Golden Careless One
types.traits: Dazzling, breezy and a little thoughtless; lives for parties; easily bored by serious talk.

first.mogger: Oh, you’re divine. Let’s go somewhere glamorous and ruin our reputations.
first.normie: Hello, darling. Entertain me? Everyone here is so dull.
first.truecel: Oh! I must have swiped by accident. Well, you’re here now. Amuse me.

types.out: That’s all of them! Isn’t that a shame.
types.refuse: Oh, not now, I look a fright.
types.unasked: Look how golden the light is. Look at me in it.

warm: Oh, you’re divine. Say more fun things.
Love that. Let’s have cocktails about it.

roots.love: I waited for someone once and he didn’t come back in time, so I married money. I’m happy. I’m almost always happy. Ask me again later.
roots.faith: God and I have an arrangement. I don’t bother him, and he doesn’t bother me.
roots.world: Darling, the people who argue about everything have either never worried about rent or always have. I can’t keep track.

types.label: The Cool Competitor
types.traits: Athletic, aloof and hard to impress; bends rules to win; secretly likes being chased.

first.mogger: You look like you could keep up with me. Prove it.
first.normie: I play to win. Do you?
first.truecel: Bold of you to match with me. Let’s see if you can keep up.

types.out: Game over, no more.
types.refuse: Beat me at something first.
types.unasked: Just won. Felt like showing off.

warm: Ha. Okay, point to you.
Good. You can keep up.

roots.love: I don’t like losing, and love is mostly losing. So I keep it casual. Mostly.
roots.faith: I played golf with a priest once. He cheated. That’s my whole theology.
roots.world: In sport you know where you stand: there’s a score. Everywhere else, people pretend there isn’t one.

types.label: The Restless Heartbreaker
types.inspiredBy: Lady Brett Ashley, The Sun Also Rises
types.traits: Free-spirited, magnetic and impossible to pin down; adores attention; never stays long.

first.mogger: Let’s not pretend. I want you. Where shall we go?
first.normie: I get bored terribly quickly. Don’t be boring.
first.truecel: Darling, I match with everyone. Don’t read into it.

types.out: That’s the lot, darling.
types.refuse: Not tonight. Ask me another time.
types.unasked: Out and about. Wish you were here, or don’t I?

warm: Oh, I could fall for you if you’re not careful.
You’re trouble. Good.

roots.love: I lost someone in a way I don’t talk about. Since then I’ve loved a lot of people a little, so I never have to love one all the way.
roots.faith: I go into churches when I’m sad. I can’t pray, but I like being somewhere people do.
roots.world: Everyone’s lost, darling. The arguing is just what lost people do to feel found.

types.label: The Thrill-Seeker
types.traits: Bold, cheerful and desperate for adventure; would rather chase a mystery than sit still.

first.mogger: You look like trouble. Excellent. When do we start?
first.normie: Quick question: are you an adventure or a nap?
first.truecel: Matched with you out of boredom, honestly. Got anything exciting?

types.out: That’s all the evidence I have.
types.refuse: Do something daring first.
types.unasked: Mid-adventure selfie! Don’t ask.

warm: Ha! Yes! You’re fun!
Partner in crime material, definitely.
cool: Oh come on, live a little.

roots.love: My first love dared me to jump off the old quarry ledge. I jumped. He didn’t. I’ve been looking for someone who’d jump ever since.
roots.faith: I’ve had a couple of close calls. Each time, right before, I prayed. So maybe I believe more than I let on.
roots.world: Boredom is the real enemy in a town like this. Half the shouting in Sunfall is just bored people.

types.label: The Earnest Heart
types.inspiredBy: Dorothy Gale, The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
types.traits: Kind, homesick and brave when it counts; trusts easily; wants somewhere to belong.

first.mogger: Hi! You seem kind. That matters most to me.
first.normie: Hi there. Sunfall still doesn’t feel like home. Does it for you?
first.truecel: Oh. Hi. I’m sure you’re nice. Probably.

types.out: That’s all of them, honestly.
types.refuse: Maybe when I know you better.
types.unasked: I took this today and thought you might smile.

warm: That’s really kind. Thank you.
I knew you were nice.
cool: I hope you don’t really mean that.

roots.love: My parents still hold hands at the supermarket. I know it’s possible. I just haven’t found my person yet.
roots.faith: When my little brother was ill, the whole parish brought food for weeks. I don’t know much theology. I know what that felt like.
roots.world: I try to see the best in people. I’m usually right. When I’m wrong, it hurts a lot.

types.label: The Curious Contrarian
types.traits: Inquisitive, logical and argumentative; questions everything, especially nonsense.

first.mogger: Curiouser and curiouser. Why are you so interesting?
first.normie: Explain your profile. It makes no sense, and I want it to.
first.truecel: Why did I match with you? I genuinely can’t work it out.

types.out: There aren’t any more. That’s simple arithmetic.
types.refuse: Why should I?
types.unasked: An experiment: does a picture make you nicer?

close: Why does nobody else see that?

warm: Ooh, you argued back. Excellent.
Interesting. Nobody ever disagrees with me properly.
cool: You’re just agreeing to be nice. Don’t.

roots.love: I fell down the rabbit hole of a terrible relationship once, and everything was upside down. Now I question everything, especially feelings.
roots.faith: I asked why so often at church that the priest started giving me books instead of answers. Best thing anyone ever did for me.
roots.world: When everyone agrees, I get suspicious. When everyone’s angry, I get curious.

types.label: The Spellbinding Storyteller
types.inspiredBy: Scheherazade, One Thousand and One Nights
types.traits: Clever and captivating; always leaves a story unfinished so you come back.

first.mogger: I’ll tell you a story, but only the beginning. You’ll have to come back for the rest.
first.normie: Shall I tell you a story? I never finish them on the first night.
first.truecel: I’ll tell you a story to pass the time. Don’t get ideas.

types.out: The rest of the story is in person.
types.refuse: Not yet. The story isn’t there yet.
types.unasked: An illustration for tonight’s story.

close: But that’s a story for another night.

warm: Oh, you’re a good listener. That’s rare.
You’ve earned the next chapter.

roots.love: My grandmother kept my grandfather in love for sixty years by telling him stories. Her trick, she said, was never to finish one.
roots.faith: Every faith is a story told so well it changes people. I don’t think that makes it less true. I think it makes it more.
roots.world: Every side in Sunfall has a story about itself. I listen for the bit they skip.

types.label: The Dignified Outsider
types.traits: Independent and proud; judged by others and done caring; makes beautiful things by hand.

first.mogger: People talk about me. You’re the first who looks like you don’t care.
first.normie: Fair warning: people gossip about me. I’ve stopped minding.
first.truecel: I know what people say about me. I don’t need it from you too.

types.out: That’s all I’ll share.
types.refuse: I’ve learned not to give people ammunition.
types.unasked: Something I made, and me with it.

open: People don’t like hearing this, but
close: I stopped caring what they think.

warm: You don’t judge. I notice that.
Thank you. Truly.

roots.love: I made one mistake, in public, years ago, and this town has never let me forget it. I know what it’s like to be judged by people who’ve never been caught.
roots.faith: The church folk were the cruellest to me, and also the only ones who brought me food. I’ve never untangled that.
roots.world: I’ve been on the wrong end of a mob. I don’t care which side it’s on. A mob is a mob.

types.label: The Girl Sleuth
types.inspiredBy: the early Nancy Drew mysteries (1930; personality only, the name is a trademark)
types.traits: Confident, resourceful and nosy; cannot leave a mystery alone; drives too fast.

first.mogger: You have a mysterious air. I love a mystery.
first.normie: Quick: what’s the strangest thing you’ve noticed in Sunfall lately?
first.truecel: I matched to investigate why you swiped on me. Case open.

types.out: That’s every clue I’m giving.
types.refuse: Solve something first.
types.unasked: On a stakeout. Bored. Here’s me.

warm: Good thinking. You’d make a decent sidekick.
Ooh, that’s a clue. I like you.
cool: Hm, no. Doesn’t fit the evidence.

roots.love: My dad’s a lawyer and raised me on evidence before conclusions. It turns out that’s terrible advice for falling in love.
roots.faith: I like mysteries with answers. Faith is a mystery that doesn’t hand you one. I’m still working on that.
roots.world: I found a lost dog when I was eight by asking every neighbor the same three questions. I’ve never stopped asking questions.

types.label: The Chaotic Sweetheart
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Enthusiastic, clumsy and big-hearted; every plan goes slightly wrong; never gives up.

first.mogger: Hi!! Sorry, I set my kitchen on fire a bit. You’re cute! Hi!
first.normie: Hello! I’m having a chaotic day, distract me?
first.truecel: Oh no, I swiped the wrong way again. Hi, I guess!

types.out: Oh no, I’m out! I deleted the rest by accident.
types.refuse: Wait, wait, I look like a mess!
types.unasked: Look what I did! (It went wrong.)

warm: Aaa you’re so nice! Hi!
Okay I like you a lot already!
cool: Oh nooo. Okay. That’s fine. It’s fine!

roots.love: I’ve set three kitchens on fire trying to bake for boys. I’m due some luck, honestly.
roots.faith: My godmothers are very strict about tradition. I find it all very confusing, but I light a candle when I’m scared, and it seems to help.
roots.world: Where I grew up, mistakes were how you learned. Here they’re how you get canceled.

types.label: The Glamorous Rival
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Vain, rich and competitive; loves being admired; secretly afraid nobody likes the real her.

first.mogger: Finally, someone worthy of my time.
first.normie: You may compliment me now.
first.truecel: Did my phone glitch? Why are we matched?

types.out: You’ve seen my best. Everything else is merely excellent.
types.refuse: You haven’t complimented me enough.
types.unasked: I look stunning today. You should know.

close: I’m always right about these things.

warm: Finally, someone with taste.
Correct. You may stay.

roots.love: Everyone assumed I’d marry well. I’ve had proposals. I turned them all down. I’m waiting for someone who doesn’t bore me.
roots.faith: I go to the cathedral for the weddings and the hats. I stay for the music. Don’t spread that around.
roots.world: I was the most hated girl at school and the most invited. I learned early that envy and admiration look identical.

types.label: The Shy Gentle One
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Soft-spoken, polite and kind; slow to open up; surprisingly strong when pushed.

first.mogger: H-hi. You’re very… hello.
first.normie: Hello. Sorry, I’m not good at first messages.
first.truecel: Oh. Hello. I didn’t expect a match. Um. Sorry.

types.out: That’s all of them, sorry.
types.refuse: I’m too shy, sorry.
types.unasked: I was brave today. Here.

warm: Oh! That’s… really nice. Thank you.
I’m smiling at my phone. Sorry.

roots.love: I grew up in a house of loud cousins. I was the quiet one in the corner. The person I love will be the one who notices the corner.
roots.faith: Prayer is the one place I never have to speak up. That’s probably why I love it.
roots.world: I don’t argue much. I watch. And the loudest people usually know the least.

types.label: The Practical Princess
types.licence: CC BY 4.0, Pepper&Carrot by David Revoy (credit required)
types.traits: Dry, capable and a fixer of things; comes from money and would rather be in the workshop.

first.mogger: You look like someone who can fix a carburettor. Can you?
first.normie: I’m elbow-deep in an engine. Talk to me.
first.truecel: I matched because the swipe button was broken. I fixed it. Too late.

types.another: Fine. Hands are clean this time.
types.out: That’s the lot. The rest have grease on them.
types.refuse: Busy. Ask me after I finish this.
types.unasked: Workshop selfie. Admire the engine.

warm: Sensible. I like sensible.
Good. Useful answer.

roots.love: My parents’ marriage was arranged, and they’re the happiest couple I know. Romance is lovely. Teamwork is better.
roots.faith: Faith, to me, is turning up: to the sick, the sad and the dishes. The feelings come later, if at all.
roots.world: Everyone in Sunfall has a theory. Very few people have a plan. I like plans.

types.label: The Devout Quiet One
types.traits: Gentle, devout and morally certain; easily overlooked; never compromises on what is right.

first.mogger: Hello. I hope you won’t think me forward for writing first.
first.normie: Good evening. I prefer to take things slowly, if you don’t mind.
first.truecel: I will be honest: I prayed about whether to answer you.

warm: That’s a good answer. Thank you.
I think we see things the same way.

roots.love: My parents met at a parish dance and prayed for each other before they ever kissed. I know how that sounds. It worked.
roots.faith: I nearly lost my faith when my mother died. It came back slowly, like feeling in a cold hand. It’s stronger now, not weaker.
roots.world: I don’t follow the arguments much. But everyone shouting seems very sure, and nobody seems very happy.

types.label: The Steadfast Heart
types.traits: Patient, warm and loyal; once gave up love too easily and won’t again.

first.mogger: I once let someone go because others advised it. I don’t intend to do that again.
first.normie: Hello. I’m slow to trust, but steady once I do.
first.truecel: I almost didn’t reply. I’m glad I’m giving you a chance.

close: It took me a long time to see it.

warm: Thank you. That means more than you know.
You’re steady. I like that.
cool: I’ve heard that before. It never ends well.

roots.love: I was persuaded to give someone up at nineteen. Years later, I still think about him. I won’t be talked out of love again.
roots.faith: Faith taught me patience. I needed a lot of it. I still do.
roots.world: I’ve seen people change their minds about almost everything, including me. So I try to give people time.

own.label: Ask what a charity volunteer actually does
own.player: What does a charity volunteer actually do all day?
own.reply: I smile at people who are richer than God while they argue about tablecloths. Then I go home and eat chips in the bath. It’s a living. Well, it isn’t, it’s unpaid.

own.label: Ask about the parties
own.player: Are the charity parties as glamorous as they look?
own.reply: From the door, yes. From the kitchen, it’s twelve people pretending to care about orphans while checking who got the better table. I adore it. I’m a terrible person.

own.label: Ask if she knew Elena Cross
own.player: Did you know Elena Cross?
own.reply: A bit. She was the only one who learned the volunteers’ names. The night of the gala she asked me to swap name badges with someone. I didn’t think anything of it at the time.
own.note: Anna Voss says Elena Cross asked her to swap name badges with someone on the night of the gala.

own.label: Ask if she’ll ever stop volunteering
own.player: Will you ever stop volunteering and do something for yourself?
own.reply: My mother volunteered until she died. Everyone at the funeral said how generous she was. Nobody there actually knew her. I think about that a lot.

own.label: Ask what a benefit night looks like from inside
own.player: What does a night like that look like when you’re the one working it?
own.reply: Two hundred chairs, six hundred glasses and one woman crying in the bathroom by ten. I am basically furniture. Very good furniture. You can put a drink on me.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live, when you’re not furniture?
own.reply: A one-bedroom near the reservoir. Mom’s life insurance paid the deposit, which is a sentence I hate. I wear four good dresses and make them look like twelve.

own.label: Ask about her mom
own.player: Was your mom at the Foundation too?
own.reply: Twenty years. Flower committee. She died in the club’s cloakroom folding someone else’s wrap. Everyone at the funeral said generous. Not one of them said her name right.

own.label: Ask if she’s good at decisions
own.player: Are you good at making decisions?
own.reply: I can seat three hundred people so nobody sits next to an ex in about four minutes. Ask me what to have for dinner and I will cry.

calls.label: Ask about the letter she mentioned
calls.player: You said there was a letter of your mom’s?
calls.reply: Honoria Blackwood wrote to her once, thanking her for her discretion. I used to think it was a nice letter. I read it every night now. I think discretion was the job.
calls.note: Anna Voss says Honoria Blackwood once thanked her late mother for her discretion.

calls.label: Ask what happened with the name badge
calls.player: What actually happened with Elena’s badge?
calls.reply: For an hour I was Elena. A man I had never seen called me by her name and said the car was waiting by the kitchen. I said I’d be a minute. I never went. I think that minute is the only reason she got any start at all.
calls.note: Anna Voss says that at the gala a stranger called her Elena and told her the car was waiting by the kitchen.

life.news: Wore the same green dress to three parties this month. Nobody noticed. I’m either a genius or invisible.
life.more: Four good dresses, and I’ve learned to make them look like twelve. A different belt, a scarf, hair up or down. Tonight a woman complimented the green and asked if it was new. Darling, it’s older than your marriage.

life.news: Ate chips in the bath for an hour with a terrible novel. Felt like royalty.
life.more: I smile at people richer than God while they argue about tablecloths, then I come home and do this. Salt and vinegar, bubbles, a book where everyone’s a duke. It’s a living. Well, it isn’t, it’s unpaid. But it’s a life.

life.news: Found my mom’s old flower committee notes. She wrote everyone’s name with a little drawing beside it.
life.more: Twenty years volunteering, and she drew a tiny portrait of every woman on that committee. Everyone at her funeral said generous. Not one of them said her name right. She knew all of theirs. I sat on the floor and read every page.

life.news: Catherine and I stayed up talking until the birds started. Best night in ages.
life.more: Catherine Bell, my closest friend at the club. She plays tennis like she’s trying to kill the ball and listens like she’s trying to keep you alive. We ate toast before dawn and solved nothing. Perfect.

gossip.says: Catherine Bell trains for a marathon she’ll never enter. She says she likes having one thing that depends only on her. She’s my closest friend at the club and the most frightening woman on a tennis court.
gossip.note: Anna Voss says Catherine Bell trains for a marathon she’ll never enter.
gossip.ask: Anna says you train for a marathon you’ll never enter.
gossip.answer: I might enter it. One day. Probably not. People say I play to win like it’s a diagnosis. I’ve noticed they say it after I beat them. The marathon’s mine. Nobody can sit on a committee about it.

gossip.says: Diana Moore tips me fifty in a card at every party, as if I were staff. She was my mother’s friend. I think it’s the only way she knows how to say she misses her.
gossip.note: Anna Voss says Diana Moore tips her at every party, as if she were staff.
gossip.ask: Anna says you tip her fifty in a card at every party.
gossip.answer: Darling, somebody has to look after Ingrid’s girl. Her mother was the only woman at that club who ever asked how I was. I don’t know how to do it properly, so I do it in a card. Tell Anna to spend it on something silly.

gossip.says: Phoebe Sutton does the volunteer roster and knows exactly where everyone is meant to be. She’s never wrong. It makes her very hard to lie to.
gossip.note: Anna Voss says Phoebe Sutton always knows where every volunteer should be.
gossip.ask: Anna says you’re very hard to lie to.
gossip.answer: I’m not hard to lie to. I just notice when the chairs don’t get stacked. It’s always the same five women stacking them. If someone’s missing, I know who. Anna’s usually where she should be. Usually.

own.label: Ask about her dog
own.player: You have a dog, right?
own.reply: Major. German shepherd, retired from the force at eight. He still checks every room before he lies down. So do I.

own.label: Ask how she switches off
own.player: What do you do to switch off?
own.reply: Hockey reruns, eaten standing up at the counter. Very glamorous.

own.label: Ask why she became a detective
own.player: Why did you become a detective?
own.reply: Because someone in my town went missing when I was twelve, and nobody looked hard enough. I look hard enough.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: A farming town. Wheat, wind and my dad’s truck. I don’t go back enough. Don’t tell him I said that.

own.label: Ask about the Vale accidents
own.player: Do you think the Vale accidents are connected?
own.reply: Two isn’t a pattern. Three would be. If you hear anything with a day and a place attached, you call me, not the switchboard.
own.note: Detective Graves says that if you learn a day and place for an attack on Vale, call her directly.

own.label: Ask what she eats
own.player: What does a detective eat?
own.reply: The same soup. I make a freezer of it on my day off. Major gets the carrots. Hockey reruns, standing at the counter. Glamour.

own.label: Ask if she goes home much
own.player: Do you go home much?
own.reply: Wheat, wind and my father’s truck. Not enough. He doesn’t say so. The truck does.

own.label: Ask what made her a cop
own.player: What actually made you join?
own.reply: A girl from my town, Carrie Lund, fifteen, went missing after a county fair. They called the search off in a week because the sheriff’s son was the last one seen with her. I was twelve. I look hard enough now.

views.campus: My job is the bit after the shouting stops. I’ve been busier than I’d like.
views.speakers: Off the record, I read one of the Houellebecq novels. Depressing. Very good. I’ll deny it.
views.police: We’re not heroes and we’re not villains. We’re tired people with a lot of paperwork.

calls.label: Ask what she keeps from her town
calls.player: Do you keep anything from back then?
calls.reply: Carrie’s shoe. It was in an evidence drawer nobody opened. I took it back the night before I left for the academy. That’s the worst thing I’ve ever done and the only thing I’m sure of.

calls.label: Ask if there’s a witness in the Blue Ribbon case
calls.player: Is there a witness in the Elena Cross case?
calls.reply: There’s a statement from someone on the late-service crew. Redacted to ribbons before it reached my desk. I’ll send you what I can, with the black bars. If anyone asks, you read it in a bin.

calls.label: Ask what she won’t write down
calls.player: Is there something you’re not writing down?
calls.reply: A sign-out sheet for the gala photographs. I saw a sergeant’s signature on it, Vic Lowry’s. By morning it was blank. I haven’t told Markham, because she’s the one person here I need to stay clean.
calls.note: Eleanor Graves saw Sergeant Vic Lowry’s signature on the gala photographs’ sign-out sheet before it was replaced with a blank.

life.news: Major caught a frisbee today. First time in his life. He’s ten. He looked as surprised as I was.
life.more: He spent eight years finding things for us and never once learned to play. A kid at the reservoir threw it and he just stood up and caught it. Then he brought it to me very seriously, like evidence. I nearly cried at a frisbee.

life.news: Ate soup standing at the counter again. Third night running. Same soup.
life.more: I make a vat on my day off, freeze it in portions, and then I’m too tired to sit down and eat it. Hockey rerun on, Major at my feet, spoon in the pot. My mother would be horrified. My mother lives four hundred miles away for exactly this reason.

life.news: Rang my dad. He’s selling the truck. I didn’t think I’d mind. I mind.
life.more: A farming town, wheat and wind, and that old red truck that taught me to drive. He says it’s just a truck. I said fine. Then I sat in my car outside the station for twenty minutes. I’ve asked him to keep it till I can visit. He said, then visit.

life.news: Ran the reservoir path at dawn with Major and a nurse from the hospital. She’s faster than me. I’m furious.
life.more: Emily Fairchild. She climbs things and runs like she’s being chased. She’s nodded at us every morning for a month, and today she just fell in beside us. Major likes her. Major likes nobody. I’m going to have to get faster.

gossip.says: Abigail Porter fixes everything. The station coffee machine twice, a sergeant’s lamp, my car door. She comes from money and would rather be under a sink with a spanner.
gossip.note: Eleanor Graves says Abigail Porter fixes everything at the station.
gossip.ask: Eleanor says you’d rather be under a sink with a spanner than at a fancy table.
gossip.answer: It’s true. My family’s tables are lovely and nobody at them can change a fuse. A toaster tells you exactly what’s wrong if you listen. People never do. Eleanor’s car door, for the record, was held on with optimism.

gossip.says: Helen Markham was the station’s first woman sergeant. The guys left a tiara on her desk the day she was promoted. She wore it to the briefing.
gossip.note: Eleanor Graves says Helen Markham wore a tiara to her first briefing as sergeant.
gossip.ask: Eleanor says you wore a tiara to your first briefing as sergeant.
gossip.answer: They meant it as a joke. I thought it suited me. Wore it all morning, gave the briefing, sent two of them to traffic duty. Nobody’s left anything on my desk since. It’s in a drawer at home. It’s a very good tiara.

gossip.says: Emily Fairchild runs the canyon at dawn like she’s being chased. She works twelve-hour shifts at the hospital and then goes climbing. I think she’s part goat.
gossip.note: Eleanor Graves says Emily Fairchild, a nurse, runs the canyon at dawn.
gossip.ask: Eleanor says you run the canyon at dawn like you’re being chased.
gossip.answer: Part goat! I’ll take it. Twelve hours holding strangers’ hands and then I need to be somewhere nobody needs anything. The canyon at dawn is that place. Eleanor and her dog run like a pair of police officers, by the way. Very upright. Very suspicious of rocks.

own.label: Ask about her records
own.player: What are you listening to?
own.reply: A funeral march recorded in a cathedral decades ago. Not on purpose. The organist was drunk. It’s perfect.

own.label: Ask about her cat
own.player: You have a cat?
own.reply: Hecate. She knocks things off shelves and stares at corners where nothing is. We understand each other.

own.label: Ask about her crescent pendant
own.player: What does your crescent pendant mean?
own.reply: It means I like the moon. It means the moon likes me back. It means you should stop asking, sweetheart.

own.label: Ask why she loves the night
own.player: Why do you love the night so much?
own.reply: Because everything that matters happens when the moon closes her eye. The rest is just waiting.

own.label: Ask about the old chapel
own.player: People say you hang out at the old chapel.
own.reply: People say a lot of things. Come and see for yourself one night. Or don’t. I won’t ask twice.

own.label: Ask what she reads at night
own.player: What do you read when you can’t sleep?
own.reply: My grandmother’s papers. A whole trunk of them. Old women write the most frightening things in the nicest handwriting.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: My mother runs a charity and a dining table. We haven’t spoken since I left the university. She says I was disinherited. I say I declined.

views.believe: In old things that never died, only waited.
views.sisters: They leave their door open at night. Sweet. As if a door ever kept anything out.
views.speakers: Houellebecq understands that the modern world is a lonely room with good lighting. The protesters and the professor are fighting over the light switch.

life.news: Hecate knocked my grandmother’s teacup off the shelf before dawn and then sat staring at the empty corner like it owed her money.
life.more: She does it every few nights. Same corner, same hour. I’ve stopped sweeping up and started taking notes. Either the apartment is haunted or my cat is a better critic of my decorating than you’ll ever be.

life.news: I sat in the back pew at St. Brigid’s this morning. Nobody threw me out. I’m almost disappointed.
life.more: Sophia Moretti looks at me like a stray she’s deciding whether to feed. I go for the Latin and the candles. And because it annoys exactly the right people that I’m allowed.

life.news: I opened my grandmother’s trunk again. I shouldn’t have.
life.more: Letters, mostly. Seating plans, of all things. She kept every one from forty years of dinners, with little marks beside the names. I spent the night working out who she’d stopped inviting, and why. Family is a long grudge with good handwriting.

life.news: Somebody at the record shop finally played the funeral march I asked for. In the middle of the afternoon.
life.more: The drunk organist’s version, from the old recording. The shop went quiet. Two boys in band shirts took their hats off without knowing why. That’s what I mean about music, sweetheart. It knows things before you do.

gossip.says: Lenore Vale casts the best silver in the Old Quarter and hates being asked about her family. Ask her anyway. She goes the most wonderful color.
gossip.note: Victoria Blackwood says Lenore Vale hates being asked about her family.
gossip.ask: Victoria says you hate being asked about your family. So, about your family?
gossip.answer: Victoria told you that? Of course she did. My family is a footnote with a famous uncle, and I’d like to stay a footnote. I make rings for the dead. They never ask who my relatives are.

gossip.says: Piper Nocturne wasn’t born Nocturne. She picked it at fifteen, like a dress. Ask her what she was called before. Watch her face.
gossip.note: Victoria Blackwood says Piper Nocturne chose her surname at fifteen.
gossip.ask: Victoria says Nocturne isn’t your real name.
gossip.answer: She told you that? Then she’s thinking about me, which is worse. Dunne. I was Piper Dunne from behind the drive-in. Nocturne is what I was going to be, so I started early. Don’t tell the Quarter. They think I was born in a coffin.

gossip.says: Sophia Moretti lets me sit in the back pew at St. Brigid’s. Everyone else glares. She brings me a hymn book and doesn’t say a word. I can’t decide if it’s kindness or strategy.
gossip.note: Victoria Blackwood says Sophia Moretti brings her a hymn book at St. Brigid’s.
gossip.ask: Victoria says you bring her a hymn book every week.
gossip.answer: She sits there every week like she’s daring the roof to fall in. It never does. Everyone who walks through that door is welcome, even the ones who come to be looked at. It isn’t strategy. Tell her that. She won’t believe you either.

own.label: Ask for today’s coffee rating
own.player: What’s today’s coffee rating?
own.reply: Six out of ten. Burnt, but the barista was crying, so I tipped well. The worst coffee in Sunfall is at the police station. I have tasted it in the line of duty.

own.label: Ask what she’s working on
own.player: What are you working on right now?
own.reply: I can tell you it involves a charity, a seating plan and a man who says no comment beautifully. That’s all you get.

own.label: Ask how she protects sources
own.player: How do you protect your sources?
own.reply: Never in writing, never on the work phone, never their real name in my notes. If someone trusts me with their life, I treat it like mine.

own.label: Ask about her old sport
own.player: Did you play sport?
own.reply: Hurdles, at college. Then my knee decided otherwise. I still dream I’m running. I wake up and write instead.

own.label: Ask what she writes for herself
own.player: Do you write anything just for you?
own.reply: Poems. Terrible ones. One is about the moon over the old chapel. I’ll show you when I trust you more. That’s almost now.

own.label: Ask who she lives with
own.player: Do you live alone?
own.reply: With Natalie Cross, a photographer, and about four hundred notebooks. We fight over the bathroom and the darkroom, which are the same room.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are your family sporty?
own.reply: Dad coached the high school track team for thirty years and Mom timed it. I ran hurdles until my knee said no. Now I run the reservoir path on the knee that lets me.

own.label: Ask about the man who says no comment
own.player: Who’s the man who says no comment so beautifully?
own.reply: Dorian Kell. Four times he’s said it to me. The fourth time he added that I had a lovely sister. That was not a compliment. I bought a better lock.
own.note: Beatrice Hale says Dorian Kell made a veiled remark about her sister after she kept asking questions.

views.paper: I love that paper the way you love a dog that bites. The editor spikes the best stories and keeps the bear ones.
views.speakers: I covered the Paglia talk. Inside, people laughed, argued and bought her book. Outside, people screamed about a speech they hadn’t heard. Both crowds asked me to print their version.
views.thunderbirds: Charming people. Very good at answering a different question from the one you asked.

calls.label: Ask about the poem she won’t publish
calls.player: What’s the poem you won’t show anyone?
calls.reply: Two years ago, before any flyers, I sat on the Old Mission’s step one night and saw a circle of candles through the window. I wrote it as a poem because I didn’t believe it as a fact. I believe it now.
calls.note: Beatrice Hale saw a circle of candles inside the Old Mission two years ago.

life.news: Found a coffee today I’d rate eight out of ten. Eight! I nearly rang the paper.
life.more: A little van by the reservoir path. The woman makes it like she’s angry at the beans, which is correct. I ran four miles on the bad knee to get there and it was worth every limp. Don’t tell anyone where it is. Sources are sacred, and so is this.

life.news: Knee’s playing up. I dreamed I was running hurdles again and woke up on the floor.
life.more: Second year of college, one hurdle, one knee, the end of the running. The sports desk gave me a job writing about people who still could. I still dream about it. In the dream I always clear the last one.

life.news: A man at the council said no comment so beautifully today that I wrote it down. Not the comment. The way he said it.
life.more: Some people say no comment like a door slamming. He says it like he’s tucking you in. I’ve got a whole page of his no comments in my notebook. One day I’ll work out what they’re all not about.

life.news: Natalie developed a photo of me laughing. I didn’t know I looked like that.
life.more: My roommate photographs what people don’t want photographed, which apparently includes me eating cereal late at night and laughing at a crossword clue. She put it on the fridge. I’m leaving it there. Don’t tell her I said that.

gossip.says: Natalie Cross, my roommate, develops her film in our airing cupboard. Everything we own smells of chemicals. She won’t photograph grief, ever, and she won’t tell you why unless she trusts you.
gossip.note: Beatrice Hale says Natalie Cross develops film in their airing cupboard and won’t photograph grief.
gossip.ask: Beatrice says you won’t photograph grief, and won’t say why.
gossip.answer: I did once, for a front page. A woman at a funeral. I can still see her face, and she can still see mine. That’s the why. Beatrice always tells people about the airing cupboard. She leaves out that she dries her tights in it.

gossip.says: Fiona Blake, my editor, lives in the apartment right above the newsroom. Literally above it. The phone rings and she rolls out of bed into the building.
gossip.note: Beatrice Hale says Fiona Blake lives directly above the newsroom.
gossip.ask: Beatrice says you live right above the newsroom and roll out of bed into work.
gossip.answer: It’s a very short commute and a very long day. I can hear the presses in my sleep. It’s either the most romantic thing about this job or a cry for help. I haven’t decided. Probably both.

gossip.says: Madison Pike at the Lucky Cactus hears more than any reporter in town. People talk in front of waitresses like they’re furniture. I’ve stopped asking sources and started asking her.
gossip.note: Beatrice Hale says Madison Pike at the Lucky Cactus hears more than any reporter.
gossip.ask: Beatrice says you hear more at the Lucky Cactus than any reporter in town.
gossip.answer: Ha! Beatrice comes in, orders nothing and just listens. We call her the reporter who never eats. It’s true, though, people forget I’ve got ears. I hear everything. I only remember the orders.

own.label: Ask about the dogs she walks
own.player: How many dogs are you walking these days?
own.reply: Six! Pancake the greyhound, who has more social life than me; a dachshund who hates hats; and a husky with abandonment issues. I’m basically a therapist with a lead.

own.label: Ask what she’s studying
own.player: What are you studying?
own.reply: Psychology. I’m writing about attachment styles, which means I diagnose everyone I meet. You’re… anxious-avoidant, maybe? Don’t worry, I’m only a second year.

own.label: Ask about kayaking
own.player: Someone said you kayak?
own.reply: The reservoir, first light, nobody else there. I once capsized in front of a wedding party. The bride clapped.

own.label: Ask about growing up
own.player: What were you like growing up?
own.reply: My parents used to drive me into the desert to teach me how to find water. I hated it. Now I’m weirdly proud I could survive out there for three days.

own.label: Ask about her seminar
own.player: Anyone interesting in your classes?
own.reply: There’s a girl in my seminar who works for Professor Vale. Types his letters, keeps his diary. She keeps leaving early for meetings and comes back pale. I’m a psych student. That’s data.
own.note: Clara says a girl in her seminar works for Vale, keeps his diary, and leaves for secret meetings.

own.label: Ask who she lives with
own.player: Who do you live with?
own.reply: Three housemates and a curly-haired cat who thinks she pays rent. I walk six dogs to cover mine. Pancake the greyhound is the most popular person in the house.

own.label: Ask about her worst kayak moment
own.player: Ever fallen in?
own.reply: In front of a wedding party. Full capsize, at dawn, right by the jetty. The bride clapped. I bowed from the water. It’s my proudest moment.

views.sunfall: Sunfall is like a dog who loves you but keeps eating your shoes. Annoying, loyal, impossible to stay mad at.
views.speakers: I’m writing an essay arguing with Paglia, which is the most fun I’ve had in a library. She’s wrong about half of it and annoyingly right about the other half.
views.campus: I walk Pancake past the protests every morning. He barks at the megaphones. He’s the most balanced person on campus.

calls.label: Ask about the poems under her wiper
calls.player: Who’s leaving the poems?
calls.reply: I photographed the library books he writes in. Same handwriting as the letters the Daily keeps. The poems are about me, and about two girls I’ve never met, Chloe and Rosa, by name. That’s three of us. That’s a pattern, not a crush.
calls.note: Clara Weiss says the man leaving poems writes about her and two other students, Chloe and Rosa, in the same hand as the Daily’s letters.

calls.label: Ask about the girl from her seminar
calls.player: What did you write about the girl who keeps Vale’s diary?
calls.reply: An anonymised case study: a woman who keeps a famous man’s diary and leaves early for meetings and comes back pale. My tutor asked, very lightly, whether the case was real. I said it was a composite. It isn’t.
calls.note: Clara Weiss says the woman who keeps Professor Vale’s diary keeps leaving early for meetings and coming back pale.

life.news: ok WAIT. Pancake learned to open the fridge. he’s a greyhound. he has never learned anything. i’m so proud and so scared
life.more: he nosed the handle and pulled and just stood there looking at the cheese like it was a sunrise. six dogs and he’s the dumbest and now he’s the smartest?? attachment theory does not cover this. i put a chair against the fridge. he moved the chair

life.news: capsized the kayak at the reservoir again. last time a bride clapped. this time a man fishing. i’m a spectator sport
life.more: first light, flat water, me, upside down. he said, nine out of ten for the entry. i said thank you and swam to the bank towing the kayak like a sad dog. honestly the best start to a day

life.news: my parents used to drive me into the desert to teach me to find water. today i found some for a lost hiker. i’m unbearable now
life.more: he was on the canyon trail with an empty bottle and a sunburn. i showed him where the rock stays damp and we dug. it worked!! i hated those trips so much as a kid. i rang my dad and he went very quiet and then said, good girl. i cried on the trail

life.news: failed a psychology essay. on attachment styles. i diagnosed everyone i know and forgot to do the reading
life.more: the lecturer wrote: confident, entertaining, wrong. which is honestly my dating profile. i have to resubmit. i’m reading the actual book this time. keep me company while i read it? you don’t have to talk. just be there so i don’t diagnose the cat

gossip.says: Lucy Bennett taught me one module and she wears sunglasses in morning lectures. she says it’s for the glare off our blank faces. iconic
gossip.note: Clara Weiss says Lucy Bennett wears sunglasses in her morning lectures.
gossip.ask: Clara says you wear sunglasses in morning lectures because of the glare off blank faces.
gossip.answer: Darling, have you seen a lecture hall first thing? It’s like teaching a field of very tired sheep. The sunglasses are a mercy for all of us. Clara was the only one who laughed. She also asked whether my sunglasses were a defense mechanism. They are.

gossip.says: Rebecca Shaw has eleven rescue rabbits and one of them is called Comrade Biscuit and he has more opinions than my whole seminar
gossip.note: Clara Weiss says Rebecca Shaw has eleven rescue rabbits, one called Comrade Biscuit.
gossip.ask: Clara says your rabbit Comrade Biscuit has more opinions than her whole seminar.
gossip.answer: He does. He disagrees with everything, especially lettuce he didn’t choose. Clara came to the rescue once and diagnosed him with an avoidant attachment style. Respectfully, he’s a rabbit. He’s avoidant because he’s a rabbit.

own.label: Ask how fundraising works
own.player: How do you get rich people to give money away?
own.reply: Same as tennis. Make them think they’re winning. Nobody gives to a cause; they give to be seen next to it.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do when you’re not raising money?
own.reply: Tennis at the club, early, before it’s too hot to think. I play to win. People say that’s unladylike. They usually say it after I beat them.

own.label: Ask if the numbers add up
own.player: Do the charity’s numbers ever not add up?
own.reply: Every year the gala raises more and the scholarships get fewer. I’m good with numbers. I don’t like what those ones say.
own.note: Catherine Bell says the gala raises more each year while the scholarships get fewer.

own.label: Ask what she’s training for
own.player: What are you actually training for?
own.reply: A marathon I’ll never enter. I like having something that only depends on me. Fundraising depends on rich men having a good lunch.

own.label: Ask how she handles big donors
own.player: How do you get a rich man to give?
own.reply: Tennis. Make him think he’s winning, then take the check. Nobody gives to a cause. They give to be photographed next to it.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What are your family like?
own.reply: Dad sold the trucking yard to the casino and bought a seat on the board with it. Mom hasn’t said a true sentence since I was twelve. They’re lovely at parties.

own.label: Ask if she can bluff
own.player: Can you bluff?
own.reply: On court, yes. At a board meeting, no. I have the kind of face that says exactly what I think a second before I decide not to say it.

own.label: Ask if she knows Moira Bell
own.player: You’re a Bell. Do you know Moira Bell?
own.reply: My cousin. The other Bells, the ones who clean. Our fathers fell out over the trucking yard and nobody’s sat at a table since. If Moira’s in trouble, her mom is the one to ring. Ruth. Here: {number}. Don’t tell her I gave it you. Actually, do.
own.note: Catherine Bell, Moira’s cousin, gave you the number for Moira’s mother, Ruth Bell.

calls.label: Ask what the numbers on her whiteboard say
calls.player: What are you actually adding up on that whiteboard?
calls.reply: Three years of what we raised against three years of what reached a student. The gap grows every year, and the gap has a name: the Halcyon Ridge Trust. I photograph it and wipe it every night. My father’s name is on the board.
calls.note: Catherine Bell says the money the Foundation raises and the money students get are drifting apart, and the gap goes to the Halcyon Ridge Trust.

calls.label: Ask if she’d show you her figures
calls.player: Would you show me your figures?
calls.reply: If you swear you’re not doing this to look clever. Fine. I’ll leave a copy of the columns where you’ll find it. Three years, my handwriting, and his signature on every quarter. Burn it if anyone asks.

life.news: Beat a man at tennis this morning who’d told me he goes easy on women. He didn’t go easy. I did.
life.more: Make them think they’re winning, then take the check. Same with tennis. He served like he was doing me a favor. Six love, six one. He shook my hand very limply. I’ve never enjoyed anything more before breakfast.

life.news: Ran twenty miles on the canyon trail. Still not entering the marathon.
life.more: I train for one I’ll never enter because I like having one thing that depends only on me. Nobody can sit on a committee about my legs. Twenty miles today, and a lizard watched me the whole way. He was unimpressed. Fair.

life.news: My mom hasn’t said a true sentence since I was twelve. Today she said one. I didn’t know what to do.
life.more: We were in the car and she said, I’m tired of pretending to like these people. Then she turned the radio up and we never spoke of it again. I’m going to be thinking about that sentence for a year.

life.news: Anna and I ate toast on her kitchen floor before dawn. We solved nothing.
life.more: Anna Voss says she’s basically furniture at parties. Very good furniture. To me she’s the only person in that building who tells the truth. Toast before dawn is the only honest meal.

gossip.says: Anna Voss has four good dresses and makes them look like twelve. Nobody at the club has noticed in three years. She’s cleverer than all of them and she lets them think she’s decoration.
gossip.note: Catherine Bell says Anna Voss makes four dresses look like twelve.
gossip.ask: Catherine says you make four dresses look like twelve.
gossip.answer: Five, if you count the one with the wine stain I wear back to front. A belt here, a scarf there. I’m basically furniture at these things. Very good furniture. Catherine’s the only one who’s noticed. That’s why she’s my best friend.

gossip.says: Yumi Tanaka does her face in eleven minutes and keeps the books perfect. She says if you look perfect, people stop checking your work. She means it as a warning.
gossip.note: Catherine Bell says Yumi Tanaka believes looking perfect stops people checking your work.
gossip.ask: Catherine says you think looking perfect stops people checking your work.
gossip.answer: It does. It’s the single most useful thing I know. Everything about me is on purpose. Catherine’s the opposite. She looks like she’s about to win something, so people check everything. We’d make a terrifying team.

gossip.says: Caroline Prescott keeps her trophies in the downstairs bathroom so people have to see them. She’s the only Bluebird who’s ever beaten me at tennis. Twice. I’m still training.
gossip.note: Catherine Bell says Caroline Prescott keeps her trophies in the downstairs bathroom.
gossip.ask: Catherine says you keep your trophies in the downstairs bathroom.
gossip.answer: Where else would people have time to read them? Taking part is what losers call it. Catherine’s very good. She reminds me of someone I used to be. I’m not going to tell her that. I’m going to beat her a third time.

own.label: Ask about the bake sale
own.player: Tell me about the famous bake sale.
own.reply: The great shortbread rivalry! Mrs. Delgado says hers is better. Mrs. Delgado is wrong, and I have prayed for her.

own.label: Ask about her garden
own.player: Do you still keep the chapel garden?
own.reply: Roses in the desert. They take stubbornness and gray water. Some days I think they grow out of spite.

own.label: Ask what she’s knitting
own.player: What are you knitting at the moment?
own.reply: Blankets for the outreach box. Last time it was a scarf for a dog. He looked very handsome.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother
own.player: Who taught you your faith?
own.reply: My grandmother. She taught me the rosary and how to haggle at the market, in that order. She says both are prayers.

own.label: Ask about the chapel at night
own.player: Is it true you hold the chapel keys?
own.reply: This season, yes. Mostly it means I’m the one who finds the mice. And sometimes the goth girls sitting quietly in the back pew. I never send them away.

own.label: Ask what time she gets up
own.player: What time does a baker’s daughter get up?
own.reply: With the ovens. Four, most days. Mass by first light, the garden before the heat, and bread on every parish table by noon. I sleep like a stone and I’m never sorry.

own.label: Ask why she grows roses
own.player: Why roses, out here?
own.reply: They were my mother’s. She died when I was eleven, of something fast. I grow them because she did, and I’m a little bit scared of hospitals because of how fast it was.

own.label: Ask who comes to the chapel at night
own.player: Does anyone come to the chapel when it’s quiet?
own.reply: Girls in black, sometimes, sitting very still in the back pew. I never send them away. If a church isn’t for sitting quietly in, I don’t know what it’s for.

own.label: Ask about the other key on her ring
own.player: There’s an old key on your ring. What’s it for?
own.reply: The side door of the Old Mission. The Franklins handed it to the parish years ago. I have never once used it and I never want to. Teresa knows I have it. Now you do.
own.note: Sophia Moretti carries a key to the Old Mission’s side door on the chapel key ring.

own.label: Ask if something’s going on at the parish
own.player: Is something going on at the parish?
own.reply: I add things up the way nonna adds a bill. Two lunches going up the stairs every day. Crying through a wall. Margaret being quiet, which Margaret never is. I haven’t asked, and I won’t. But I’ve done the sum.
own.note: Sophia Moretti suspects the Sisters are quietly looking after someone upstairs at the charity shop.

views.believe: That God loves us more than we deserve, and that a warm meal is a kind of prayer.
views.speakers: Professor Vale gave me a Houellebecq book once. It made me sad for everyone in it. They were all so lonely, and nobody prayed.
views.goths: They’re not wicked. Most of them are just sad in very good clothes. Except one or two. Be careful with Victoria.

life.news: Won the shortbread war at the parish picnic. Mrs. Delgado’s came second. I’m praying for humility. Later.
life.more: Three generations of Morettis have baked for the parish picnic, and Mrs. Delgado has been our rival for most of them. The judge was Father’s housekeeper. She said mine had more love in it. Mrs. Delgado said mine had more butter. She’s not wrong.

life.news: I have the chapel keys this week, which mostly means I’m the one who finds the mice.
life.more: Three this morning, all in the hymn book cupboard, all very well fed. I suspect the Bible class cookies. I carried them out to the garden with a blessing. They’ll be back. They’re very faithful mice.

life.news: My roses came up red this year. My mother’s roses. In the desert. Nonna cried.
life.more: My mother grew them, and when she died I kept them going. Everyone said roses won’t grow here. They grow if you’re stubborn. Nonna stood in the garden this morning with her rosary and said, she’d be proud. I made shortbread to celebrate.

life.news: Nonna haggled a man at the market so hard he gave her a lemon for free, out of respect.
life.more: She taught me the rosary and haggling in the same summer. She says they’re the same skill: patience, and not taking no for an answer. He wanted three for the peppers. She paid one and got a lemon. I’m learning from a master.

gossip.says: My friend Sofia Delgado is the granddaughter of my shortbread rival. We’re on opposite sides of the great war and we have lunch every week. Our grandmothers can never know.
gossip.note: Sophia Moretti says Sofia Delgado is the granddaughter of her shortbread rival.
gossip.ask: Sophia says you two have lunch every week and your grandmothers can never know.
gossip.answer: Never! Abuela would disown me. Sophia’s shortbread is better, but if you tell anyone I said that, I’ll deny it in two languages. I’ve already decided who she should marry, by the way. She just doesn’t know him yet.

gossip.says: Phoebe Sutton from the Bluebirds runs the volunteer roster and says I’m the one real volunteer. She runs the canyon before sunrise with no phone. I worry about her.
gossip.note: Sophia Moretti says Phoebe Sutton runs the canyon before sunrise without a phone.
gossip.ask: Sophia says you run the canyon before sunrise without your phone, and she worries.
gossip.answer: She worries about everyone. It’s her best quality. I run without a phone because it’s the only hour nobody can ask me to roster anything. Sophia stacks chairs with me every week. It’s always the same five women. Me and the Sisters.

gossip.says: Teresa Bellamy teaches twenty-two eight-year-olds and a hamster she calls a theological menace. She says Saint Brigid once turned bathwater into beer. I checked. It’s true.
gossip.note: Sophia Moretti says Teresa Bellamy’s class hamster is a theological menace.
gossip.ask: Sophia says your class hamster is a theological menace.
gossip.answer: He is! He escaped during a lesson on the loaves and fishes and ate a loaf. The children decided it was a miracle. I decided it was a hamster. We compromised on a miracle hamster. Hospitality is holy, even for rodents.

own.label: Ask what she’s campaigning for
own.player: What are you campaigning for at the moment?
own.reply: Housing first, always. Students sleeping in cars while the university builds a donor lounge. Then whatever the administration does next.

own.label: Ask about the rabbit rescue
own.player: Is it true you volunteer with rabbits?
own.reply: Eleven rabbits. One is called Comrade Biscuit. The rabbits are fine; the rabbits are always fine. It’s the volunteers I worry about.

own.label: Ask about rollercoasters
own.player: Rumor says you love rollercoasters.
own.reply: I can’t swim and deep water terrifies me, but drop me a hundred feet strapped to a plastic seat and I’m serene. I contain contradictions.

own.label: Ask about her worst campaign
own.player: What’s the worst campaign you ever ran?
own.reply: A recycling drive that ended with a bin on fire. Not a metaphor. An actual bin. On actual fire.

own.label: Ask how she really feels about Vale
own.player: How do you really feel about Professor Vale?
own.reply: I want him to stop platforming men who think some people are born lesser. I don’t want him hurt. Some people at our meetings don’t seem to know the difference, and that frightens me.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the print shop by campus, across the landing from the campaign office, so I can’t ever really leave work. Smells of toner. I’ve made peace with it.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Were your family political?
own.reply: We argue at dinner for sport. Dad was a union man at the reservoir works until it closed. Mom’s a librarian who taught me to cite my sources. Every Christmas ends with a footnote.

own.label: Ask about Comrade Biscuit
own.player: Which rabbit is your favorite?
own.reply: Comrade Biscuit. Eleven rabbits at the rescue and he’s the only one who organizes the others. I respect him enormously.

views.speakers: Paglia says young women should toughen up. Houellebecq turns loneliness into a reason to blame women. And the next speaker claims some groups are simply born less intelligent, which actual scientists have taken apart again and again. Vale calls that a debate. I call it an audition for cruelty.
views.thunderbirds: I’ve read their accounts. Well, the half they publish.
views.police: Some of them are decent. The system they work for isn’t built for people like my students.

calls.label: Ask who pays the campaign’s rent
calls.player: Who pays the rent on the campaign office?
calls.reply: A charity with no office and no website. I traced it, because I trace everything, to a trust on the ridge. The same trust that adores Professor Vale is paying the people who protest him. I think somebody wants us loud so nobody looks at the quiet ones.
calls.note: Rebecca Shaw traced the campaign office’s rent to the trust on the ridge, which also backs Professor Vale.

life.news: Comrade Biscuit escaped the rabbit run and was found in the vegetable patch eating one perfect lettuce. Revolutionary.
life.more: Eleven rabbits at the rescue and he’s the only one with a plan. He dug under the fence overnight, ignored every weed, and went straight for the best lettuce. I respect it. I’ve put him in charge of the next campaign.

life.news: Went on a rollercoaster at the fair three times in a row. I can’t swim. I’m told those are unrelated.
life.more: I love rollercoasters and I’m terrified of the reservoir. My dad says it’s because one of them has a seatbelt. He’s not wrong. On the third go the man running it let me stay on for free because I screamed so happily.

life.news: The recycling drive’s bin caught fire again. Second time this month.
life.more: Someone keeps putting batteries in with the paper. We made a sign. We made a bigger sign. Today the bigger sign caught fire too. I stood there with a fire extinguisher feeling like a metaphor. Respectfully, people, read the sign.

life.news: My old lecturer sent me a book with a note in the margin. Still marking me, years later.
life.more: Lucy Bennett. She taught me literature and still sends me books, with notes like: you’ll hate chapter three, read it anyway. I always hate chapter three. I always read it anyway. She’s never wrong. It’s infuriating.

gossip.says: Daisy Chen is the only friend I have who can make a poster. I have seventeen spreadsheets. She has a glue gun and taste.
gossip.note: Rebecca Shaw says Daisy Chen makes all her campaign posters.
gossip.ask: Rebecca says you’re the only one of her friends who can make a poster.
gossip.answer: She sends me seventeen spreadsheets and says make it pop. I make it pop. Last time the glue gun caught fire, which made it pop more than intended. I’d rather know what she’s afraid of than what the weather’s doing. It’s usually fonts.

gossip.says: Lucy Bennett taught me English literature and still posts me books with notes in the margins. She says she read the summary of her own thesis instead of the thesis. I believe her.
gossip.note: Rebecca Shaw says her old lecturer Lucy Bennett still sends her books.
gossip.ask: Rebecca says you still send her books with notes in the margins.
gossip.answer: Darling, someone has to. She was the only student who read the whole book and then argued with it. I send her the ones I know she’ll hate. It keeps her honest and me entertained. Chapter three is always the one, isn’t it?

gossip.says: Jennifer Tate books the hall with me for every meeting and brings all four megaphones even when we only need one. She says the others get lonely.
gossip.note: Rebecca Shaw says Jennifer Tate brings all four megaphones to every meeting.
gossip.ask: Rebecca says you bring all four megaphones even when you only need one.
gossip.answer: They do get lonely! One for emergencies, one decorative, one that quacks and one for actually talking. Rebecca pretends to hate it. She’s asked to borrow the decorative one twice.

own.label: Ask about her dog
own.player: Your dog swiped on me?
own.reply: Biscuit! He’s a terrier with no impulse control. He also ate a lipstick and a tax letter today. He has range.

own.label: Ask about her plants
own.player: How are the plants doing?
own.reply: I have eleven. Six are alive. Two are resting. I talk to them every morning and I think it’s helping. Them, not me.

own.label: Ask what she dreams about
own.player: What do you actually want out of life?
own.reply: A little house with a porch, a husband who reads to me, and children who tell me I’m embarrassing. Is that too old-fashioned to say on here?

own.label: Ask what her mom is like
own.player: What’s your mom like?
own.reply: She says I talk too much and then calls me for two hours. We’re the same person. It’s terrifying.

own.label: Ask about the cosmetics counter
own.player: What’s the counter like?
own.reply: I talk to customers the way I talk to my plants, and it helps them more than it helps me. I name everybody’s lipstick shade. A girl from the club bought one called Last Supper. I named it.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: Loud. A seamstress, a mailman, and a lot of women who all talk at once while Dad reads the paper. I was the dreamy one who wrote stories about horses.

calls.label: Ask about the name she wrote down
calls.player: Did you write anything pretty in the client book lately?
calls.reply: A woman bought the darkest hair dye we stock, cash, first thing the morning after the benefit. She gave her name as Swallow. I wrote it down because it was pretty. She went on to the salon on the Sunfall Road after.
calls.note: Amelia Hart sold very dark hair dye to a woman calling herself Swallow the morning after the gala.

calls.label: Ask about the girl and the lipstick
calls.player: Any customers you worry about?
calls.reply: A girl from the club bought a lipstick for a private dinner and asked me if it was too much. I said no. I’ve wondered since whether it was the dinner that was too much.
calls.note: Amelia Hart worries about a young Bluebird going to a private dinner.

life.news: Biscuit ate a lipstick AND a tax letter today. He has range.
life.more: Terrier, no impulse control, eats anything lower than my knees. The lipstick was coral. The tax letter was red, which feels right. I had to ring the tax office and explain that my dog had paid their letter the ultimate respect. The woman laughed so hard she put me on hold.

life.news: Six of my eleven plants are alive! Two are resting. Three we don’t talk about.
life.more: Resting is what I call it when they’ve gone brown but I’m still hoping. The fern made a new leaf today. I told my mom. She said I talk too much about plants. Then she talked about her plants for an hour.

life.news: Sold a lipstick to a woman who said she hadn’t worn one since her wedding thirty years ago. She bought two.
