life.more: Her husband used to say she looked like a film star in red. He’s been gone three years. I did it for her at the counter and she looked in the mirror for ages and said, there she is. I had to pretend to tidy a drawer.

life.news: My mom and I said the exact same sentence at the exact same time on the phone. Terrifying.
life.more: We both said, well, you know what they’re like. About the same neighbor. I’m becoming her. She’s always been her. A little house with a porch and a husband who reads to me, that’s what I want. Mom says that’s what she wanted. Then she got Dad, who reads the paper.

gossip.says: Megan Torres works on the floor below me and she’s the only quiet person I’ve ever been friends with. She says more in one text than in a whole shift. Braver in writing, she says.
gossip.note: Amelia Hart says her friend Megan Torres is braver in writing than in person.
gossip.ask: Amelia says you say more in one text than in a whole shift.
gossip.answer: In person I mostly nod and hope someone else talks. With Amelia that’s easy, because she talks for both of us. It’s restful. I send her very long messages at night and she replies with forty exclamation marks. It works.

gossip.says: Mei Chen does hair on the Sunfall Road and she’s the quietest woman in town, so everyone tells her everything. I’ve told her things I haven’t told my mom. That’s saying something.
gossip.note: Amelia Hart says everyone tells Mei Chen their secrets at the salon.
gossip.ask: Amelia says she’s told you things she hasn’t told her mom.
gossip.answer: She has. Mostly about a boy who reads, and her plants. I never repeat anything. Amelia talks for the whole hour and I just cut. She tips in cookies sometimes. Her dog ate one once, I think. She mentioned the dog a lot.

gossip.says: Camila Reyes from the beauty college does my eyebrows for free because she needs the practice. She’s done me forty times. She says I’m better than the mannequin. High praise.
gossip.note: Amelia Hart says Camila Reyes practises eyebrows on her.
gossip.ask: Amelia says you’ve done her eyebrows forty times for practice.
gossip.answer: Forty-one! And she’s so much better than Brenda, the mannequin. Brenda never thanks me. Amelia thanks me and then tells me about every boy she’s ever liked while I work. I teach women to look like themselves, just more. She’s very easy. She’s already very her.

own.label: Ask what it’s like being a donor
own.player: What’s it like being the one who writes the checks?
own.reply: Lovely. Everyone laughs at your jokes. You never quite know if they’re funny.

own.label: Ask if she’s been married
own.player: Have you ever been married?
own.reply: Twice, darling. The first was for love and the second was for the house. The house was nicer to me.

own.label: Ask if money makes her happy
own.player: Does the money make you happy?
own.reply: It makes me comfortable, which people confuse with happy. I’ve a twelve-seat dining table and I eat alone at the end of it. Don’t tell anyone at the club.

own.label: Ask if she gets lonely
own.player: Do you get lonely in that big house?
own.reply: The house has eleven rooms and I use two. Money buys space. It doesn’t fill it.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: Above a feed store on the state road, darling. You can take the girl out of the sacks of chicken pellets. I have, at enormous expense.

own.label: Ask about her first husband
own.player: What was the first one like?
own.reply: Tommy Moore rode bulls and couldn’t keep a horse or a promise and I loved him anyway. A bull killed him two years in. I kept his name because it was the only thing he owned that wasn’t in hock.

own.label: Ask what her days are like
own.player: What does a day look like for you?
own.reply: A housekeeper comes three mornings and leaves food with labels on it, as if I might forget what soup is. I sleep on the small sofa. The big one is for being photographed on.

own.label: Ask if people are honest with her
own.player: Is anyone honest with you?
own.reply: Everyone laughs at my jokes now. I have stopped being able to tell if they’re funny. You’re not laughing, which is either very rude or very refreshing.

calls.label: Ask what she signed
calls.player: You said you signed something once. What was it?
calls.reply: On my second wedding night, at the lodge up on the ridge, after the champagne, with Celeste Van Doren’s hand on my shoulder. A paper. I have never been shown it since. Walter died within the year. I decided to be comfortable instead of knowing. It’s stopped working.
calls.note: Diana Moore signed something at the lodge on Halcyon Ridge on her second wedding night, with Celeste Van Doren beside her.

calls.label: Ask about Walter
calls.player: What happened to Walter?
calls.reply: He fell. That’s what it says. There’s a blue ribbon on his stone at the Cemetery Chapel. Go and look at the stones near him, sometime. Count the blue ribbons. Then don’t tell me the number.
calls.note: Diana Moore says many husbands’ graves at the Cemetery Chapel carry the same blue ribbon as her husband Walter’s.

life.news: Ate dinner at the end of my twelve-seat table again. Talked to the candlesticks. They agreed with everything.
life.more: Eleven rooms. I use two. The rest are for the silence to live in. The housekeeper leaves food with labels as if I were a child, and I eat it at the end of the table like a queen in exile. The candlesticks are excellent company. They never ask.

life.news: Went to the rodeo. First time in years. My first husband rode there.
life.more: The first was for love and the second was for the house. Tommy was a rodeo rider who couldn’t keep a horse or a promise, and I loved him anyway. I sat in the stands and a girl selling tickets told me her grandad rode with him. I had to leave.

life.news: A joke I made at lunch got a real laugh. I could tell. It was the sound.
life.more: Everyone laughs at my jokes now, darling. I’ve stopped being able to tell if they’re funny. But today a waiter laughed by accident, through his nose, and then apologized. That was real. I tipped him like it was the opera.

life.news: Slept on the sofa in the little sitting room again. Eleven rooms, and I sleep on a sofa.
life.more: The bedroom is very large and very quiet. The sofa is small and near the kitchen, where the light comes in. I grew up above a feed store. My body still knows where the warm room is. Don’t tell the club. They think I sleep in a swan.

gossip.says: Audrey King sells tickets at the rodeo. Her grandfather rode with my first husband. She told me Tommy was the bravest stupid man she’d ever heard of. She meant it kindly. I think.
gossip.note: Diana Moore says Audrey King’s grandfather rode with her first husband at the rodeo.
gossip.ask: Diana says your grandfather rode with her first husband.
gossip.answer: Grandpa still talks about Tommy Moore. Said he’d get on anything with four legs and a temper. Brave in a way that’s mostly stupid, which is the rodeo in one sentence. I didn’t know she was his widow till she went white. I bought her a lemonade.

gossip.says: Anna Voss’s mother was the only woman at that club who ever asked how I was. Now I tip Anna at every party because I can’t think what else to do. She’s the image of Ingrid.
gossip.note: Diana Moore says Anna Voss’s mother was the only woman at the club who asked how she was.
gossip.ask: Diana says your mother was the only one at the club who ever asked how she was.
gossip.answer: That sounds like Mom. She asked everyone how they were and actually waited for the answer. Diana tips me fifty in a card like I’m staff, and I let her, because I think it’s really for Mom. One day I’ll ask her how she is. Properly.

own.label: Ask what she teaches
own.player: What do you lecture in?
own.reply: English literature, to students who’ve read the summary. Darling, I don’t blame them. I read the summary of my own thesis.

own.label: Ask what campus is like now
own.player: What’s it like teaching on campus right now?
own.reply: Everyone is terrified of saying the wrong thing, so nobody says anything interesting. My seminars used to be fights. Now they’re hostage videos.

own.label: Ask about Professor Vale
own.player: Do you know Professor Vale?
own.reply: We had dinner once. He’s cleverer than he is kind, and braver than he is careful. Someone in his own department hates him far more than the protesters do.
own.note: Lucy Bennett says someone in Professor Vale’s own department hates him more than the protesters do.

own.label: Ask what her students are like
own.player: What are your students like these days?
own.reply: Bright, frightened and permanently online. They’re terrified of saying the wrong thing, so they don’t say anything. I miss arguments.

own.label: Ask how she’s a lecturer so young
own.player: How are you a lecturer at twenty-two?
own.reply: I finished a doctorate at twenty-one and the department needed someone cheap and brilliant. I was cheap. Brilliant was the bonus.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Who are the Bennetts?
own.reply: Gallery district. Dad’s a surgeon on the hospital board, Mom’s on the museum’s. They find it charming that I lecture. Charming is what my family calls things they don’t understand.

calls.label: Ask who hates Vale in his own department
calls.player: Who in his department hates Vale?
calls.reply: Dr. Hal Pemberton. He leaks Vale’s diary to the newsroom. He told me so himself, drunk, at a faculty party, as a joke. I laughed. I didn’t forget.
calls.note: Lucy Bennett says Dr. Hal Pemberton leaks Professor Vale’s diary to the newsroom.

calls.label: Ask about a student who worried her
calls.player: Has a student ever frightened you?
calls.reply: Vanessa Greer. She wrote me an essay so angry I marked it with a note saying anger isn’t an argument. She wrote back that it wasn’t meant to be one.
calls.note: Lucy Bennett says her former student Vanessa Greer told her that her anger wasn’t meant to be an argument.

life.news: Gave a seminar on a novel nobody had read. I hadn’t read it either. Best discussion all year.
life.more: English literature, to students who’ve read the summary. Darling, I don’t blame them. I read the summary of my own thesis. Today we all admitted it in the first five minutes and made the plot up together. It was better than the book.

life.news: Champagne at the club as somebody’s guest. I was charming for three hours and nobody noticed I said nothing.
life.more: I grew up in the rooms where Sunfall decides things, and the trick is to agree with everyone in a slightly different tone. Tonight a man asked my opinion of his opinion. I said, gosh. He was delighted.

life.news: My seminars used to be fights. Now they’re hostage videos. I miss being argued with.
life.more: Students are bright, frightened and online. Nobody wants to be quoted saying the wrong thing, so they say nothing in a very clever way. Today I begged someone to disagree with me. A girl at the back said, respectfully, no. I nearly kissed her.

life.news: A student came to my office hours to argue about a poem. A real argument. I’ve framed the moment, metaphorically.
life.more: Emma Frost. Shy, writes everything in a notebook, says the safe thing out loud. Today she said the true thing out loud instead, about a sonnet, and it was wrong, and brilliant. I gave her a cookie and told her to do it more.

gossip.says: Alice Beaumont and I drink champagne at the club and agree with every man in slightly different tones. She’s going to run that place one day. Honestly, I hope she does.
gossip.note: Lucy Bennett says Alice Beaumont will run the Bluebird Club one day.
gossip.ask: Lucy says you two agree with every man at the club in slightly different tones.
gossip.answer: It’s an art form. Lucy agrees with a man so beautifully he goes home wondering what he said. I agree with him so precisely he goes home with a committee job. We’re very different talents. Same champagne.

gossip.says: Emma Frost writes what she really thinks in a notebook and says something safe in my seminars. I’ve seen the notebook once. It’s the best criticism on campus.
gossip.note: Lucy Bennett says Emma Frost writes her real opinions in a notebook.
gossip.ask: Lucy says your notebook is the best criticism on campus.
gossip.answer: She saw it? Oh no. I left it open on the desk once. You can’t say anything in seminars, so I write it down instead. She’s the only lecturer who’s ever asked what I think. I told her the truth about a sonnet. She gave me a cookie.

own.label: Ask about her photography
own.player: What do you photograph?
own.reply: Whatever people don’t want photographed. Which in Sunfall is most things.

own.label: Ask if she’s related to Elena Cross
own.player: Are you related to Elena Cross?
own.reply: No. Everyone asks. Same surname, different town. But it means I can’t stop thinking about her.

own.label: Ask what she caught on camera
own.player: Did you photograph the gala?
own.reply: From across the road. One frame shows a gray sedan with its lights off, idling by the kitchen door. My editor said it was nothing.
own.note: Natalie Cross photographed a gray sedan idling by the gala kitchen door with its lights off.

own.label: Ask what she won’t photograph
own.player: Is there anything you won’t photograph?
own.reply: Grief. I did once, for a front page. I can still see that woman’s face, and she can still see mine.

own.label: Ask what she drives
own.player: What do you drive?
own.reply: An old hatchback with a long lens on the passenger seat. The lens gets the seat belt. I have my priorities.

own.label: Ask where she’s from
own.player: Where’s home?
own.reply: A mining town two hours east. Dad’s alive and silent. Mom ran the town paper until it closed. I think I take photographs so somebody keeps a record.

own.label: Ask about the wall in her apartment
own.player: What’s on your wall?
own.reply: Everything I won’t print. Grief, children, one woman at a funeral who can still see my face. You keep those, so you remember not to take them again.

calls.label: Ask about the frame after the one she showed
calls.player: Was there another frame after the one your editor binned?
calls.reply: The next one shows the car’s back door open and a woman’s hand on the roof, with a ring, and a man’s shape behind it. I printed it once and burned it. The negative is in my mother’s old camera.
calls.note: Natalie Cross has an unprinted frame from gala night: a woman’s ringed hand on the roof of the gray car, a man behind her.

life.news: Everyone in this town asks if I’m related to someone. Today it was the man at the gas station.
life.more: Same surname, different town. I say no and they look disappointed, like I’ve canceled something. I tried saying distant cousin once to see what would happen. Nothing good. I’ve stopped.

life.news: Developed a roll from the reservoir at dawn. Three frames came out perfect. Three out of thirty-six is a good day.
life.more: Herons, a man fishing in a suit, and the light hitting the water like it had somewhere to be. Nobody will buy them. They’ll go on the wall with all the others nobody buys. That wall is my favorite thing I own.

life.news: My mom’s old paper would have been fifty this year. It closed when I was fifteen.
life.more: A town two hours east. She ran it for twenty years, then printed one story the mine’s owner didn’t like. Six months later it was gone. That’s when I learned what a town does to a paper that tells the truth. I took her camera when we cleared the office. I still use it.

life.news: Beatrice made dinner. It was nearly edible. I’m counting it as a love language.
life.more: Burnt pasta, a sauce she called rustic, and a candle she found in a drawer. We ate on the floor because the table’s covered in my prints. She rated it six out of ten. Generous. She rates everything like a coffee.

gossip.says: Beatrice Hale rates every coffee in Sunfall out of ten in a notebook. The police station’s gets a two. She says the barista there is a crime scene.
gossip.note: Natalie Cross says Beatrice Hale rates every coffee in Sunfall out of ten.
gossip.ask: Natalie says you rate every coffee in Sunfall out of ten. What does the police station get?
gossip.answer: Two, and that’s being kind to the cup. Burnt, sad, and served by a sergeant who watches you drink it. Natalie’s coffee is a seven, by the way. Don’t tell her. She’ll get ideas.

gossip.says: Celina Rojas holds my reflector and carries my bags, and in about two years she’ll be better than me. I haven’t told her. She rereads messages six times before she answers them.
gossip.note: Natalie Cross says Celina Rojas, her assistant, will be better than her in two years.
gossip.ask: Natalie says you’ll be a better photographer than her in two years.
gossip.answer: She said that? Out loud? I’m going to read this message six times. Mostly I hold the bag and get blamed for the weather. One day I’ll take the picture. Two years, then. That’s a date. Sort of.

gossip.says: Linh Tran once sold a photo of the bear for more than I make in a month, and she’ll never let any of us forget it. She’s writing a novel with everyone in it, too, so be careful what you say near her.
gossip.note: Natalie Cross says Linh Tran’s bear photo outsold a month of real journalism.
gossip.ask: Natalie says I should be careful what I say near you, in case I end up in your novel.
gossip.answer: You’re already in it, buddy. Chapter nine. You’re doing fine so far, a bit mysterious. Natalie’s in chapter three as a woman who won’t photograph anything sad, which is accurate, and she hates it.

own.label: Ask about the airport line
own.player: Did you ever get out of that line?
own.reply: Eventually. I made friends with a grandmother from Tucson. She showed me forty photos of her cat. It was the best part of my trip.

own.label: Ask if she’s shy
own.player: Are you shy, or is it just texting?
own.reply: Both. I’m braver in writing. In person I mostly nod and hope someone else talks.

own.label: Ask what she hopes for
own.player: What do you hope for?
own.reply: Someone who doesn’t mind quiet. Most people treat silence like an emergency.

own.label: Ask about the last brave thing she did
own.player: What’s the last brave thing you did?
own.reply: Messaging you, honestly. Before that, I sent soup back. It was cold. I apologized four times.

own.label: Ask what she does at the store
own.player: What do you do at the store?
own.reply: Menswear. I measure men for dinner jackets. They talk over my head as if I’m a hat stand, so I hear everything. I remember most of it.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: Dad mends shoes in one of the last old shopfronts on the street. Mom’s a lunch lady at the parish school. I was the girl nobody noticed who noticed everybody.

calls.label: Ask about the men she measures
calls.player: Anything strange about the men you measure?
calls.reply: We keep a book: every club dinner jacket, the man, the woman who paid. Four of the men I’ve fitted in two years were voted into the family. I wrote in my notebook that I measure men who won’t need the jacket long. I’ve seen the Cemetery Chapel.
calls.note: Megan Torres has fitted four voted-in Bluebird husbands for dinner jackets, and fears for every one of them.

life.news: Wrote something brave in my notebook today. Then I did it. I asked for a day off.
life.more: I’m braver in writing. In person I mostly nod and hope someone else talks. I wrote: ask for the day off, you’ve earned it. Then I read it to my manager, word for word, from the notebook. He said yes. I spent the day in the reading room by the radiator.

life.news: A grandmother in the line showed me forty photos of her cat. I looked at every one.
life.more: It happened once at an airport too, a woman from Tucson. I think I have a face that says show me your cat. This one was ginger and very fat and called Duke. My own cat is called Tucson, after the first grandmother. I might need another cat.

life.news: Sent soup back at a café. It was cold. I apologized four times. The waiter apologized five.
life.more: That’s the bravest thing I do, apart from messaging people. We apologized at each other until the soup came back hot. I left a huge tip out of guilt. I don’t think I’m built for complaints.

life.news: My dad fixed a pair of shoes for a man who cried when he saw them. His late wife’s.
life.more: Dad mends shoes in a little shop on our street. The man brought in his wife’s dancing shoes to keep. Dad made them new without making them different. The man held them like a baby. Dad pretended to be very busy with the glue.

gossip.says: Amelia Hart works upstairs from me and talks enough for both of us. Her dog ate a tax letter. She wants a porch and a husband who reads to her. I hope she gets both.
gossip.note: Megan Torres says Amelia Hart wants a porch and a husband who reads to her.
gossip.ask: Megan says you want a porch and a husband who reads to you.
gossip.answer: A little house with a porch, a husband who reads to me and children who tell me I’m embarrassing! Is that too old-fashioned? Megan doesn’t think so. She’s the only quiet person I’ve ever been friends with. She listens like it’s her job.

gossip.says: There’s another Megan, Megan O'Keefe, a dental hygienist, and our manager keeps mixing us up. She’s my exact opposite. She’s been engaged three times. I’ve been on four dates.
gossip.note: Megan Torres says Megan O'Keefe, the dental hygienist, is her opposite.
gossip.ask: Megan Torres says you’re her exact opposite.
gossip.answer: Three engagements, eleven times in love, and the other Megan has been on four dates and remembers every one. I think she’s got the better system. She can read a man from his shoulders. I do it from his teeth. Same job, different end.

gossip.says: Priya Nair runs the parish reading room and lets me sit there on my days off. Nobody talks. The radiator sings. It’s the best room in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Megan Torres says Priya Nair’s reading room is her favorite quiet place.
gossip.ask: Megan says your reading room is the best room in Sunfall.
gossip.answer: She sits in the armchair by the window, reads for four hours, and leaves a thank-you note in the returns box every time. I’ve filed them under pending. Like my feelings. Tell her the armchair is hers.

own.label: Ask about nursing
own.player: What’s nursing really like?
own.reply: Twelve-hour shifts, holding hands with strangers, and eating chips standing up. I love it. Don’t tell my back.

own.label: Ask what she does for thrills
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: Skydiving, once. Rock climbing, often. After a night in the ER, jumping out of a plane feels relaxing.

own.label: Ask about a patient she remembers
own.player: Is there a patient you can’t forget?
own.reply: A woman came in the night of the gala with a cut hand and a blue dress, gave a false name, and left before the doctor saw her.
own.note: Emily Fairchild treated a woman in a blue dress on gala night who gave a false name and left early.

own.label: Ask what the night shift teaches you
own.player: What does the night shift teach you?
own.reply: That everyone is the same at four in the morning. Rich, poor, angry, holy. Everyone wants their mom.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where do you get your nerve from?
own.reply: Dad drove the last passenger train out of Sunfall. He taught me fear is a signal, not an instruction. Mom’s a midwife at the hospital. I was raised by people who don’t panic.

own.label: Ask what she does on days off
own.player: What do you do on a day off?
own.reply: Climb, or run the canyon trail early. Once I found a girl crying on the third bend and just ran past slowly so she had company. She still nods at me.

calls.label: Ask what happened with the chart
calls.player: What happened with that patient’s chart?
calls.reply: She said thank you and the word swallow when I asked her name, so I wrote Mrs. Swallow. She smiled. The doctor signed the chart later without ever seeing her. The chart still exists. Most things in a hospital do.
calls.note: Emily Fairchild says the hospital chart for Mrs. Swallow still exists, signed later by a doctor who never saw her.

calls.label: Ask about the nurse beside her
calls.player: Has anyone at work told you something they shouldn’t?
calls.reply: Beth Porter, who nurses beside me. Her sister Abigail is a police officer. Beth says Abigail left the club’s door for nine minutes that night and hasn’t slept since.
calls.note: Emily Fairchild heard from Beth Porter that her sister Abigail left the club’s door for nine minutes on gala night.

life.news: Climbed a route at the canyon I’ve been scared of for a year. Did it. Shaking. Brilliant.
life.more: After a night in the ER, climbing feels relaxing. This route has a bit near the top where you trust a tiny ledge with two fingers. My dad drove trains and always said fear is a signal, not an instruction. I listened to the signal. Then I went anyway.

life.news: Twelve-hour shift. Held hands with three strangers. Ate chips standing up. Don’t tell my back.
life.more: Everyone’s the same in the small hours. Everyone wants their mom. I held an old man’s hand while he told me about his wife and a bus they missed in another country. Then I ate a packet of chips in the sluice room. I love this job. My back doesn’t.

life.news: Ran the canyon at dawn and fell in with a detective and her police dog. We didn’t speak. We just ran.
life.more: Eleanor Graves and Major. They run like they’re looking for clues. Very upright. Very suspicious of rocks. I’ve nodded at them every morning for a month. Today I just joined in. She’s slower than me. I’m not going to mention it. Yet.

life.news: My mom delivered twins today. She’s been a midwife thirty years and she still called me crying.
life.more: She says every baby is the first one. Today it was two at once and both came out shouting. She called me from the parking lot and just said, two! I could hear her smiling. Then she asked if I’d eaten. I hadn’t. She knew.

gossip.says: Maya Serrano and I work emergency together. She eats a whole packet of cookies in her car after a bad shift and won’t share. I’ve stopped asking. I bring my own.
gossip.note: Emily Fairchild says Maya Serrano eats cookies in her car after bad shifts.
gossip.ask: Emily says you eat a whole packet of cookies in your car after a bad shift and won’t share.
gossip.answer: It’s not not sharing, it’s survival! Emily brings her own now, which is growth. We sit in two cars side by side in the parking lot eating cookies and not talking. It’s the best part of the job. Don’t tell the consultant.

gossip.says: Phoebe Sutton runs the canyon before sunrise without her phone. I found her once on the third bend, just sitting. I sat with her for a bit, then ran on. Some people need someone to sit, not someone to talk.
gossip.note: Emily Fairchild says she once sat with Phoebe Sutton on the canyon trail.
gossip.ask: Emily says she sat with you once on the third bend and didn’t say anything.
gossip.answer: She didn’t say a word. Then she ran off, very fast, like it was nothing. It wasn’t nothing. I’ve never told anyone at the club that I sit on that bend. Tell her I owe her a run, and I’ll try to keep up.

own.label: Ask how karaoke went
own.player: How did the karaoke go?
own.reply: I sang a power ballad, forgot the second verse and freestyled. People clapped out of fear. I count that as a win.

own.label: Ask about marketing
own.player: What’s marketing actually like?
own.reply: We sell feelings to people who are too tired to feel them. Today I wrote elevate your hydration journey about a water bottle. I need a shower.

own.label: Ask what she’s honest about
own.player: What’s something you’d never post online?
own.reply: That I’m lonely. Everyone posts the party. Nobody posts the drive home.

own.label: Ask if she believes in her job
own.player: Do you actually believe in what you market?
own.reply: I sold a shampoo as self-love once. It was shampoo. I think that was the day I started looking for a new job.

own.label: Ask who her agency works for
own.player: Who does your agency work for?
own.reply: The Foundation, the casino, and the free weekly’s adverts. I sell feelings to people too tired to feel them. Today it was hydration. Tomorrow it’s probably grief.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your family do?
own.reply: Dad runs a gas station on the state road. Mom does the register. I sang at every school thing and was told I had a voice. Turns out voices don’t pay.

calls.label: Ask about the campaign she can’t discuss
calls.player: What campaign aren’t you allowed to talk about?
calls.reply: The Foundation’s anniversary. Members only, never public. The mood board has a crescent, a bell, nine women on old chapel steps from a postcard, and the line welcome into the family. I have it on my laptop and it gives me the creeps.
calls.note: Brooke Chandler says the Foundation’s private anniversary campaign uses a crescent, a bell, nine women on chapel steps and the line welcome into the family.

calls.label: Ask about the self-love shampoo
calls.player: Why did the shampoo job make you want to quit?
calls.reply: I sold it as self-love. The brand belongs to the wellness company that’s trying to buy the tattoo studio, and that company belongs to the trust on the ridge. I was selling self-love for a landlord.
calls.note: Brooke Chandler says the wellness brand she advertised belongs to the trust on the ridge.

life.news: Karaoke tonight. Forgot the second verse of a power ballad and freestyled. People clapped out of fear. I count that as a win.
life.more: I rhymed heart with shopping cart and held a note so long the barman turned the music down to check I was all right. I was. I was glorious. Everyone posts the party. I’m posting the freestyle.

life.news: Wrote elevate your hydration journey about a water bottle today. I need a shower.
life.more: Marketing doesn’t sell products, it sells feelings people don’t have yet. The bottle is just a bottle. I spent four hours making it a lifestyle. Then I went home and drank tap water out of a mug, out of spite.

life.news: Drove home alone after a party again. Nobody posts the drive home.
life.more: Everyone posts the party. The lights, the pool, the glitter. Nobody posts the twenty minutes in the car afterwards with the radio on and your shoes on the passenger seat. That’s the honest bit. I’m lonely. I said it. On an app. Brave or stupid?

life.news: Sang at my cousin’s wedding. Nobody clapped out of fear this time. They actually clapped.
life.more: My dad cried, my mom cried, the vicar cried, which I don’t think vicars are supposed to do. At school they told me I had a voice and voices don’t pay. Today it didn’t need to pay. It just needed to get through the first verse without me inventing one.

gossip.says: Tiffany Nash throws the parties I post about. Pool, playlist, strict no-boring-people policy. She keeps a list of who’s pretty, rich or interesting. She’s on it under interesting. She wrote it herself.
gossip.note: Brooke Chandler says Tiffany Nash keeps a list of who’s pretty, rich or interesting.
gossip.ask: Brooke says you keep a list of who’s pretty, rich or interesting.
gossip.answer: Two out of three gets you in, babe. Brooke’s interesting and pretty, which is the best combination, because rich people are mostly boring. She sings at my parties after two drinks. After three, she freestyles. I book the third drink.

gossip.says: Lauren Bishop teaches the fitness classes my agency advertises. She tells everyone they’re fine as they are. Then she goes home and eats toast. So much toast.
gossip.note: Brooke Chandler says Lauren Bishop the fitness instructor lives on toast.
gossip.ask: Brooke says you live on toast.
gossip.answer: Don’t tell my clients! They think I live on kale and gratitude. Walk, sleep, eat a vegetable, call your mom. That’s the whole program. The toast is between me and God. Brooke wrote my class poster and it said transform your soul. I teach squats.

own.label: Ask about the diner
own.player: What’s it like at the diner?
own.reply: The Lucky Cactus! Same twelve regulars, same pie, same jukebox that only works when you kick it. It’s my favorite place on earth.

own.label: Ask about the regulars
own.player: Who are the regulars?
own.reply: A retired cowboy who tips in quarters, two old ladies who argue about the bishop, and a reporter who never eats, just listens.

own.label: Ask what she overheard
own.player: Do you overhear things at the diner?
own.reply: Everything. The night of the gala, two men in suits sat in the back booth and one said, She’s not coming back, so stop asking.
own.note: Madison Pike overheard two men at the Lucky Cactus on gala night: She’s not coming back, so stop asking.

own.label: Ask who tips worst
own.player: Who tips worst at the diner?
own.reply: Men in expensive watches and people who say they’re influencers. The truckers tip like saints.

own.label: Ask who raised her
own.player: Who brought you up?
own.reply: My sister Rowan, the tattooist, from when I was ten. Most frightening person in Sunfall. I talk for both of us. She thinks I talk too much. She’s right.

own.label: Ask about the jukebox
own.player: Does the jukebox have a name?
own.reply: Dolores. After the woman who ran the diner forty years. It plays what it wants. The day she died, it played her song by itself. Everyone swears it.

calls.label: Ask who paid in the back booth
calls.player: Do you know who the two men in the booth were?
calls.reply: One was the treasurer, from the paper. The other paid by card, and I read everything, so I read the name. Marchbanks. Nobody asked me, so I never said.
calls.note: Madison Pike says the men in the Lucky Cactus booth on gala night were Augustus Pell and a man who paid as Marchbanks.

calls.label: Ask who she keeps a slice of pie for
calls.player: Who’s the slice of pie behind the counter for?
calls.reply: Zara, Dolores’s niece. She hasn’t been in for a meal in four years. I save her a slice every night and throw it away in the morning. One day she’ll come in hungry.

life.news: Kicked the jukebox at the Lucky Cactus and it played my favorite song first time! It never does that!
life.more: Same twelve regulars, same pie, same jukebox that only works when you kick it. It’s my favorite place on earth. Today I kicked it exactly right and it played the slow one, and old Mr. Hollis at the counter started singing, and so did everyone. Best shift ever.

life.news: A man tipped me in pennies. Forty of them. In a little stack.
life.more: I keep count of who tips worst. It’s always men in expensive watches and people who say they’re good tippers. This man was neither. He built a little tower of pennies and said, for the lady. Rowan says it’s an insult. I think it’s architecture.

life.news: Rowan wouldn’t tell me about our dad again. She just changed the subject to the dishwasher.
life.more: My sister’s raised me since I was ten. She knows things about the motel strip she won’t say. I asked about our dad and she said the dishwasher’s making a noise. The dishwasher’s fine. I made her pancakes anyway. She ate them. That’s how we hug.

life.news: Remembered a man’s order from three years ago. He nearly fainted.
life.more: Two eggs, one up, one over, rye toast, no butter, and a side of nothing. He came in today for the first time since, and I just put it through. He said, how? I said, it’s a superpower but useless. He tipped me twenty. Okay. Useful today.

gossip.says: Nadia Okafor does cryptic crosswords at my counter in pencil, and I read them upside down while I pour. I got two clues before her. She’s still not over it.
gossip.note: Madison Pike says she solved two of Nadia Okafor’s crossword clues first.
gossip.ask: Madison says she got two of your crossword clues before you did.
gossip.answer: Two. Out of thirty. In a cryptic. Upside down. She tells everyone like she won the lottery. To be fair, she’s frighteningly good. She also refills my coffee before I ask, which is the only reason I let it go.

gossip.says: Beatrice Hale from the paper comes in, orders nothing and just listens. We call her the reporter who never eats. I’ve started bringing her toast anyway. She eats it without noticing.
gossip.note: Madison Pike says Beatrice Hale the reporter comes to the Lucky Cactus just to listen.
gossip.ask: Madison says you come to the Lucky Cactus, order nothing and just listen.
gossip.answer: Everything’s off the record until it isn’t, and the Lucky Cactus is where Sunfall forgets to be careful. I do eat. I eat Madison’s toast. It’s a seven out of ten, which from me is practically a medal.

gossip.says: Arielle Brooks lives upstairs from the diner and tells me stories from the old newspapers on my breaks. Today it was a man who sued a goose. A hundred years ago. He lost.
gossip.note: Madison Pike says Arielle Brooks tells her stories from the old newspapers.
gossip.ask: Madison says you told her about a man who sued a goose.
gossip.answer: He did! He lost because the goose had a better lawyer. Well, the goose’s owner did. Madison laughs at every story like it’s the first funny thing that’s ever happened. I save the best ones for her breaks.

own.label: Ask about the housing market
own.player: How’s the housing market?
own.reply: For buyers? A horror film. For sellers? A heist film. For anyone under thirty? A tragedy.

own.label: Ask about estate-agent language
own.player: What does characterful mean in a listing?
own.reply: Haunted or damp. Cozy means you can touch both walls. Up-and-coming means bring a dog.

own.label: Ask about a strange sale
own.player: Have you had any strange sales?
own.reply: Someone bought three empty houses near the old chapel, cash, through a company with a made-up name. Nobody buys out there.
own.note: Olivia Reid sold three empty houses near the old chapel for cash to a company with a made-up name.

own.label: Ask what home means to her
own.player: What does home mean to someone who sells them?
own.reply: A door you can close. Everything else is staging. I’ve sold a hundred homes and I rent a room above a laundromat.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the laundromat on Sunfall Road. If you’re the new one in the room across the landing, hello. The radiator sings, the walls are cardboard, and I know you snore.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Did your family always rent?
own.reply: We lost a house to the reservoir’s second wall and never got another. Dad maintains the dam that drowned it. Mom cleans at the club. That’s how I learned the people who own houses aren’t the people who clean them.

calls.label: Ask who signed the strange sale
calls.player: Who actually bought the three houses?
calls.reply: A company with a made-up name. But the signature on the completion is real: Adeline Marsh, from the club. And the buyer’s address for letters is the Bluebird Club’s east wing. I have the file.
calls.note: Olivia Reid says the three houses by the Old Mission were bought by a shell company signed for by Adeline Marsh, care of the Bluebird Club.

calls.label: Ask what else she’s been asked to value
calls.player: Have you valued anything odd lately?
calls.reply: The parish reading room and the Sisters’ shop building, for the diocese’s property company. The contact is a monsignor called Ferrante. It’s on my desk marked confidential, and now I’ve told you, which isn’t very confidential.
calls.note: Olivia Reid valued the Sisters’ reading room and shop for the diocese’s property company, via Monsignor Ferrante.

life.news: Showed an apartment today that I described as cozy. Cozy means you can touch both walls. The buyer touched both walls.
life.more: Up-and-coming means bring a dog. Characterful means haunted or damp. He stood in the middle, put his arms out, touched both walls, and said, I’ll take it. Respect.

life.news: Valued a house for a couple selling the home they raised four kids in. They cried. I cried. I’m meant to be a professional.
life.more: For buyers it’s a horror film, for sellers it’s a heist, and sometimes it’s just a tragedy. They’d measured the kids on the kitchen door frame. I asked if they wanted to take the frame. They did. We unscrewed it together.

life.news: The laundromat under my apartment gives free dryer time if you kick machine four. Life-changing.
life.more: Twenty free minutes if you kick it on the corner. A woman in a bathrobe taught me. I’m keeping it a secret from everyone on the landing. Except you.

life.news: Somebody bought three empty houses this month for cash. No viewings. No questions. Nobody buys houses like that.
life.more: People who don’t look at a house have already decided what it’s for. The company name on the forms doesn’t exist anywhere I can find. I filed it. I’m still thinking about it. That’s the bad part of this job.

gossip.says: Linh Tran lives down the landing and she’s writing a novel with everyone in Sunfall in it. I’m in chapter four as a real estate agent who’s secretly a poet. I’m not a poet. I’m a little bit a poet.
gossip.note: Olivia Reid says she is in chapter four of Linh Tran’s novel.
gossip.ask: Olivia says she’s in chapter four of your novel as a secret poet.
gossip.answer: She is. She’s good in it. A bit mean, very funny, writes sonnets about kitchens. I didn’t make up the sonnets. She leaves them on the laundromat noticeboard, unsigned. Everyone knows.

gossip.says: Celina Rojas used to live across the landing from me. She left in one night in the spring and didn’t say why. She left a plant on my doorstep. It’s still alive. I talk to it.
gossip.note: Olivia Reid says Celina Rojas left the landing suddenly in the spring.
gossip.ask: Olivia says you left the landing in one night and gave her a plant.
gossip.answer: I had to go. It’s a long story and not a nice one. I left her the plant because she left me cookies when I was crying through the wall. It’s a spider plant. They’re very hard to kill. I chose it on purpose.

own.label: Ask about accounting
own.player: Is accounting as dull as people say?
own.reply: People think numbers are cold. They’re not. A budget is just a list of what someone loves.

own.label: Ask if she’s a romantic
own.player: You seem like a romantic.
own.reply: Hopelessly. I cried at a wedding I was only catering for. I believe in the whole thing: the vows, the cake, the forever.

own.label: Ask if forever is realistic
own.player: Do you think forever is realistic any more?
own.reply: My grandparents managed sixty years with one argument a decade. If they could do it on worse wages, we can do it with better phones.

own.label: Ask what she’d never put a price on
own.player: Is there anything you’d never put a price on?
own.reply: My grandmother’s recipe box. And a man who turns up when he says he will. Those are both rarer than they should be.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: They run the feed store on the state road. Diana Moore grew up above it. Our families know each other’s debts, which in a small town is closer than marriage.

own.label: Ask about her wedding scrapbook
own.player: Do you really have a wedding scrapbook?
own.reply: Since I was twelve. Cakes, dresses, a church with a good door. I’m crushed by coldness and my new office is a very cold place.

calls.label: Ask what the Foundation’s budget says
calls.player: What does the Foundation’s budget say about it?
calls.reply: A budget is a list of what someone loves. This one loves a trust on the ridge most, a catering firm second, and the scholarships come below the upkeep of a lodge. I drew a heart round the numbers. It’s the wrong shape.
calls.note: Sarah Whitcomb says the Foundation’s budget puts the trust on the ridge first and the scholarships below the lodge’s upkeep.

life.news: Found my grandmother’s wedding cake recipe in her recipe box. In her handwriting. With a note: don’t skimp on the brandy.
life.more: My grandparents managed sixty years with one argument a decade. Under the recipe she wrote: made for us, fifty years ago, still good. I’m going to make it one day. For the right reason.

life.news: Did a stranger’s budget for free at the library. It was a list of everything he loved. His dog came first.
life.more: People think numbers are cold. They’re not. A budget is just a list of what someone loves. His went: dog food, his mom’s phone bill, a bus pass, then everything else. I didn’t change a thing. I told him he was doing it right.

life.news: Cried at a wedding again. I was only there to drop off a cake order.
life.more: I catered weddings at sixteen and cried at every one. I’ve stopped catering. I haven’t stopped crying. Today I walked in with a box and the bride was reading her vows to her nana, and that was it. I left the cake on a chair and fled.

life.news: Went to the feed store where I grew up. Mom and Dad still argue about the price of oats. Lovingly.
life.more: They run the feed store on the state road and they’ve argued about oats for thirty years, and never about anything else. My grandad says that’s the secret. Pick one thing to fight about and make it something small.

gossip.says: Julia Mercer makes wedding cakes and she can tell from the tasting whether the marriage will last. It’s the fork. If they share one fork, they’ll make it.
gossip.note: Sarah Whitcomb says Julia Mercer predicts marriages from how couples share a fork.
gossip.ask: Sarah says you can tell from the cake tasting whether a marriage will last.
gossip.answer: It’s the fork! One fork, they’ll make it. Two forks, they’ll be polite. One fork each and they won’t look at each other’s plate? Run. Sarah cried at one of my tastings. The couple shared a fork. She knew before I did.

gossip.says: Nicole Ashbury plans weddings and once watched a cannon set fire to a hedge at a gender reveal. She says her own wedding would be tiny. A church, a dress, nobody filming.
gossip.note: Sarah Whitcomb says Nicole Ashbury wants a tiny wedding for herself.
gossip.ask: Sarah says you’d have a tiny wedding: a church, a dress, nobody filming.
gossip.answer: Tiny! After two hundred weddings for other people, all I want is one where nobody shouts at a florist. The hedge is fine now, by the way. The baby was always fine. Spend more on counseling than on cake. Sarah agrees. Sarah cries at both.

gossip.says: Yumi Tanaka had my desk before me. She left a note in the drawer that said, check everything twice. I do. I’ve started checking things three times.
gossip.note: Sarah Whitcomb says Yumi Tanaka left her a note to check everything twice.
gossip.ask: Sarah says you left her a note to check everything twice.
gossip.answer: Twice is the minimum. Three times is sensible. Four is a personality. Sarah is very kind and very honest, and she needs to be careful. Not everything at that desk adds up the way it should. She’ll find that out. Check everything.

own.label: Ask about her parties
own.player: What kind of parties do you throw?
own.reply: The kind people pretend they didn’t go to. Pool, playlist, a strict no-boring-people policy.

own.label: Ask about VIP lists
own.player: How do you get on your VIP list?
own.reply: Be pretty, rich or interesting. Two out of three, darling. One if you’re very interesting.

own.label: Ask about the gala after-party
own.player: Did you run the gala after-party?
own.reply: I did the after-party. A charity man paid me double to keep one room off the guest list. I spent the money. I didn’t ask.
own.note: Tiffany Nash was paid double by a charity man to keep one room off the gala after-party guest list.

own.label: Ask if she ever gets tired of parties
own.player: Do you ever get tired of parties?
own.reply: Every night, around the third hour. Everyone’s having the best time of their lives, every single weekend. Nobody is.

own.label: Ask what list she’s on
own.player: Are you on your own list?
own.reply: Under interesting. Which is a lie. I’m under pretty, on a good day. I sleep till noon and work till four. My apartment has a wardrobe and no kitchen.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The trailer park behind the drive-in. A goth, a Bluebird, a lab analyst, a jeweler and me. Someone says that’s statistically significant.

calls.label: Ask which room was kept off the list
calls.player: Which room was kept off the after-party list?
calls.reply: The boathouse at the club’s sailing annex. The charity man who paid me was Dorian Kell. The barman told me, frightened, that a woman’s coat and bag were put in there the morning after, and then they were gone.
calls.note: Tiffany Nash says Dorian Kell paid to keep the boathouse off the after-party list, and Elena Cross’s coat and bag were left there the morning after.

calls.label: Ask how she paid her debt
calls.player: Do you owe anyone anything?
calls.reply: I played cards at the lodge once and lost. The favor they wanted was a room. They asked for it before the benefit. So it was always planned.
calls.note: Tiffany Nash says the lodge asked her for the after-party room before the gala.

life.news: Threw a party last night that people will pretend they didn’t go to. Best compliment there is.
life.more: Pool, playlist, strict no-boring-people policy. Be pretty, rich or interesting, two out of three. A man tried to get in on rich alone. I said, babe, that’s one. He went home. He’ll be back with a personality.

life.news: The third hour of a party: everyone’s having the best night of their lives. Nobody is. Watched it happen again.
life.more: Everyone’s having the best time of their lives, every single weekend. Nobody is. In the third hour I stand by the pool and watch people pretend. It’s my favorite moment. It’s also the saddest. I’m complicated.

life.news: My mom asked what I actually do for a living. I said I make people happy. She said, do you?
life.more: She cleans for a living, real work, with her hands. I make playlists and guest lists. I sent her a photo of the pool at sunrise with nobody in it. She said it looked lonely. She’s right. Don’t tell her.

life.news: Slept till lunch, worked till dawn, had cereal for dinner. I’m living my truth.
life.more: An apartment with a wardrobe and no kitchen. One bowl, one spoon and a box of cereal I share with no one. My accountant hates me. My mirror loves me. Somewhere in the middle there’s a person. She’s fine.

gossip.says: Erin Doyle lifeguards the pool at my parties and has saved four children and one very proud businessman. She stays sober all night and judges everyone. She’s always right.
gossip.note: Tiffany Nash says Erin Doyle lifeguards her pool parties.
gossip.ask: Tiffany says you stay sober all night at her parties and judge everyone.
gossip.answer: It’s eight hours of watching people almost drown and then not. Somebody has to stay sober. Tiffany’s parties are mostly influencers who never touch the water and one man who always tries a backflip. I’ve pulled him out twice. He thinks we’re friends.

gossip.says: Brooke Chandler posts my parties better than I throw them. She makes a quiet night look like a film. Then she drives home alone and sings in the car. I’ve seen her at the lights.
gossip.note: Tiffany Nash says Brooke Chandler sings alone in her car after parties.
gossip.ask: Tiffany says she’s seen you singing alone in your car at the lights.
gossip.answer: She saw that?! I was doing a power ballad. The second verse. I freestyled it. Everyone posts the party. Nobody posts the drive home. That’s my drive home. It’s the best concert in Sunfall and it’s free.

gossip.says: Piper Nocturne and I grew up in the same trailer park behind the drive-in. She went goth, I went parties. Same girls. Different lighting.
gossip.note: Tiffany Nash says she and Piper Nocturne grew up in the same trailer park.
gossip.ask: Tiffany says you two grew up in the same trailer park, just with different lighting.
gossip.answer: Tiffany said that? She’s not wrong. Three doors apart. She had the pink bike and I had the one I’d painted black with nail varnish. I sell velvet and despair, she sells glitter and despair. Don’t tell my customers.

own.label: Ask about her classes
own.player: What are your classes like?
own.reply: Loud music, louder screaming, and a man called Derek who insists on doing everything at half speed. I love Derek.

own.label: Ask about wellness culture
own.player: What do you think of all the wellness stuff?
own.reply: Half of it is good advice and the other half is selling powders to sad people. Walk, sleep, eat a vegetable, call your mom. That’s my whole program.

own.label: Ask about her body image
own.player: Is it hard working in a world obsessed with bodies?
own.reply: Some days. I spend all day telling people they’re fine as they are, then go home and hate my thighs. Fitness is a weird religion.

own.label: Ask what she actually eats
own.player: What do you actually eat, honestly?
own.reply: Toast. So much toast. Don’t tell my clients. They think I live on kale and gratitude.

own.label: Ask if she’s related to the bishop
own.player: Any relation to the bishop?
own.reply: None, which is the joke of my life, so I tell it first. Dad drives trucks. Mom’s a lunch lady at the hill school. No incense, just toast.

own.label: Ask what she tells clients
own.player: What do you tell people at the gym?
own.reply: That they’re fine as they are. Then I go home and hate my thighs. Fitness is a weird religion. I’m a doubting priest.

calls.label: Ask what she saw from the gym’s back window
calls.player: Seen anything from the gym window?
calls.reply: It faces the alley behind the jeweler’s on Fifth Avenue. One night with no moon I saw the jeweler hand a box to a girl in sunglasses. The box was about the size of a bell clapper. Don’t ask me how I know what size a bell clapper is.
calls.note: Lauren Bishop saw the Fifth Avenue jeweler hand a box the size of a bell clapper to a girl in sunglasses on a moonless night.

calls.label: Ask who trains at her gym
calls.player: Who trains at your gym?
calls.reply: A Bluebird, a police officer, a reporter and a goth, all on the same page of the membership list. It’s the only room in Sunfall where they’d ever share a towel.

life.news: Derek did a full squat today. At half speed, but full. I cried in front of the class.
life.more: Loud music, louder screaming, and Derek, who insists on doing everything at half speed. He’s seventy and he’s been coming for a year. Today he went all the way down and all the way up and the whole class clapped. I love Derek.

life.news: Told twenty people they were fine as they are. Went home and hated my thighs. Fitness is a weird religion.
life.more: I mean it when I tell them. I don’t mean it when I tell me. Walk, sleep, eat a vegetable, call your mom. That’s my whole program. Tonight I’m doing two of those. Toast doesn’t count as a vegetable. I’ve checked.

life.news: Ate so much toast today the man at the bakery asked if I was feeding a family.
life.more: Don’t tell my clients. They think I live on kale and gratitude. I said yes, I’m feeding a family. Of me. He gave me a free loaf. I think he felt sorry for my imaginary children.

life.news: Ran a class for the over-sixties. They outlasted me. One woman did twenty press-ups and asked if that was all.
life.more: Mrs. Delgado did the whole hour and then challenged me to an arm-wrestle. She won. I think she trains on shortbread. They want a weekly class now. I’m going to need more toast.

gossip.says: Alisha Benton boxes at my gym and I broke her nose by accident. Twice. She came back both times. She’s either the bravest woman I know or the most stubborn.
gossip.note: Lauren Bishop says she accidentally broke Alisha Benton’s nose sparring, twice.
gossip.ask: Lauren says she broke your nose twice and you came back both times.
gossip.answer: Technically once, and once it was the same break saying hello again. She’s lovely and she has no idea how strong she is. I came back because it’s the only hour of the week I’m not looking at evidence. Also, I’m going to land one on her eventually.

gossip.says: Heather Collins teaches at the hill school and climbs everything. Our moms were lunch ladies together. She was the girl who climbed the water tower. I was the girl who held her shoes.
gossip.note: Lauren Bishop says Heather Collins climbed the water tower as a girl.
gossip.ask: Lauren says you climbed the water tower and she held your shoes.
gossip.answer: She held my shoes AND called my mom, which is the most Lauren thing anyone’s ever done. I was eleven. The view was worth the grounding. Now I teach eight-year-olds not to climb things. Hypocrisy, but supervised.

own.label: Ask about teaching
own.player: What’s teaching seven-year-olds like?
own.reply: Like herding philosophers on sugar. One asked me today if worms have feelings. I didn’t have an answer.

own.label: Ask about kids and screens
own.player: Are kids different now, with all the screens?
own.reply: They’re brilliant and they can’t wait. They’ve never been bored. Boredom is where imagination comes from.

own.label: Ask about the bear at school
own.player: Has the bear come near the school?
own.reply: Last week it left prints by the playground fence. The kids named it. Nobody told the parents. You didn’t hear that from me.

own.label: Ask what she wishes parents knew
own.player: What do you wish parents knew?
own.reply: That their kids are fine if you let them be bored. Boredom is where imagination lives. We’ve paved over it with tablets.

own.label: Ask about her house
own.player: What’s your place like?
own.reply: A house on the hill with a dog, a view of the ridge road and my grandfather’s rifle in a locked cabinet. He was the fire warden. I’ve never fired it. I keep it oiled for him.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What does your dad do?
own.reply: He was a logger until the logging went. Then the ridge’s quarry. He came back with a cough and a quiet. He won’t say what they quarry up there.

calls.label: Ask what was beside the bear prints
calls.player: Was there anything else by the bear prints?
calls.reply: Boot prints and a van’s tire marks, which I didn’t tell the children. The fence had been cut and mended. Somebody tried to take that bear off our playing field. I’ve seen a van with no plates on the hill road twice, at dawn, going up.
calls.note: Heather Collins found boot prints, tire marks and a cut fence beside the bear prints at the hill school.

calls.label: Ask about a child’s drawing
calls.player: Has a child ever drawn something that worried you?
calls.reply: A six-year-old whose father works on the ridge drew a man in a cloak reading to his dad at a gate. I kept the drawing. Children draw what they see. That’s the frightening bit.
calls.note: Heather Collins has a child’s drawing of a man in a cloak reading to a worker at a gate on the ridge.

life.news: A child asked me today if worms have feelings. I didn’t have an answer. We spent an hour on it.
life.more: Like herding philosophers on sugar. We went outside, found a worm, and the class voted on whether it was sad. Nineteen said happy, three said shy. The worm declined to comment. Best lesson I’ve taught all year.

life.news: Took the class to the field and let them be bored for twenty minutes. No tablets. They invented a whole kingdom.
life.more: They’re brilliant and they can’t wait. They’ve never been bored. Boredom is where imagination lives and we’ve paved over it. After ten minutes of moaning they built a kingdom out of sticks with a king who was a stone. I nearly cried.

life.news: The bear left prints by the playground fence again. The kids want to write it a letter.
life.more: They named it last term, and we’re not supposed to tell the parents, so you didn’t hear this from me. They’ve drafted a letter asking it to visit at break. I told them bears can’t read. They said, then we’ll draw it.

life.news: My dad’s cough was bad today. He came back from the quarry with it and it hasn’t gone.
life.more: He was a logger until the logging went, then he worked up at the quarry on the ridge and came back quieter. He won’t see a doctor. We sat on the porch and watched the ridge road and didn’t say anything. The hills are very loud when nobody talks.

gossip.says: Tessa Larkin from the wildlife rescue brought an injured owl to my class for show and tell. The owl hated everyone. The kids loved it. Tessa makes clay birds that look like potatoes.
gossip.note: Heather Collins says Tessa Larkin brought an owl to her class.
gossip.ask: Heather says your clay birds look like potatoes.
gossip.answer: They do. Potatoes with opinions. I love birds and I can’t make them. The owl was called Doris and she did hate everyone, but she was very well behaved about it. You can’t love something into staying, but you can bring it to a classroom for an hour.

gossip.says: Marisol Fuentes from the park service came to talk to my class about the bear. She said he’s a young male pushed out by an older one, lost and hungry and too curious. A girl put her hand up and said, me too.
gossip.note: Heather Collins says park ranger Marisol Fuentes talked to her class about the bear.
gossip.ask: Heather says one of her pupils related a bit too much to your bear.
gossip.answer: Honestly? Relatable. He’s lost, hungry and too curious, and so is everyone under ten and most people over thirty. I told them never to feed him and never to run. The girl who said me too asked if he gets lonely. I said probably. She drew him a friend.

own.label: Ask about art school
own.player: What’s art school like?
own.reply: Everyone makes installations about their feelings. I paint landscapes. They think I’m a reactionary.

own.label: Ask why she paints landscapes
own.player: Why landscapes, when everyone else does installations?
own.reply: Because the desert is beautiful and my classmates are not. Beauty isn’t old-fashioned. It’s just hard.

own.label: Ask what she sketched
own.player: Have you sketched anything strange lately?
own.reply: I sketch the old chapel at night for the light. Last time there were people inside, in a circle. I drew them before I got scared.
own.note: Chloe Farrow sketched people standing in a circle inside the old chapel at night.

own.label: Ask what she thinks art is for
own.player: What do you think art is for?
own.reply: Beauty. I know that’s unfashionable. My tutors want everything to be a statement. A sunset isn’t a statement. It’s just true.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Who taught you to paint?
own.reply: My dad painted signs. The Lucky Cactus, the casino’s letters, the Rialto. He taught me a letter is a landscape. Mom’s a lunch lady. I paint what he taught me to see.

own.label: Ask where she draws
own.player: Where do you go to draw?
own.reply: Out the Old Mission road on my bike. I sit on an old lady’s back step without asking and draw the cracked tower. She brings me lemonade. Neither of us has ever said a word.

calls.label: Ask where the man in the cloak lives
calls.player: Do you know where the man who draws you lives?
calls.reply: I followed him home once. The apartment above the old Rialto. Every window is covered in drawings of me. I saw them from the street and went home and didn’t sleep.
calls.note: Chloe Farrow followed Theon home to the apartment above the old Rialto, its windows covered in drawings of her.

calls.label: Ask about her sketch of the old chapel
calls.player: What did you draw at the old chapel?
calls.reply: Thirteen figures in a circle, with candles. And something on the floor in the middle that I drew as a shadow. I don’t think it was a shadow.
calls.note: Chloe Farrow sketched thirteen figures in a candlelit circle inside the Old Mission, around something on the floor.

life.news: Painted the desert at sunset on the dry river. My classmates made an installation about their feelings. Mine had a sky.
life.more: Everyone makes installations about their feelings. I paint landscapes. They think I’m a reactionary. Today I painted a mesa going purple and a man walking his dog stopped and watched me finish. He said, that’s exactly it. That’s the only review I wanted.

life.news: My tutor said beauty is old-fashioned. I said beauty isn’t old-fashioned, it’s just hard. He gave me a C.
life.more: A C is a badge of honor. I’ve stuck it on my sketchbook. My dad painted signs for a living: the Lucky Cactus, the Rialto, the casino’s letters. He says a letter is a landscape. He’d have given me an A.

life.news: Our kettle broke and we boiled water in a saucepan for a week. Civilization has fallen.
life.more: Emma and I share a house on the dry river. She writes everything in a notebook and says the safe thing out loud. This week she said the unsafe thing: this is barbaric. We bought a kettle together. It’s the most grown-up thing either of us has ever done.

life.news: Sold a painting! A sunset. To someone at a club I’ll never be allowed into.
life.more: Somebody’s sister bought it for a big room with a chandelier. I’ll never see it again. I painted it on the old mission road, sitting on a stranger’s back step. She let me, and brought me lemonade. I’m going to paint her one for free.

gossip.says: Hana Park designs logos and says everything’s beige now. She gave me a sticker that says UGLY AND ALIVE. It’s on my easel.
gossip.note: Chloe Farrow says Hana Park gave her a sticker that says ugly and alive.
gossip.ask: Chloe says you gave her a sticker that says ugly and alive.
gossip.answer: I print them for anyone who’s sick of beige. Every client wants clean and minimal. I want ugly and alive. Chloe paints the most beautiful landscapes in Sunfall, which is the most rebellious thing an art student can do now. She doesn’t need the sticker. She is the sticker.

gossip.says: Emma Frost is my housemate. She writes what she really thinks in a notebook and says the safe thing out loud. Her notebook is terrifying. I’d read it before any novel.
gossip.note: Chloe Farrow says her housemate Emma Frost keeps a terrifying notebook.
gossip.ask: Chloe says your notebook is terrifying.
gossip.answer: It’s not terrifying. It’s honest. Which, in a seminar, is the same thing. Chloe’s the brave one. She says the true thing out loud and then paints a sunset to prove it. We bought a kettle together. That’s the closest I’ll ever come to a mortgage.

gossip.says: Heather Collins teaches my little brother at the hill school. He came home and said worms have feelings and Miss Collins agrees. My parents are very confused.
gossip.note: Chloe Farrow says Heather Collins teaches her little brother.
gossip.ask: Chloe says you told her little brother worms have feelings.
gossip.answer: I said we didn’t know, which is different! We had a vote. The worms won. Her brother voted shy. He’s a lovely boy who draws everything, like his sister. I’ve got his drawing of the worm on my wall.

own.label: Ask about pastry
own.player: What’s your best thing to bake?
own.reply: Croissants. Three days of folding butter for something people eat in four bites. Love is a lot like laminated dough.

own.label: Ask about her café dream
own.player: Would you ever open your own place?
own.reply: A tiny bakery with a bell on the door and no music, just the smell. I have the name already. I won’t tell you. You’ll steal it.

own.label: Ask about wedding cakes
own.player: Do you make wedding cakes?
own.reply: Dozens. I can tell which marriages will last from how the couple taste the samples. If they share one fork, they’re fine.

own.label: Ask what the dough has taught her
own.player: What has baking taught you?
own.reply: That you can’t rush anything worth having. Bread, trust, men. Especially men.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: Is your mother a baker too?
own.reply: Josephine Mercer. She makes rings, reserved and meticulous. Dad was the baker. He left for a woman with a café when I was nine. I mean to open a better one, out of spite.

own.label: Ask about the bell on her door
own.player: Why is there a bell on your apartment door?
own.reply: For practice. My bakery will have a bell and no music. I’ve been listening to that bell for years so I know exactly how it should sound.

calls.label: Ask what her tasting book shows
calls.player: What do you write down at wedding tastings?
calls.reply: The couple, the flavor, the fork. Every Bluebird wedding is in there. None of the voted-in couples shared a fork. Three of my predictions now have ribbons on their stones.
calls.note: Julia Mercer’s wedding-tasting book shows no voted-in Bluebird couple ever shared a fork, and three of those husbands are dead.

life.news: Three days of folding butter, and today the croissants came out perfect. People ate them in four bites.
life.more: Love is a lot like laminated dough. Patience, cold hands, and folding it again when you’d rather give up. Today every single one shattered when you bit it. A man ate one standing at the counter with his eyes shut. I’ll think about his face for a week.

life.news: I have the name for my café written in a drawer. I won’t tell you. You’ll steal it.
life.more: A tiny bakery with a bell on the door and no music, just the smell. I’ve had the name for three years. I’ve put a bell on the inside of my own front door so I can practice hearing it. My downstairs neighbor thinks I’m running a shop. I am. In my head.

life.news: Did a wedding tasting. They shared one fork. They’ll make it.
life.more: I can tell which marriages will last from how they eat the cake. They fed each other the lemon one and argued about the chocolate. Arguing about chocolate is a very good sign. It means they’ll argue about small things forever and nothing big.

life.news: Years ago I sent a letter to a man I loved. He never answered. Today I saw him in the line.
life.more: A letter I still remember word for word. He bought a loaf and paid and said, nice to see you, Julia, like I was the weather. I said, you too. I folded butter for an hour afterwards. Bread forgives you if you’re patient. Men, I’m not so sure.

gossip.says: Nina Petrov runs the bakery across town, and she followed a man here from St. Petersburg. The man left. The ovens stayed. She says she chose the ovens. We’re rivals. We play cards every week.
gossip.note: Julia Mercer says Nina Petrov stayed in Sunfall for her ovens after the man left.
gossip.ask: Julia says you chose the ovens over the man.
gossip.answer: The man left. The ovens stayed. I chose the ovens. Ten years, and they’ve never once lied to me. Julia plays cards the way she bakes, very slowly and with feeling. I win. She pays in croissants. Everyone wins.

gossip.says: Sarah Whitcomb cried at one of my tastings. She wasn’t even getting married, she’d come to drop off an order. Kindest woman in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Julia Mercer says Sarah Whitcomb cried at one of her cake tastings.
gossip.ask: Julia says you cried at a cake tasting that wasn’t yours.
gossip.answer: They shared a fork! She told me what it meant and I just went. My grandparents shared one fork for sixty years, with one argument a decade. I’m a hopeless romantic with a calculator. Don’t tell my clients about the crying.

gossip.says: Nicole Ashbury plans the weddings I make cakes for. She once caught a falling three-tier cake with her whole body. Saved the top tier. Ruined the dress.
gossip.note: Julia Mercer says Nicole Ashbury once caught a falling wedding cake.
gossip.ask: Julia says you once caught a three-tier cake with your whole body.
gossip.answer: Every event goes slightly wrong and turns out fine. The table leg went, I went, the cake went into me. The bride got her top tier. I got buttercream in places buttercream shouldn’t go. Julia made me a medal out of fondant. It’s on my fridge.

own.label: Ask about the animals
own.player: What’s it like working with animals?
own.reply: Better than people. Animals bite you honestly.

own.label: Ask about the owners
own.player: Who’s worse, the pets or the owners?
own.reply: The owners. A man brought in a ferret dressed as a pirate and asked if it was depressed. Sir, look at its hat.

own.label: Ask about the bear
own.player: Has the bear hurt any animals?
own.reply: No. But a ranger brought in a tranquilizer dart we didn’t issue. Someone’s been trying to catch that bear privately.
own.note: Rachel Lowe says someone has been privately trying to tranquillise the bear.

own.label: Ask about the hardest part of her job
own.player: What’s the hardest part of the job?
own.reply: The goodbyes. Old dogs and old men holding them. The men always say sorry to the dog. It breaks me every time.

own.label: Ask about her pets
own.player: Do you have pets of your own?
own.reply: A three-legged dog, a one-eyed cat and a tortoise nobody can date. Between them they have most of an animal.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Was your dad a vet?
own.reply: The county’s large-animal vet for thirty years. The Whitlock ranch, the lodge’s stables, everyone. Then the lodge stopped calling him and he never said why.

calls.label: Ask about the tranquilizer dart
calls.player: What do you know about that dart?
calls.reply: It’s logged in our fridge. The vet says leave it. I photographed the markings. The supplier is the same one on an invoice to the trust on the ridge. Somebody’s trying to catch that bear privately, with money that’s meant for conservation.
calls.note: Rachel Lowe says the tranquilizer dart’s supplier matches an invoice to the trust on the ridge.

calls.label: Ask why her dad stopped going to the lodge
calls.player: Why did your dad stop going to the lodge?
calls.reply: His last call-out, he came home and said there was a horse with a man’s saddle on it that hadn’t been ridden in a year, and a stall at the end with a chain on the door. He never went back. They got a vet from the city.
calls.note: Rachel Lowe’s father saw a chained stall and an unridden horse with a man’s saddle at the lodge’s stables.

life.news: A man brought in a ferret dressed as a pirate and asked if it was depressed. Sir. Look at its hat.
life.more: Animals bite you honestly. People don’t. The ferret had an eyepatch, a little tricorn and the face of a ferret who’d had enough. I took the hat off. He perked up immediately. Diagnosis: hat.

life.news: An old man said sorry to his old dog in the end room today. It breaks me every time.
life.more: I’m breezy about everything except that room. He sat on the floor with her and said, sorry, girl, sorry, over and over, as if he’d done something wrong. He hadn’t. He’d done everything right. I went out to the parking lot and had a little cry with the trash cans.

life.news: The three-legged dog, the one-eyed cat and the tortoise nobody can date all slept in one basket. A miracle.
life.more: My apartment above the clinic is a home for things nobody else would take. Tonight they piled into one basket, the tortoise on top like a lid. I took forty photos. I’d send you all forty. That’s love.

life.news: A ranger brought in something the clinic didn’t issue. I’m not allowed to say what. I photographed it anyway.
life.more: We logged it and my boss said to leave it. I don’t like leaving things. My dad was the county’s vet for thirty years and he said, Rachel, when something doesn’t add up, write it down. So I wrote it down. Then I went to the bar. Balance.

gossip.says: Marisol Fuentes is a park ranger and she pulls cactus out of tourists for a living. She has the best stories in Sunfall and the worst taste in men. We drink together. She’s my favorite.
gossip.note: Rachel Lowe says Marisol Fuentes the ranger pulls cactus out of tourists.
gossip.ask: Rachel says you have the best stories and the worst taste in men.
gossip.answer: Both true. I tell tourists not to touch cacti, then pull cactus out of tourists. Today it was a man’s hand and his pride. As for men, I like them lost and curious, same as the bear. Rachel says that’s a red flag. Rachel dates vets.

gossip.says: Tessa Larkin runs the rescue and has a lizard called Gregory who lives in a shoebox and judges everyone. Gregory has better taste than most of Sunfall.
gossip.note: Rachel Lowe says Tessa Larkin’s lizard Gregory judges everyone.
gossip.ask: Rachel says your lizard Gregory has better taste than most of Sunfall.
gossip.answer: He does. He judged Rachel on sight and then let her stroke his chin, which means she passed. He lives in a shoebox and looks at me like I’ve let him down. Eventually he’ll go back to the rocks. You can’t love something into staying.

gossip.says: Amelia Hart’s terrier Biscuit is my most frequent patient. He’s eaten a lipstick, a tax letter, a sock and half a birthday card. He has range.
gossip.note: Rachel Lowe says Amelia Hart’s terrier Biscuit eats everything.
gossip.ask: Rachel says your dog is her most frequent patient.
gossip.answer: Biscuit! He’s a terrier with no impulse control. The birthday card was for my mom, so honestly he did me a favor. Rachel’s so lovely with him. She talks to him like he’s a person. He talks back. Mostly about lipstick.

own.label: Ask about her job
own.player: Is it weird looking in people’s mouths all day?
own.reply: You learn everything about a person from their teeth. Coffee, wine, grinding. Grinding means they’re hiding something.

own.label: Ask about her first love
own.player: Who was your first love?
own.reply: A boy who wrote me a poem that rhymed Megan with vegan. I married him in my head for three years.

own.label: Ask who grinds their teeth
own.player: Who in Sunfall grinds their teeth the worst?
own.reply: Can’t say names. But a certain foundation treasurer has cracked two crowns since the gala.
own.note: Megan O’Keefe says the foundation treasurer has cracked two crowns grinding his teeth since the gala.

own.label: Ask what a smile tells her
own.player: What does someone’s smile tell you?
own.reply: Everything. Whether they’re nervous, whether they’re lying, whether they had coffee. Yours looks honest, for what it’s worth.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Were your family dentists?
own.reply: Bar people. Dad ran a bar, sold it, and became a dental technician. I followed him. Mom reads the same romances I do. We swap them.

own.label: Ask about working for the mayor
own.player: What’s it like working for the mayor?
own.reply: He’s a dentist. He talks in the chair about the planning committee because I’m the hygienist and don’t count. I write it in my scrapbook between the poems.

calls.label: Ask about the charts she keeps
calls.player: What do your patients’ charts tell you lately?
calls.reply: The treasurer has cracked two crowns. The events director had a tooth replaced, knocked out, he says, by a car door. Car doors don’t usually swing that hard.
calls.note: Megan O’Keefe says Augustus Pell has cracked two crowns and Dorian Kell had a tooth knocked out after the gala.

calls.label: Ask what the mayor talks about
calls.player: What does the mayor talk about in the chair?
calls.reply: Canal side. Variance. The Sisters. In that order, every time. I don’t know what a variance is, but I know it’s about the Sisters’ land.
calls.note: Megan O’Keefe says the mayor keeps talking about a canal-side planning variance and the Sisters’ land.

life.news: Cleaned the teeth of a woman who smiled the whole time. You can’t fake that with your gums. She was in love.
life.more: You learn everything about a person from their teeth. Coffee, wine, grinding. Grinding means they’re hiding something. Hers were relaxed and she kept smiling at nothing. I asked. Engaged yesterday. I knew before she said it.
