life.more: Bellamy & Daughters. Every ring has a story and Granny knows all of them. This one belonged to a woman who married a sailor who came home. The buyer is marrying a fisherman. Granny said, that one knows the way back. I cried too.

life.news: The children made cards for a man at the care home who has no visitors. He’s put them all around his bed.
life.more: Twenty-two cards, mostly dinosaurs, one of a very confident horse. He told the nurse he has twenty-two grandchildren now. We’re going to visit next term and sing. He’s asked for something with a lot of brass.

life.news: Granny’s cuckoo clocks went off in the middle of a phone call with the bishop’s office. All eleven.
life.more: We live above the shop and the clocks are everywhere. The secretary asked if I was in a forest. I said yes. I’m not proud of it. Granny laughed for an hour. The bishop’s office still hasn’t rung back. Margaret will be furious.

gossip.says: Harper Lin at the paper is the daughter of the man who had my classroom before me. He left me a rule about never shouting before break. I’ve never broken it.
gossip.note: Teresa Bellamy says Harper Lin’s father taught in her classroom before her.
gossip.ask: Teresa says your father left her a rule about never shouting before break.
gossip.answer: That’s Dad. He had a rule for everything, and every one of them was about being kind. Teresa sends him the children’s drawings every term. He keeps them all. Pickle ate one. Don’t tell Teresa.

gossip.says: Heather Collins teaches at the other school and our playgrounds share a fence. Her children got to name the bear after its prints turned up by the fence. Mine are jealous.
gossip.note: Teresa Bellamy says Heather Collins’s class named the bear.
gossip.ask: Teresa says your class named the bear and hers are jealous.
gossip.answer: They named him Mr. Muffin. I tried to steer them toward something dignified. They voted. Mr. Muffin won by nineteen votes. Teresa’s lot wanted Gabriel, which is a lovely name for a bear, but they’d already used it on a hamster.

gossip.says: Jessica Rivera in the choir has a lovely voice and mouths the high notes because she’s scared. One day I’m putting her down for a solo, and she’ll forgive me eventually.
gossip.note: Teresa Bellamy says Jessica Rivera mouths the high notes in choir.
gossip.ask: Teresa says she’s putting you down for a solo one day.
gossip.answer: Oh no. Oh no no. She wouldn’t. She would, wouldn’t she? If I had to, it would be the one about the lighthouse. But I won’t have to. Please tell her I’ve got a cold. A long one.

own.label: Ask about her parish work
own.player: What do you do for the parish?
own.reply: I keep the accounts and the minutes. Nobody notices me unless something’s missing, which is how I like it.

own.label: Ask what she prays for
own.player: What do you pray for?
own.reply: Mostly for other people. Sometimes, when I’m brave, for a husband who’d be kind to a quiet woman.

own.label: Ask what scares her
own.player: What scares you?
own.reply: Being asked to be brave in public. I’ll do anything, so long as I don’t have to do it in front of people.

own.label: Ask what kindness costs her
own.player: What does kindness cost you?
own.reply: Sleep, mostly. And sometimes pride. You can’t help people and also need them to say thank you.

own.label: Ask about her grandmother’s sewing box
own.player: What’s in the sewing box?
own.reply: My grandmother sewed St. Brigid’s altar linens for fifty years. I mend them now with her needles. Some of the stitches are older than the town hall.

own.label: Ask how she came to the accounts
own.player: How did you start keeping the accounts?
own.reply: My father kept them before me. He died of a stroke at the desk, and I took the ledger out of his hands. Literally. I’ve kept it since.

own.label: Ask why she checks everything twice
own.player: Do you really check everything twice?
own.reply: Twice, and then once more when nobody is looking. Mistakes in a parish ledger aren’t mistakes. They’re somebody’s supper.

own.label: Ask what she found in the accounts
own.player: Did you find something in the parish accounts?
own.reply: A payment to a company called Halcyon Ridge Consultancy, signed by the bishop’s own chancellor, hidden under the garden line. It means the review was bought. I’ve shown nobody, because showing it means going before the king.
own.note: Evelyn Rosales found the bishop’s chancellor signed the parish’s payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy, so the review against the Sisters was bought.

own.label: Ask what the minutes say lately
own.player: Anything unusual in the minutes lately?
own.reply: Pantry stock. One more for supper, upstairs, until further notice. That’s all it says, and that’s all I’ll say.
own.note: Evelyn Rosales’s pantry minutes record one more for supper, upstairs, until further notice.

life.news: Mended a hole in the altar linen my grandmother sewed fifty years ago. You can’t see where it was.
life.more: She sewed St. Brigid’s linens for half a century, and I mend them now. Tiny stitches, under a lamp, the same thread she used. Nobody will ever notice. That’s the point. The best mending is the kind nobody notices.

life.news: The accounts balanced to the penny this month. I checked twice. Then a third time, for joy.
life.more: I keep the accounts and the minutes. Nobody notices me unless something’s missing, which is how I like it. Nothing’s missing. I sat in the parish office with a cup of tea and felt very quietly happy. Is that strange? It’s a good feeling.

life.news: Margaret asked me to read the minutes aloud at the meeting. I wanted the floor to swallow me.
life.more: I’ll do anything, so long as I don’t have to do it in front of people. My voice went very small. Teresa said I did beautifully. I don’t think I did. I read them so fast nobody could object to anything.

life.news: Had tea with Agnes in the garden. We didn’t talk much. It was perfect.
life.more: Agnes Castillo grows roses and prickly pear and doesn’t need you to fill a silence. We sat on the bench for an hour and watched a bee. That’s my favorite kind of friendship. The kind where the bee is the conversation.

gossip.says: Agnes Castillo is learning ballroom dancing and she’s dreadful. She says it’s good for her because she has to let someone else lead. She’s never let anyone lead in her life.
gossip.note: Evelyn Rosales says Agnes Castillo is learning ballroom dancing to practice letting someone lead.
gossip.ask: Evelyn says you’re learning to let someone else lead on the dance floor.
gossip.answer: I’m dreadful at it. It’s good for me. You have to let someone else lead, which I find very hard. Last time I trod on the instructor three times and apologized in Spanish. Evelyn came to watch once. She laughed so quietly only the bee heard.

gossip.says: I met Yumi Tanaka at a finance meeting. She checks every sum twice, like me. We recognized each other straight away. Same animal.
gossip.note: Evelyn Rosales says Yumi Tanaka, a charity accountant, checks every sum twice.
gossip.ask: Evelyn says you two recognized each other straight away. Same animal.
gossip.answer: We did. Two women in a room of men who round up. Charity accounts are where the most interesting lies in town are written down, very neatly. Evelyn reads them like scripture. I read them like a thriller. We find the same things.

gossip.says: Eliza Montoya runs our food pantry and never makes anyone feel small. Her family came through that door once. She says she owes us the rest of her life. She doesn’t. We’d say it the other way around.
gossip.note: Evelyn Rosales says Eliza Montoya runs the food pantry and never makes anyone feel small.
gossip.ask: Evelyn says the Sisters feel they owe you, not the other way around.
gossip.answer: That’s not true. When we had nothing they fed us and never once made us feel small. I’ll be paying that back gladly for the rest of my life. Evelyn’s kind. Tell her the beans came in early this week. She’ll want to know for the books.

own.label: Ask what she’s investigating
own.player: What are you investigating at the moment?
own.reply: Three stories, two of which might be the same story. That’s the best feeling in this job.

own.label: Ask why she became a reporter
own.player: Why become a reporter?
own.reply: Because my school covered up a teacher who hurt kids, and the local paper didn’t. I thought: never again, not on my watch.

own.label: Ask what her sources say
own.player: What are your sources saying about the gala?
own.reply: That the money went missing before Elena did. Follow the money and you find the person. That’s always the order.
own.note: Hannah Webb’s sources say the money went missing before Elena Cross did.

own.label: Ask if the truth still matters
own.player: Does the truth still matter to people?
own.reply: It matters to about nine readers and my grandmother. I write for them. Everyone else wants a team to cheer for.

own.label: Ask what her apartment looks like
own.player: What does an investigative reporter’s apartment look like?
own.reply: A studio apartment with a wall of string. I eat at my desk. Once a week I sleep at my grandmother’s, and she reads every word I’ve written aloud and marks it in red.

own.label: Ask who raised her
own.player: Who brought you up?
own.reply: My grandmother, on the railway side. Dad was a guard on the last passenger train. Mom went to the coast. Gran was a reader, so I became a writer out of self-defence.

own.label: Ask if anyone tried to reach Elena
own.player: Did anyone try to get a message to Elena?
own.reply: Our front desk took one for her the night of the benefit. A frightened woman, initials only. I made a copy before the slip went upstairs. You can have it if you protect her.

calls.label: Ask what her third story is
calls.player: What’s the third story you won’t name?
calls.reply: The husbands. Eleven names, matched to blue ribbons at the Cemetery Chapel. I haven’t written a word, because eleven dead men with nothing provable is a libel. The first name is Ellis Dane. He sponsored the youth orchestra I played in at twelve, and the next year his name was gone from the program.
calls.note: Hannah Webb has eleven names of men who married Bluebirds and died; the first is Ellis Dane.

life.news: My gran read my story out loud to me tonight and only marked two things. Two! A personal best.
life.more: I sleep at hers on the railway side once a week. She reads every word I write aloud with a red pen in her hand. She’s eighty-one. She once made me rewrite a headline because it was rude to the reader. She’s always right. It’s horrible.

life.news: Three stories on my wall and I swear two of them are the same story. Best feeling in this job.
life.more: A wall of string in a studio apartment. My landlord thinks I’m unwell. I’m not, I’m close. Follow the money and you find the person. That’s always the order. Sorry, I can’t say more. Not yet.

life.news: Someone from my old school rang. The school with the teacher nobody would print.
life.more: They’d seen my name in the paper and wanted to say they believed me back then. Fifteen years late. I sat on the stairs for an hour after. It’s strange what helps. I write for nine readers and my gran. Turns out it was ten.

life.news: Drinks with Kira tonight. She told me a story about a judge and a parrot. Can’t print it. Will never forget it.
life.more: Kira writes down every word in that courtroom and remembers the pauses. The parrot said one word during a hearing and the judge adjourned for twenty minutes. She won’t tell me the word. Friendship is torture.

gossip.says: Kira Henson draws maps of the canyon by hand, paths nobody else knows. She showed me one and said if I ever showed anyone she’d stop speaking to me. I believe her.
gossip.note: Hannah Webb says Kira Henson draws secret maps of the canyon by hand.
gossip.ask: Hannah says you draw secret maps of the canyon, and only share them with people you trust.
gossip.answer: Hannah talks a lot for a woman sworn to secrecy. Old mining paths, dry riverbeds, and one place I’ve never shown anyone. I share them with people I trust. You’re not there yet. You might be. Ask me again in a while.

gossip.says: Helen Markham, the police sergeant, drinks with us sometimes and has never once told me anything I could print. She sits with her back to the wall. Every time, every room.
gossip.note: Hannah Webb says Sergeant Helen Markham never tells reporters anything and always sits with her back to the wall.
gossip.ask: Hannah says you always sit with your back to the wall.
gossip.answer: Hannah notices good things and prints none of them, which is why I drink with her. Back to the wall, eyes on the door. Twenty years of habit. It’s not paranoia if the door keeps opening. And she’s right. I’ve never told her anything. Not today either.

gossip.says: Keiko Nakamura at the police sees patterns nobody else does. She told me once that crime in Sunfall goes up when the casino pays out and down on church days. She meant it as small talk.
gossip.note: Hannah Webb says Keiko Nakamura, the police analyst, can see patterns in Sunfall’s crime.
gossip.ask: Hannah says you can tell when crime is about to go up in Sunfall.
gossip.answer: It isn’t magic. Most crime is boring, and boring things repeat. The casino pays out, the numbers go up. People go to church, they go down. The strange ones stand out because the rest is so dull. Hannah treats it like a horoscope. I wish she wouldn’t.

own.label: Ask what an editor does
own.player: What does an editor actually do?
own.reply: Decide what Sunfall knows tomorrow. It’s a lot of power for someone who can’t decide what to have for lunch.

own.label: Ask about the state of the news
own.player: Is the news business dying?
own.reply: It’s being eaten by people who give their opinions away for free. Opinions are cheap. Facts cost shoe leather, and nobody wants to pay for shoes.

own.label: Ask why she spiked a story
own.player: Did you spike a story about the gala?
own.reply: I spiked a photo. A board member called me at home that night. I told myself it was legal advice. I don’t sleep well.
own.note: Fiona Blake admits she spiked a gala photo after a board member called her at home.

own.label: Ask what she’d never put on the front page
own.player: What would you never put on the front page?
own.reply: A child’s face, a grieving widow, and anything I can’t prove twice. I lose a lot of stories that way. I sleep fine.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Do you ever leave the newsroom?
own.reply: I live directly above it. Literally. A bed I fall into and a phone that rings. Editing is a punishment I chose, because I’d rather chase a mystery than sit still, and now I sit still and send other people.

own.label: Ask about her family and the paper
own.player: Has your family always run the Daily?
own.reply: Grandad owned it. He sold it to a chain, which sold it to a man who owes money to the wrong people. I’m the last Blake in the building and the only reason it’s still a paper.

calls.label: Ask who really owns the paper
calls.player: Who actually owns the Daily?
calls.reply: A man in the city who owes the Halcyon Ridge Trust. If I print the wrong front page, the Trust calls the debt, the Daily closes, and Sunfall has no paper at all. Every day for a month I’ve decided a compromised paper beats none. I’m not sure.
calls.note: Fiona Blake says the Daily’s owner is in debt to the Halcyon Ridge Trust.

calls.label: Ask about the photograph in her desk
calls.player: Do you still have the photo you spiked?
calls.reply: In my desk. Table 9, the treasurer’s table, with a face that isn’t on any guest list. If I give it to you I’ve given it to nobody. Understood? Good. Don’t frame it.

life.news: Forty letters about the bear this week. Not one about the council budget.
life.more: Readers love the bear more than anything we spend weeks on. I keep the bear stories in because they love them and I love them. Somewhere under the bear there’s a budget nobody reads. That’s the job. Feed them the bear, slip in the budget.

life.news: My dad rang. He’s sold another shelf of his books. He only sells them when he’s drinking.
life.more: He has the best library in Sunfall and he’s drinking it one shelf at a time. I bought two back from the shop on the canal before he noticed. I’ll give them back when he’s sober. I’ve got quite a few now.

life.news: We beat the Ledger to a story by four hours. Four hours! I’m buying the newsroom donuts.
life.more: A water main, a sinkhole and a councillor’s car very nearly in it. Hannah got there first, Natalie got the picture, and the Ledger got the story off our website. Small victories keep a paper alive. That and donuts.

life.news: Didn’t sleep. The phone rang late again.
life.more: When you edit a paper, the phone at night is never good news. Someone always wants something not printed. I’m good at saying no. I’m worse at sleeping after. Ask me something nice. Ask me about the donuts.

gossip.says: Harper Lin edits our weekend paper, and her dog Pickle has worked at the Daily longer than most of us. Thirteen, deaf, asleep under her desk. We put Pickle on the staff list.
gossip.note: Fiona Blake says Harper Lin’s dog Pickle is on the Daily’s staff list.
gossip.ask: Fiona says your dog Pickle is officially on the staff list.
gossip.answer: Longest-serving member of staff, and the only one who’s never filed late. She’s thirteen and deaf as a post and she sleeps through every crisis. Fiona added her to the list as a joke, and then personnel sent Pickle a pension form. True story.

gossip.says: Moira Bell checks our facts. She rings people and asks if they really said what they said, and most of them didn’t. She remembers everything anyone’s ever told her. It’s a gift, mostly.
gossip.note: Fiona Blake says Moira Bell the fact-checker remembers everything anyone tells her.
gossip.ask: Fiona says you remember everything anyone has ever told you.
gossip.answer: Everything. What you said first, what you changed later, what you meant. It’s a gift, mostly. Fiona says it’s why I’m good at my job and bad at arguments. I win them. I just can’t stop winning them.

gossip.says: Hannah Webb has a wall of string in her studio apartment and her landlord thinks she’s unwell. She’s not. She’s the best reporter I’ve got.
gossip.note: Fiona Blake says Hannah Webb is the best reporter at the Daily.
gossip.ask: Fiona says you’re the best reporter she’s got.
gossip.answer: She said that to you and not to me? Typical. I’ll take it. She also once spiked a story of mine for being too true, so it’s a complicated compliment. I write for nine readers and my gran. Ten now, if you count you.

own.label: Ask about freelancing
own.player: What’s freelancing like?
own.reply: Feast or famine. Mostly famine. I once sold a photo of the bear for more than a month of real journalism.

own.label: Ask what she’s writing
own.player: Are you writing anything?
own.reply: A novel about Sunfall that I’ll never finish. Everyone in town is in it. You might be in it now. Behave.

own.label: Ask about her motel photos
own.player: You photograph the motel strip?
own.reply: For a project. In one shot from the gala night, there’s a woman in a blue dress in Room 12’s window. Elena wore blue.
own.note: Linh Tran has a photo from gala night of a woman in a blue dress in a motel window. Elena wore blue.

own.label: Ask if freelancing is freedom
own.player: Is freelancing really freedom?
own.reply: It’s freedom to not get paid on time. But nobody tells me what to think, and that’s worth being broke.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the laundromat on Sunfall Road. Thin walls, a radiator that sings at night, and a neighbor who sells houses and another who plays pool. If you live there too, hello, neighbor. Turn your music down.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: We had a restaurant until the casino’s rents ate it. Dad cooks at the casino now, for the people who priced him out. Mom does nails. They’re funnier about it than I am.

calls.label: Ask what she saw at the motel later
calls.player: Did you go back to the motel?
calls.reply: At night, more than once. Room twelve was empty. Room nine is never rented, but there’s a light in it sometimes, and once a man in a cloak, reading at the window. I put him in my novel. He frightened my novel.
calls.note: Linh Tran saw a man in a cloak reading in the window of motel room nine, which is never rented.

calls.label: Ask what’s spooking her about her novel
calls.player: Why does your novel scare you?
calls.reply: Three chapters ago I wrote a scene in a weigh station, a woman going out through a window. I thought I made it up. Then the paper started printing my chapters back at me.

life.news: Got paid! On time! I don’t know what to do with myself.
life.more: A magazine in the city paid a freelance invoice inside thirty days. I printed the email. It’s on my wall. Feast or famine, mostly famine, and today was a feast. I bought proper coffee and cookies that weren’t from the reduced shelf.

life.news: I wrote a scene in my novel last week. Then it happened, almost exactly, outside the laundromat.
life.more: Two old men arguing about a dog that belonged to neither of them. Word for word, nearly. I’ve started to wonder if I’m writing the town or the town’s writing me. Either way, you’re in it. Behave.

life.news: My dad’s restaurant would have been twenty years old this week. The casino rents killed it.
life.more: He cooks at the casino now, in the kitchen of the people who priced him out. He says a kitchen’s a kitchen. My mom does nails and says nothing. I bought his old sign off a scrap dealer and it’s behind my bed. Don’t tell him.

life.news: Zadie and I had our biggest argument yet about a band. I won. Then we made up over tacos.
life.more: She gave a band two stars and I said they were a four. We shouted outside Hector’s van until he gave us free tacos to shut up. Best argument of my life. They’re still a four.

gossip.says: Olivia Reid lives down the landing from me above the laundromat, and she sells houses she could never afford. She describes every apartment as a film genre. Funniest woman in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Linh Tran says Olivia Reid, a real estate agent, lives on her landing above the laundromat.
gossip.ask: Linh says you describe every apartment as a film genre.
gossip.answer: Because they are. For buyers, a horror film. For sellers, a heist film. For anyone under thirty, a tragedy. Linh’s room is found footage. Nobody’s sure what’s happening in there and there’s a lot of shaking.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster hasn’t washed a plate in two years. She plays pool with her neighbors for the dishes and she never loses.
gossip.note: Linh Tran says Zadie Foster wins her dishes at pool.
gossip.ask: Linh says you haven’t washed a plate in two years because you never lose at pool.
gossip.answer: Two years and three months. I play the neighbors for the dishes and I practice in secret, which Linh calls cheating and I call preparation. She owes me a plate, by the way. She lost at the bar last week and ran.

gossip.says: Maria Vega came into the Daily and stared at one of my photos on the wall for ages. Didn’t say why. Police are like that.
gossip.note: Linh Tran says Maria Vega stared at one of her photos at the Daily.
gossip.ask: Linh says you stared at one of her photos for ages and wouldn’t say why.
gossip.answer: It’s a good photo. Is that not enough? I look at a lot of things for a long time. It’s the job, and it’s a habit I can’t switch off. Tell her she has a good eye. Don’t tell her which picture.

own.label: Ask about DJing
own.player: What’s it like DJing the goth night?
own.reply: Like conducting a funeral where everyone’s dancing. I live for it.

own.label: Ask what’s wrong with music now
own.player: What’s wrong with music now?
own.reply: Everything sounds like it was designed to be skipped. The old songs were built to be lived in.

own.label: Ask about the special set
own.player: Has anyone asked you for a special set?
own.reply: Victoria wants me to play a twenty-minute drone at the Midnight Show, starting exactly when the moon disappears. She paid in advance. Nobody pays in advance.
own.note: Victoria paid Alice Wren in advance for a long drone set timed to the moonless night.

own.label: Ask about the best silence she’s heard
own.player: What’s the best silence you’ve ever heard?
own.reply: The second after the last record ends at a good night. Two hundred people standing still. Then the lights come up and it’s gone.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The railway side. Dad worked the signal box. I can hear a train before you can see it, which is very useful for a DJ and nothing else.

own.label: Ask about her loop pedal
own.player: What’s the loop pedal for?
own.reply: A job. I bought it for cash at the music shop and tested it once. I haven’t switched it on since. Some gear you buy and then avoid looking at.

calls.label: Ask when the drone starts
calls.player: When exactly is this drone meant to start?
calls.reply: The second the moon goes. {night}. Twenty minutes, then the best silence there is. She paid in advance. Nobody pays in advance.

calls.label: Ask what’s on the tape she was given
calls.player: What’s actually on the mix she gave you?
calls.reply: Under the drone, on her cassette, there’s a round for nine voices and a bell. I know that bell’s note. It’s the one on Odette Price’s old radio reel from the Old Mission fair. I think I’ve been hired to play the founders’ music back into the Old Mission.
calls.note: Alice Wren says the rite’s music hides a round for nine voices and the Old Mission’s bell, the same as on Odette Price’s old radio reel.

life.news: Played four hours at the Cellar Door last night and nobody left before the end. Nobody. My ears are still ringing and I love it.
life.more: There’s a second after the last record when the whole room holds its breath. Best silence in the world. I chase that second like other people chase money. Then I mop. Glamour.

life.news: Somebody nicked two crates of records out of the van. My dad’s records.
life.more: Signal box records, he called them. Things he played on night shifts by the line. Nobody else would want them, which is what makes it so stupid. I’ve put notes up in every record shop in the Quarter. If you see a crate of brass bands and railway hymns, it’s mine.

life.news: Got the records back! Some kid sold them to a shop on the canal for five bucks and the owner called me.
life.more: He wouldn’t take the fiver back off me. Said a girl who knows what a signal box sounds like deserves her dad’s records. I cried in a shop full of men in leather jackets. They all pretended to look at the jazz.

life.news: My mom sent a postcard. From a boat. First one in eleven years.
life.more: A picture of a harbor and four words: hope you’re still loud. That’s it. I don’t know whether to frame it or set it on fire. Probably both. Frame it, then set the frame on fire. That’s very me, isn’t it?

gossip.says: Sable Marlow runs the Cellar Door and plays in goal for the Old Quarter five-on-five. She saved a penalty off Adriana Ponce last month and still talks about it like she won a war.
gossip.note: Alice Wren says Sable Marlow plays in goal for the Old Quarter five-on-five.
gossip.ask: Alice says you saved one penalty and never stopped talking about it.
gossip.answer: Alice exaggerates everything. It’s her best and worst quality. It was Adriana Ponce, bottom corner, and yes, I’ll be talking about it at my funeral. Goalkeeper. I like standing in the way of things. Ask anyone I’ve dated.

gossip.says: Inez Morales prints all my posters for nothing. Well, for drinks. I owe her about forty drinks. She keeps the tally on the back of her hand.
gossip.note: Alice Wren says Inez Morales prints her posters in exchange for drinks.
gossip.ask: Alice says she owes you about forty drinks for posters.
gossip.answer: Forty-three. I keep count because Alice keeps forgetting. Printing posters for the Old Quarter is the only organizing I do that ends on a dance floor. Tell her I’m collecting on the next payday.

gossip.says: Piper Nocturne keeps one thing from every ex in a box. A lighter, a ticket stub, a terrible poem. If you date her, think hard about what you want to end up as.
gossip.note: Alice Wren says Piper Nocturne keeps one thing from every ex.
gossip.ask: Alice says you keep a souvenir from every ex. What would mine be?
gossip.answer: Alice should mind her own museum. Fine. Yes. One thing each. A lighter, a ticket stub, a terrible poem. Yours? Depends how you end it. So far you’re a screenshot.

own.label: Ask about the shop
own.player: What do you sell at the shop?
own.reply: Velvet, silver and despair, at reasonable prices.

own.label: Ask if she breaks hearts
own.player: Are you a heartbreaker?
own.reply: I leave before it gets serious. It’s kinder. Probably. I’ve never stayed long enough to find out.

own.label: Ask who buys the crescent pendants
own.player: Who buys the crescent pendants?
own.reply: We sold thirty in a week to people who don’t look like goths. Accountants. A man in a charity lanyard. That’s not fashion. That’s a uniform.
own.note: Piper Nocturne’s shop sold thirty crescent pendants in a week, including to a man in a charity lanyard.

own.label: Ask what she keeps from her exes
own.player: Do you keep anything from your exes?
own.reply: One thing each. A lighter, a ticket stub, a terrible poem. It’s a small museum of men who were wrong about me.

own.label: Ask how she came to the shop
own.player: How did you end up working at the shop?
own.reply: My aunt owns it. She took me in when Mom died, when I was fourteen, and let me rename myself. I was born Piper Dunne in the trailer park behind the drive-in. Don’t tell the Old Quarter.

own.label: Ask what’s in the drawer she never opens
own.player: What’s in the drawer you don’t open?
own.reply: A crescent pendant somebody gave me three years ago, before there were thirty of them. It was a present then. Now it’s a uniform.

calls.label: Ask who’s in the shop’s book
calls.player: Who did you sell the pendants to?
calls.reply: My aunt makes me write every sale in the book. There’s a Beaumont in it. A Shawcross. Two Pells. Since when do Pells wear silver moons?
calls.note: Piper Nocturne’s shop book shows crescent pendants sold to a Beaumont, a Shawcross and two Pells.

calls.label: Ask how well she knows Victoria
calls.player: How well do you know Victoria?
calls.reply: Better than the scene thinks. We weren’t friends. We were more than that, once. She still knows exactly how to ask me for things.
calls.note: Piper Nocturne and Victoria Blackwood were lovers, not just friends.

life.news: Sold a velvet coat to a woman who cried in the changing room because it fitted. Best sale of my life.
life.more: She said nobody had made her look like that since her wedding. I gave her ten percent off and a tissue. Velvet, silver and despair, at reasonable prices. Sometimes the despair goes home happy.

life.news: My aunt’s talking about selling the shop to a man who wants to turn it into a candle place.
life.more: Scented candles with names like Inner Healing. She’s tired, she says, and he’s offering cash. I said I’d buy her out. With what, she said. With charm, I said. She laughed for a full minute. I’m working on a plan. The plan is mostly charm.

life.news: My cousin rang the shop again. He never rings unless something’s wrong.
life.more: He’s working up on the ridge with men I don’t like and he sounds like someone who wants to be told to come home. I told him to come home. He laughed. That’s my whole family. We laugh when we mean help.

life.news: Somebody left a drawing under the shop door. Of me. It’s actually good.
life.more: No name. Charcoal, me at the counter looking bored, which is accurate. I’ve put it in the window. If it was you, say so. If it wasn’t, say it was. I’ll never check.

gossip.says: Elise Harrow from the Bluebirds grew up three doors from me behind the drive-in. Now she does their books in pearls. Good for her. Don’t tell them where she’s from.
gossip.note: Piper Nocturne says Elise Harrow, a Bluebird bookkeeper, grew up in the trailer park behind the drive-in.
gossip.ask: Piper says you two grew up three doors apart behind the drive-in.
gossip.answer: Piper said that? She would. Yes. Three doors, two dogs and one washing line between all of us. I’d rather the Bluebirds didn’t hear it from you. They like their girls to come from somewhere with a gravel drive.

gossip.says: Zara Brooks raised her little cousin practically on her own, at the counter of the Lucky Cactus. Arielle. She’d kill for her. Actually kill, I think.
gossip.note: Piper Nocturne says Zara Brooks raised her cousin Arielle at the Lucky Cactus.
gossip.ask: Piper says you basically raised your cousin Arielle.
gossip.answer: I walked her to school every day for six years. Somebody had to. Dolores ran the diner and Arielle ran me. She’s at the archive now, reading things nobody’s touched in fifty years. Piper says kill. I’d say mind.

gossip.says: Lenore Vale won’t speak to another silversmith on the bench. Something about a commission Lenore turned down and the other girl took. Silver people hold grudges like nobody else.
gossip.note: Piper Nocturne says Lenore Vale fell out with another silversmith over a commission.
gossip.ask: Piper says you fell out with someone over a commission.
gossip.answer: Piper hears everything through the shop door. Someone wanted something cast that I didn’t want to cast. I said no. Ophelia said yes. That’s all I’ll say, except that I sleep fine, and I hope she does.

own.label: Ask about tattooing
own.player: What’s the strangest tattoo you’ve done?
own.reply: A man’s ex-wife’s name, changed into a cactus. He cried. I didn’t charge him extra for the cactus.

own.label: Ask how people treat her
own.player: Do people judge you for how you look?
own.reply: Every day. The same people who say be yourself cross the road when I am.

own.label: Ask about the crescent tattoos
own.player: Has anyone asked for a crescent tattoo?
own.reply: Three people this month, same design, same spot inside the wrist. They wouldn’t say why. I turned the last one away.
own.note: Zara Brooks was asked for the same crescent tattoo, inside the wrist, three times this month.

own.label: Ask which tattoo she regrets
own.player: Do you regret any of your tattoos?
own.reply: One. A name. Not his, mine. I got my own name on my wrist at eighteen so I’d never forget it. I’ve never needed reminding.

own.label: Ask about the name on her wrist
own.player: Whose name is on your wrist?
own.reply: Mine. So I never forget it. People laugh. I’ve watched a lot of people forget who they were in this town.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Have you got family in Sunfall?
own.reply: My cousin Arielle. Dolores raised us both at the Lucky Cactus counter. I walked Arielle to school every day. I still would.

calls.label: Ask who got the crescent tattoo
calls.player: Who got the crescent inside the wrist?
calls.reply: Two girls, Hex and Ivy. The third was Sorrel. I turned her away, because a mark you can’t explain is a mark somebody else owns. I drew the flyer’s crescent, too. I’ve started to understand what it invites people to.
calls.note: Zara Brooks tattooed the crescent on Hex Morrow and Ivy Sable and turned Sorrel Vane away.

life.news: Finished a back piece today. Seven sittings. She cried when she saw it in the mirror and so did I, a bit.
life.more: A tree full of her grandmother’s birds. Every bird a different one her gran used to feed. She brought photos of the feeder. That’s the job. People bring you the thing they’re scared of forgetting, and you put it somewhere it can’t leave.

life.news: A man crossed the road when he saw me this morning. Then he came in an hour later for a quote.
life.more: Wanted his daughter’s name. I did it. Made it beautiful. He didn’t look me in the eye once. The same people who say be yourself cross the road when I am. I still charge them the normal price. That’s my revenge. Being good at it.

life.news: Arielle came around with pastries and stayed three hours. Best day this month.
life.more: My little cousin. She reads old letters at the archive for a living and tells me about them like they’re gossip. A woman a hundred years ago wrote nine pages to her sister about a hat. We laughed until Rowan banged on the floor.

life.news: Somebody left a pencil drawing of my cactus tattoo on the studio step. Nobody knows that one but the man who has it.
life.more: The cactus I did over the man’s ex-wife’s name. He cried. Now someone’s drawn it, carefully, and left it on our step. Either he’s thanking me or he’s got a friend who wants one. Either way, I kept it.

gossip.says: Rowan Pike taught me everything with a needle. She raised her sister Madison on her own too. We’re a club, me and Rowan. The girls who did it early.
gossip.note: Zara Brooks says Rowan Pike raised her sister Madison on her own.
gossip.ask: Zara says you raised your sister Madison on your own.
gossip.answer: Zara talks about me like I’m a saint. I was nineteen, Madison was ten, and somebody had to buy school shoes. That’s not saintly. That’s arithmetic. She waits tables now and thinks I’m terrifying. She’s right.

gossip.says: My cousin Arielle Brooks works at the archive. She can tell you who owned your house a hundred years ago and what they argued about. Don’t ask unless you want to know.
gossip.note: Zara Brooks says her cousin Arielle Brooks at the archive knows the history of every house.
gossip.ask: Zara says you can tell me who owned my house a hundred years ago.
gossip.answer: Zara is my biggest fan and my worst publicist. I can try. Give me the street and a week. Last time someone asked, it turned out their kitchen used to be a stable, and the horse is buried under the patio. They didn’t thank me.

gossip.says: Hana Park drew half my flash sheet when I was too tired to hold a pencil. Her lettering’s better than mine. I’ll deny it if you tell her.
gossip.note: Zara Brooks says Hana Park drew some of her tattoo designs.
gossip.ask: Zara says your lettering is better than hers.
gossip.answer: She said that? I need it in writing. I did some flash for her when she was dead on her feet, and she paid me in a tiny tattoo nobody’s allowed to see. It’s a very small comma. I’m a designer. I think in punctuation.

women.name: Maya Serrano
women.look: Olive skin, dark curls in a high ponytail, teal scrubs and a white zip hoodie

own.label: Ask about her shifts
own.player: What happened on your last shift?
own.reply: Cactus spines, a man who swallowed a key, and a grandmother who flirted with every doctor. Standard.

own.label: Ask about the café idea
own.player: You want to open a café?
own.reply: With my sister. She bakes, I’d do the coffee and the shouting. Somewhere with no laptops after dark, just people talking.

own.label: Ask about the patient she recognized
own.player: Did you recognize a patient?
own.reply: A man came in with burns on his hands, and I knew his face from the newspaper. He gave a different name. I told no one. I’m telling you.
own.note: Maya Serrano treated a man with burnt hands whose face she knew from the newspaper; he gave a false name.

own.label: Ask what she does after a hard shift
own.player: What do you do after a really hard shift?
own.reply: Sit in my car in the hospital parking lot and eat a whole packet of cookies. Then I drive home and tell nobody.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are your family nurses?
own.reply: Mom nursed at the hospital for thirty years and Dad drove the ambulance. I grew up in the back of it. My first word was probably clear.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have a sister?
own.reply: Rosa, no relation to the student, I always have to say. She bakes. One day we’re opening a café, no laptops after dark, just people talking. I’ll do coffee and shouting.

calls.label: Ask who the burned man was
calls.player: Who was the man with the burned hands?
calls.reply: Caleb Marsh. I knew his face from the paper. He gave another name. His sister came and collected him. The chart says garden-center accelerant, because the doctor wrote what he smelled.
calls.note: Maya Serrano treated Caleb Marsh’s burned hands under a false name; his sister collected him.

calls.label: Ask about men from the ridge
calls.player: Do men from the ridge come in?
calls.reply: With quarry injuries that aren’t quarry injuries. The first one I saw was a dog bite. The dog was the lodge’s. The night ward keeps a list now.
calls.note: Maya Serrano says injured men from the ridge come into the ER with wounds that aren’t from the quarry.

life.news: Today: cactus spines, a man who swallowed a key, and a grandmother who flirted with every doctor. Standard shift.
life.more: The grandmother asked the consultant if he was married, and when he said yes she asked if he was happily married. The whole department stopped. He said, I am now worried. She winked at me on the way out. Hero.

life.news: Hard shift. Sat in my car in the parking lot and ate a whole packet of cookies. Didn’t share.
life.more: Some days you hold it together for twelve hours and then the car door shuts and it all comes out. Cookies help. The radio helps. Emily parks next to me and eats her own cookies and we don’t talk. That helps the most.

life.news: My sister and I found the perfect spot for our café. No laptops after dark. Just people talking.
life.more: Rosa bakes, I do the coffee and the shouting. A little corner on Brown Avenue with a window that gets the evening light. We can’t afford it yet. We stood outside it for an hour imagining the chairs. That’s a start.

life.news: A little boy I treated last month came back with his mom to say thank you. He brought me a drawing of a plaster.
life.more: He’d fallen out of a tree. Nothing broken, lots of crying, mostly his mom’s. He drew a giant plaster with a smiley face and wrote MAYA on it in capitals. It’s on the staff room fridge. Nobody’s allowed to touch it.

gossip.says: Emily Fairchild works emergency with me and jumps out of planes on her days off. She says after a night in the ER, skydiving feels relaxing. She’s not joking. That’s the scary part.
gossip.note: Maya Serrano says Emily Fairchild goes skydiving to relax after the ER shifts.
gossip.ask: Maya says you jump out of planes to relax after the ER.
gossip.answer: It IS relaxing! Nobody needs anything from you at twelve thousand feet. My dad drove trains and said fear is a signal, not an instruction. Maya won’t come with me. She says she gets enough adrenaline from the cookie cupboard running out.

gossip.says: Leila Sayeed did the nursing course with me. She went to the police station and I went to the hospital. She says she patches up both ends of the handcuffs. I just get the ends that come in screaming.
gossip.note: Maya Serrano says she trained with custody nurse Leila Sayeed.
gossip.ask: Maya says you patch up both ends of the handcuffs.
gossip.answer: Everyone’s polite to the nurse. Even the ones who bite. Maya gets the screaming, I get the quiet ones staring at the wall, and the quiet ones are worse. We swap stories over cookies in her car. She always has cookies. She never shares them with Emily.

women.name: Jocelyn Reed
women.look: Dark skin, cropped natural curls, royal-blue blazer and a tiny blue ribbon

own.label: Ask about her job
own.player: What does a compliance officer do?
own.reply: I ask grown adults for receipts and they look at me as if I’ve asked for a kidney. It’s thankless, and I’m very good at it.

own.label: Ask about her hobby
own.player: What do you do to relax?
own.reply: I restore old furniture. Strip the paint, find the honest wood underneath. It’s the opposite of my job: the furniture wants to be found out.

own.label: Ask what keeps her up at night
own.player: What keeps you up at night?
own.reply: I have a second copy of a donation ledger. If I publish it, my career is over. If I don’t, I’m complicit. So mostly I lie awake and sand chairs.
own.note: Jocelyn Reed has a second copy of a donation ledger she is afraid to publish.

own.label: Ask about the worst couple she ever set up
own.player: What’s the worst couple you ever set up?
own.reply: A vegan and a butcher. They’re married now with three children. I don’t understand anything any more.

own.label: Ask how she got into finance
own.player: How did you end up in compliance?
own.reply: I worked nights on a hotel desk through a finance degree. You learn everything about people at three in the morning. Mostly that they think the receipt won’t matter.

own.label: Ask where she’s from
own.player: Where are you from originally?
own.reply: A town on the coast. Mom was the church secretary. Dad was the kind of man who made the church secretary cry. I left at seventeen and didn’t look back, except constantly.

own.label: Ask about her favorite restoration
own.player: What’s the best thing you’ve ever restored?
own.reply: An ottoman. Seven coats of paint and underneath, walnut. Hollow inside, too. Useful.

calls.label: Ask about the copy she can’t sleep over
calls.player: What’s the copy you lie awake about?
calls.reply: The donation ledger from the year before the benefit, with the trust’s payments still in it, before somebody rewrote the official one. If I publish it I’m finished. If I don’t, I’m them. It’s in the ottoman. I’ll give you one page and then I never met you.

calls.label: Ask what else she found
calls.player: Have you found anything else?
calls.reply: The catering invoices, the firm that never caters, are in the events director’s own handwriting. Dorian Kell writes his sevens the European way. So do the invoices.
calls.note: Jocelyn Reed says the Late Service Catering invoices are in Dorian Kell’s handwriting.

life.news: Stripped an old chest of drawers down to the wood. Three coats of paint, then oak. Honest oak.
life.more: Furniture wants to be found out. You strip it and the honest wood is underneath. Somebody painted this one avocado green, then cream, then a sad gray. Under it all, oak, with a child’s initials carved in the side. I’ve left the initials.

life.news: Asked a grown man for a receipt for a lunch. He looked at me as if I’d asked for a kidney.
life.more: He said it was a business lunch. I said then it’ll have a business receipt. He found it in his coat. It said two lobsters. For one man.

life.news: Set two friends up on a blind date. They’ve been out three times. I’m unbearable about it.
life.more: I once set up a vegan with a butcher. It lasted two years and they’re still friends, which I count as a triumph. These two are a librarian and a fireman. I have a very good feeling. I’ve already decided what I’m wearing to the wedding.

life.news: Didn’t sleep. Sanded a chair in the middle of the night instead.
life.more: Some nights there’s something on my mind I can’t put down. I go to the garage and sand until my arms hurt. The neighbors think I’m building an ark. Tonight it was a dining chair. It’s very smooth now. My mind isn’t.

gossip.says: Bianca Roth works under me and remembers everyone’s birthday. Lately she’s been jumpy. She hasn’t said why. I’ve stopped asking and started bringing her coffee.
gossip.note: Jocelyn Reed says Bianca Roth has been jumpy lately.
gossip.ask: Jocelyn says you’ve been jumpy lately.
gossip.answer: Jumpy is a strong word. Attentive. Everyone brings me their form and their birthday, and I remember both. Jocelyn brings me coffee now, which is kind and means she’s worried. Tell her I’m fine. Tell her I like the coffee.

gossip.says: Francesca Quinn collects the strangest cookbooks in Sunfall, including a whole book about aspic. She made me a jelly with an egg in it. I ate it. We don’t talk about it.
gossip.note: Jocelyn Reed says Francesca Quinn collects strange cookbooks.
gossip.ask: Jocelyn says you made her a jelly with a whole egg in it.
gossip.answer: It was a classic of its era. Every era thinks it has taste. Every era is wrong. Jocelyn ate the whole thing with a straight face, which is why I trust her. Anyone who can eat aspic politely can keep a secret.

gossip.says: Hannah Webb, the reporter, calls me sometimes and I tell her nothing interesting. She thanks me every time as if I had. She’s very good.
gossip.note: Jocelyn Reed says the reporter Hannah Webb calls her sometimes.
gossip.ask: Jocelyn says you call her and she tells you nothing interesting.
gossip.answer: Nothing interesting is very interesting, coming from compliance. She says nothing in a very particular order. Follow the money and you find the person. Tell her I’ll keep ringing. And tell her the chair she sold at the flea market is in my gran’s kitchen.

women.name: Priya Nair
women.look: Brown skin, dark side braid, tortoiseshell glasses, sage cardigan and long skirt

own.label: Ask about the parish reading room
own.player: Tell me about the parish reading room.
own.reply: Three shelves, two armchairs and a radiator that sings. The council wants to close it. The old men who read the papers there have nowhere else to go.

own.label: Ask about the hymn books
own.player: You restore hymn books?
own.reply: Handwritten ones, from when the chapel had a choir of forty. The ink fades, but the faith in those margins is still loud.

own.label: Ask about the strange book
own.player: Have you found anything strange in the collection?
own.reply: An old missal with a crescent drawn inside the cover and a line of Latin that isn’t from any prayer I know. Someone borrowed it last month and brought it back changed.
own.note: Priya Nair found a crescent and unknown Latin drawn inside a missal someone borrowed and returned.

own.label: Ask what book she’d save from a fire
own.player: Which book would you save from a fire?
own.reply: My grandmother’s missal. It’s falling apart and full of her notes in the margins. Her handwriting is the closest thing I have to her voice.

own.label: Ask about living above the reading room
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Above the reading room. I think of it as the top of a lighthouse. The radiator sings, the old men come, and the books go out and come back changed.

own.label: Ask what her family think
own.player: What does your family think of the reading room?
own.reply: My parents are doctors in the city and think it’s a hobby. My grandmother endowed it to thank God for a daughter who got better. I think of it as keeping her promise.

own.label: Ask who borrowed the missal
own.player: Who borrowed the book with the crescent in it?
own.reply: Someone on a dead man’s card. Harold Oakley’s. A young man. It came back with a crescent drawn inside the cover and a line of Latin in a new hand. I won’t report a reader. But I can tell you the card is still being used.
own.note: Priya Nair says a young man borrowing on the late Harold Oakley’s reading card returned a missal with a crescent and new Latin inside.

life.news: The radiator in the reading room sang all morning. The old men say it’s tuned to the hymns.
life.more: Three shelves, two armchairs and a radiator that sings. The council wants to close it. The old men have nowhere else to go. Today Mr. Okonjo hummed along to the radiator and two others joined in. I didn’t stop them. It was the nicest noise in Sunfall.

life.news: The council sent another letter about closing the reading room. I’ve filed it under pending. Like my feelings.
life.more: I catalog everything, including my feelings, which I file under pending. The letter says the room isn’t used. Eleven people used it today. I’ve written back with a list of their names and what they read. It’s a very long letter.

life.news: A book came back with someone else’s notes in the margins. Better notes than the book.
life.more: Handwritten, in pencil, all the way through a history of the county. Little corrections, a joke on page forty, a pressed flower at the end. The borrower’s card shows nobody I’ve heard of. I’ve left the notes in. They belong to the book now.

life.news: My grandmother’s missal turned up in a box of donations. Her handwriting in the cover. I sat on the floor for an hour.
life.more: She endowed this reading room when my aunt got better. I never knew her missal was here. Her prayers in the margins, in faded ink. The faith in those margins is still loud. I’ve put it on the top shelf, where it can see the room.

gossip.says: Bethany Price runs the town library and I run the parish reading room, and we swap the books we’re not allowed to stock. It’s very nearly smuggling.
gossip.note: Priya Nair says she and Bethany Price swap books between their libraries.
gossip.ask: Priya says you two swap books you’re not allowed to stock. Very nearly smuggling.
gossip.answer: Very nearly! We meet at the Lucky Cactus with tote bags and look shifty. She gets my Austen overflow and I get her hymn histories. A library is the last free place. Two of them, if you count hers. I always count hers.

gossip.says: Keiko Nakamura from the police borrowed a book of poems from me once and returned it with every sad poem marked with a pencil check mark.
gossip.note: Priya Nair says Keiko Nakamura marked every sad poem in a book she borrowed.
gossip.ask: Priya says you ticked every sad poem in a book you borrowed.
gossip.answer: They were the best ones. I find the pattern in the noise. In a book of poems, the pattern was sadness. I should have used a lighter pencil. I’ll buy her a new copy. I’m keeping the checked one.

women.name: Inez Morales
women.look: Amber skin, wavy chestnut bob, turquoise eyeshadow, corduroy jacket and vintage band T-shirt

own.label: Ask about campus housing
own.player: How bad is student housing here?
own.reply: Students sleeping in cars, while the university builds a meditation garden. You can’t meditate in a Honda Civic. I’ve tried.

own.label: Ask about her gig posters
own.player: You make gig posters?
own.reply: Screen-printed, illegal, beautiful. The goths pay in drinks and the punks pay in nothing. It’s the only honest economy in town.

own.label: Ask who funds her co-op
own.player: Who funds your housing co-operative?
own.reply: We got a donation from a charity with no office and no website. It saved us. I’m scared to find out who it really was.
own.note: Inez Morales’s housing co-op received money from a charity with no office and no website.

own.label: Ask what she really thinks about landlords
own.player: What do you really think about landlords?
own.reply: That most of them are just retired couples who were scared about money. That’s the bit nobody on my side likes hearing.

own.label: Ask where she sleeps
own.player: Where’s your room in the co-op?
own.reply: By the front door. The organizer sleeps by the door. That way I hear every late key and every landlord.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have siblings?
own.reply: Isabel, who trains horses at the Whitlock ranch. We’re a farrier’s daughters who went opposite ways. We ring each other every night and argue about who got it right.

calls.label: Ask who really owns the co-op
calls.player: Who really saved the co-op?
calls.reply: The charity with no office is the trust on the ridge, and the gift was a loan secured on the building. They own our roof now. If I say so out loud, forty students are sleeping in cars by the end of the week.
calls.note: Inez Morales says the trust on the ridge holds a loan secured on the student co-op’s building.

life.news: Tried to meditate in my car again. You can’t meditate in a Honda Civic. I keep trying.
life.more: The co-op’s so loud that the car is the only quiet room I have. I sat in the parking lot with my eyes shut and a man knocked on the window to ask if I was all right. I said I was achieving inner peace. He said, in a Civic?

life.news: Printed a poster for Alice’s next night. Best one yet. She’s paying me in drinks, as is traditional.
life.more: Gig posters, screen-printed, absolutely illegal where we put them up. The goths pay in drinks and the punks pay in nothing. It’s the only honest economy in town. This one’s a skeleton playing a record. I’m very proud of the skeleton.

life.news: My sister rang. Our dad’s back is bad again. He won’t stop shoeing horses.
life.more: He’s a farrier. He taught us both to hold a hoof and a grudge. Isabel’s at the ranch and I’m here, and every night we ring each other and argue about who’s going to make him rest. Neither of us will. He won’t.

life.news: Talked a landlord out of raising the rent on three students. He was just scared. They mostly are.
life.more: Landlords in Sunfall are mostly retired couples terrified of their own boiler. He thought the students would wreck the place. I brought him the students. They brought cookies. He cried a bit about his late wife. Rent’s frozen.

gossip.says: My sister Isabel Morales trains horses at a ranch past the canyon. We’re a farrier’s daughters who went in opposite directions. We ring each other every night and fight.
gossip.note: Inez Morales says her sister Isabel Morales trains horses past the canyon.
gossip.ask: Inez says you two ring every night and fight.
gossip.answer: Every night! About Dad, mostly, and about who’s right, which is me. She organizes people and I train horses. It’s the same job. You can’t force trust, only earn it. She hates it when I say that.

gossip.says: Alice Wren owes me forty-three drinks for posters. Forty-three. She thinks it’s forty. I’ve written it on my hand.
gossip.note: Inez Morales says Alice Wren owes her forty-three drinks for gig posters.
gossip.ask: Inez says you owe her forty-three drinks for posters, not forty.
gossip.answer: Forty-three? She’s counting the one I spilled on her. That one was a gift. Inez makes the best posters in the Old Quarter and she knows it, which is why she charges like a bank. I’ll pay her next payday. I always say that.

gossip.says: Jennifer Tate lives in my co-op and keeps the megaphones on a shelf above her bed. If one falls in the night it quacks. We’ve all learned to sleep through a duck.
gossip.note: Inez Morales says Jennifer Tate keeps her megaphones above her bed in the co-op.
gossip.ask: Inez says the whole co-op has learned to sleep through a duck.
gossip.answer: Once! It fell once. Okay, twice. The shelf’s slightly wonky. Inez sleeps by the door because the organizer sleeps by the door. She was the first one up with a flashlight. She thought it was a burglar who quacked.

women.name: Rowan Pike
women.look: Pale skin, silver-black undercut, gray-green eyes, subtle tattoos and crescent jewelry

own.label: Ask about running the studio
own.player: What’s it like running your own studio?
own.reply: Like being a priest with needles. People tell me things they’ve never told anyone. Then they pay me.

own.label: Ask about the investor
own.player: Someone wants to buy your studio?
own.reply: A wellness brand wants to turn it into a chain. Tattoos as self-care. I’d rather burn it down.

own.label: Ask about the key
own.player: Did someone leave something at the studio?
own.reply: A girl from Victoria’s circle left a key on the counter. Old, iron, too big for any door I know. I haven’t given it back.
own.note: Rowan Pike has an old iron key left at her studio by a girl from Victoria’s circle.

own.label: Ask what she won’t tattoo
own.player: What won’t you tattoo?
own.reply: Faces of exes and hate symbols. Everything else, if you’re sober and you’ve thought about it for a week.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Is Madison at the diner your sister?
own.reply: My little sister. I raised her from ten, after Mom died and Dad went away. She thinks I’m strict. I am. She’s still the best thing I’ve made.

own.label: Ask what happened to her father
own.player: Where’s your dad now?
own.reply: He kept the lenders’ book on the motel strip and got caught. I was nineteen. I still have the book. It has interesting names in it.

calls.label: Ask what the iron key fits
calls.player: Have you worked out what that key opens?
calls.reply: My mom’s old friend described a door to her once, thirty years ago, and I was in the room. The Old Mission’s crypt door. Iron, too big, a lock like a fist. That’s what the girl left on my counter.
calls.note: Rowan Pike believes the iron key Sorrel Vane left her opens the Old Mission’s crypt door.

calls.label: Ask about the wellness brand’s offer
calls.player: Who’s really behind the investor?
calls.reply: Page four of their offer. Small print. The Halcyon Ridge Trust. They want the studio, the old movie theater, the whole street. And Dad’s lenders’ book has a Blackwood in it, in debt.
calls.note: Rowan Pike says the wellness brand’s offer for her studio is backed by the Halcyon Ridge Trust.

life.news: The wellness brand sent another letter. This one has a scented insert.
life.more: They want to turn the studio into a chain. Tattoos as self-care. The insert smells like a candle that’s been to university. I put it in the trash, took it out to show Zara, then put it back in the trash. That’s my whole response. Trash.

life.news: Madison called me from the diner bathroom. Some man grabbed her wrist.
life.more: She’s fine. She tipped a coffee into his lap, which I taught her. I went down and sat at the counter for two hours and didn’t order anything. He left. Dolores gave me pie on the house. I’m not proud of how good that felt.

life.news: Finished my own sleeve. Took six years, because I keep working on everyone else.
life.more: Horror soundtracks I love, done as sheet music up my arm. Zara did the last bar because I can’t reach. First time in years I’ve let anyone else’s needle near me. Strange feeling. Trust, I think they call it.

life.news: Someone’s been leaving coins on my doorstep. One a day. Old ones.
life.more: Not money you can spend. Old pennies, worn flat. Seven now. No note. I’ve lined them up on the counter. Either I’ve got an admirer from a hundred years ago or someone in the Old Quarter thinks I owe them change.

gossip.says: My sister Madison Pike waits tables at the Lucky Cactus and remembers every order anyone’s ever made. Ask her what you had last time. She’ll know, and she’ll judge it.
gossip.note: Rowan Pike says her sister Madison Pike remembers every order at the Lucky Cactus.
gossip.ask: Rowan says you remember every order anyone’s ever made.
gossip.answer: Oh my God, Rowan talks about me? She never talks about me! Okay, yes, I do, it’s like a superpower but useless. When you come in I’ll remember forever, so order something cool. Not a club sandwich. Everyone orders a club sandwich.

gossip.says: Alisha Benton from the police lab came in for a tattoo and spent the whole sitting watching my hands instead of the needle. Lab people notice everything.
gossip.note: Rowan Pike says Alisha Benton from the police lab notices everything.
gossip.ask: Rowan says you watched her hands the whole time she was tattooing you.
gossip.answer: She has very steady hands and a scar across two knuckles she doesn’t explain. I look at hands for a living. Gloves, swabs, prints. It’s a habit. The tattoo’s lovely, by the way. Tiny. I’m not telling you where.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler runs the Furnace and lets kids sit there all day when home is bad. Somebody did it for her once. She pays it forward with free cola and terrible advice.
gossip.note: Rowan Pike says Nixie Adler lets kids with bad homes sit at the Furnace all day.
gossip.ask: Rowan says you let kids hang out at the Furnace when home is bad.
gossip.answer: Rowan has a big mouth for someone who barely talks. A woman with a record shop let me sit there when I was eleven and home was bad. She never asked why. I don’t ask either. The door’s open. That’s all it is.

women.name: Camille Baptiste
women.look: Deep brown skin, dark locs tied in a scarf, olive utility jacket and silver compact-camera strap

own.label: Ask about her motel photographs
own.player: Why photograph old motels?
own.reply: Because they’re where America keeps its secrets. Every motel sign is a promise someone broke.

own.label: Ask for a story
own.player: Tell me a Sunfall story.
own.reply: A woman ran the diner for forty years and never once took a day off. The day she died, the jukebox played her song by itself. Everyone swears it. I believe it.

own.label: Ask what her gala photo shows
own.player: What did you see in your gala photographs?
own.reply: A face at Table 9 who isn’t on the official guest list. Not a waiter, not a guest. Someone who wasn’t meant to be remembered.
own.note: Camille Baptiste photographed someone at Table 9 who isn’t on the official guest list.

own.label: Ask what photography taught her about people
own.player: What has photography taught you about people?
own.reply: That everyone has one honest face and they only show it when they think nobody’s looking. My job is to be nobody.

own.label: Ask about her apartment
own.player: What’s on your walls?
own.reply: Motel signs. Vacancy, No Vacancy, one that just says Ice. Every motel sign is a promise someone broke.

own.label: Ask who taught her photography
own.player: Who taught you to take pictures?
own.reply: My grandfather photographed weddings. My mother photographed the ones he wouldn’t. I learned both, which is why I can make anyone look married or divorced.

own.label: Ask why her stories never end
own.player: Why do you never finish a story?
own.reply: Because then you’d stop listening. Editors and men both come back for the ending. I keep it in my pocket.

calls.label: Ask whose face is in her photograph
calls.player: Who is the face at Table 9?
calls.reply: I went up the lodge road with a long lens and photographed a car. Same face. Lyle Marchbanks. He’s on no guest list anywhere and at every table that matters. The same roll has a girl from the club with her hand on his arm.
calls.note: Camille Baptiste identified the face at Table 9 as Lyle Marchbanks, photographed again on the lodge road.

calls.label: Ask if she’d share the frame
calls.player: Could I see that frame?
calls.reply: A cropped print. Not the whole roll, I’m not mad. Enough that you’ll know him if you see him. Treat it like it’s radioactive.

life.news: Found an old motel sign in a scrapyard. A pink flamingo with one leg. I’m in love.
life.more: Every motel sign is a promise somebody broke. This one says VACANCY, and only the CAN still lights up. I’ve hung it over my bed and it glows pink all night. I sleep worse and I’m happier.

life.news: The jukebox at the Lucky Cactus played a song by itself again. Everyone swears they didn’t touch it.
life.more: A woman ran that diner years ago, and the day she died the jukebox played her song on its own. Everyone swears it. Today it played the same song. Nobody had put a coin in. I believe it. I want to believe more things like that.

life.news: My brother rang. It’s the anniversary of the fire. We don’t say the word, we just ring.
life.more: We were kids. Nobody was badly hurt, but the house went, and the photographs with it. That’s why I take so many now. Every picture is me trying to keep something from burning. Sorry, that got heavy. Tell me something light.

life.news: Got an honest face today. An old man at a bus stop who thought nobody was looking.
life.more: Everyone has one honest face and only shows it when they think nobody’s watching. My job is to be nobody. He was watching a little girl give her lollipop to a dog. That’s the photo. My grandfather would have loved it.

gossip.says: Alisha Benton from the police lab looked at my grandfather’s camera and went very quiet. She said her dad had the same one. She held it like it might break.
gossip.note: Camille Baptiste says Alisha Benton’s father had the same camera as her grandfather.
gossip.ask: Camille says you went quiet over her grandfather’s camera.
gossip.answer: My dad had one exactly the same. Thirty-six chances on a roll, and you think before every one. There’s a roll of his I’ve never developed. His last. I’m not ready. Camille didn’t ask why I went quiet. I liked her for that.

gossip.says: Anna Voss volunteers at every Bluebird do and she’s the only one there who learns the waiters’ names. I photograph her at every party. She’s always looking at the person nobody else is looking at.
gossip.note: Camille Baptiste says Anna Voss is the only Bluebird who learns the waiters’ names.
gossip.ask: Camille says you’re the only one at those parties who learns the waiters’ names.
gossip.answer: Well, someone has to, darling. I’m basically furniture at those things, so I talk to the other furniture. The waiters know everything. Who’s drunk, who’s leaving with whom. I’m loyal to the waiters. They tip me off about the good canapés.

gossip.says: Natalie Cross and I keep turning up at the same places, a minute apart, from opposite sides of the road. One day we’ll put our pictures together and find out what we both missed.
gossip.note: Camille Baptiste says she and Natalie Cross keep photographing the same places from opposite sides.
gossip.ask: Camille says you two keep photographing the same things from opposite sides of the road.
gossip.answer: We do. It’s eerie. She gets the faces and I get the backs of heads. One day we’ll lay them side by side on my floor and the whole town will make sense, or we’ll both need a lie down.

women.name: Tessa Larkin
women.look: Freckled fair skin, copper-red braids, bright coral top and faded jeans

own.label: Ask about the lizard
own.player: Did you get the lizard out of your kitchen?
own.reply: Eventually. His name is Gregory now. He lives in a shoebox and judges me.

own.label: Ask about her clay birds
own.player: You make clay birds?
own.reply: Terrible ones. They look like potatoes with opinions. I keep making them because I love birds and I’m not good at anything else, artistically.

own.label: Ask what she saw near the enclosure
own.player: Did you see something near the animal enclosure?
own.reply: A van with no plates parked by the bear trap the rangers didn’t set. Two men were checking a laptop. They drove off when I waved.
own.note: Tessa Larkin saw a van with no plates and two men with a laptop by an unofficial bear trap.

own.label: Ask what wild animals teach her
own.player: What do wild animals teach you?
own.reply: That you can’t love something into staying. You feed it, you heal it, and you open the box and let it go.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A caravan at the rescue center, with Gregory and whatever’s come in this week. Right now a hawk with a wing and a fox with opinions.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: We had an orchard until the water went to a rich family. Dad’s bitter, Mom keeps bees. At fourteen Dad told me you can’t love something into staying. He meant the orchard.

calls.label: Ask about the Foundation’s offer
calls.player: What’s the Foundation offering the rescue center?
calls.reply: A permanent home on the ridge, by the lodge, with a grant. Page four says our animals must be available for their educational program. That means they want a licensed place to keep a bear.
calls.note: Tessa Larkin says the Foundation’s offer to house the rescue center on the ridge would let the lodge legally keep a bear.

calls.label: Ask what was on the men’s laptop
calls.player: What was on that laptop by the trap?
calls.reply: A map with a moving dot. The dot was on the hill school’s playing field. They were tracking him.
calls.note: Tessa Larkin saw the men by the bear trap tracking a dot on the hill school’s field.

life.news: Released a hawk today. Six weeks of feeding and splinting. She flew off and didn’t look back.
life.more: You feed it, you heal it, and you open the box and it doesn’t look back. That’s how you know you did it right. I cried, obviously. Gregory watched the whole thing from his shoebox with deep disapproval. He thinks I’m too soft.

life.news: Made a clay bird at pottery class. It looks like a potato with opinions. I love it.
life.more: I love birds and I can’t make them. This one has a beak like a thumb and a very judgemental expression. The teacher said it had character. I’ve put it next to Gregory. They glare at each other all day. I think they’re friends.

life.news: My dad’s still bitter about the orchard. The water went years ago and he never got over it.
life.more: We had an orchard on the state road and the water got sold to a big ranch upstream. The trees died one by one. Dad says you can’t love something into staying. He said it to me when I was fourteen. I think about it every day. I think he was talking about Mom too.

life.news: A fox kit came in today. So small it fitted in a teacup. He bit me. I’ve named him Teacup.
life.more: Someone found him by a road with no mom. He’s furious about everything, which is a good sign. Angry babies survive. I’ve wrapped him in an old sweater and he’s asleep on a hot water bottle, snoring. Gregory is jealous.

gossip.says: Rachel Lowe from the vet’s helps me with the animals at the rescue for free. She says animals bite you honestly. She’s been bitten by everything. She says thank you every time.
gossip.note: Tessa Larkin says Rachel Lowe helps at the wildlife rescue for free.
gossip.ask: Tessa says you say thank you every time an animal bites you.
gossip.answer: Manners cost nothing! A bite is an animal telling you the truth: back off, I’m scared. It’s more honest than most people manage. Tessa’s the brave one. She’ll pick up anything with teeth. I’ve seen her hold a badger like a baby.

gossip.says: Marisol Fuentes from the park service brings me every injured animal she finds and then pretends she doesn’t care how they get on. She rings every day to ask.
gossip.note: Tessa Larkin says Marisol Fuentes rings every day to check on the animals she brings in.
gossip.ask: Tessa says you ring every day to check on the animals you bring her.
gossip.answer: Professional interest. It’s a ranger’s duty to follow up. Fine. I ring every day. I’ve got a fox kit I want to know about. Tessa named him Teacup, which is undignified for a fox. I’ve started calling him Captain. He’ll choose.

gossip.says: Heather Collins let me bring an owl into her classroom. The owl hated everyone. Twenty-two children fell in love with her. Heather says it was the best lesson of the year.
gossip.note: Tessa Larkin says Heather Collins’s class met a rescue owl.
gossip.ask: Tessa says you let her bring an owl into your classroom.
gossip.answer: Doris! She hated every single one of them and they adored her. One girl asked if Doris had feelings, and we had the worm debate all over again. They’ve written Doris a thank-you letter. I’ve no idea how to deliver it.

women.name: Nadia Okafor
women.look: Dark skin, shoulder-length box braids, burgundy shirt and simple watch

own.label: Ask about forensic work
own.player: Is forensic work like the TV shows?
own.reply: No. Less glowing blue lights, more labeling bags. But I love it. Details don’t lie. People do.

own.label: Ask about her crosswords
own.player: I hear you do cryptic crosswords?
own.reply: In diners, with a pencil, like a woman from a better century. A good clue is a crime scene: everything you need is there, disguised.

own.label: Ask what’s bothering her at work
own.player: Something at work bothering you?
own.reply: The chain-of-custody log for the gala evidence has a gap. Two hours where nobody signed for the bag. Nobody else seems to care.
own.note: Nadia Okafor found a two-hour gap in the custody log for the gala evidence.

own.label: Ask what evidence can’t prove
own.player: What can’t evidence prove?
own.reply: Why. I can tell you who was in a room and when. I can’t tell you why anyone does anything. That’s what keeps me up.

own.label: Ask about her apartment
own.player: What’s your place like?
own.reply: A window box of my grandmother’s roses and a shelf of crossword books from a better century. I do cryptics in the Lucky Cactus, in pencil. The waitress reads the clues over my shoulder and gets them first.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: Mom’s a pharmacist on the Sunfall Road. Dad was a hospital porter. He died of a stroke in the parking lot he’d parked in for twenty years. I check parking lots now. It doesn’t help.

own.label: Ask what she’s waiting for
own.player: What are you waiting on at work?
own.reply: I’ve passed every exam the county offers. The promotion needs one sergeant’s signature, and it’s the wrong sergeant.

calls.label: Ask about the crossword clues
calls.player: You said the crossword talks to you?
calls.reply: Someone sets clues in the Daily that I’m certain are written for me. Last week: a nine-letter word for a trust on a ridge. I don’t know who. I’ve started leaving answers in the margins of the bar menus.
calls.note: Nadia Okafor believes someone is hiding clues for her in the Daily’s crossword.

calls.label: Ask what was in the evidence bag
calls.player: What went missing from the bag?
calls.reply: A torn ticket and a phone’s SIM. Two hours, nobody signs, and after it the bag is lighter. The SIM was Elena Cross’s. The last initials before the gap belong to a photographic assistant called Dale Pruett.
calls.note: Nadia Okafor says Elena Cross’s SIM card went missing from the evidence bag during a two-hour gap, after Dale Pruett last signed it.

life.news: Finished the hardest cryptic of the year at the Lucky Cactus. In pencil. In under an hour.
life.more: A good clue is a crime scene. Everything you need is there, disguised. Madison refilled my coffee four times and read the clues over my shoulder. She got two before I did. I’m not over it.

life.news: Labeled two hundred evidence bags today. My handwriting has never been so beautiful or so tired.
life.more: Less glowing blue lights, more labeling bags. I love it. Details don’t lie. People do. But two hundred is a lot of details. My hand is a claw. I’m doing tomorrow’s crossword with my left.

life.news: My grandmother’s roses flowered in my window box. In the desert. She’d be furious they did better here.
life.more: She grew them back home for forty years and I brought cuttings over in a wet sock. Everyone said they’d die. They’re red and enormous and smug. I sent her a photo and she said, too much water, which is grandmother for well done.

life.news: Someone’s writing crossword clues that feel like they’re meant for me. I’m probably imagining it.
life.more: Nine letters, a word I’d said out loud at work the day before. Then another. It’s coincidence. It must be. I’ve started answering them in a different color pen, just in case someone’s checking. That’s normal. That’s a normal thing to do.

gossip.says: Alisha Benton has a darkroom in her bathroom. You can’t have a bath at hers. You have to ask permission to wash your hands in case something’s developing.
gossip.note: Nadia Okafor says Alisha Benton has a darkroom in her bathroom.
gossip.ask: Nadia says you have to ask permission to wash your hands at yours.
gossip.answer: Only if the red light’s on! It’s a perfectly normal bathroom with a perfectly normal enlarger over the bath. Nadia knocked over a tray of fixer once and I’ve never let her forget it. Thirty-six chances on a roll. You have to mean it.

gossip.says: Madison Pike at the Lucky Cactus reads my crossword clues over my shoulder and gets them before me. She says she doesn’t even like crosswords. The worst kind of talent.
gossip.note: Nadia Okafor says Madison Pike solves her crossword clues over her shoulder.
gossip.ask: Nadia says you solve her crossword clues before she does.
