calls.reply: To win something that’s mine. Not a husband somebody picked. A race, a cake that stands up, one night where nobody is measuring me for anything.

calls.label: Ask if she’s seeing anyone
calls.player: Are you seeing anyone?
calls.reply: There’s a swimmer from the city. Tomas. Nobody knows about him. Not my father, not my mother, not the club. I’m keeping him. If you tell anyone I’ll drown you, politely.

life.news: Cake number nine collapsed. The Sisters served it in bowls again and called it a trifle.
life.more: Raspberry, three layers, a ganache I was very proud of. It sank in the middle like a sigh. Sister Eliza looked at it, didn’t blink, got out the bowls. She hugged me on the way out. I think I’m the only one who hugs her. I should do it more.

life.news: Swam two miles in the reservoir at dawn. No lanes, no coach, nobody timing me. Best I’ve felt in months.
life.more: The club pool has my name on a board. The reservoir doesn’t know my name. A heron watched me the whole way like it was judging my stroke. I got out shaking and laughing and drove home with my hair dripping all over my father’s car seats.

life.news: My mother had me measured for a dress. She won’t say what it’s for. My father won’t either. They won’t say it to each other.
life.more: Cream, long, very plain. The dressmaker kept smiling at me the way you smile at a bride. I asked if somebody was getting married. She said not yet and pinned the hem.

life.news: Somebody sent me a postcard from the city with a swimming pool on it. No name. I know exactly who.
life.more: One line on the back: lane four, whenever you’re ready. I keep it inside my running shoe so my mother can’t find it. Running shoes are the only thing she never touches.

gossip.says: Sister Eliza Montoya serves my collapsed cakes in bowls at the pantry and calls them trifle. She’s never once laughed at me. I think she’s the kindest person in Sunfall.
gossip.note: Eloise Rainer says Eliza Montoya serves her collapsed cakes in bowls at the Sisters’ pantry.
gossip.ask: Eloise says you serve her cakes in bowls.
gossip.answer: I do, and I’ll keep doing it. Every week a beautiful ruin arrives with a girl behind it who wants so badly to get something right. The bowls are the easy part. She hugs me at the door. I don’t think she knows how long it had been.

gossip.says: Alice Beaumont runs the ball. She looked at my presentation list for a long time and then crossed out one name with a very sharp pencil. She wouldn’t say whose. I keep the records and I still can’t read it.
gossip.note: Eloise Rainer says Alice Beaumont crossed a name off her ball presentation list.
gossip.ask: Eloise says you crossed a name off her list.
gossip.answer: I did. A girl should be presented to people who will still be alive at her wedding. Eloise keeps the records. I keep the girls. Tell her the pencil was sharp because I meant it.

women.name: Lorna Sutton
women.look: Fair skin, brown waves with teal tips, tortoiseshell glasses, powder-blue twinset

women.name: Penelope Kline
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, copper waist-length waves, tortoiseshell glasses, powder-blue twinset

women.name: Maren Caldwell
women.look: Fair skin, platinum pixie cut, hazel eyes, cream blazer over a silk camisole

women.name: Estelle Parker
women.look: Rosy fair skin, platinum pixie cut, hazel eyes, pale pink sheath dress

women.name: Irene Vaughn
women.look: Freckled fair skin, rose-gold bob, freckles across her nose, gold-buttoned navy blazer

women.name: Whitney Ashford
women.look: Pale skin, dark French braid, a gap-toothed smile, navy shift dress with pearls

women.name: Delphine Moreau
women.look: Rosy fair skin, copper waist-length waves, strong dark brows, powder-blue twinset

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do at the Foundation?
own.reply: I keep the stationery account. The smallest line in the budget. I write the invitations, by hand. The club thinks that’s quaint. The club is wrong about a great many things, very politely.

own.label: Ask what she does in the mornings
own.player: What do you do in the mornings?
own.reply: I row on the reservoir at dawn, alone. Nearly national, until my shoulder went. The water doesn’t know who signed what. That’s the whole appeal.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: With my mother, who is ninety, and her nurse, and a room given over entirely to paper. Nobody goes in there but me. My mother is very strict about the guest list, even now.

own.label: Ask if she makes anything
own.player: Do you make anything?
own.reply: Paper collages. Cut from the society pages, bordered with offcuts from the invitations. They hang in the committee rooms. People call them decorative. They are the minutes.
own.note: Delphine Moreau’s paper collages in the committee rooms record the club’s private dinners: who was invited, who came, who is next.

own.label: Compliment her handwriting
own.player: You have beautiful handwriting.
own.reply: Which one? I can do anyone’s hand after an hour with a sample. It’s a small gift. The club has found it large. I keep every sample I ever worked from, because I’m a clerk, and clerks keep.
own.note: Delphine Moreau can copy anyone’s handwriting after an hour with a sample, and keeps every sample she has worked from.

calls.label: Ask if she’s ever been in love
calls.player: Have you ever been in love?
calls.reply: Once. A court reporter. She left me for six months for someone at the club, and then she left Sunfall. I put the other woman’s name in the border of a collage every year. Never in the center. One day I’ll decide what that means.

calls.label: Ask what she’s working on
calls.player: What are you making at the moment?
calls.reply: A big piece. It isn’t finished. The center is empty. I’m waiting to find out whose face goes there. If you hear anything about a woman who isn’t where she’s supposed to be, I would very much like to know.
calls.note: Delphine Moreau’s newest collage has an empty center: she is waiting to learn whose face goes there.

life.news: Rowed the length of the reservoir before sunrise. A heron raced me for half a mile and lost.
life.more: Flat water, no wind, my shoulder only complaining a little. I sang to myself on the way back, which I haven’t done in years. Then I came home and cut out a whole page of wedding announcements and enjoyed it more than I should have.

life.news: A woman at the club asked me to write her name the way her mother used to. I did. She cried.
life.more: A widow, very old, holding her mother’s letter in a plastic sleeve. I practiced the hand for an hour and wrote her name on a card. She held it against her face. It was the first time the gift has ever done anything kind. I didn’t know what to do with my hands afterward.

life.news: My mother didn’t know me this morning. Then she did, and asked who I’d invited.
life.more: She kept the club’s minutes for forty years and she still asks about the guest list before she asks about breakfast. I told her everyone she’d want. She said good, and then she asked who was next, and I didn’t answer.

life.news: A craft fair. A woman selling collages made of bus tickets and receipts. I bought three and talked to her for an hour.
life.more: Cheerful, paint on her wrists, no idea who I am. We argued about glue for twenty minutes. I laughed out loud in public. I may go back next month. I may not. That’s the best kind of decision.

gossip.says: Daisy Chen makes collages out of bus tickets and receipts. I met her at a craft fair and we argued about glue for twenty minutes. It was the happiest afternoon I’ve had in years.
gossip.note: Delphine Moreau says she met Daisy Chen at a craft fair and argued with her about glue.
gossip.ask: Delphine says you two argued about glue at a craft fair.
gossip.answer: We did, and I was right. She was so serious and so funny about it, this woman in a twinset who wouldn’t let a glue stick go. She bought nothing, then came back and bought my three best pieces. Tell her I kept her card. Tell her it’s in my wallet.

gossip.says: Ruth Calder has the most beautiful handwriting at the Foundation. Round, honest, impossible to hurry. I admire it more than she will ever know.
gossip.note: Delphine Moreau says Ruth Calder has the most beautiful handwriting at the Foundation.
gossip.ask: Delphine says she admires your handwriting.
gossip.answer: Does she? How strange. Delphine writes the invitations and has the best hand in the building. She once asked me for a page of my notes to study. I gave it to her. I hope she found it useful. I never got it back.

women.name: Catalina Reyes
women.look: Deep brown skin, rose-gold bob, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, white linen trouser suit

women.name: Danica Holt
women.look: Deep brown skin, golden-brown ringlets, a silver ear cuff, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask about photographing crime scenes
own.player: What’s it like photographing crime scenes?
own.reply: You learn to look at the worst day of someone’s life as a problem of light. Then you go home and look at nothing for an hour.

own.label: Ask about the watches
own.player: You repair watches?
own.reply: Badly, slowly, happily. A watch is a crime scene in reverse: every part tells you exactly what happened, if you’re patient.

own.label: Ask what’s missing at work
own.player: Something missing at work?
own.reply: The key to the filing cabinet with the gala photographs. It was there, then it wasn’t, and the sign-out sheet is blank. Somebody in our own building wanted those prints.
own.note: Danica Holt says the key to the cabinet holding the gala crime-scene photographs went missing inside the police station.

own.label: Ask what color she sees most at work
own.player: What color do you see most at work?
own.reply: Beige. Carpets, walls, coats. The worst things happen in the most boring rooms.

own.label: Ask how she started so young
own.player: How did you get the job at seventeen?
own.reply: I photographed the drive-in’s back field every dawn for a year, where my cousin Dana was found. I sent the station the photos. They hired me. I think they didn’t know what else to do with me.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: At my aunt’s, Dana’s mom’s. It’s a house of grief, and I’ve decided to be the light in it. Some days I’m a very small light.

own.label: Ask what she notices at scenes
own.player: What do you notice first at a scene?
own.reply: Beige. Carpets, walls, coats. The worst things happen in the most boring rooms. I bring a red scarf to every scene, just to see one color.

calls.label: Ask about her practice photos
calls.player: Did you take any photos of your own that night?
calls.reply: Practice frames, of the club’s kitchen door. I wasn’t meant to. They show a gray car with its door open and a shape in the back seat. I haven’t told Katrina. I don’t know who I’d be telling after her.
calls.note: Danica Holt’s practice photos from the gala show a gray car at the club’s kitchen door with a shape in the back seat.

life.news: Got a watch working that’s been dead for forty years. It ticked. I may have shouted.
life.more: A watch is a crime scene in reverse. Every part tells you exactly what happened, if you’re patient. This one belonged to a man who wound it every morning for thirty years and then stopped. Now it’s going again. Somewhere, I hope, he knows.

life.news: Long one today. I’m going to look at nothing for an hour.
life.more: You learn to look at the worst day of someone’s life as a problem of light. Then you go home and look at nothing for an hour. I’m on my bed looking at the ceiling. It’s beige. The worst things happen in beige rooms. My ceiling knows this.

life.news: My aunt laughed at dinner. Properly. First time in a long time.
life.more: We live in a house that’s been sad for a while, and I’ve decided to be the light in it. Tonight I did impressions of the station sergeant and my aunt laughed so hard she had to put her fork down. I’m going to practice more impressions.

life.news: A watch repairer gave me a box of broken movements to practice on. One has initials scratched inside.
life.more: Tiny letters inside the case, where nobody would ever look. Someone wanted it to be theirs even in the dark. I’m going to fix that one last, slowly, properly. Whoever they were, they deserve to hear it tick.

gossip.says: Abigail Porter caught the man who killed my cousin. She never talks about it. She just checks on my aunt every few months and fixes whatever’s broken in the house.
gossip.note: Danica Holt says Abigail Porter caught the man who killed her cousin.
gossip.ask: Danica says you still check on her aunt and fix things in the house.
gossip.answer: Someone has to fix the kitchen tap. That’s all it is. I don’t talk about the case because there’s nothing to say that would help. Danica takes better photographs than anyone in that building. Tell her I said so. She won’t believe me either.

gossip.says: Bianca Roth from the Bluebirds is learning to repair watches at the same shop as me. She won’t say why. She’s very good at the tiny screws.
gossip.note: Danica Holt says Bianca Roth from the Bluebirds is learning watch repair.
gossip.ask: Danica says you’re learning to repair watches and won’t say why.
gossip.answer: A woman is allowed a hobby. It’s very calming. Every part has its place and nobody argues about it. If you must know, a watch stopped in my family and I’d like to be the one who starts it again. That’s more than I meant to say. Remember my birthday instead.

women.name: Sasha Mahoney
women.look: Olive skin, natural afro puff, deep dimples, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask what the numbers say about Sunfall
own.player: What do the numbers say about Sunfall?
own.reply: Most accidents happen in the kitchen. Statistically, your toaster is a bigger threat than any stranger. Sleep well.

own.label: Ask about her book club
own.player: What’s your book club reading?
own.reply: Officially, a serious novel about grief. Actually, we drink wine and talk about our exes. Nobody has finished a book since we started.

own.label: Ask how a statistician can be impulsive
own.player: How is a statistician impulsive?
own.reply: I know the odds, so I ignore them. Knowing a thing is unlikely just makes me want to see it happen.

own.label: Ask which number she can’t forget
own.player: Is there a number you can’t forget?
own.reply: Seventeen. The number of calls a woman made before anyone came. I built a model so it would never happen again. It still happens.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Who taught you numbers?
own.reply: Mom teaches math at the high school and taught me to count cards at family poker. Dad runs the boat hire on the reservoir. Between them, I don’t trust water or luck.

own.label: Ask what actually kills people
own.player: What’s actually dangerous in Sunfall?
own.reply: Your kitchen. Most accidents happen there. Then ladders. Then the reservoir at the regatta. Strangers come a long way down the list, which nobody wants to hear.

calls.label: Ask about the seventeen calls
calls.player: Why did nobody come for seventeen calls?
calls.reply: The nearest patrol car was on a private job: escorting a Foundation vehicle up to the ridge, signed off by Sergeant Lowry. I found it in the data my first year. They told me it was a coding error. I kept the raw log.
calls.note: Sasha Mahoney says the patrol car that never came was escorting a Foundation vehicle to the ridge on Sergeant Lowry’s orders.

calls.label: Ask about her dad and the regatta
calls.player: Did your dad ever see anything at the reservoir?
calls.reply: He gave a statement once, years ago. A man called Ellis Dane drowned at a club regatta. Dad said Dane was sober and the boat had been tampered with. The case was closed as misadventure. Dad hasn’t hired a boat to the club since.
calls.note: Sasha Mahoney’s father says Ellis Dane, who drowned at a club regatta, was sober and his boat had been tampered with.

life.news: Book club tonight. Nobody’s read the book. We’ve been on chapter two since spring.
life.more: Officially it’s a serious novel about grief. Actually it’s wine and exes. Tonight Hollis tried to read a paragraph aloud and we voted her down. She sulked beautifully. Nobody has finished a book since we started. I think that’s the point.

life.news: Told my dad the odds of a good summer for his boat hire. He ignored me. He was right.
life.more: I know the odds of everything and ignore them, which I get from him. He runs the boats on the reservoir. I told him rain was likely. It wasn’t. He’s been insufferable all week. I said statistics aren’t predictions. He’s printed that on a T-shirt.

life.news: Ran the numbers on a model I built years ago. It still isn’t good enough.
life.more: It’s about how fast help reaches people who call. It’s better than it was. It’s not good enough. One number in it is someone who waited too long. I rebuild it every year, and tonight I’m rebuilding it again. Sorry. Sometimes it’s not a fun job.

life.news: Beat my mom at poker. She taught me to count cards. She’s furious and proud.
life.more: She teaches math at the high school and taught me to count the deck at eight. Tonight I took her for forty matchsticks. She said, I’ve created a monster, and asked for a rematch. Next week I’m going to lose on purpose. Maybe.

gossip.says: Keiko Nakamura comes to my book club and says one sentence every six months. It’s always the best sentence of the night.
gossip.note: Sasha Mahoney says Keiko Nakamura speaks once every six months at her book club.
gossip.ask: Sasha says you say one perfect sentence every six months.
gossip.answer: I listen. Everyone else talks. Somebody has to listen, and I’m better at it. The last sentence was about a dog. They’re still quoting it. That’s enough for a year.

gossip.says: Joanne Kendrick on dispatch makes pottery bowls that aren’t round. Eleven of them. Her mom uses every one.
gossip.note: Sasha Mahoney says Joanne Kendrick makes pottery bowls that aren’t round.
gossip.ask: Sasha says none of your eleven bowls are round.
gossip.answer: Twelve now. Still none round. My mom says they have character. They have holes. I’m going to make one round bowl before I die. Sasha’s worked out the odds. She won’t tell me what they are.

gossip.says: Kimberly Brooks rides a motorcycle to her office job and has never once let anyone photograph her on it. She says photographs jinx bikes.
gossip.note: Sasha Mahoney says Kimberly Brooks won’t be photographed on her motorcycle.
gossip.ask: Sasha says you won’t let anyone photograph you on your motorcycle.
gossip.answer: Bad luck. Every bike I’ve seen photographed ended up in a hedge. I’m not superstitious, I’m statistical. Ask Sasha. She’ll call it nonsense, then refuse to stand near my bike with a camera.

women.name: Imani Harper
women.look: Pale skin, layered caramel shoulder-length hair, freckles across her nose, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask about the evidence archive
own.player: What’s the evidence archive like?
own.reply: Rows of boxes holding the worst days of people’s lives, sorted by number. I label them carefully. It feels like the least I can do.

own.label: Ask about her cactus garden
own.player: I heard you keep cacti indoors?
own.reply: Thirty-one of them. They’re the only things in Sunfall that thrive on neglect, and I respect that.

own.label: Ask what’s weighing on her
own.player: You seem like something’s weighing on you.
own.reply: I promised my mom I’d go home to Atlanta by now. I keep not going. Sunfall gets its hooks in you.

own.label: Ask about the box nobody opens
own.player: Is there a box in the archive nobody opens?
own.reply: Shelf nine, bottom row. It’s labeled with a case number that doesn’t exist. I’ve never opened it. I think about it every day.

own.label: Ask where she’s from
own.player: You’re not from here, are you?
own.reply: Atlanta. I promised my mom I’d come home after a year. That was two years ago. She’s a hospital administrator and wanted me to be a lawyer. I label boxes. We’re both disappointed in very organized ways.

own.label: Ask who cuts her hair
own.player: Who cuts your hair?
own.reply: Me, in the bathroom, with the good scissors. Freckles I’ve stopped hiding, windbreaker for the archive cold. I’m very low maintenance. The cacti are high maintenance about being ignored.

calls.label: Ask what’s strange about the box
calls.player: What’s strange about that box?
calls.reply: There’s no such case. I checked. And somebody dusts that box every week, and it isn’t me. My boss says it’s an old filing error. Filing errors don’t get dusted.
calls.note: Imani Harper says the evidence box on shelf nine has no real case number and someone dusts it every week.

life.news: Thirty-two cacti. I bought another one. It was on sale and looked lonely.
life.more: They thrive on neglect. I respect that in a plant. This one’s tiny and lopsided and had a sticker saying reduced. I’ve put it in the middle of the windowsill so the others can teach it. It’s called Detective. They all have names.

life.news: My mom rang from Atlanta and asked when I’m coming home. I said soon. I always say soon.
life.more: I promised I’d go home after a year. It’s been three. She doesn’t shout, she just goes quiet, which is worse. I love it here and I can’t explain why to her. Everything in the archive is finished. Nothing at home is.

life.news: Labeling boxes today, I found a ticket stub from a concert forty years ago tucked inside a file.
life.more: Rows of boxes holding the worst days of people’s lives. I label them carefully. It feels like the least I can do. The stub was in there like a bookmark. Someone went to a concert once, before the worst day. I put it back exactly where it was.

life.news: Dinner with Naoko. We laughed so hard at a pasta shape that the waiter came to check on us.
life.more: We eat together most nights. The station calls us the twins because we’re always together and look nothing alike. Tonight the pasta was shaped like little ears and Naoko said it was listening. We couldn’t breathe. I needed that more than I knew.

gossip.says: I met Rosalie Kemp, the chapel archivist, at a records conference. She told me every archive has one box nobody opens. I haven’t stopped thinking about it.
gossip.note: Imani Harper says Rosalie Kemp told her every archive has one box nobody opens.
gossip.ask: Imani says you told her every archive has one box nobody opens.
gossip.answer: It’s true. In mine it’s a hatbox of letters from a priest to a woman who married someone else. I’ve never opened it and I never will. Some things are kept by not being read. I think Imani has one too. I think she knows that.

gossip.says: Nadia Okafor does cryptic crosswords in pencil in diners and says a good clue is a crime scene. I watched her solve one in ten minutes. I couldn’t get the first clue.
gossip.note: Imani Harper says Nadia Okafor solves cryptic crosswords at astonishing speed.
gossip.ask: Imani says you solve cryptic crosswords at frightening speed.
gossip.answer: Frightening is a strong word. Efficient. Everything you need is there in the clue, disguised, same as a scene. Imani files better than I ever will, so we’re even. Tell her I’ll teach her. Pencil first. Never pen.

gossip.says: Vanessa Greer has more books than furniture. A friend of mine goes to her meetings and comes back with a new book every time.
gossip.note: Imani Harper says Vanessa Greer lends out books at her meetings.
gossip.ask: Imani says you hand out a book at every meeting.
gossip.answer: Books are the only thing I’m generous with. History is a list of people who stopped asking nicely. If someone comes to a meeting, they leave with one. Imani should come herself. I’ve got a whole shelf about archivists who said no.

women.name: Leila Sayeed
women.look: Olive skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, hazel eyes, plain white shirt and slim black pants

own.label: Ask what a custody nurse does
own.player: What does a custody nurse actually do?
own.reply: I patch up people on the worst night of their lives, usually at both ends of the handcuffs. Everyone is polite to the nurse. Even the ones who bite.

own.label: Ask where she wants to be in ten years
own.player: Where do you want to be in ten years?
own.reply: Running the whole place. Or a little clinic by the sea. I change my mind every shift. Ambition is just restlessness with a plan.

own.label: Ask what she grows on her balcony
own.player: What are you growing out there?
own.reply: Mint for dinner and chillies for revenge. Lavender too, for the nights I come home smelling of the station.

own.label: Ask what scares her at work
own.player: Does anything at work scare you?
own.reply: The quiet ones. The ones who say they’re fine and look at the wall. I’ve learned to sit with them a bit longer.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: They run a drugstore on the Sunfall Road, two doors from Nadia Okafor’s mom’s. The mothers are best friends and sworn enemies. Their window displays are a cold war.

own.label: Ask how she stays so neat
own.player: How do you stay that tidy in custody?
own.reply: I change my shirt twice a shift. Some nights three times. Clean white is a kindness to the next person. They’re having a bad enough night.

calls.label: Ask about the quiet girl
calls.player: Who was the quiet one you sat with?
calls.reply: A graduate student held overnight after a protest. She looked at the wall for an hour and said one thing: that she knew about the car and didn’t know how to stop it. Her name was Rosa Gutierrez. The custody sergeant was listening at the door, so I wrote nothing down.
calls.note: Leila Sayeed says Rosa Gutierrez, held overnight after a protest, said she knew about the car and didn’t know how to stop it.

life.news: My chillies are finally red. I’ve been waiting all summer. Revenge chillies.
life.more: Mint for dinner, chillies for revenge, lavender for the nights I come home smelling of the station. The chillies are for my brother, who said I couldn’t grow anything hotter than a radish. He’s coming to dinner. He’s not ready.

life.news: Long shift. Someone bit me. Everyone’s polite to the nurse. Even the ones who bite.
life.more: He apologized afterwards, which happens more than you’d think. I patch people up at both ends of the handcuffs, and tonight it was a lot of both ends. I’m on the balcony with the lavender, a cup of mint tea and my arm in a bandage. I’m fine.

life.news: Changed my mind again. Today I’m going to run the whole place one day. Yesterday it was a clinic by the sea.
life.more: I change my mind every shift. On good shifts I want to run the custody suite. On bad ones I want a little clinic by the sea where people come in with sunburn and splinters. Today was a good shift. Ask me tomorrow.

life.news: My mom and Nadia’s mom had a fight about whose pharmacy has the better window display. Again.
life.more: They’re two doors apart on Sunfall Road, best friends and worst enemies. This month it’s tinsel in the wrong season. Both of them called me to complain about the other. I love them both. I’m staying out of it.

gossip.says: A graduate student, Rosa Gutierrez, was brought in after a protest and sat looking at the wall all night. I sat with her. The quiet ones scare me more than the loud ones.
gossip.note: Leila Sayeed says Rosa Gutierrez was brought in after a protest and sat staring at the wall.
gossip.ask: Leila says she sat with you the night you were brought in.
gossip.answer: She did. She didn’t ask anything, she just stayed. I’d checked the lock on that cell twice in my head, which is a thing I do. She brought me tea in a paper cup. I haven’t thanked her. Tell her I will.

gossip.says: Nadia Okafor’s mom and my mom run pharmacies two doors apart and fight about everything. Nadia and I stay out of it and eat the cookies they both send.
gossip.note: Leila Sayeed says her mother and Nadia Okafor’s mother run rival pharmacies.
gossip.ask: Leila says your moms run rival pharmacies and you two just eat the cookies.
gossip.answer: Correct. Both mothers send cookies as weapons. We eat the weapons. Leila’s mom does a very good shortbread, but my mom’s is better, and if you repeat that in front of Leila I’ll deny it under oath.

gossip.says: Maya Serrano did the nursing course with me. She went to the hospital and I went to the station. We swap horror stories over cookies in the parking lot.
gossip.note: Leila Sayeed says she trained with Maya Serrano.
gossip.ask: Leila says you two swap horror stories in the parking lot.
gossip.answer: Every week! She wins on bites, I win on swallowed objects. Last week she had a man who’d glued himself to a police car. I had a man who’d swallowed a key. It’s a draw. The cookies are always mine.

women.name: Joanne Kendrick
women.look: Freckled fair skin, natural afro puff, thin wire-rimmed glasses, maroon fleece and jeans

own.label: Ask what dispatch is like
own.player: What’s it like being a dispatcher?
own.reply: People call me on the worst day of their lives and I have to sound calm. Then I hang up and shake. Then the next one rings.

own.label: Ask about her pottery
own.player: How’s the pottery going?
own.reply: I’ve made eleven bowls and none of them are round. My mom uses them anyway. She says they have character. They have holes.

own.label: Ask about the strangest call she’s taken
own.player: What’s the strangest call you’ve ever taken?
own.reply: A man who wanted us to arrest the moon because it was too bright. I logged it. Politely. You never know.

own.label: Ask how she switches off after a shift
own.player: How do you switch off after a shift?
own.reply: I don’t, really. I lie awake wondering how they all got on. You never find out. That’s the worst part.

own.label: Ask about Doreen
own.player: What’s Doreen like to work for?
own.reply: Twenty-two years on the phones and she’s heard everything twice. She taught me to sound calm. She didn’t teach me how to stop shaking after. I don’t think she has.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is it just you and your mom?
own.reply: Dad was a guard on the last passenger train out of Sunfall. He’s gone now. Mom cleans at the museum. She uses my bowls even though they leak. She says they have character.

calls.label: Ask about the call she can’t forget
calls.player: Is there a call you can’t get out of your head?
calls.reply: A woman, out of breath, on a payphone at the weigh station by the old junction. Someone was coming. I put her through to patrol. Patrol was on a private escort. Doreen said log it as a prank. I did. I hear her when I close my eyes.
calls.note: Joanne Kendrick took a payphone call from a frightened woman at the old junction’s weigh station on gala night, logged as a prank.

calls.label: Ask if she’s noticed anything at the station
calls.player: Seen anything odd at the station?
calls.reply: The guy from the motor pool keeps washing the gray sedan. Every day. Nobody washes a police car every day. Not here.
calls.note: Joanne Kendrick says a station mechanic keeps washing the gray sedan every day.

life.news: A man rang dispatch tonight and asked us to arrest the moon. He was very polite about it.
life.more: He said it was keeping him awake and looking at him funny. I sounded calm, like you have to. I told him we’d send someone to have a word with it. He thanked me and went to bed. Best call of the night.

life.news: Bad call tonight. I sounded calm. Then I hung up and shook.
life.more: You never find out how they got on. That’s the worst part. I lie awake wondering. I’m lying awake now. Talk to me about anything. Your day, the weather, what you had for dinner. Anything that ends well.

life.news: Made bowl number twelve at pottery. Still not round. It does hold soup, though.
life.more: My mom uses every one. She says they have character. They have holes. This one has no holes, which is progress, but it leans, so the soup goes to one side. Mom says that’s where the flavor goes.

life.news: My boyfriend fixed my car without being asked and then pretended he hadn’t.
life.more: Tyler works in the motor pool. My car was making a noise like a goose. Next morning, no goose. He said he didn’t touch it. There was oil on his sleeve. I’ve decided to let him keep his secret.

gossip.says: Sasha Mahoney built a model of how fast help reaches people who call us. I feed it every call I take. She checks on me after the bad ones, without saying that’s what she’s doing.
gossip.note: Joanne Kendrick says Sasha Mahoney built a model of how fast help reaches callers.
gossip.ask: Joanne says you check on her after bad calls without saying that’s what you’re doing.
gossip.answer: I ask her about her bowls. That’s all. If she talks about the bowls, she’s all right. If she doesn’t, I sit with her for a while. Statistically, the bowls are a very good indicator. Don’t tell her I’ve worked that out.

gossip.says: Cassidy Boone in records is my boyfriend’s big sister. She basically raised him on her own. She owns a van and turns up whenever anyone needs moving. Never asks for anything.
gossip.note: Joanne Kendrick says Cassidy Boone raised her brother and turns up with her van when anyone needs help.
gossip.ask: Joanne says you turn up with your van whenever anyone needs moving.
gossip.answer: Loyalty means turning up. I own a van, so I turn up with a van. Tyler’s a good guy. I raised him on chainsaw oil and canned spaghetti and he turned out all right. Joanne’s good for him. Tell her the van’s free whenever.

women.name: Cassidy Boone
women.look: Fair skin, short silver-dyed crop, amber eyes, denim shirt with rolled sleeves

own.label: Ask what the records room is like
own.player: What’s it like down in the records room?
own.reply: Quiet. Dusty. Every file is somebody’s worst week, filed alphabetically. I like it down there. Paper doesn’t lie to you.

own.label: Ask about her sketches
own.player: What do you sketch?
own.reply: Old shopfronts before they’re knocked down. The barber’s, the cobbler’s, the old movie theater. Somebody should remember what this town looked like.

own.label: Ask what loyalty means to her
own.player: What does loyalty mean to you?
own.reply: Turning up. Twice, if needed. Most people say they’d help you move house. I actually own a van.

own.label: Ask if a file ever stayed with her
own.player: Has a file ever stayed with you?
own.reply: One. An old case nobody closed. I read it every few weeks. Someone ought to keep looking, even if it’s only me.

own.label: Ask if she’s good at helping people move
own.player: Are you the friend with the van?
own.reply: I am the friend with the van, and I actually turn up. That’s rarer than it should be. Bring cookies and lift the heavy end.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Where are the Boones from?
own.reply: Up in the hills. Logging, until the logging went. Dad repairs chainsaws and says about nine words a day. Mom left for a preacher when I was eleven. Dad and I are fine. Quiet, but fine.

calls.label: Ask about the case she rereads
calls.player: Which old case do you keep rereading?
calls.reply: Ellis Dane, fourteen years ago. Married a Bluebird. Drowned at a club regatta. A witness said he was sober and the boat was tampered with. Closed as misadventure by a young detective constable called Vic Lowry. I read it every few weeks.
calls.note: Cassidy Boone says the Ellis Dane drowning was closed as misadventure by Vic Lowry when he was a young detective.

calls.label: Ask what her pull cards show
calls.player: Who’s been pulling files lately?
calls.reply: I keep the stubs of every file pulled and by whom. Lately the stubs say a sergeant took the sign-out sheet for the gala cabinet the week a man vanished, and the sheet that came back was blank.
calls.note: Cassidy Boone’s records show Sergeant Lowry pulled the gala cabinet’s sign-out sheet, which came back blank.

life.news: Drew the old movie theater lobby this morning before they board it up. Got every bit of the ceiling.
life.more: Somebody should draw the town before they knock it down. Apparently it’s me and one other girl. The ceiling has painted stars on it, faded almost to nothing. I got them all. I’ll give a copy to the man who used to sell the tickets. He’s ninety.

life.news: Spent my lunch break reading an old case nobody ever closed. I do it every few weeks.
life.more: Every file is somebody’s worst week, filed alphabetically. Paper doesn’t lie. This one’s fourteen years old and nobody’s looked at it but me. Someone ought to keep looking, even if it’s only me. Sorry. Records room thoughts.

life.news: Helped Pat at the hardware shop move a cabinet. Got paid in screws.
life.more: I live over her shop. She’s seventy-eight and stronger than me. They’re very good screws, and I’ve been wanting them for a shelf. She knew that. That’s how Old Town pays you: in exactly what you needed.

life.news: Dad’s chainsaw repair business is slow again. He won’t take money.
life.more: He came down from the hills when the logging went and now he fixes chainsaws for the few people who still need them. I drove out with a pie. He fixed my van instead of eating it. That’s my family. We fix things instead of talking.

gossip.says: Helen Markham comes down to records more than any other sergeant. She reads old files standing up and never signs anything out. I’ve stopped asking.
gossip.note: Cassidy Boone says Helen Markham reads old files in records and never signs them out.
gossip.ask: Cassidy says you read old files standing up and never sign them out.
gossip.answer: Cassidy notices more than anyone in that building and says less. I read standing up because it’s quicker. I don’t sign out because I’m only looking. If she’s noticed, she’ll have noticed which ones. That’s between her and me. And now, apparently, you.

gossip.says: Eleanor Graves brings me a coffee every time she wants a file, and it’s always from the good van, not the station. That’s how you know she means it.
gossip.note: Cassidy Boone says Eleanor Graves brings her good coffee when she wants a file.
gossip.ask: Cassidy says you bring her good coffee whenever you want a file.
gossip.answer: The station coffee is a crime. Cassidy finds things in that basement nobody else could. The least I can do is bring her something that tastes like coffee. Bribery is a strong word. It’s a thank-you in advance.

gossip.says: Joanne Kendrick on dispatch is going out with my little brother Tyler. She makes bowls that aren’t round and she’s the best thing that’s ever happened to him.
gossip.note: Cassidy Boone says Joanne Kendrick is going out with her brother Tyler.
gossip.ask: Cassidy says you’re the best thing that’s ever happened to her brother.
gossip.answer: She said that? Cassidy doesn’t say things like that. She says them with her van. Tyler’s lovely. He fixed my car and pretended he didn’t. I’m making Cassidy a bowl. It won’t be round. She’ll use it anyway.

women.name: Naoko Watanabe
women.look: Light-brown skin, blunt black bob, rosy cheeks, windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do at the station?
own.reply: Victim liaison. I sit with the families of the dead and the missing and explain what the police are doing, mostly when the police are doing nothing. I’m very good at silence.

own.label: Ask how she switches off
own.player: How do you switch off after work?
own.reply: I drive out past the canyon, lie on the hood of the car and look up. Out there the sky’s so full you forget the lodge has lights.

own.label: Ask why she’s so quiet
own.player: You don’t say much.
own.reply: I say exactly enough. People in the worst week of their lives don’t want a talker. They want someone who stays in the chair.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: They run a restaurant. The club’s smaller dinners used to be in our back room. I grew up carrying plates past women who never looked at me once.

own.label: Ask how work has been
own.player: Rough week at work?
own.reply: A man I work with has gone missing. Dale. He showed me where the kettle was on my first day. His last call was to his wife, saying he’d be late because the sergeant wanted him to sign something in the basement. The guys say he ran off with a woman. His wages are sitting in an envelope nobody will give her.
own.note: Naoko Watanabe says Dale Pruett’s last call was from the station basement, about signing something for the sergeant; his wages sit in an envelope the station won’t give his wife.

calls.label: Ask her to tell you about a star
calls.player: Tell me about a star.
calls.reply: There’s one low in the west in the evening that isn’t a star at all. It’s a planet. It doesn’t twinkle, because it isn’t far enough away to lie. I like things that aren’t far enough away to lie.

calls.label: Ask how she spends her evenings
calls.player: What do you do in the evenings now?
calls.reply: I’m at the Pruett house most nights. Homework with the boys, the shopping for Carla. Liaison is supposed to mean you don’t take sides. I’ve taken one.

life.news: Clear night past the canyon. I counted shooting stars until I lost count.
life.more: Lay on the hood with a blanket and a thermos of my mother’s tea. No radio, no signal, just the hum of the car cooling. I felt like a person again by the end of it. I drove home very slowly so it would last.

life.news: Sat with a mother whose son hasn’t come home. Six hours. I didn’t have one single thing to tell her.
life.more: She made me tea three times because she needed to do something with her hands. I drank every cup. The detective never came. At the end she thanked me for staying, and that’s the part that gets me, every single time.

life.news: Someone left a bag of oranges on my desk with no note. Third time this month.
life.more: Good ones, the expensive kind. I asked everyone. Nobody admits it. I’ve started to suspect the custody sergeant, who has never said a kind word to anyone in his life. If it’s him I’m going to have to rethink everything.

life.news: My mother taught me her dumpling fold. Fifty dumplings later I can almost do it.
life.more: Pleat, pinch, turn. Hers look like little purses. Mine look like they’ve been in an accident. She ate one of mine first, on purpose, and said it tasted the same. It didn’t. That’s the nicest lie anyone’s told me all year.

gossip.says: Imani Harper is the only person at the station who asks how I am and waits for the answer. She knows where everything in the building is kept. Everything.
gossip.note: Naoko Watanabe says Imani Harper knows where everything at the station is kept.
gossip.ask: Naoko says you know where everything in the building is kept.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to. Naoko sits with the worst news in Sunfall and still says thank you to the cleaners. If she ever asks me where something is, I’ll tell her, and I won’t ask why. Tell her that. She’ll know what I mean.

gossip.says: Cassidy Boone has a file on her desk she won’t let anyone touch, not even to move it for a coffee cup. I sat next to her for a week. She never opened it once.
gossip.note: Naoko Watanabe says Cassidy Boone keeps a file on her desk that nobody may touch.
gossip.ask: Naoko says you keep a file nobody’s allowed to touch.
gossip.answer: It’s old, it’s mine, and it was closed by someone who shouldn’t have closed it. I don’t open it at work because I don’t want anyone to see my face while I read it. Naoko notices everything. That’s why I like her.

women.name: Brenda Velasco
women.look: Lean and wiry, golden-tan skin, high sharp cheekbones, hooded dark eyes, a strong nose, a chestnut high ponytail, thin wire-rimmed glasses, an olive field jacket

own.label: Ask what a collision investigator does
own.player: What does a collision investigator actually do?
own.reply: I measure skid marks and work out who’s lying. Everyone says the other car came out of nowhere. Nothing comes out of nowhere.

own.label: Ask about her rescue dog
own.player: Tell me about your dog.
own.reply: Biscuit. He’s fourteen, half blind and convinced the mailman is the devil. He sleeps on my feet. I’d die for him.

own.label: Ask what she’s most skeptical about
own.player: What are you most skeptical about?
own.reply: Men who say they’re great drivers. Every single one. I have the photographs.

own.label: Ask if the job changed how she drives
own.player: Has the job changed how you drive?
own.reply: I drive like my grandmother now. I hold my breath at every junction. I’ve seen what a second does.

own.label: Ask about her dad
own.player: How did you end up in collisions?
own.reply: Dad ran the breakdown truck in the canyon for thirty years. He pulled every wreck off that road. I used to ride along. You learn to read a road from the tow hook end.

own.label: Ask what she’s like off duty
own.player: What are you like when you’re not measuring skid marks?
own.reply: Exactly the same, but in slippers. Biscuit sleeps on my feet and growls at the mailman, and I drink tea out of a mug that says world’s okayest driver.

calls.label: Ask about Paul Sanderson’s crash
calls.player: What was wrong with the crash at the old junction?
calls.reply: No skid marks. A man brakes when he’s about to die. Paul Sanderson didn’t, or couldn’t. There was a second set of tire tracks. I said so and was moved off the case. Four crashes at that junction in nine years. All Foundation men. All weather.
calls.note: Brenda Velasco says the four crashes at the old junction, all Foundation men, had no skid marks and a second set of tire tracks.

calls.label: Ask what she found at the weigh station
calls.player: Did you find anything at the weigh station?
calls.reply: Fresh tracks in the yard, a gray sedan’s, beside a window with blood on the frame. I photographed the window. The photo’s in Markham’s drawer.
calls.note: Brenda Velasco found gray sedan tracks and blood on a window frame at the old junction’s weigh station.

life.news: Biscuit barked at the mailman for a full minute. He’s half blind, so he barked at a bin. I’m so proud.
life.more: He’s fourteen and sure the mailman is the devil. Today the devil came and Biscuit stood up and defended the house against a trash can. The mailman watched the whole thing and gave him a treat. Biscuit still doesn’t trust him.

life.news: A man told me today he’s a great driver. He’d just reversed into a lamppost.
life.more: Men who say they’re great drivers are the reason I measure skid marks. Everyone says the other car came out of nowhere. Nothing comes out of nowhere. He said the lamppost moved. Lampposts don’t move. I wrote that down.

life.news: My dad’s breakdown truck sold today. Thirty years of pulling wrecks off the canyon road.
life.more: He’s been gone a while and the truck’s been sitting in a yard. A young man bought it for his own business. I gave him Dad’s gloves with it. He didn’t understand why I was crying. I didn’t explain. I drove home like my grandmother, holding my breath.

life.news: Cycled out past the canyon on my day off. Saw a road runner. It was faster than me.
life.more: I cycle on days off because it’s the only way I can be on a road without measuring anything. The road runner ran alongside me for a bit like we were racing. I lost. It didn’t even look back. Smug bird.

gossip.says: Isabel Morales trains horses on a ranch past the canyon. Five generations on that land. I pass it on the road and she always waves with her whole arm.
gossip.note: Brenda Velasco says Isabel Morales trains horses on a five-generation ranch past the canyon.
gossip.ask: Brenda says you always wave with your whole arm when she drives past.
gossip.answer: You have to wave with your whole arm on that road or nobody sees you! Brenda drives so slowly I could ride alongside her. I think she’s lovely. Horses can tell, you know. Mine all stand still when her car goes past.

gossip.says: Nine years ago I was the young officer on Sofia Delgado’s father’s accident. My dad’s truck pulled the van off the canyon road. I sat with her in the cab. She doesn’t know that was me.
gossip.note: Brenda Velasco says she was the young officer at Sofia Delgado’s father’s accident.
gossip.ask: Brenda says she was the officer who sat with you in the breakdown cab, the night of your father’s van.
gossip.answer: That was her? I remember a young officer with a blanket who sat with me in the cab and didn’t say it would be all right, because she didn’t know. I’ve always been grateful for that. Tell her I’m buying her a coffee. I’ll find her. I always find people.

women.name: Alisha Benton
women.look: Lean and athletic, olive skin, a slightly crooked nose from an old break, intense dark eyes, honey-blonde beach waves, a windbreaker over a sports top

own.label: Ask if forensics is like on television
own.player: Is forensic work like it is on television?
own.reply: On television it takes an afternoon and a dramatic zoom. Here it takes two weeks and a form. Nobody has ever said enhance to me.

own.label: Ask about her old cameras
own.player: What’s the appeal of old film cameras?
own.reply: You only get thirty-six chances, so you have to mean it. Phones turned everyone into people who take a thousand pictures of nothing.

own.label: Ask what she notices about people first
own.player: What do you notice about people first?
own.reply: Their hands. Bitten nails, paint, rings they keep turning. Hands tell you what faces are trained to hide.

own.label: Ask if there’s a film she’s never developed
own.player: Is there a roll of film you’ve never developed?
own.reply: One. My dad’s last roll. I’m scared it’s just the garden. I’m more scared it isn’t.

own.label: Ask where she develops film
own.player: Where do you develop your film?
own.reply: My bathroom’s a darkroom. My towels are a tragedy. Every camera on my shelf was dead when I found it. I like bringing things back.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: Who taught you about cameras?
own.reply: Dad. Ray Benton, wedding photographer, the kindest man in the county. He died of a heart attack in the club’s garden, mid-wedding, with a roll in the camera. The club sent flowers.

own.label: Ask about her nose
own.player: How did you break your nose?
own.reply: Sparring. A fitness instructor called Lauren broke it and then cried more than I did. I kept the bend. It’s my favorite thing about my face now.

calls.label: Ask what the fire chemistry said
calls.player: What did the lab say about Vale’s fire?
calls.reply: Set by somebody who knew nothing about fire, with something bought at a garden center. Amateurs leave a lot of chemistry. Whoever it was burned their hands, I’d bet my best camera.
calls.note: Alisha Benton says Vale’s fire was set by an amateur using garden-center accelerant, who probably burned their hands.

calls.label: Ask who asked about the lab’s negatives
calls.player: Has anyone been asking about the lab?
calls.reply: A woman from the club, Genevieve Locke, twice, very lightly, whether we keep negatives of what we process. Nobody asks that lightly twice.
calls.note: Alisha Benton says Genevieve Locke has twice asked whether the police lab keeps negatives.

life.news: Brought an old camera back to life tonight. It hadn’t taken a picture in thirty years. First frame: my toast.
life.more: You get thirty-six chances on film, so you have to mean it. I meant the toast. It’s a very good piece of toast. Phones turned everyone into people who take a thousand pictures of nothing. I took one picture of something. Breakfast.

life.news: Boxing class. Lauren hit me on the nose by accident. Same nose as last time.
life.more: It’s already a bit crooked from an old break. Lauren teaches the class and she was mortified. I told her it’s my good side anyway. Ice and a film tonight. Don’t ask me to smile in any photos for a week.

life.news: A sample came back from the lab with a fingerprint on the outside of the bag. Mine. I’m very embarrassed.
life.more: On television it takes an afternoon and a dramatic zoom. Here it takes two weeks and a form, and sometimes the form is because you touched the bag. Everyone laughed. I’m taping a sign to my own glove.

life.news: Looked at my dad’s last roll of film again. Didn’t develop it. Again.
life.more: I keep it in a drawer. I’m scared it’s just the garden. I’m more scared it isn’t. Some nights I take it out, hold it and put it back. Tonight was one of those. Tell me something good. Something with a happy ending.

gossip.says: Lauren Bishop teaches boxing at my gym and she’s the cheeriest person who’s ever punched me in the face. She apologized for twenty minutes. Then she did it again.
gossip.note: Alisha Benton says Lauren Bishop, the fitness instructor, broke her nose by accident.
gossip.ask: Alisha says you’re the cheeriest person who’s ever punched her in the face.
gossip.answer: It was an ACCIDENT. Twice! She’s got very fast feet and a very slow face! I brought her flowers and a bag of frozen peas with a bow on it. We’re fine. Derek in my class says she’s a menace. Derek’s not wrong.

gossip.says: Nadia Okafor sits next to me in the lab and labels bags so neatly you could frame them. She hums when she’s concentrating. Always the same song. Nobody knows what it is.
gossip.note: Alisha Benton says Nadia Okafor hums the same song while she works.
gossip.ask: Alisha says you hum the same song at work and nobody knows what it is.
gossip.answer: It’s my grandmother’s. She sang it while she watered the roses. I didn’t know I hummed it at work. Now I’ll be thinking about it all week. Thank you so much. Details don’t lie, and apparently neither does my humming.

gossip.says: Delia Maher restores old cameras like I do. She’s eighteen and more patient than anyone in my lab. I’d hire her tomorrow if she’d stop being a reporter.
gossip.note: Alisha Benton says Delia Maher restores old cameras and is extraordinarily patient.
gossip.ask: Alisha says she’d hire you tomorrow if you’d stop being a reporter.
gossip.answer: That’s a lovely offer and I’m going to decline it on principle. I’m patient for a young person. That’s the trick. Everyone my age wants to go viral. I want to be right. Alisha wants to be right too. We get on.

women.name: Miranda Sowerby
women.look: Fair skin, a sleek low bun, a wide bright smile, charcoal blazer and turtleneck

women.name: Yvette Palmer
women.look: Rosy fair skin, brown waves with teal tips, sharp winged eyeliner, black leather jacket over a white tee

women.name: Katrina Ford
women.look: Pale skin, chestnut curly bob, freckles across her nose, windbreaker over a sports top

women.name: Monica Herrera
women.look: Golden-tan skin, auburn shag with a curtain fringe, rosy cheeks, charcoal blazer and turtleneck

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What does a public safety statistician do?
own.reply: I build models that count things. Protests, calls, car crashes. Sasha Mahoney is my boss. She tells me the odds. I go and look anyway.

own.label: Ask how she gets around
own.player: How do you get around town?
own.reply: The station’s pool car, too fast. I can’t leave a mystery alone, and I can’t drive slowly toward one either. I’ve had two warnings from my own department.

own.label: Ask what she does on her day off
own.player: What do you do on your day off?
own.reply: I teach my cousin Mateo guitar, because my mom taught me. He’s twelve and he only wants to play one song. It’s a good song. I’m starting to hate it.

own.label: Ask who’s at home
own.player: Who’s at home?
own.reply: My dad, who’s slow since his stroke. My big sister Paz comes for family lunch every week, argues with him about everything, then does the dishes. I’m the one who stays.

own.label: Ask about her mom
own.player: What was your mom like?
own.reply: A school secretary who knew every kid’s name. On her last night she asked me to look after Paz. Paz was always the one with the matches. I promised. Paz doesn’t know.

own.label: Ask what she’s been counting lately
own.player: Counting anything interesting lately?
own.reply: The Back Row’s meetings, against the professor’s accidents. Nobody asked me to. The pattern was just there. The campus security logs have names in them, and one of the names is my sister’s.
own.note: Monica Herrera has counted the Back Row’s meetings against Professor Vale’s accidents; campus security logs put her sister Paz Herrera in the room.

calls.label: Ask if anything has turned up twice in her data
calls.player: Has anything turned up twice in your data?
calls.reply: A grey sedan. Logged on campus the night before the fire, and on the Sunfall Road after the gala, same plate. I have the registration. I haven’t told anyone. The first person I’d tell is the problem.
calls.note: Monica Herrera says the same grey sedan was logged on campus the night before Vale’s fire and on the Sunfall Road after the gala.

calls.label: Ask if she’s ever been engaged
calls.player: Have you ever been engaged?
calls.reply: Once, to a Bluebird’s cousin. He took me to dinner at the lodge, and the dinner had a guest list. I read it. I gave him the ring back in the parking lot.

life.news: Mateo played the whole song through without stopping. Twelve years old and he bowed. I cried a bit.
life.more: Three months of the same four chords. Today he got the change in the middle right and looked up at me like he’d invented music. My mom taught me that song. I didn’t tell him. I just clapped too long.

life.news: My model says more trouble happens on nights with no moon. Sasha says that’s a coincidence. Sasha also says coincidences are rare.
life.more: I ran it three ways. Burglaries, calls about lights, a bear. Nights with no moon win every time. Keiko Nakamura saw the same thing and stopped talking about it. I haven’t stopped. I just talk about it more quietly.

life.news: Paz and Dad had the big fight at lunch again. I did the dishes this time. She left without saying bye.
life.more: Politics, always. Dad says she wants to burn everything down. She says somebody has to. I stood at the sink and didn’t take a side, which is the only side anyone in my family ever leaves for me.

life.news: Got a speeding warning from my own department. In the pool car. On the way to a meeting about road safety.
life.more: The officer was very kind about it. He said, Monica, you made the slides. I said I know. He said, the slide with the speed limits. I said I know. It was a really good slide.

gossip.says: Sasha Mahoney, my boss, knows the odds of everything and runs a book club where nobody has finished a book since spring.
gossip.note: Monica Herrera says her boss Sasha Mahoney runs a book club where nobody finishes the book.
gossip.ask: Monica Herrera says nobody in your book club has finished a book since spring.
gossip.answer: Statistically, somebody should have by now. We’re on chapter two. We drink wine and talk about our exes. Monica came once, finished the book in a night and was never invited back. She broke the model.

gossip.says: Keiko Nakamura gets a box of crime novels from her grandmother every few weeks and reads them all. She’s the only analyst I know who solves the made-up ones too.
gossip.note: Monica Herrera says Keiko Nakamura reads the boxes of crime novels her grandmother sends.
gossip.ask: Monica says you solve the crime novels your grandmother sends before the end.
gossip.answer: Usually by chapter four. Grandmother chooses them to defeat me. She has not succeeded in two years. Monica borrows them and tells me who did it before I start. I have stopped lending.

women.name: Kelsey Donovan
women.look: Fair skin, rose-gold bob, a gap-toothed smile, black leather jacket over a white tee

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What’s it like in the evidence archive?
own.reply: Nine years in the basement with the boxes. Quiet. I like the quiet. Imani Harper started a while back and labels everything like it’s a birthday present. I’ve got very protective of her.

own.label: Ask what she does after hours
own.player: What do you do after hours?
own.reply: I play records in the archive. Singers who made one album and vanished. The archive doesn’t mind. The boxes have heard worse.

own.label: Ask about her leather jacket
own.player: Is that leather jacket a statement?
own.reply: I bought it at seventeen and I’m not giving it up. I know how it looks. Some things you keep because they knew you before.

own.label: Ask how she ended up at the station
own.player: How did you end up at the station?
own.reply: I was seventeen and in trouble. A young detective got me a civilian job instead of a record. Eighteen years ago. I’d do anything for him. He’s never once noticed.

own.label: Ask what’s new with her
own.player: Anything new with you?
own.reply: New furniture. An inheritance from an aunt in the city. Nobody asks which aunt. The guys at work don’t ask much. You’re not going to ask, are you?
own.note: Kelsey Donovan’s apartment is newly furnished with what she calls an inheritance from an aunt in the city.

calls.label: Ask about her mom
calls.player: Is your mom in Sunfall?
calls.reply: In a home on the edge of town. A nice one now. I see her every week. She ran room service on the motel strip when I was a kid. She still folds napkins into swans for the nurses.

calls.label: Ask if anything in the archive bothers her
calls.player: Is there anything in the archive that bothers you?
calls.reply: Shelf nine, bottom row. A box with a case number that doesn’t exist. It was there before Imani started. If anything ever happens to me, I want Imani to open it. Not anyone else. Promise me that.
calls.note: Kelsey Donovan says a box on shelf nine of the evidence archive has a case number that does not exist, and wants Imani Harper to open it if anything happens to her.

life.news: Found a record at the market by a singer who made one album and vanished. Played it in the archive until the lights clicked off.
life.more: A woman with a voice like a cracked bell. Nine songs and then nothing. I like the ones who stopped. You wonder if they were happier after. I hope so. Somebody should be.

life.news: Imani labeled an evidence box today with a little drawing of a cactus on it. Against regulations. I let it go.
life.more: It was a box of stolen garden gnomes, so honestly, it fit. She looked so worried when I noticed. I said it was the best label in the building. It is. I may start drawing on mine.

life.news: Saw my mom today. She didn’t know who I was for a minute. Then she did. That minute.
life.more: Some weeks she’s sharp as anything and folds napkins into swans for the nurses. Today she looked at me like a stranger, and then she said, Kels, you’ve cut your hair. I haven’t. I said yes.

life.news: A detective I’ve known forever said thanks today. Just thanks. I’ve been floating all afternoon.
life.more: Eighteen years and he says thanks maybe twice a year. I filed something for him fast, and he tapped the desk on his way past and said, thanks, Kels. That’s it. That’s the whole story. I’m embarrassed by how good it was.

gossip.says: Imani Harper labels every evidence box like it’s a birthday present and keeps thirty-two cacti at home. I’d fight anyone who was mean to her.
gossip.note: Kelsey Donovan says she is protective of Imani Harper at the evidence archive.
gossip.ask: Kelsey Donovan says she’d fight anyone who was mean to you.
gossip.answer: She would. She nearly did, once, to a detective who called me the new girl for six months. Kelsey plays old records in the archive after hours. Sad ones. I pretend I don’t notice she’s crying. She pretends I’m not there. It works.

gossip.says: Nadia Okafor from the lab does the hardest crossword in the paper in pencil, in under an hour. She looks at people like they’re clues. Including me.
gossip.note: Kelsey Donovan says Nadia Okafor looks at people like crossword clues.
gossip.ask: Kelsey says you look at people like they’re clues, including her.
gossip.answer: Everyone’s a clue. Most are easy. Kelsey is a hard one. Lovely, kind, plays sad records, and lately she wears a watch that costs more than my car. A good clue hides in plain sight.
