women.name: Adriana Ponce
women.look: Golden-tan skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, a beauty mark above her lip, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask why she campaigns
own.player: Why climate campaigning?
own.reply: Because my town in Sonora ran out of water when I was twelve. People argue about models. I remember the taps.

own.label: Ask about her soccer
own.player: Five-on-five, I heard?
own.reply: Every week with women half my age. I’m slower and dirtier. They’re learning a lot.

own.label: Ask what she makes of the young activists
own.player: What do you make of the younger activists?
own.reply: They’re brave and they’re online. They mistake a hashtag for a hard week’s work. I tell them: knock on doors, or go home. They hate me. They come back.

own.label: Ask what she got wrong when she was young
own.player: What did you get wrong when you were young?
own.reply: I thought shouting was the same as winning. It isn’t. The people I changed were the ones I had a coffee with.

own.label: Ask about the photographs on her wall
own.player: What are all the photos on your wall?
own.reply: Towns that ran out of water. Mine is the first one, top left. A river sold upstream when I was twelve. My family came north the year the taps stopped.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: What did your parents do here?
own.reply: Dad was a mechanic who became a janitor. Mom cleaned houses and sang while she did it. I learned organizing from watching her get six rich houses to pay on time.

calls.label: Ask about the torn page in the journal
calls.player: What was on the page torn out of the journal?
calls.reply: The night before we voted to join the protest, someone wrote in the shared journal: three names and a parking lot bay number. Vanessa’s hand. The next morning the page was gone. I read it before it went.
calls.note: Adriana Ponce read a torn-out journal page in Vanessa Greer’s hand listing three names and a parking lot bay.

life.news: Scored at five-on-five. Not against Sable, she was off injured, but I’m counting it.
life.more: Soccer with women half my age. I’m slower and dirtier and I’ve got more to prove. They’re learning a lot. I scored with my shin. A goal off the shin counts double when you’re thirty-six.

life.news: My daughter told me I’m embarrassing. In front of her friends. In my soccer uniform.
life.more: Lupe’s sixteen. Everything I do is embarrassing, and the soccer uniform is the worst of it. I said I’ll stop embarrassing you when the reservoir’s full. She rolled her eyes. Later she asked when the next match is. That’s my girl.

life.news: Knocked on forty doors today. Thirty-eight people shut them. Two invited me in for coffee.
life.more: They mistake a hashtag for a hard week’s work. Knock on doors or go home. I thought shouting was winning, once. The people I changed were the ones I had coffee with. Two today. That’s a good day. Most days it’s none.

life.news: Saw a photo of my town in Sonora. The river’s still dry.
life.more: It ran dry when I was twelve. Somebody sold it upstream. People argue about models. I remember the taps. I keep a wall of photos of towns that ran out of water. Today I added one more. I’d like to stop adding them.

gossip.says: Rosa Gutierrez wrote the only honest thing about water anyone in Sunfall has written this year. Her thesis. I’ve tried to take her for coffee twice. She keeps saying she’s busy.
gossip.note: Adriana Ponce says Rosa Gutierrez’s water thesis is the only honest thing written in Sunfall this year.
gossip.ask: Adriana says your thesis is the only honest thing anyone’s written in Sunfall this year.
gossip.answer: She said that? Adriana doesn’t say nice things. She says true things, and they sometimes happen to be nice. I’ll have coffee with her. I keep meaning to. Tell her yes. Tell her I said yes before I could check the lock.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland gives most of her wages away and brings soup to every meeting. She’s blunt because the world’s on fire. I told her to knock on doors. She did. She’s better at it than me.
gossip.note: Adriana Ponce says Eden Sutherland gives away most of her wages and is brilliant at knocking on doors.
gossip.ask: Adriana says you’re better at knocking on doors than she is.
gossip.answer: I’m not better. I’m younger, and nobody slams a door on a girl holding soup. Adriana taught me to say one sentence and then shut up. It works. She’s terrifying and right, which is the worst combination.

gossip.says: Sasha Mahoney plays for the other five-on-five team and she counts my touches. Literally. She knows the odds of me scoring before I take the shot.
gossip.note: Adriana Ponce says Sasha Mahoney calculates the odds at five-on-five.
gossip.ask: Adriana says you work out her odds of scoring before she shoots.
gossip.answer: Eleven percent from outside the box, thirty-two inside. She knows that. She shoots from outside anyway. I know the odds and ignore them. She doesn’t know them and ignores them anyway. We’re very well matched.

women.name: Sienna Navarro
women.look: Olive skin, burgundy-dyed curls, gray-green eyes, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask what she’s organizing
own.player: What are you organizing at the moment?
own.reply: A mural on the underpass. Forty volunteers, three committees and one argument about whether a cactus is problematic. It’s a cactus.

own.label: Ask about the drums
own.player: How are the drums going?
own.reply: Loudly. My neighbor bangs on the wall in time now. I think we’re a band.

own.label: Ask what she overthinks most
own.player: What do you overthink the most?
own.reply: Group chats. If I put a period, am I angry? If I don’t, am I unserious? I once drafted a thumbs-up for ten minutes.

own.label: Ask if she ever tires of causes
own.player: Do you ever get tired of causes?
own.reply: All the time. Some days I just want to paint something pretty that doesn’t mean anything. I’m not allowed to say that at meetings.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What do your parents do?
own.reply: Dad painted houses and Mom sold them. That’s the whole economy in one marriage. I paint walls nobody can sell. I think that’s growth.

own.label: Ask how she got into organizing
own.player: How did you end up organizing?
own.reply: I was a shy art student. Organizing turned out to be a way of being in a room without anyone looking at me. Everyone looks at the clipboard.

calls.label: Ask about the crescent on the mural
calls.player: Why is there a crescent moon on the underpass mural?
calls.reply: A volunteer added it and we voted to keep it, for the desert nights. Then Hana Park told me that crescent is a design somebody paid cash for, and it’s on a flyer for something called the Midnight Rite. The volunteer was a girl called Sorrel, and she paints the night sky like she’s been told where the stars go.
calls.note: Sienna Navarro says the mural’s crescent was added by Sorrel Vane, and the same design is on the Midnight Rite flyer.

life.news: Forty volunteers, three committees and a two-hour argument about whether a cactus is problematic. It’s a cactus.
life.more: The underpass mural. Someone said the cactus was a lazy symbol of the desert. Someone else said it was a symbol of resilience. Someone else said the cactus was a cactus. That was me. We voted. The cactus stays.

life.news: Zadie banged on the wall in time again. We did a whole new song. Neither of us said a word about it after.
life.more: My neighbor. I drum badly when I’m stressed, and she bangs on the wall in time, and over months it’s become a kind of band. We nod in the hallway like strangers. It’s the best band in Sunfall and it has a wall in the middle.

life.news: Drafted a thumbs-up in a group chat for ten minutes. Sent nothing.
life.more: If I put a period, am I angry? If I don’t, am I unserious? Committees have destroyed me. I just wanted to say yes to a paint order. From now on I’m only communicating by mural.

life.news: Painted something pretty that doesn’t mean anything. A cup of tea. Best thing I’ve done all year.
life.more: Some days I just want to paint something that isn’t a cause. A cup of tea on a windowsill, with steam. No message, no committee, no cactus. It’s going in my kitchen, and nobody’s allowed to ask what it represents.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster lives next door and reviews bands for the paper, and she’s in my band without ever having touched a drum. She bangs on the wall. In time.
gossip.note: Sienna Navarro says Zadie Foster plays in her band by banging on the wall.
gossip.ask: Sienna says you’re in her band and you’ve never touched a drum.
gossip.answer: I’m the rhythm section. The wall is my instrument. She thinks I can’t tell her stress drumming from her happy drumming. I can. Stress is faster. Tell her the bridge last night was a four. Possibly a four and a half.

gossip.says: Hana Park designs logos for companies that won’t exist next year. She redid the lettering on our mural for free because she said the original was a crime.
gossip.note: Sienna Navarro says Hana Park redid the mural’s lettering for free.
gossip.ask: Sienna says you redid the mural lettering because the original was a crime.
gossip.answer: It was a crime! Somebody used a font that looked like it was apologizing. I couldn’t sleep. I did it for free so I could walk through that underpass without wincing. Ugly and alive is fine. Ugly and apologetic is not.

gossip.says: Cassandra Finch brings cake to every meeting and votes however she likes. Nobody can argue with her because she’s holding the cake.
gossip.note: Sienna Navarro says Cassandra Finch brings cake to every meeting and votes as she pleases.
gossip.ask: Sienna says nobody can argue with you because you’re holding the cake.
gossip.answer: That’s the strategy. Bring a lemon drizzle and vote how you like. I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down, and cake helps. Sienna once tried bringing a cake too. A cactus-shaped one. Very brave.

women.name: Nora Hadley
women.look: Warm brown skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, a silver ear cuff, vintage windbreaker

own.label: Ask what her heresy is
own.player: What’s an opinion your friends hate?
own.reply: That nuclear power is the best thing for the climate. Say that in our group chat and watch people combust. Ironically.

own.label: Ask about learning Italian
own.player: You’re learning Italian?
own.reply: Badly. I want to read Dante in the original before I die. Ambitious, for someone who still says grazie wrong.

own.label: Ask what’s bothering her
own.player: Something on your mind?
own.reply: A woman from our march saw something on gala night. She told me, then a week later she told the police the exact opposite. Someone got to her.
own.note: Nora Hadley says a witness changed her story about gala night after someone got to her.

own.label: Ask what she believes that her friends don’t
own.player: What do you believe that your friends don’t?
own.reply: That men and women want different things, mostly, and that’s fine. Saying it at a meeting is like admitting you eat meat.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What does your dad do?
own.reply: He’s a surveyor. He surveyed the ridge road once and said it was fine. Mom’s a school nurse. I’m the nobody in particular they made, with opinions.

own.label: Ask what she reads
own.player: What are you reading?
own.reply: Italian grammar, badly, and everything in the library by people who were wrong in public and survived it. I’d like to be wrong in public one day. Properly.

calls.label: Ask about her father’s survey
calls.player: Is something wrong with your dad’s survey?
calls.reply: He said the ridge road was fine. It isn’t fine. Trucks go up it at night that the survey says can’t. I think somebody paid him to say so, and I think he knows I think it.
calls.note: Nora Hadley suspects her father was paid to sign off the ridge road as safe.

life.news: Said nuclear power in the group chat. Three people left. One came back to argue. Progress.
life.more: Nuclear is the best thing for the climate. Say that in our group chat and watch people combust. Ironically. The one who came back wrote me four paragraphs. I wrote five. We’re meeting for coffee. It might be a date. Or a duel.

life.news: Read a canto of Dante in the original. It took four hours. I understood about a third.
life.more: I want to read Dante in the original before I die. Ambitious for someone who still says grazie wrong. I read it with a friend from the library and we argued about one word for forty minutes. She was right. I’ll never admit it.

life.news: Years ago I argued with a teacher until she cried. Today I saw her in the supermarket.
life.more: I was right. I was also fifteen and cruel about it. That’s when I learned that being right is something you have to carry carefully. I said hello. She said hello back and asked what I’m reading. I nearly cried in the cereal aisle.

life.news: My dad took me out surveying for the day. Measuring the desert. Very calming.
life.more: He says the land never lies, only the people who pay for the report. I held the pole while he squinted down the sight. We ate sandwiches on the tailgate. He’s quieter than he used to be. Today he laughed twice.

gossip.says: Adriana Ponce tells us young ones to knock on doors or go home. We hate her. We come back. She’s the only grown-up in the movement who argues with me properly.
gossip.note: Nora Hadley says Adriana Ponce is the only grown-up who argues with her properly.
gossip.ask: Nora says you’re the only grown-up who argues with her properly.
gossip.answer: She argues properly too. She’s wrong about some things and right about nuclear, which I’ll never say in public. Arguing with her is like playing soccer with someone who’s read the rule book. Exhausting. Good for you.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland sings alto in a church choir she doesn’t believe in. She says it’s the only place she feels calm. She’d kill me for telling you.
gossip.note: Nora Hadley says Eden Sutherland sings in a church choir she doesn’t believe in.
gossip.ask: Nora says you sing in a church choir you don’t believe in.
gossip.answer: Of course she told you. Fine. Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell the group. They’d make it a debate. It’s not a debate. It’s just singing.

women.name: Daisy Chen
women.look: Dark skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, tortoiseshell glasses, hand-knitted sweater

own.label: Ask what she makes her collages from
own.player: What do you make the collages from?
own.reply: Old magazines, bus tickets, receipts people drop. I like turning things people threw away into something they’d stop to look at.

own.label: Ask why she’s bad at small talk
own.player: Why are you so bad at small talk?
own.reply: Because I’d rather know what you’re afraid of than what the weather is doing. It makes me very bad at parties and very good at funerals.

own.label: Ask about the worst crisis she’s handled
own.player: What’s the worst crisis you’ve handled?
own.reply: A pensioners’ craft fair where the glue gun caught fire. I put it out with a dish towel and nobody stopped knitting. Best day of my career.

own.label: Ask what she’s like when nobody’s watching
own.player: What are you like when nobody’s watching?
own.reply: Sillier. I dance in the kitchen and talk back to the radio. Most people only ever meet the organizer.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Do you have family here?
own.reply: My sister Mei, downstairs. She does hair and hears everything. I make art and say nothing. Between us we know the whole street.

own.label: Ask about her parents
own.player: What happened to your parents?
own.reply: Dad ran a restaurant and died in it. Mom sold it and went to the coast. Mei and I stayed, which nobody expected, least of all us.

calls.label: Ask what odd thing she’s picked up lately
calls.player: Found anything odd for your collages?
calls.reply: A garden center receipt dropped on campus, for a quantity of something nobody gardens with. I glued it into a piece called Sunfall. Nobody’s read it yet. Somebody will.
calls.note: Daisy Chen found a garden-center receipt on campus for a quantity of something nobody gardens with.

life.news: Found a receipt on the sidewalk for one birthday candle and a single cupcake. It’s going in the middle of my next collage.
life.more: I make collages from what people drop. Bus tickets, receipts, a shopping list that just said courage. One candle and one cupcake. Someone had a birthday alone, or a very small party. Either way it goes in the middle, where it’ll be looked at.

life.news: Danced in the kitchen to the radio for an hour. Nobody saw. Best hour of my week.
life.more: Sillier, when nobody’s watching. I talk back to the radio, I dance badly, I sing the wrong words loudly. Only my sister knows. She lives downstairs and bangs on the ceiling. Not in time, unlike some people’s neighbors.

life.news: Went to a friend’s mom’s funeral. I’m good at funerals. I wish I wasn’t.
life.more: I’d rather know what you’re afraid of than what the weather’s doing. It makes me bad at parties and good at funerals. I sat with her in the parking lot afterwards and we didn’t say anything for half an hour. That’s the bit I’m good at.

life.news: Mei did a woman’s hair today who told her a secret so big that Mei won’t even tell me. She always tells me.
life.more: My sister does hair and hears everything. I make art and say nothing. Between us we know the whole town. But today she came upstairs, made tea and just said, don’t ask. I’ve never seen her like that. I’m not asking. I’m dying.

gossip.says: My sister Mei Chen does hair on the Sunfall Road and hears everything. People tell their hairdresser things they wouldn’t tell a priest. She’s quieter than most, so they tell her even more.
gossip.note: Daisy Chen says her sister Mei Chen hears everyone’s secrets at the salon.
gossip.ask: Daisy says people tell you things they wouldn’t tell a priest.
gossip.answer: They do. I don’t know why. I think because I don’t talk much, so there’s a lot of room. I never repeat anything. Not even to Daisy, and she lives upstairs and bribes me with cookies. She’s very good at bribing.

gossip.says: Rebecca Shaw has seventeen spreadsheets and exactly one friend who can make a poster. That’s me. She once sent me a spreadsheet about a poster.
gossip.note: Daisy Chen says Rebecca Shaw once sent her a spreadsheet about a poster.
gossip.ask: Daisy says you once sent her a spreadsheet about a poster.
gossip.answer: It had a tab for fonts and a tab for feelings. That’s thorough, not strange. Daisy made something beautiful out of it and ignored every tab. I’ve learned to send her the spreadsheet and then leave the room.

gossip.says: Khadija Rahman runs our film night and turned it from twelve people at a documentary into a full hall for slapstick. She says nobody wants to be educated after a long day. She’s right.
gossip.note: Daisy Chen says Khadija Rahman filled the film night hall with slapstick.
gossip.ask: Daisy says you turned twelve people at a documentary into a full hall for slapstick.
gossip.answer: Twelve people and one of them asleep. Now it’s popcorn and men falling off ladders, and the hall’s full. My friends think everything is a system. I think people just want to laugh at the end of a long day. That’s not a system. That’s sense.

women.name: Zoe Whitaker
women.look: Light-brown skin, golden-brown ringlets, freckles across her nose, oversized thrifted cardigan

own.label: Ask what she does in the climate group
own.player: What do you do in the climate group?
own.reply: I write the minutes. I say very little. People think that means I don’t notice anything. It means I’m writing it down.

own.label: Ask about the journal she carries
own.player: What’s that journal you carry?
own.reply: A trip I haven’t taken yet. The coast, a train, a city with a river. I’ve written the whole thing already. I’ll go when the jar is full. The jar is slow.

own.label: Ask what she does in the mornings
own.player: What do you do in the mornings?
own.reply: Three mornings a week at the Lucky Cactus with Madison Pike. She talks enough for both of us, which suits me. I carry plates and listen. You learn a lot about a town from what it orders.

own.label: Ask why she joined the climate group
own.player: Why the climate group?
own.reply: A girl called Nora Hadley argued with me in a seminar, and I’d never been argued with before. I went to a meeting to argue back. I’m still there. So is the argument.

own.label: Ask who’s at home
own.player: Who’s at home?
own.reply: My aunt. She raised me, kindly, with no money. I got to the university on a scholarship that wasn’t the Foundation’s. I’m proud of that in a way I know is small.

own.label: Ask about the evening before the fire
own.player: Were you at the campaign office the evening before the fire?
own.reply: Late, writing up the minutes. Two people left. Since then the two people I trust most have each told me a different reason why. Vanessa Greer says she took Rosa home because Rosa was in a state. Dev Okafor says Vanessa left with Caleb Marsh and a bag from a garden center. One of them is lying. I have to decide which. I don’t want to.
own.note: Zoe Whitaker was at the campaign office the evening before Vale’s fire: Vanessa Greer says she took Rosa home, Dev Okafor says Vanessa left with Caleb Marsh and a garden-center bag.

calls.label: Ask what she saw with her own eyes
calls.player: What did you see with your own eyes?
calls.reply: Only one thing, and I wrote it in my travel journal under the city with a river, where nobody would look. The bag was heavy. Caleb Marsh carried it with both hands.
calls.note: Zoe Whitaker saw Caleb Marsh carry a heavy garden-center bag out of the campaign office with both hands.

calls.label: Ask if she’s okay
calls.player: You sound tired. Are you okay?
calls.reply: I went to the city today. I go once a month. My mom’s in a hospital there, and her mind comes and goes. Today it came. She knew me for an hour. Don’t tell anyone. I don’t.

life.news: Put four dollars in the jar today. Tips from the Lucky Cactus. The jar is getting less slow.
life.more: Madison told a man his pie was her grandma’s recipe, which it isn’t, and he tipped like he believed her. She gave me half. I wrote it in the journal under the train. Four dollars closer to a city with a river.

life.news: Somebody at the meeting asked me to stop writing everything down. I wrote that down.
life.more: He said the minutes should be a summary, not a transcript. I said a summary is just a transcript somebody edited. Nobody laughed except Nora, and Nora never laughs, so I’m counting it.

life.news: Long day. I don’t want to talk about where I was. Tell me something about yours instead.
life.more: I was in the city. It’s family. I’m fine. Mostly I’m tired from pretending I’m fine on the bus home. Tell me something stupid that happened to you. Please.

life.news: Nora argued with me for an hour about trains versus planes. I won. She says I didn’t.
life.more: Trains, obviously. You can write on a train. Nora says the carbon math is closer than I think and pulled up a chart. I said a chart can’t look out of a window. She said that isn’t an argument. It’s the best one I have.

gossip.says: Madison Pike tells customers the pie is her grandma’s recipe. It comes frozen in a box. They tip double.
gossip.note: Zoe Whitaker says Madison Pike tells diner customers the frozen pie is her grandma’s recipe.
gossip.ask: Zoe says you tell customers the pie is your grandma’s recipe.
gossip.answer: It is my grandma’s recipe. My grandma also bought it frozen. That’s the recipe. Zoe won’t lie to a customer, so she carries the plates and I do the talking. Together we’re one great waitress.

gossip.says: Nora Hadley is the only person who has ever argued with me properly. She says nuclear in the group chat just to watch people leave.
gossip.note: Zoe Whitaker says Nora Hadley says nuclear in the group chat to watch people leave.
gossip.ask: Zoe says you say nuclear in the group chat just to watch people leave.
gossip.answer: Not to watch them leave. To see who stays to argue. Zoe stayed. She writes down everything I say and reads it back to me when I contradict myself. It’s the most annoying thing anyone’s ever done for me.

women.name: Khadija Rahman
women.look: Warm brown skin, cornrows into a low bun, strong dark brows, embroidered peasant blouse

own.label: Ask about her film nights
own.player: What do you show at the film nights?
own.reply: Old comedies, mostly. I tried a serious documentary once. Twelve people came and one of them was asleep. Now it’s slapstick and popcorn and the hall is full.

own.label: Ask what community meetings are really like
own.player: What are community meetings really like?
own.reply: Two hours, three people talking and a cookie tin nobody opens until the end. The cookies are the only thing everyone agrees on.

own.label: Ask what she disagrees with her friends about
own.player: What do you disagree with your friends about?
own.reply: Quite a lot, quietly. They think everything is a system. I think a lot of things are just people being rude. You can’t fix rude with a workshop.

own.label: Ask what she misses most
own.player: What do you miss most?
own.reply: My grandmother’s kitchen. Everyone shouting and nobody angry. Sunfall is very polite. I miss being shouted at with love.

own.label: Ask how she runs film night
own.player: Where do you get a projector?
own.reply: I share one with Gwen, who runs a yard film night on alternate weeks. It travels between us in a shopping trolley. It has seen things.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What does your family do?
own.reply: Mom runs a pharmacy on the Sunfall Road and has a strong view on everything. Dad died when I was twenty. In our house you were shouted at with love or not at all.

calls.label: Ask what went wrong at film night
calls.player: What happened at the film night you stopped?
calls.reply: Four minutes of film that wasn’t mine came up between reels. A room with candles, a circle of people, and a bell. I said it was a fault. It came in the shared projector from Gwen’s yard night. A man asked her to show it as a favor. Brad Keller. The reel is in my apartment. I don’t want it there.
calls.note: Khadija Rahman has a reel showing a candlelit circle and a bell, passed on by Brad Keller.

life.news: Film night was full again. A man laughed so hard at a pie fight he fell off his chair. Then everyone laughed at him.
life.more: Old comedies, slapstick, popcorn. The documentary nights had twelve people and one asleep. Tonight a man in a cardigan fell off his chair at the pie scene and the whole hall cheered him back up. Better than any film.

life.news: Sat in a committee meeting for two hours. Three people and a cookie tin. Decided nothing.
life.more: They think everything’s a system. I think a lot of things are just people being rude, and you can’t fix rude with a workshop. I said that in the meeting. There was a long silence. Someone ate the last cookie out of spite.

life.news: Missing my grandmother’s kitchen today. Everyone shouting and nobody angry.
life.more: It was in the city, full of aunts and pans and my grandmother shouting with love at everybody. Sunfall is very polite. Nobody shouts here unless they mean it. I rang my aunt just to be shouted at. She obliged.

life.news: Recorded the canal at night on my old reel machine. It sounds like a city breathing.
life.more: I record sounds around town. People think it’s strange. I think in fifty years someone will want to know what Sunfall sounded like when it was quiet. Ducks, a radio from a window, someone laughing two streets away. That’s the reel.

gossip.says: Vanessa Greer comes to our meetings and talks to everyone like they’re the only person who’s ever listened to them. People leave in love with her. I watch the cookie tin.
gossip.note: Khadija Rahman says Vanessa Greer talks to everyone as if they’re the only person who’s ever listened.
gossip.ask: Khadija says people leave your meetings in love with you.
gossip.answer: People leave my meetings thinking, which is rarer. Khadija thinks I’m a cult leader with good books. I think she’s a cynic with a projector. We’re both a little right. She guards the cookie tin like it’s the treasury.

gossip.says: Daisy Chen makes art out of receipts people drop in the street. She’ll pick up your shopping list if you drop it. Don’t drop anything embarrassing.
gossip.note: Khadija Rahman says Daisy Chen makes collages from things people drop.
gossip.ask: Khadija says you’ll pick up my shopping list if I drop it.
gossip.answer: Only if it’s interesting. A list that just says milk is no use to me. A list that says milk, rope, apology card? That’s going in the middle of a collage. Drop interesting things. It’s the least you can do.

gossip.says: Cleo Rook let me record her old church while it was empty. It hums. A real note. I haven’t worked out where it comes from.
gossip.note: Khadija Rahman says she recorded a hum in Cleo Rook’s old church.
gossip.ask: Khadija says your church hums when it’s empty, and she’s recorded it.
gossip.answer: It does. It’s hummed for twelve years. I leave the light on for it. Khadija sat in the vestry with her machine for an hour, completely still. She’s the only person who’s ever listened to it properly. Whatever it is, it liked her.

women.name: Esther Yu
women.look: Medium-brown skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, oversized thrifted cardigan

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Climate group. I’m the one who opens the office in the morning, puts the kettle on, reads the journal and writes the first line of the day. Somebody has to be the first line.

own.label: Ask what she collects
own.player: Do you collect anything?
own.reply: Roadside souvenirs. A motel snow globe, a spoon from a diner that burned down, a plastic saguaro from a gas station on the state road. The group thinks it’s weird. They’re relics. Somebody should keep them.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: My parents run a laundry on the Sunfall Road. I grew up folding other people’s shirts and learning more about this town from its pockets than from the paper.

own.label: Ask what she looks for in a man
own.player: What do you look for in a man?
own.reply: Respect, before anything. I’ve walked away from two boyfriends because they didn’t have it. I lost no sleep either time. Romance is lovely. It isn’t load-bearing.

own.label: Ask what she does on her days off
own.player: What do you do on your days off?
own.reply: Junk markets, with an older woman from the club I met over a box of spoons. We hunt souvenirs once a week and talk about nothing. The rule is we never talk about her club. It’s the best friendship I have.

calls.label: Ask if anything strange has happened
calls.player: Anything strange going on lately?
calls.reply: A gray car has been parked outside the office every morning for two weeks. Two men in it. They never get out. They leave the minute anyone else arrives. I write the plate down in the journal every day. I write everything down.
calls.note: Esther Yu says two men in a gray sedan wait outside the climate group’s office every morning; she writes the plate in the journal every day.

calls.label: Ask about her market friend
calls.player: Tell me about your market friend.
calls.reply: Marianne. She has a spoon from the same burned diner as mine. Last week I read a license plate out loud as a joke and she went completely still. We don’t talk about her club. I’m starting to think I should.
calls.note: Esther Yu says Marianne Keene went completely still when Esther read the gray sedan’s plate out loud as a joke.

life.news: Opened the office before sunrise and the whole street was pink. I wrote the first line of the journal about the sky instead of the campaign.
life.more: Nobody minded. Jennifer read it when she came in and said it was the best first line we’ve had all year. Then she put the kettle on for me, which has never once happened. I’m framing the page.

life.news: Found a souvenir I’ve hunted for years: a pennant from a drive-in that closed before I was born.
life.more: Faded orange felt, a cartoon car, a phone number with only five digits. The man wanted twenty dollars. Marianne talked him down to six by pretending to be my aunt. We were very pleased with ourselves all the way home.

life.news: Somebody threw an egg at the office window. I cleaned it off before anyone else got in.
life.more: It was still runny, so it can’t have been long before I arrived. I didn’t write it in the journal. Some things the group doesn’t need first thing in the morning. I wrote it in mine instead.

life.news: Two people in the group stopped arguing long enough to agree with each other. Historic.
life.more: It was about the bike racks. Twenty minutes of shouting and then, suddenly, the same opinion. Everybody looked embarrassed. I made a cake to mark the occasion. It said truce in green icing.

gossip.says: Marianne Keene is my junk market partner. She’s twice my age, from the club, and she can talk a man down from twenty dollars to six without blinking. We never talk about her club. That’s the rule.
gossip.note: Esther Yu says Marianne Keene is her junk market partner and that they never talk about the club.
gossip.ask: Esther says you hunt souvenirs together and never talk about the club.
gossip.answer: That’s the rule, and it’s the best rule I’ve ever kept. Esther writes everything down and asks nothing she doesn’t need to. One day she’ll ask me something, and I think I’ll answer, and I think that will be the end of the rule. Not yet.

gossip.says: Jennifer Tate lives next door at the co-op and plays the same record every night. I know every word now. I’ve never told her.
gossip.note: Esther Yu says Jennifer Tate, her neighbor at the co-op, plays the same record every night.
gossip.ask: Esther says you play the same record every night and she knows every word.
gossip.answer: She does? Oh no. It was my mother’s favorite and I can’t sleep without it. Tell Esther I’ll buy her earplugs. Actually, tell her to come over and sing it. I’ve always wanted someone to sing the harmony.

women.name: Cassandra Finch
women.look: Bird-like and slight, warm brown skin, cropped bleached hair, enormous dark tired eyes with a sullen look, a small gap between her front teeth, a slim small-busted figure, a linen shirt and a canvas tote

own.label: Ask how she stays so cheerful
own.player: How do you stay so cheerful?
own.reply: Stubbornness. I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down now. Out of spite, mainly.

own.label: Ask what she paints
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: Skies. Sunfall has the best skies in the world and everyone is looking at their phones under them. Sorry. Not you. Well, a bit you.

own.label: Ask if she fits in with her group
own.player: Do you fit in with the others?
own.reply: Not really. I go to the meetings, bring the cake and vote how I like. They keep me for the cake.

own.label: Ask what she’ll never give up on
own.player: What will you never give up on?
own.reply: People. Even the awful ones. Especially the awful ones. Someone gave up on me once, and it took years to undo.

own.label: Ask where she paints
own.player: Where do you paint?
own.reply: On the roof above the Sisters’ charity shop. I rent the room underneath from Lucia. Best sky in Sunfall and nobody up there but me and the pigeons.

own.label: Ask about growing up
own.player: What were you like as a teenager?
own.reply: Ill, mostly. Thin and tired with a thing the doctors were slow to name. Mom left. Dad sold farm machinery and sat with me. I decided to be cheerful out of spite and I’ve never backed down.

calls.label: Ask about her neighbor
calls.player: Who lives next door to you?
calls.reply: Nobody, for two years. Now the light comes on behind the blind at night and goes off before dawn. Lucia takes two lunches up the stairs. Through the wall I heard a woman crying, and once, laughing. I painted the blind with the light behind it. I won’t say more.
calls.note: Cassandra Finch says someone has been living secretly in the apartment next to hers, above the Sisters’ charity shop.

calls.label: Ask what she kept from a meeting
calls.player: Did you keep anything from the group’s meetings?
calls.reply: Vanessa Greer’s cup. She left it, and I don’t give up on anyone. There’s a crescent painted on the bottom. I’m trying to decide if that means anything.
calls.note: Cassandra Finch kept a cup Vanessa Greer left behind, with a crescent on the base.

life.news: Painted the sky from the roof again. Everyone below was looking at their phones. Sorry. A bit you.
life.more: Sunfall has the best skies in the world and everyone looks at their phones under them. Tonight it went orange, then pink, then a purple I don’t have a name for. I painted it fast. I’ll give it to the first person who looks up.

life.news: Brought a lemon drizzle to the meeting and voted against everyone. Delicious and principled.
life.more: I decided to be cheerful years ago and I refuse to back down. Out of spite, mainly. They wanted to spend the grant on a logo. I wanted to spend it on paint for children. I lost the vote. They ate the cake. I count it as a draw.

life.news: Wrote to an old friend. Fourth letter. No reply yet.
life.more: Someone gave up on me once. It took years to undo. I don’t give up on people now. Even the awful ones. Even the ones who don’t answer. Especially those. I’ll write a fifth. I’ve got plenty of stamps.

life.news: Sat at the back of the Sisters’ vigil again. I don’t believe. I go anyway.
life.more: It’s the quietest room in Sunfall, full of women who mean every word. I sit at the back with my hands in my lap and think about who I’m worried about. I suppose that’s a kind of praying. Don’t tell the Sisters. They’d be too pleased.

gossip.says: Lavinia Gravesend was in a home with me for six months when we were young. I’ve never stopped trying to reach her. If she’s talking to you, keep talking to her.
gossip.note: Cassandra Finch says she has been trying to reach Lavinia Gravesend for years.
gossip.ask: Cassandra asked me to keep talking to you.
gossip.answer: Did she? She draws me, you know. From memory. She always gets the hands right. I don’t call her back because I don’t know what to say. Tell her the purple desert’s coming along. She’ll know what that means.

gossip.says: Margaret Holloway visited me every week when I was in the home. She brought books and lists. She still makes lists. I’ve kept one she wrote me years ago. It says: get better.
gossip.note: Cassandra Finch says Margaret Holloway visited her every week when she was young and ill.
gossip.ask: Cassandra says you visited her every week when she was ill, and wrote her a list.
gossip.answer: She kept it? Of course she did. It was a very short list, for me. Item one: get better. Item two: be difficult about it. She managed both. I’m proud of her. Don’t tell her I said proud. I’ll deny it on parish paper.

gossip.says: Sienna Navarro organizes forty volunteers and then goes home and paints cups of tea. She says she’s tired of causes. She’s not. She’s tired of committees.
gossip.note: Cassandra Finch says Sienna Navarro is tired of committees, not causes.
gossip.ask: Cassandra says you’re not tired of causes, just committees.
gossip.answer: That’s annoyingly accurate. I love the mural. I hate the three committees about the mural. Cassandra brings cake and votes how she likes and somehow gets away with it. I’ve tried bringing cake. I just get asked to take the minutes.

women.name: Eden Sutherland
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, light-brown skin, freckles across her nose, huge dark sleepy eyes with a sullen stare, buzz-cut dark hair, a gap-toothed smile, overalls and a bandana

own.label: Ask what campaigning is like day to day
own.player: What’s campaigning actually like day to day?
own.reply: Leaflets, rain and men in big cars telling me to get a job. This is my job. It pays less than their car.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell my friends.

own.label: Ask why she’s so blunt
own.player: Why are you so blunt?
own.reply: Because the world’s on fire and I haven’t got time to be nice about it. I’m nice afterwards. I bring soup.

own.label: Ask what she gives away
own.player: What do you give away?
own.reply: Most of my wages, honestly. My roommate calls it a problem. I call it the only bit of my life that makes sense.

own.label: Ask who she lives with
own.player: Do you live with anyone?
own.reply: Jasmin, on the dry river. She calls my giving my wages away a problem. She also eats my soup, so she’s part of the problem.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Grandad was a founding family’s lawyer, struck off. Dad is a kind drunk who teaches piano. Mom is a Bluebird’s lady’s maid, which I don’t say on campus. Don’t you say it either.

calls.label: Ask about the grant letter
calls.player: Did your group ever get a grant?
calls.reply: A letter signed Ruth Calder says it’s approved, pending a private meeting at the lodge. Just me. On a night I worked out has no moon. I wrote to thank her. She didn’t know anything about it. I haven’t told the group, because they’d say no and the water kit is real.
calls.note: Eden Sutherland has a grant letter signed with Ruth Calder’s name inviting her alone to the lodge on a moonless night; Ruth Calder never sent it.

calls.label: Ask who cries in her choir
calls.player: Does anyone in your choir get upset?
calls.reply: There’s a hymn about the deep that makes a girl from the club cry. Elise. I’m blunt, so I asked her why. She’s started telling me. It’s about an invitation.
calls.note: Eden Sutherland says Elise Harrow has started confiding in her about a frightening invitation.

life.news: Leafleted in the rain for four hours. A man in a big car told me to get a job.
life.more: This is my job. It pays less than his car. I gave him a leaflet anyway and he took it, through the window, in the rain. Small wins. The leaflet was soaked, so he got a very wet argument.

life.news: Choir practice. We sang the old hymn with the high bit and nobody’s voice cracked. A miracle, possibly.
life.more: Alto. Church hall, old ladies, hymns I don’t believe in. It’s the only place I feel calm. Don’t tell my friends. Raven and Jessica and I stood in a row and nailed the alto line. It felt like flying.

life.news: My roommate found out how much of my wages I give away. She’s calling it a problem. I’m calling it the only honest thing I do.
life.more: Jasmin sat me down with a calculator and a very concerned face. I said I’ve got rent and soup money, what else do I need. She said, shoes. I looked at my shoes. She had a point. I’ve bought shoes.

life.news: My dad played piano at the old people’s home and they all sang. He hasn’t been sober that long in years.
life.more: He teaches piano and drinks, mostly in that order. Today he did a whole hour and the residents sang every word, and he cried at the end, and so did I. I don’t know how long it’ll last. Today it lasted an hour. I’ll take an hour.

gossip.says: Elise Harrow from the Bluebirds sings alto next to me in the choir. Pearls and a cardigan and the filthiest laugh in the church hall. Nobody at the club would believe it.
gossip.note: Eden Sutherland says Elise Harrow, a Bluebird, sings alto in the church choir.
gossip.ask: Eden says you have the filthiest laugh in the church hall.
gossip.answer: Eden exaggerates for effect. It’s a perfectly normal laugh that occasionally frightens a vicar. I was charming at the right party to get my job, and in choir I don’t have to be charming at all. That’s why I go.

gossip.says: Adriana Ponce told me to knock on doors or go home. I knocked. Forty doors. Two cups of coffee. She said that’s a good day. It was.
gossip.note: Eden Sutherland says Adriana Ponce taught her to knock on doors.
gossip.ask: Eden says you taught her to knock on doors instead of shouting.
gossip.answer: I told her what I wish someone had told me. I thought shouting was winning. The people I changed were the ones I had coffee with. Eden learned it in a month. It took me fifteen years. Kids these days. Better than us.

gossip.says: Jessica Rivera sings in the choir too and mouths the high notes because she’s scared. She has the best voice in the room and she’d rather die than do a solo.
gossip.note: Eden Sutherland says Jessica Rivera mouths the high notes in choir because she’s scared.
gossip.ask: Eden says you have the best voice in the choir and mouth the high notes.
gossip.answer: I don’t mouth all of them. Just the ones that might be heard. It’s fine. I’m fine. If I ever did a solo it would be the one about the lighthouse, but I won’t, so it doesn’t matter. Please don’t tell Teresa. She’d put me on the roster.

women.name: Lucille Pembrook
women.look: Fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, rosy cheeks, linen shirt and canvas tote

women.name: Lara Newsome
women.look: Freckled fair skin, auburn shag with a curtain fringe, a wide bright smile, embroidered peasant blouse

women.name: Willow Greene
women.look: Rosy fair skin, sandy shag with a fringe, amber eyes, band T-shirt under dungarees

women.name: Jasmin Malik
women.look: Warm beige skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, deep dimples, hand-knitted sweater

own.label: Ask what she does in the climate group
own.player: What do you do in the climate group?
own.reply: I make the leaflets funny. Somebody has to. You can’t save the planet in a font that looks like a tax form. I also make Adriana Ponce laugh, which nobody else can do. That’s my real job.

own.label: Ask what she does in the evenings
own.player: What do you do in the evenings?
own.reply: Book club on the sofa. We drink, we argue, we never finish the book. It’s the most honest reading group in Sunfall.

own.label: Ask if she writes
own.player: Do you write?
own.reply: Plays nobody stages and stories nobody reads. I was the funny girl at school. Now I’m the funny girl with a stack of unstaged plays. It’s a living. It is not a living.

own.label: Ask where her sweater is from
own.player: Where’s that sweater from?
own.reply: My grandmother knits. She’s made me one every winter since I was born. They get bigger every year, like she’s worried I’ll stop growing. I wear them all.

own.label: Ask if she’s always in other people’s drama
own.player: Are you always this busy with other people’s drama?
own.reply: Since I was six. Somebody has to hold the coats. Eden and the group, Nora and everyone, my best friend Tamsin Wilde and the whole world. I’m the coat rack.

own.label: Ask if her friend is okay
own.player: Is your friend okay?
own.reply: Two men came to Tamsin’s kitchen while I was in the next room. One of them said scholarship. The other one said mother. Her mom is in a home the Foundation pays for. The next morning she went to the police and said she saw nothing. I drove her.
own.note: Jasmin Malik heard two men in Tamsin Wilde’s kitchen say scholarship and mother; the next morning Tamsin told the police she saw nothing.

calls.label: Ask if she has any enemies
calls.player: Got any enemies?
calls.reply: One. Zadie Foster, the music reviewer. She gave my brother’s band two stars and called his drumming enthusiastic. Enthusiastic! He sends her a postcard every year that just says no. I helped him pick the first one.

calls.label: Ask what her mom does
calls.player: What does your mom do?
calls.reply: She sews for Rinaldi Bridal. Forty years of hems. She says the owner wears a little swallow brooch every day and never takes it off, and she says it the way you’d say someone keeps a gun in the drawer.

life.news: Book club tonight. Nobody read the book. Eden cried at the blurb. Best meeting yet.
life.more: It was a short novel about a lighthouse keeper. Eden read the back cover out loud and burst into tears before chapter one. Adriana laughed so hard she had to go outside. I wrote it all down for a play. Nobody will stage it.

life.news: Grandma knitted me a sweater with a polar bear on it for the climate group. The ice floe is unraveling. On purpose.
life.more: She said she wanted to support the cause. The bear is standing on a little ice floe and the ice floe is coming apart, stitch by stitch. My grandmother is the most effective activist in the whole group, and she’s never been to a meeting.

life.news: Eden gave away her wages again. I bought the groceries again. I love her. I’m also broke.
life.more: She meets someone who needs it more and that’s it, gone. I can’t even be mad, because she’s right, they did need it more. But somebody in this apartment has to eat, so I made a pot of lentils the size of a bathtub.

life.news: My brother’s band played the Furnace tonight. He drummed like the building owed him money. I screamed myself hoarse.
life.more: Nixie Adler put them on second, which is a huge deal. Twelve people in the crowd and I was three of them. He threw a drumstick into the crowd at the end and I caught it. He wants it back. He’s not getting it back.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland, my roommate, gives most of her wages away and then sings in a church choir she doesn’t believe in. I feed her lentils. Somebody has to.
gossip.note: Jasmin Malik says Eden Sutherland gives most of her wages away.
gossip.ask: Jasmin Malik says you give most of your wages away and she feeds you lentils.
gossip.answer: Most of them. Not all. I kept enough for soup. Jasmin makes lentils in a pot the size of a bathtub and complains the whole time she’s stirring. It’s the nicest thing anyone does for me.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster gave my brother’s band two stars and called his drumming enthusiastic. We are at war. She knows.
gossip.note: Jasmin Malik is feuding with Zadie Foster over a two-star review of her brother’s band.
gossip.ask: Jasmin says you gave her brother’s band two stars, and now it’s war.
gossip.answer: Two stars was generous. He plays like he’s angry at the drums. He sends me a postcard every year that just says no. I’ve kept every one. Tell Jasmin I’d give him three now. Don’t tell her I said that.

women.name: Freya Castillo
women.look: Medium-brown skin, twist-out coils, freckles across her nose, mustard turtleneck

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do for the art collective?
own.reply: I write the grants and tell everyone when the money’s gone. Somebody has to be the kitchen. I keep the film night’s projector running on paperwork alone.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: My grandmother’s house on the Old Mission road. I built a little desert inside it: a glass room full of cacti. Yes, I know there’s a desert outside. Mine has rules.

own.label: Ask if money is hard to find
own.player: Is it hard keeping the collective funded?
own.reply: A trust up on the ridge offered us money for our membership list. Twice. I said no twice. The projector can starve.

own.label: Ask what she does with her weekends
own.player: What do you do with your weekends?
own.reply: Some weekends I have my goddaughter. She’s eight and she names every cactus. There’s one called Mr. Stabs. He is thriving.

own.label: Ask if she has family in town
own.player: Do you have family in town?
own.reply: A sister, Agnes. We haven’t spoken in six years. After our dad died, I said God let him die in that chapel. She said he died happy. It was in a kitchen. It’s always a kitchen.

own.label: Ask who lives next door
own.player: Who lives next door to you?
own.reply: Nobody, for a year. Then, on the last three nights with no moon, candles behind the blinds and cars outside. I count the cars. I’ve heard singing. I’ve heard a bell that can’t ring.
own.note: Freya Castillo says the dark house next to hers on the Old Mission road has candles behind the blinds and cars outside on nights with no moon, and she has heard a bell.

calls.label: Ask if her dad left her anything
calls.player: Did your dad leave you anything?
calls.reply: His sacristan’s diary. It stops the week before his stroke, with one line I didn’t understand until now: they are coming back to the crypt, and the bell knows. I haven’t shown my sister. I’d have to speak to her.
calls.note: Freya Castillo has her father’s sacristan diary; its last line says they are coming back to the crypt, and the bell knows.

calls.label: Ask if she still goes to church
calls.player: Do you still go to church?
calls.reply: No. I drive past St. Brigid’s every day and don’t look. My sister is in there somewhere, pruning roses and praying for me by name. I know she is. That’s worse than if she weren’t.

life.news: A cactus I’d given up on flowered today. Bright pink. Out of nowhere. I said thank you out loud.
life.more: Three years it sat there doing nothing, sulking in the corner of the glass room. I nearly threw it out. Then this morning, a flower the size of my fist. My goddaughter says it was waiting for me to stop looking. She’s usually right.

life.news: Counted six cars on the Old Mission road last night. On a road with four houses.
life.more: I count things. It’s a grant writer’s habit. Six cars, no moon, nobody walking. They were gone by morning. I wrote the plates down, because I don’t know what else to do with a feeling like that.

life.news: Drove past St. Brigid’s and caught myself looking. Six years, and today I looked.
life.more: Just for a second. The roses by the gate were pruned the way our dad taught us. Agnes did those. I know her cuts. I nearly stopped the car. I didn’t. I drove around the block twice instead, like an idiot.

life.news: Got the projector grant renewed. Film night lives. Khadija hugged me so hard my glasses fell off.
life.more: Eleven pages of forms for a machine that shows pie fights. Worth every page. Khadija says the hall would riot without it. She brought cookies to the meeting and opened the tin first, which has never happened. History.

gossip.says: Khadija Rahman runs the film night and guards the cookie tin like it’s the collective’s treasury. I write the grants that keep her projector alive.
gossip.note: Freya Castillo writes the grants that keep Khadija Rahman’s film night projector running.
gossip.ask: Freya Castillo says she writes the grants that keep your projector alive.
gossip.answer: She does, and she reminds me at every meeting. Freya is the only person in the collective who says exactly what she means. No workshop needed. I give her the first cookie. Nobody else gets the first cookie.

gossip.says: My sister Agnes Castillo looks after the gardens at St. Brigid’s. We haven’t spoken in six years. I still know her pruning when I see it.
gossip.note: Freya Castillo says she and her sister Agnes Castillo have not spoken in six years.
gossip.ask: Freya Castillo says you two haven’t spoken in six years.
gossip.answer: Six years. I pray for her every night, by name. She drives past the gate every day and doesn’t look. I always look. One of us has to keep the door open, and God gave me the gate.

women.name: Nicolette Parrish

women.name: Sloane Mercer
women.look: Dark skin, chestnut curly bob, gray-green eyes, hand-knitted sweater

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Climate group. I’m the mischief. I joined for the arguments and stayed because nobody else argues properly. Somebody has to make the meetings worth sitting through.

own.label: Ask where she goes at night
own.player: Where do you go at night?
own.reply: Black’s bar, downstairs from my apartment. I play pool with the goths and win their dish duty. I’m the only campaigner they tolerate. It’s because I don’t try.

own.label: Ask about her sweater
own.player: Nice sweater. Yours?
own.reply: Stolen. From Jasmin’s grandmother’s knitting pile. Jasmin knows. Her grandmother doesn’t. I wear it to every meeting so Jasmin has something to be furious about besides the planet.

own.label: Ask if she’s seeing anyone
own.player: Are you seeing anyone?
own.reply: Sometimes. Billie. She runs the goth night at the casino lounge. She tells me things in bed, laughing, that she shouldn’t. I find it funny. It isn’t.

own.label: Ask what she gets up to when she’s drunk
own.player: What do you get up to when you’re drunk?
own.reply: Riddles on coasters, mostly. People keep them. Once I wrote a whole plan into a journal as a poem. A professor, a parking bay, a day, a device, all in rhyme, because I could. Alma tore it out and burned it. I watched her. I think I love her for it.
own.note: Sloane Mercer once wrote the plan against the professor into a journal as a rhyming poem: a professor, a parking bay, a day, a device. Alma tore it out and burned it.

calls.label: Ask if her jokes ever go too far
calls.player: Do your jokes ever go too far?
calls.reply: Always. There’s a code word going around a certain group. Garden shed clearance. That was my joke. I found a man’s number in the classifieds for a laugh and invented the phrase. It’s not a joke now. That’s what happens to my jokes.
calls.note: Sloane Mercer invented the code word garden shed clearance and found Lenny’s number in the classifieds for Vanessa Greer.

calls.label: Ask what Billie tells her in bed
calls.player: What does Billie tell you?
calls.reply: Where her friends meet on nights with no moon. Which chapel. She said it laughing, with her head on my stomach. I haven’t told anyone. It isn’t anyone’s business. I’m telling you because you asked nicely.
calls.note: Sloane Mercer knows from Billie Wraith which chapel the circle meets in on moonless nights.

life.news: Beat three goths at pool in a row. They’re doing the bar’s dishes all week. I’m a hero of the people.
life.more: The last one bet his eyeliner. I didn’t take it. I have standards. Then he asked me to teach him the bank shot and we were there until closing, and now he’s better than me. That’s the problem with teaching people things.

life.news: Somebody framed one of my drunk coasters and hung it behind the bar. I don’t remember writing it.
life.more: It says: the moon owes me money and the river knows why. In my handwriting. Wren swears a customer brought it in already framed. I stared at it all night trying to work out what I meant. I think I meant it.

life.news: Big fight at the climate meeting. I started it. I won it. Nobody’s speaking to me. Worth it.
life.more: It was about whether to chain ourselves to the water board or just write a letter. I said a letter is a way of asking permission to be ignored. Jasmin threw a muffin at me. I ate it. Delicious muffin, terrible argument, great evening.

life.news: Jasmin’s grandmother knitted me a second sweater. On purpose. Jasmin is furious.
life.more: Her grandmother caught me in the stolen one and said if I was going to steal, I should at least have one in my color. Green, cable knit, fits perfectly. Jasmin says it’s a betrayal. I say it’s a peace treaty.

gossip.says: Billie Wraith runs the goth night at the casino lounge and laughs at my jokes in all the wrong places. She’s the best person I’ve ever lost an argument to.
gossip.note: Sloane Mercer says she is sometimes seeing Billie Wraith.
gossip.ask: Sloane says you laugh at her jokes in the wrong places.
gossip.answer: Only the wrong places are funny. Sloane is the cleverest person in any room and the least careful. I tell her things I shouldn’t because she makes me laugh first. One day one of her jokes is going to hurt somebody. I hope it isn’t her.

gossip.says: Jasmin Malik’s grandmother knits sweaters for the whole climate group, and I stole one. Jasmin has never forgiven me. I wear it to every meeting.
gossip.note: Sloane Mercer says she stole a sweater knitted by Jasmin Malik’s grandmother.
gossip.ask: Sloane says she stole your grandmother’s sweater.
gossip.answer: She did, and then my grandmother knitted her another one, which is somehow worse. Sloane is a menace and the only person in the group who argues like it matters. Tell her I want the first one back. Tell her I know she won’t give it.

women.name: April Kearney
women.look: Fair skin, golden-brown ringlets, a gap-toothed smile, mustard turtleneck

women.name: Isla Jameson
women.look: Rosy fair skin, loose spiral curls, rosy cheeks, vintage windbreaker

women.name: Kiki O’Dell
women.look: Freckled fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, thin wire-rimmed glasses, hand-knitted sweater

women.name: Annika Joseph
women.look: Freckled fair skin, brown waves with teal tips, a gap-toothed smile, corduroy jacket with enamel pins

women.name: Annabel Yates
women.look: Fair skin, a long braid to the waist, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, band T-shirt under dungarees

women.name: Rhea Cooper
women.look: Freckled fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, tortoiseshell glasses, corduroy jacket with enamel pins

women.name: Tamsin Wilde
women.look: Olive skin, golden-brown ringlets, a wide bright smile, band T-shirt under dungarees

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Community art collective. I run the workshop at the underpass and I bake for our dinners. Elaborate cakes. Badly, but with enormous confidence.

own.label: Ask if art is her only job
own.player: Is art your only job?
own.reply: I do late service at the club when they need waitresses. The collective doesn’t pay and my mother’s home costs money. I carry plates past people who once gave me a scholarship. They never look up.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you close to your family?
own.reply: My father drove for the Foundation and died at the junction when I was twelve. My mother is in a home now. Her mind is going, slowly. I visit every other day. Sometimes she knows me.

own.label: Ask who her best friend is
own.player: Who’s your best friend?
own.reply: Jasmin. Since we were six. She’s held my coat at every fight I’ve ever been in. Lately I’ve started to understand what else she’d hold.

own.label: Ask why she stopped baking
own.player: Why did you stop baking?
own.reply: Everyone noticed. Nobody asked, which was kind. I’ll tell you one thing. There’s a tin in my cupboard with my last collapsed cake in it, and the lid is more interesting than the cake.

calls.label: Ask how she really is
calls.player: How are you, really?
calls.reply: Quiet. I was funny before, quick, loud. That woman is in a cupboard with the cakes. I think whoever gets me talking again will get her back. I don’t think it’ll be the police.

calls.label: Ask what’s weighing on her
calls.player: Something’s weighing on you. Tell me.
calls.reply: I worked late service that night. I saw a man in a lanyard walk a woman through the kitchen to a car with its door open. She had her hand in her pocket. She said not here. Afterward two men came to my kitchen. One said scholarship. One said mother. I told the police I saw nothing. I wrote it all inside a cake tin’s lid, in pencil.
calls.note: Tamsin Wilde saw a man in a lanyard take a woman through the gala kitchen to a waiting car; after two men threatened her scholarship and her mother’s care, she told police she saw nothing, but wrote it inside a cake tin’s lid.

life.news: Workshop at the underpass today. A little boy painted a horse with six legs and refused to fix it. Correct decision.
life.more: He said it was a fast horse. His mother wanted to paint over the extra legs and he stood in front of the wall with his arms out. We left it. It’s the best thing on the whole mural now.

life.news: My mother called me by my father’s name today. Then she apologized, very politely, like I was a stranger.
life.more: The nurse said it happens, that names come loose before faces do. I held her hand for an hour and she told me about a man who drove too fast at the junction. She didn’t know she was talking about him. I did.

life.news: Jasmin cooked for me. Burned the onions, salted it twice, made me eat all of it. Best meal of the month.
life.more: She sat on the counter and watched me finish like a prison guard. Then she washed up and sang badly the whole time. I laughed, properly, for the first time in a while. She looked so pleased she dropped a plate.

life.news: Somebody left a box of good paintbrushes at the underpass with a note: for the horse. No name.
life.more: Sable brushes, the expensive kind. The boy’s mother swears it wasn’t her. I put them on the shelf where the workshop can reach them. Maybe there are just kind people around. I’m trying to believe that again.

gossip.says: Jasmin Malik has been my best friend since we were six. She’s held my coat at every fight I’ve been in. She feeds me now. I don’t know what I’d do without her.
gossip.note: Tamsin Wilde says Jasmin Malik has been her best friend since they were six.
gossip.ask: Tamsin says you’ve held her coat at every fight.
gossip.answer: Every single one, and I’d hold more than her coat if she asked. She’s been somewhere far away lately, even sitting right next to me. I feed her and I wait. When she comes back, I’ll be the first thing she sees. That’s been the plan for years.

gossip.says: Eden Sutherland’s overflow lives in our apartment. Boxes of leaflets, a bicycle, a cactus that’s definitely dead. Eden swears she’ll collect it all. Eden has been swearing that for a year.
gossip.note: Tamsin Wilde says Eden Sutherland keeps boxes, a bicycle and a dead cactus in her apartment.
gossip.ask: Tamsin says your boxes and your dead cactus are still in her apartment.
gossip.answer: The cactus is resting. And those boxes are history, every leaflet the movement ever printed. Tell Tamsin I’ll collect them when I have a home with a door that locks. She’ll laugh. Then she’ll make me a cake.

women.name: Paz Herrera
women.look: Golden-tan skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, deep dimples, hand-knitted sweater

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Climate group, direct action. I chain myself to things. I’ve been arrested twice and charmed both custody sergeants. One of them drinks with the nurse. Everyone drinks with the nurse.

own.label: Ask what she does at night
own.player: What do you do at night?
own.reply: I photograph the neon signs on the motel strip. There’s a woman who does the same from the other end. We don’t speak until the fortieth sign. Then we talk about nothing. It’s the best friendship I have.

own.label: Ask about her worst campaign
own.player: What’s your worst campaign?
own.reply: The bin fire at the recycling drive. Rebecca tells it as her worst campaign. It was me. I let her have it. It was a very good fire.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: What’s your family like?
own.reply: A younger sister in the police, Monica, who promised our mother she’d look after me. A father on Brown Avenue I argue with once a week while I wash his dishes. It works. Don’t ask how.

own.label: Ask if she regrets anything
own.player: Anything you regret?
own.reply: I sat in on some meetings once. A woman called Vanessa, a louder campaign, bigger ideas. I left when the talk went quiet. Quiet is when campaigns turn into something else. I’d like to think I was in that room by accident.
own.note: Paz Herrera sat in on Vanessa Greer’s meetings and left when the talk went quiet.

calls.label: Ask if anything odd is going on
calls.player: Anything odd going on near you?
calls.reply: A gray car’s been parked under my window for two weeks. I figured it was scouting the neon. My neighbor across the landing never turns her lights on. Maybe it’s watching her. Maybe it’s watching me. Either way, I wave at it.
calls.note: Paz Herrera says a gray sedan has been parked under her window for two weeks; her neighbor Rosa Gutierrez sits in the dark across the landing.

calls.label: Ask what she’s planning
calls.player: What are you planning?
calls.reply: The co-op got a donation from a trust on the ridge. A friend told me. I set fire to bins for a living, so I’ve decided to go and find the ridge. With a camera. And a can of something. Don’t tell my sister.
calls.note: Paz Herrera learned the co-op’s donation came from a trust on the ridge and plans to go up there with a camera.

life.news: Got arrested this morning. Charmed the sergeant. Out by lunch. He bought me a sandwich.
life.more: I’d locked myself to the water board’s railing with a bicycle lock and a very good sign. They cut me loose in four minutes. The sergeant asked if I’d done this before. I said twice. He said he could tell. Then he bought me a sandwich.

life.news: Fortieth sign tonight. We finally spoke. She likes the same diner sign I do. We’re practically married.
life.more: The one with the coffee cup that only half lights up. Forty signs of silence, and then we both pointed at it at the same time from opposite ends of the strip and laughed. We talked about nothing for an hour. It was perfect nothing.

life.news: Argued with my father about the dishes. Then politics. Then my mother. In that order. Every week.
life.more: He says I’m too angry. I say he’s not angry enough. Then I wash and he dries and neither of us says anything, and that’s the part that counts. I cried on the bus home. Don’t tell him.

life.news: My sister turned up at my door in uniform, late at night, to check I was home. I was home.
life.more: Monica says she drove past and my light was on and she worried. I said a light being on is the opposite of something to worry about. She came in, ate my leftovers standing up, told me to be careful, and left. She takes promises very literally.

gossip.says: Monica Herrera is my little sister and a police officer, which is a sentence I still can’t say with a straight face. She promised our mother she’d look after me. She takes it very literally.
gossip.note: Paz Herrera says her sister Monica Herrera promised their mother she’d look after Paz.
gossip.ask: Paz says you take your promise to look after her very literally.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to. Paz chains herself to railings and charms the sergeants who cut her loose. I drive past her window on my way home. Every night. She thinks I don’t. Tell her I saw the light on and I’m glad.

gossip.says: Rebecca Shaw tells the story of the recycling drive bin fire as her worst campaign. It was mine. I let her keep it. She tells it so well.
gossip.note: Paz Herrera says Rebecca Shaw tells the recycling drive bin fire as her own worst campaign.
gossip.ask: Paz says the bin fire was hers, not yours.
gossip.answer: She would say that! It was my campaign, my bin, my disgrace. She just held the matches. Fine. She lit them. But I made the sign. Tell Paz I’ll split the credit if she splits the fine.

women.name: Agnes Castillo
women.look: Deep brown skin, box braids to the waist, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, soft cream sweater and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the parish garden
own.player: What grows in a desert parish garden?
own.reply: Roses, if you’re stubborn. Prickly pear, if you’re sensible. We grow both, which is very Catholic of us.

own.label: Ask about the ballroom dancing
own.player: You’re learning ballroom dancing?
own.reply: Yes, and I’m dreadful. It’s good for me. You have to let someone else lead, which I find very hard.

own.label: Ask what she’s worried about
own.player: You seem worried about something.
own.reply: There’s a payment in the parish books to a company I’ve never heard of. Nobody will explain it. I’ve prayed about it and I still want an answer.
own.note: Agnes Castillo found an unexplained parish payment to an unknown company.

own.label: Ask what grows best in the desert
own.player: What grows best in the desert?
own.reply: Things that wait. Seeds sit for years until the rain comes. My grandmother called it faith with roots.

own.label: Ask what else happens in the garden
own.player: What goes on in the chapel garden?
own.reply: Roses, vegetables for the pantry, and a kiln where Alma fires her pots one evening a week. On firing nights the whole garden smells like bread and stones.

own.label: Ask about her father
own.player: What did your father do?
own.reply: He was the Old Mission’s last sacristan. He died there, of a stroke, in the crypt, while he was locking it. My mother still sings in the choir. She won’t go up the mission road.

own.label: Ask if she has a sister
own.player: Do you have any sisters?
own.reply: Freya. Two doors from the Old Mission, with a house full of cacti. We haven’t spoken in six years, over God. I pray for her every night. She’d hate that.

own.label: Ask what her father said at the end
own.player: What did your father say, at the end?
own.reply: He called me from the crypt, before the stroke took him. He said the bell was ringing, and that it couldn’t ring. That bell has been cracked since before my grandmother was born. I’ve told nobody but God, and now you.
own.note: Agnes Castillo’s father called her from the Old Mission’s crypt before he died, saying the cracked bell was ringing.

own.label: Ask about the payment in her accounts
own.player: Why is a strange payment in your garden accounts?
own.reply: Because nobody reads the garden accounts. Somebody chose my line on purpose to hide a payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy. I’ve prayed about it. God hasn’t told me who. I’m still asking.
own.note: Agnes Castillo says a payment to Halcyon Ridge Consultancy was hidden in her garden accounts.

life.news: The prickly pear flowered. Bright yellow, all at once, as if it had been saving it up.
life.more: Roses if you’re stubborn, prickly pear if you’re sensible. We grow both, which is very Catholic of us. The prickly pear waited three years. Things that wait grow best. My grandmother called it faith with roots.

life.news: Ballroom class. Trod on my partner four times. He said I was improving. I wasn’t.
life.more: I’m dreadful at it. It’s good for me. You have to let someone else lead, which I find very hard. Naomi from the Bluebirds is in my class and she leads with her head. Between us we’re a hazard. The instructor has started wearing steel toes.

life.news: Walked past my sister’s house. Six years since we spoke. Didn’t knock.
life.more: Freya and I were a year apart and inseparable until our father died. I prayed and she raged and we said things in a kitchen. Today the curtain moved. I don’t know if it was her. I kept walking. I’ll pray about it.

life.news: Taught a boy from the pantry to plant a seed. He checked on it every hour.
life.more: He’s seven and very serious. He put the seed in the pot like he was posting a letter, then came back every hour to see if it had answered. Seeds sit for years until the rain comes. He doesn’t have years. I watered it twice to help.

gossip.says: Naomi Whitlock from the Bluebirds is in my ballroom class and dances like she’s doing her accounts. We’re the two worst dancers in Sunfall and we’ve become friends out of shame.
gossip.note: Agnes Castillo says Naomi Whitlock, a Bluebird, is in her ballroom class.
gossip.ask: Agnes says you dance like you’re doing your accounts.
gossip.answer: That’s fair! I count the steps in a spreadsheet in my head. I’ve never felt anything I didn’t put in a spreadsheet first. Agnes counts in Spanish under her breath and apologizes to the floor. We’re terrible. It’s the best part of my week.

gossip.says: Sophia Moretti grows her mother’s roses in the desert, and they came up red this year. She brought me a cutting and wouldn’t let me thank her.
gossip.note: Agnes Castillo says Sophia Moretti grows her late mother’s roses.
gossip.ask: Agnes says you gave her a rose cutting and wouldn’t let her thank you.
gossip.answer: She’d have thanked me with a whole speech! Agnes is the best gardener in the parish and she doesn’t say much, so a thank-you from her is like a sermon. I just wanted Mamma’s roses in her garden too. That’s all. God bless you for asking.

women.name: Eliza Montoya
women.look: Warm brown skin, box braids to the waist, freckles across her nose, soft cream sweater and long pleated skirt

own.label: Ask about the food pantry
own.player: What’s the food pantry like?
own.reply: Busy and quiet at the same time. People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed. That’s the real work. The cans are just the excuse.

own.label: Ask why she volunteers
own.player: Why do you give so much of your time?
own.reply: Because it was given to me first. When my family had nothing, the Sisters fed us and never once made us feel small. I owe them the rest of my life, gladly.

own.label: Ask what’s troubling her
own.player: You seem troubled.
own.reply: The pantry’s storeroom has a filing cabinet nobody uses, and now it’s locked and the key is gone. Someone is keeping something in a place nobody thinks to look.
own.note: Eliza Montoya says an unused filing cabinet in the food pantry’s storeroom is now locked and its key is missing.

own.label: Ask who comes to the pantry
own.player: Who comes to the food pantry?
own.reply: People you’d never guess. A nurse. A man in a suit who cried. Pride is the hardest thing anyone carries through that door.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Tell me about your family.
own.reply: Three little brothers, a mom who cleans, and a dad who drove the casino’s deliveries until they let him go without a reason. We had nothing once. We have a little now. The Sisters’ name is said in our house like a saint’s.

own.label: Ask about the cakes she serves
own.player: What do you serve at the pantry?
own.reply: Whatever comes in. A girl from the club brings cakes that always collapse, so I serve them in bowls and call it trifle. Nobody has ever complained.

own.label: Ask about the locked cabinet
own.player: What do you think is in the locked cabinet?
own.reply: Something Margaret is afraid of the bishop finding. Her hand goes to that cabinet when he’s mentioned, and Evelyn’s hand goes to her collar. I’ve worked out they’re the same thing. I haven’t said so. I’m saying it to you because you won’t tell.
own.note: Eliza Montoya believes the pantry’s locked cabinet holds what Margaret Holloway is hiding from the bishop, and Evelyn Rosales wears its key.

life.news: A woman came into the pantry ashamed this morning and left laughing. Best can of beans I’ve ever handed over.
life.more: People come in ashamed and leave a little less ashamed. That’s the real work. The cans are just the excuse. Today she told me a joke about her husband and the beans. I’m not repeating it. It was very rude. I laughed till I cried.

life.news: Got a watch ticking at the repair bench. It was my practice watch, but still.
life.more: My father’s watch stopped, so I’m learning to mend them on my day off. Today the practice one ticked. Danica, who sits next to me, clapped very quietly. When I can do my father’s, I’ll tell him. Not before.

life.news: My dad’s been out of work a month now. He sits in the yard fixing things that aren’t broken.
life.more: He drove deliveries for the casino until they let him go for a reason they didn’t give. He’s a proud man. When we had nothing the Sisters fed us and never made us feel small. I’m trying to do the same for him at home. It’s harder with your own father.

life.news: A man in a suit cried in the pantry storeroom today. I’ll never say who.
life.more: Pride is the last thing to go. He came in for a parcel for a neighbor, he said. Then he sat on a box of cans and cried for ten minutes. I gave him a cup of tea and a parcel and didn’t ask whose neighbor. Everyone’s somebody’s neighbor.
