own.reply: Thirteen crescent pendants, paid in cash, collected by a girl who wouldn’t take her sunglasses off. I make a mark on everything I cast. I’d know them anywhere.
own.note: Lenore Vale cast thirteen crescent pendants for a cash order, and marks everything she makes.

own.label: Ask what she’d make for someone she loved
own.player: What would you make for someone you loved?
own.reply: A ring that doesn’t look like a ring. Something only the two of us would know meant anything.

own.label: Ask who taught her
own.player: Who taught you to make jewelry?
own.reply: Josephine Mercer, at the Canal Bench. I’m her best apprentice and she’ll never say so. She tells me my solder is lazy. It isn’t. It’s confident.

own.label: Ask what she does after work
own.player: What do you do when the bench closes?
own.reply: I play drums in a lock-up. There’s another woman in the next lock-up who plays even worse. We’ve never spoken. It’s the best relationship I’ve had.

calls.label: Ask who’s wearing her pendants
calls.player: Have you seen your crescents on anyone?
calls.reply: I’d know my mark across a room. A reporter bought a thirtieth. Hex and Ivy wear theirs. A man in a charity lanyard had one at the Vestry. And there’s one painted on the bottom of a cup somebody brought me.
calls.note: Lenore Vale has seen her crescent pendants on Hex Morrow, Ivy Sable and a man in a charity lanyard.

calls.label: Ask about the ring nobody collected
calls.player: Is there anything at the bench nobody collected?
calls.reply: My uncle’s ring. The Bluebirds gave it to him, a husband’s signet, as a favor. I resized it. He never came for it. There’s a crescent inside the band.
calls.note: Lenore Vale has Professor Vale’s uncollected signet ring from the Bluebirds, with a crescent inside.

life.news: A widow asked me to set her husband’s hair in a locket today. I did it under a lamp, very slowly. Best thing I’ve made this year.
life.more: People think it’s morbid. It’s love that refuses to stop. She held it a long time before she put it on. She said it was heavier than she expected. I told her they always are.

life.news: My lock-up neighbor left me a note. It said: you’re out of time. That’s all.
life.more: I play drums in a lock-up late at night when the bench is quiet. The woman next door plays too. We’ve never spoken. Now she’s written me a review. I’ve written back: so are you. It’s the most romantic thing that’s happened to me in a year, which says a lot about my year.

life.news: Burnt my hand on the torch. Proper burn. I’m typing with one finger.
life.more: Lost-wax casting doesn’t forgive daydreaming, and I was daydreaming. Veda found me and held my hand under the cold tap for twenty minutes, swearing at me the whole time. She’s very caring in a way that sounds like being told off.

life.news: Sat at Cassandra’s collective today with people who have no idea what I make. Bliss.
life.more: Nobody asked about the silver. We painted terrible watercolours of a lemon. Mine looked like a sad moon. Cassandra said it had integrity. I’m going to frame it and price it at a thousand.

gossip.says: Cassandra Finch runs an art collective where nobody’s allowed to be good at anything. It’s the most restful place in Sunfall. She makes everyone paint a lemon first.
gossip.note: Lenore Vale says Cassandra Finch runs an art collective where everyone paints a lemon first.
gossip.ask: Lenore says you make everyone paint a lemon first.
gossip.answer: A lemon tells me everything. People who paint it yellow are fine. People who paint the shadow first are the ones I keep an eye on. Lenore painted the shadow first. Then she painted a moon by mistake.

gossip.says: Veda Thorn shows horror films on a bedsheet in a back room on the canal. She talks through all of them and she’s right every time.
gossip.note: Lenore Vale says Veda Thorn runs horror film nights on a bedsheet by the canal.
gossip.ask: Lenore says you talk all the way through your own film nights.
gossip.answer: I do commentary. It’s a service. Somebody has to point out the vampire is a landlord. Come to the next one. Bring something to throw when the projector jumps. It always jumps. That’s the best bit.

gossip.says: Morrigan Hale’s bridesmaid orders have all dried up at once. Every one canceled. She won’t say why, and she’s too proud to ask.
gossip.note: Lenore Vale says Morrigan Hale’s bridesmaid orders have all been canceled at once.
gossip.ask: Lenore says all your bridesmaid orders have been canceled at once.
gossip.answer: Lenore notices too much. Yes. Five canceled in two weeks, and the envelopes all came the same way. I’m not saying anything else over text. Ask me in person one day, if you’re brave.

women.name: Ashlyn Vex
women.look: Dark skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, a small nose stud, velvet choker and black slip dress

own.label: Ask about running the venue
own.player: What’s it like running a music venue?
own.reply: Mopping beer off the floor at the end of the night while a band argues about their fee. I wouldn’t swap it for anything. The floor is sticky with history.

own.label: Ask why she’s learning Italian
own.player: Why are you learning Italian?
own.reply: So I can be dramatic in a language that deserves it. English doesn’t have enough words for despair. Italian has a whole opera.

own.label: Ask about the worst band she’s booked
own.player: Who’s the worst band you’ve ever booked?
own.reply: A trio who played one note, very slowly, for an hour. They called it a protest. Against what, nobody found out. They sold out.

own.label: Ask what she’s restless for
own.player: What are you restless for?
own.reply: Somewhere that isn’t here. Then I get there and miss the sticky floor. I think home is just the place you complain about most.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: My mom ran a boarding house in Old Town. I grew up among lodgers. One was a young drama tutor called Leonard Kitteridge, who taught me to project. It’s flats now.

own.label: Ask how she started
own.player: How did you end up running the Rialto?
own.reply: I came in at nineteen as a barmaid and never left. Nine years managing the ballroom now. The floor’s sticky with history and I know every board that creaks.

calls.label: Ask who lives above the ballroom
calls.player: Who lives in the apartment above your ballroom?
calls.reply: Theon. The one who reads in verse through my ceiling every night. He climbs those stairs at all hours. The apartment above the old Rialto, if you need it on a map.
calls.note: Ashlyn Vex says Theon lives in the apartment above the old Rialto’s ballroom.

calls.label: Ask why she lets him stay
calls.player: Why do you let him stay up there?
calls.reply: The landlord’s company asked me to, in a letter, with a rent cut. A company with a made-up name. I’ve worked out why since: the Rialto is the next shopfront to go, and a tenant like him is a reason to close it.
calls.note: Ashlyn Vex says a company with a made-up name pays to keep Theon in the Rialto apartment, to have an excuse to close the building.

life.news: The one-note trio are back at the Rialto. Sold out again. I don’t understand people and I love them.
life.more: They play one note for an hour. People weep. A man proposed during it and she said yes during it, so nobody heard. I’ve been mopping beer off this floor for sixteen years and that’s the first proposal it’s seen. The floor’s sticky with history.

life.news: My landlord sent a letter signed by a company that doesn’t exist. I checked.
life.more: The Rialto’s lease is with a company whose name I can’t find anywhere. No office, no phone, just a signature I don’t recognize, and the rent went down, not up. Landlords who lower the rent are either saints or up to something. I’ve never met a saint.

life.news: My Italian teacher quit. She says I only want to learn the swearing.
life.more: Unfair. I also wanted the word for betrayal, the word for storm, and how to say I told you so with my hands. She said that’s still swearing. I’ve found a new teacher. He’s eighty and he loves it.

life.news: Nyx did the whole door on her own tonight. Took the money, threw out a drunk, kept the line happy.
life.more: She’s my assistant and she was terrified six months ago. Tonight she told a man twice her size he wasn’t coming in, and he said sorry and left. I nearly cried. I didn’t. I said not bad, in Italian, which she doesn’t speak.

gossip.says: Ruth Calder, the Bluebird with the clipboard, is Nyx’s sister. She’d rather die than set foot in the Rialto, and she pays toward Nyx’s wages anyway. Don’t tell either of them I told you.
gossip.note: Ashlyn Vex says Ruth Calder secretly pays toward her sister Nyx’s wages at the Rialto.
gossip.ask: Ashlyn says you’ve been paying toward your sister’s wages at the Rialto.
gossip.answer: Ashlyn has a lovely voice and a terrible sense of discretion. Nyx doesn’t know, and she won’t, because you’re going to forget this conversation. Families pay for things. Mine pays quietly.

gossip.says: Cassidy Boone from police records keeps coming to the Rialto to sketch the ballroom. She says she wants to draw it before it goes. Before what goes? She won’t say.
gossip.note: Ashlyn Vex says Cassidy Boone keeps sketching the Rialto ballroom before it goes.
gossip.ask: Ashlyn says you’re drawing the Rialto before it goes. Before what goes?
gossip.answer: Before anything goes. Buildings like that don’t last in this town. Old ballrooms become parking lots, so I draw them first. Ashlyn thinks I know something. I always know something. It’s rarely the thing she means.

gossip.says: Odette Price from Sunfall FM recorded the Rialto floor creaking for a radio piece. An hour of creaking. People rang in to say it made them cry.
gossip.note: Ashlyn Vex says Odette Price recorded an hour of the Rialto floor creaking for the radio.
gossip.ask: Ashlyn says you made a radio piece out of her floor creaking.
gossip.answer: An hour of a ballroom breathing. Every board has its own note, did you know? Some of them are a hundred years of waltzes. The station manager hated it. The phones didn’t stop. I keep the tape at home like a pet.

women.name: Morrigan Hale
women.look: Fair skin, chin-length raven bob with a fringe, tortoiseshell glasses, black lace corset top

own.label: Ask about her jewelry
own.player: What kind of jewelry do you make?
own.reply: Silver bats, tiny coffins, rings shaped like thorns. Brides buy them for their bridesmaids now. Goth has gone mainstream, and I’ve never been richer or sadder.

own.label: Ask about her collages
own.player: What do you make collages from?
own.reply: Old funeral cards and pressed flowers. It sounds morbid. It’s the most hopeful thing I do. Everyone in them was loved by someone.

own.label: Ask if she really breaks hearts
own.player: Is it true you break hearts?
own.reply: I don’t break them. I just leave before they get attached, and that hurts more than breaking. I’m working on staying. Slowly.

own.label: Ask what would make her stay
own.player: What would make you stay?
own.reply: Someone who notices when I go quiet and doesn’t panic. Someone who makes tea and waits. That’s all. Nobody waits.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Are you related to the Hales at the Daily?
own.reply: Beatrice and Brittany are my cousins. Dad sells sports goods and never understood a daughter who wore black at twelve. I renamed myself. He still calls me Mo.

own.label: Ask about the empty chair in her apartment
own.player: Who’s the spare chair for?
own.reply: Someone who notices when I go quiet and doesn’t panic. I keep it free. Optimism, in furniture form.

calls.label: Ask why her orders stopped
calls.player: Why have your bridal orders stopped?
calls.reply: I said no to Victoria in the Black Lace shop, in front of Piper. She smiled. Since then my brides have canceled one by one, and every cancellation comes with a crescent drawn on the envelope.
calls.note: Morrigan Hale refused Victoria Blackwood’s invitation, and since then her customers cancel with a crescent drawn on the envelope.

life.news: Made a collage out of an old funeral card and three pressed violets. I love it more than people.
life.more: The card was for a woman called Edith who died at ninety-one. Her family wrote: she made the best scones and never forgave anyone. I’ve framed her with violets. Everyone in these was loved by someone. It’s the most hopeful thing I do.

life.news: Having a quiet day. The kind where I don’t talk much. It’s not you.
life.more: Some months I go down into a quiet I don’t need fixing out of. I make tea, I sit with it, I come back. If you can not panic about it, you’re already better at this than most people I’ve dated.

life.news: My cousin Beatrice says my glasses make me look like a librarian who bites. She meant it as a compliment. I think.
life.more: Beatrice is a reporter and she’s never said anything nice to me that wasn’t also a headline. We grew up at the same Christmas table, her in a tracksuit, me in black. My dad sells sports gear. I was a disappointment in a very specific way.

life.news: Somebody made me a cup of tea at the bench without asking how I take it, and got it exactly right.
life.more: Milk first, which is a crime, and two sugars, which is a confession. Juno watched me make one once and remembered. That’s the most romantic thing anyone’s done for me in years. Don’t tell her I said romantic.

gossip.says: My cousin Beatrice Hale is a reporter at the Daily and she was the worst kid at hide and seek in history. She’d tell you where she was. She still can’t keep a secret, so be careful what you give her.
gossip.note: Morrigan Hale says her cousin Beatrice Hale, the reporter, can’t keep a secret.
gossip.ask: Morrigan says you can’t keep a secret to save your life.
gossip.answer: That is slander and I’ll be printing a correction. I keep sources’ secrets forever. It’s family secrets I can’t keep, because family secrets are so much better. Morrigan used to be called something else, you know. Ask her. Actually, don’t. She bites.

gossip.says: My other cousin, Brittany Hale, is a florist, and she’s the only Hale who ever liked my black clothes. She does the funeral flowers and she’s very good at sad.
gossip.note: Morrigan Hale says her cousin Brittany Hale does beautiful funeral flowers.
gossip.ask: Morrigan says you’re very good at sad flowers.
gossip.answer: Aww, did she say that? I am! Lilies are easy, anyone can do sad lilies. The trick is one bright thing in the middle, so people have something to look at when they can’t look at the coffin. Morrigan taught me that, actually. Don’t tell her.

gossip.says: Daisy Chen makes collages too, at the community art place. She’s better than me at color and worse than me at sadness. We’re rivals. She doesn’t know.
gossip.note: Morrigan Hale says Daisy Chen is her secret collage rival.
gossip.ask: Morrigan says you’re her secret rival at collage.
gossip.answer: Her secret rival? I’ve had her work pinned over my desk for a year. I thought she didn’t know I existed. Tell her my color is just cowardice with good lighting. Hers is braver. Actually, don’t tell her that bit.

women.name: Cleo Rook
women.look: Pale skin, box braids to the waist, sharp winged eyeliner, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask about her venue
own.player: What’s your venue like?
own.reply: An old converted church with bad acoustics and a good bar. I’ve run it for twelve years. The bands get younger. The ghosts stay the same.

own.label: Ask about her travel journal
own.player: Where has your travel journal been?
own.reply: Lisbon, Prague, a bus station in the middle of nowhere for nine hours. I write by hand, because a phone forgets and paper doesn’t.

own.label: Ask what she’s proudest of
own.player: What are you proudest of?
own.reply: Never selling the venue to the people who wanted to turn it into apartments. They offered a lot. I told them it was haunted. It is.

own.label: Ask about the ghost
own.player: Is your venue really haunted?
own.reply: Something hums in the old vestry when the room is empty. I leave the light on for it. Everyone deserves someone who leaves a light on.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Do you live at the Vestry?
own.reply: In the old presbytery next door. The priest’s rooms. I sleep where a man used to write sermons. I write set lists. Same energy.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Have you got family?
own.reply: My mom was a nurse. She died when I was twenty. My father is unknown, including to my mother, she said, laughing. I came here from nowhere in particular and stayed.

calls.label: Ask what the hum really is
calls.player: What’s actually humming in the old vestry?
calls.reply: A bell. When the church was deconsecrated they meant to send it to the Old Mission to replace its cracked one. It never went. It’s in my cellar under the bar. On nights with no moon it hums, as if something somewhere is ringing a note it answers.
calls.note: Cleo Rook says the Vestry’s old bell, meant for the Old Mission, is in her cellar and hums on moonless nights.

calls.label: Ask if anyone wants the bell
calls.player: Has anyone asked about the bell?
calls.reply: A woman from the club, Delphine, asked to borrow it for the founders’ anniversary. I said I’d think about it. I’ve thought about it. The answer is getting louder.
calls.note: Cleo Rook says Delphine Moreau asked to borrow the Vestry’s bell for the Bluebirds’ founders’ anniversary.

life.news: The hum in the old vestry was louder last night. I left the light on again.
life.more: Twelve years I’ve run this place and the room still hums when it’s empty. Not the pipes, not the fridges, I’ve had them checked. I leave the light on for it. Whatever it is, it’s been here longer than me. You don’t turn the lights off on your elders.

life.news: Found a bus ticket from Lisbon in an old coat. Sat on the stairs and read my own journal for an hour.
life.more: I traveled five years on nothing. Slept in bus stations. Nine hours once in the middle of nowhere with a woman who sold me half a melon and taught me a card game I’ve never seen since. I write it all by hand. A phone forgets. Paper doesn’t.

life.news: The apartments people came around again with a bigger number.
life.more: They want the church. They always want the church. I told them it was haunted and the man laughed. Then the vestry hummed, right on cue, and he stopped laughing and left without his pen. I’ve kept the pen. It’s a nice pen.

life.news: A sixteen-year-old played her first gig here tonight. Her hands shook so much she dropped her pick twice.
life.more: Then she found it. Halfway through the third song the room went quiet in the good way. The bands get younger and the ghosts stay the same. I gave her a drink voucher for when she’s old enough. She’s going to frame it.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster reviews every band in Sunfall and she’s only ever given five stars to one act, a girl with a broken guitar. The bands are terrified of her. I love her.
gossip.note: Cleo Rook says Zadie Foster has only ever given one act five stars.
gossip.ask: Cleo says you’ve only ever given five stars once.
gossip.answer: Once. A girl with a broken guitar in the back room of the Lucky Cactus, playing like the room held thousands. My editor rang to check I wasn’t drunk. I wasn’t. I’d give it again. Everyone else is a four on a good night.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler collects roadside junk. Snow globes of gas stations, a spoon from a town of nine. Best taste in the Quarter, worst shelves.
gossip.note: Cleo Rook says Nixie Adler collects roadside souvenirs.
gossip.ask: Cleo says you own a spoon from a town of nine people.
gossip.answer: Population nine. Ten, the day I bought it, because I stopped for gas. It’s the best spoon in Sunfall. Cleo’s jealous because her souvenirs are all bus tickets, and you can’t stir tea with a bus ticket.

gossip.says: Khadija Rahman records sounds around town on an old reel machine. She came to the Vestry to record my hum and says she’s heard the same note somewhere else.
gossip.note: Cleo Rook says Khadija Rahman recorded the Vestry’s hum and heard the same note somewhere else.
gossip.ask: Cleo says you’ve heard her vestry hum somewhere else in town.
gossip.answer: It’s a real note, you know. I’ve got it on tape twice, from two places, which is the bit I can’t explain. I’m not telling you where until I’ve worked it out. Contrarian instinct. Also, I don’t know yet.

women.name: Veda Thorn
women.look: Dark skin, honey-blonde beach waves, freckles across her nose, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask how she makes her jewelry
own.player: How do you make your pieces?
own.reply: Lost-wax casting, a gas torch and swearing. The swearing is what gives them character.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: What do you show at your film night?
own.reply: Old horror films in a back room with a bedsheet for a screen. The jumps are better when the projector jumps too.

own.label: Ask why she skips small talk
own.player: Why do you skip the small talk?
own.reply: Because I’d rather argue with you about whether vampires are romantic. They’re not. They’re landlords.

own.label: Ask how she stays calm in a crisis
own.player: How do you stay so calm in a crisis?
own.reply: I fall apart beforehand, in private, in great detail. When the crisis comes I’m all used up. Calm is just exhaustion with good posture.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Is your family arty too?
own.reply: Nurses. Mom’s a ward sister, Gran was the hospital’s first matron. They fix bodies. I cast silver and swear. We’re all in the business of things that last.

own.label: Ask about her torch
own.player: Is that torch dangerous?
own.reply: It was Juno’s. She gave it to me when her hands got tired. I’ve set fire to one eyebrow and two opinions. Both grew back.

calls.label: Ask what the deleted film-night photo showed
calls.player: What was in the frame someone deleted?
calls.reply: My film night’s front row. Hex Morrow, next to a man in a charity lanyard and a boy holding a library book. Hex borrowed my camera to check the shot and deleted it. I restore things. I restored it.
calls.note: Veda Thorn restored a film-night photo of Hex Morrow beside a man in a charity lanyard and a boy with a library book.

life.news: Horror night tonight. The projector jumped at exactly the scariest moment and a man screamed so loudly a dog outside started barking.
life.more: Old black and white thing, a woman alone in a big house, the knock at the door. Projector jumped, man screamed, dog barked, whole room screamed at the dog. Best night I’ve ever run. The jumps are better when the projector jumps too.

life.news: Someone asked me out by telling me vampires are romantic. I’ve blocked him.
life.more: They’re not romantic. They’re landlords. They live forever off other people and never fix the boiler. He said I was being negative. I said I was being accurate. Then I unblocked him to send him an essay. Then I blocked him again.

life.news: My mom’s on night shifts on the ward again. I hate it when she does nights.
life.more: She’s a ward sister. My gran was the hospital’s first matron. I did a year of nursing and couldn’t. I fall apart first and then I’m calm, and nursing doesn’t give you time to fall apart first. So I make rings instead, and worry about her nights.

life.news: Cast a ring today that came out perfect first time. Never happens. I swore at it anyway, out of habit.
life.more: A little silver hand holding a smaller silver hand. It came out so clean I didn’t trust it, so I swore at it for luck. The swearing is what gives them character. Somebody’s going to propose with it. Not you. Sit down.

gossip.says: Lenore Vale plays drums in a lock-up late at night and won’t admit it. You can hear her from the canal. She’s actually good.
gossip.note: Veda Thorn says Lenore Vale secretly plays drums in a lock-up.
gossip.ask: Veda says you play drums in a lock-up late at night.
gossip.answer: Veda has excellent ears and no shame. Yes. Late, when the bench is quiet and I need to hit something that isn’t silver. The woman in the next lock-up plays too. We’ve never met. We review each other in notes. It’s the best relationship I’ve ever had.

gossip.says: Khadija Rahman lent me her projector for horror night, and she sits at the back and laughs at the scary bits. Every time. Very off-putting. I love her for it.
gossip.note: Veda Thorn says Khadija Rahman laughs at the scary bits at horror night.
gossip.ask: Veda says you laugh at the scary bits of her films.
gossip.answer: Fear is funny if you look at it properly. A man in a cape walking very slowly. It’s comedy nobody’s allowed to laugh at, so I laugh for everyone. Veda pretends to tell me off. She saves me the good seat.

gossip.says: Morrigan Hale goes quiet for days sometimes. Don’t panic when she does. Make tea, wait. She hates being fixed more than anything.
gossip.note: Veda Thorn says Morrigan Hale goes quiet for days and hates being fixed.
gossip.ask: Veda says you go quiet sometimes, and I shouldn’t panic.
gossip.answer: Veda’s kind in a way that sounds like a warning. Yes. Some months I go very quiet. It isn’t a crisis and it isn’t about you. If you can make tea and wait, you’ll be the first. Thank you for asking instead of guessing.

women.name: Nixie Adler
women.look: Freckled fair skin, dark French braid, thin wire-rimmed glasses, plum corset dress

own.label: Ask about her roadside souvenirs
own.player: What’s in your souvenir collection?
own.reply: A snow globe of a gas station, a plastic alien from a diner and a spoon from a town with a population of nine. I love things nobody else would keep.

own.label: Ask what running the venue taught her
own.player: What has running the venue taught you?
own.reply: That the quiet kid at the back will be famous in five years, and the loud one will owe me money. Every time.

own.label: Ask what she’s skeptical of
own.player: What are you skeptical of?
own.reply: Anyone who says they’re an old soul. Babe, you’re twenty-two. I have socks older than your soul.

own.label: Ask who looked after her when she was young
own.player: Who looked after you when you were young?
own.reply: A woman who ran a record shop and let me sit there all day when home was bad. I run the venue for kids like me. Somebody has to leave the door open.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The motel strip, in a bad house. At eleven I found a record shop in the Old Quarter where a woman let me sit all day and never asked why. She left me enough for the Furnace’s first year.

own.label: Ask why she runs the venue
own.player: Why run a venue?
own.reply: For kids like me. Somebody has to leave the door open. Mind you, sometimes the wrong people walk in through it.

calls.label: Ask who the record shop woman was
calls.player: Who was the woman at the record shop?
calls.reply: Marjorie. Honoria Blackwood’s cousin, disowned for the shop. Before she died she wrote me a letter telling me who Victoria really was, before the scene knew. It says the Blackwood women aren’t to be trusted with the moon.
calls.note: Nixie Adler has a letter from Honoria Blackwood’s cousin saying Victoria is a Blackwood and the Blackwood women aren’t to be trusted with the moon.

calls.label: Ask about the kids who go missing into the scene
calls.player: Who have you seen get pulled in?
calls.reply: Three lost kids this year: Hex, Sorrel, and a boy called Ethan Oakley. I watched the circle find them in my room and I didn’t stop it. I don’t stop kids finding things. I’m starting to think I should have.
calls.note: Nixie Adler watched the circle recruit Hex Morrow, Sorrel Vane and Ethan Oakley at the Furnace.

life.news: The quiet kid from the back of open-mic signed a deal today. I called it five years ago. Every time.
life.more: She used to sit on the stairs with a notebook and never sing. One night she sang one song and left. Now she’s got a contract and she sent me a photo of it with the words: you said. I keep that photo with my snow globes. The loud one from that night still owes me money.

life.news: Bought a plastic alien at the market today off a woman who swore it was haunted. Haggled her down because of it.
life.more: She wanted twelve. I said haunted’s a defect. Got it for four. It’s on the shelf next to the gas station snow globe, staring at the wall. It does seem to move a bit at night. Worth every penny of four.

life.news: Coffee at dawn after a long shift. Someone I care about is in trouble and I can’t fix it.
life.more: I run the venue for kids like I was, and sometimes one of them stops coming and you hear things. I don’t stop kids finding their way. I’m starting to wonder if that’s a rule or an excuse. Sorry. Long night. Ask me something easy.

life.news: A woman once let me sit in her record shop all day when I was eleven. I found her old shop sign in a dumpster today.
life.more: Faded, half the letters gone. I carried it home on the bus with everyone staring. It’s going over the Furnace door. Somebody left the door open for me. I leave it open for the next one. Now there’s a sign for it.

gossip.says: Rowan Pike won’t let anyone near her with a needle except Zara. I’ve known her ten years and I’ve seen her laugh twice. Both times at me.
gossip.note: Nixie Adler says Rowan Pike only lets Zara Brooks tattoo her.
gossip.ask: Nixie says she’s only seen you laugh twice in ten years. Both times at her.
gossip.answer: Three times. She doesn’t count the one where she fell off the stage at her own venue. That one was the best. She knows I’m counting. Neither of us will say what this is. That’s what makes it work.

gossip.says: Marianne Keene from the Bluebirds and I fight over the same market stall every month. Roadside junk. She wants the snow globes. She’s ruthless.
gossip.note: Nixie Adler says Marianne Keene, a Bluebird, competes with her for junk at the market.
gossip.ask: Nixie says you two fight over snow globes at the market.
gossip.answer: We don’t fight. I simply arrive earlier. Nixie thinks the market is an art form. It’s a negotiation. I collect roadside snow globes because they’re beautiful and nobody at the club would ever guess. Keep it that way.

women.name: Lavinia Gravesend
women.look: Thin and very pale, a long narrow face with hollow cheeks, kohl-smudged dark sullen eyes, a slim small-busted figure, a glossy black ponytail, a black mesh top and a tartan skirt

own.label: Ask about her jewelry
own.player: What do you make?
own.reply: Lockets, mostly. People put photographs and locks of hair in them, the way people did a hundred and fifty years ago. It sounds creepy. It’s the most romantic thing in the world.

own.label: Ask about her watercolours
own.player: What do you paint?
own.reply: The desert in the evening, very badly. I paint everything purple. My tutor said that’s not how color works. I said that’s how it works for me.

own.label: Ask what she’s noticed about you
own.player: What have you noticed about me?
own.reply: You ask questions and then actually wait for the answer. That’s rarer than you’d think. Most men are just reloading.

own.label: Ask what she’d put in her own locket
own.player: What would you put in your own locket?
own.reply: Nothing yet. I keep it empty on purpose. It feels like a promise I haven’t made to anyone.

own.label: Ask where she grew up
own.player: Where did you grow up?
own.reply: The trailer park behind the drive-in. It produced a goth, a Bluebird, a lab analyst and me. My friend Taryn says that’s a representative sample.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: Halfway up the ridge road, with Brad. The view is amazing. Ask me about the view. Don’t ask me about Brad.

calls.label: Ask about the purple painting
calls.player: What’s the purple painting in your apartment?
calls.reply: From my balcony I watched a van with no plates, a crate with air holes, and men with a laptop. And Brad getting in. I painted it all purple. It hangs on our wall and he thinks it’s a sunset.
calls.note: Lavinia Gravesend saw her boyfriend Brad Keller with the van with no plates and a crate with air holes on the ridge road.

life.news: Painted the desert purple again on the balcony this morning. The light was perfect.
life.more: My tutor said that’s not how color works. I said that’s how it works for me. The ridge goes violet before the sun’s up, and I get about twenty minutes before anyone needs anything from me. Twenty minutes is enough for a desert.

life.news: A woman came in wanting a locket for her dog’s fur. I said yes.
life.more: People put photographs and locks of hair in them, the way they did a hundred and fifty years ago. It sounds creepy. It’s the most romantic thing in the world. The dog was called Biscuit and he was fourteen. She held the locket like it was warm.

life.news: Bad night. Can we talk about something else?
life.more: I’m fine. Really. Tell me something about your day. Something boring. I like boring. Boring means nobody’s shouting.

life.news: My mom came to see my paintings for the first time.
life.more: She stood in front of the purple desert for ages and then said, that’s the view from your gran’s caravan. It is. I didn’t know I’d painted it from memory. We had tea and didn’t mention anything difficult. Nicest afternoon in a year.

gossip.says: Cassandra Finch and I were in the same home for six months when we were sixteen. She drew me then. She still draws me sometimes, from memory, and gets the hands right.
gossip.note: Lavinia Gravesend says she and Cassandra Finch were in the same home at sixteen.
gossip.ask: Lavinia says you two were in the same home at sixteen, and you still draw her.
gossip.answer: She told you that? She doesn’t tell people that. Yes. Six months, two thin girls and one window. I draw her when I’m worried about her. I’ve been drawing her a lot lately. If you’re her friend, be a good one.

gossip.says: Valerie Huxley went to my school. Two thin pale girls in the same class, and they made her a Bluebird and me a goth. Same girl, different paint.
gossip.note: Lavinia Gravesend says she went to school with Valerie Huxley, now a Bluebird.
gossip.ask: Lavinia says you two were the same girl at school, just different paint.
gossip.answer: Ha! That’s very Lavinia. We were both the girl who read in the bathroom at lunch. Then I got pearls and she got eyeliner. I still think she got the better deal. Tell her I said hi. Tell her properly.

gossip.says: There’s a barmaid called Lena on the ridge road who asks too many questions and tips too well for a barmaid. I saw her real name on a parking ticket. Maria Vega. I think she’s police.
gossip.note: Lavinia Gravesend thinks the ridge road barmaid Lena is Maria Vega, a police officer.
gossip.ask: Lavinia thinks you’re a barmaid called Lena on the ridge road.
gossip.answer: Lavinia should be careful who she says that to. Not because she’s right. Because the ridge doesn’t like guesses. If she ever needs a number to ring, she can ring mine. Tell her that, and nothing else.

women.name: Raven Solis
women.look: Pale skin, platinum pixie cut, strong dark brows, black mesh top and tartan skirt

own.label: Ask what it’s like running a venue so young
own.player: What’s it like running a venue at your age?
own.reply: Bands think I’m the merch girl until I tell them their fee. Then they think I’m terrifying. Both are true.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: I sing hymns in black lipstick. The old ladies were scared of me for a month. Now they knit me scarves. Black ones, specially.

own.label: Ask why she’s so mysterious
own.player: Why are you so mysterious?
own.reply: I’m not. I just don’t know what to say most of the time, so I say nothing, and people decide it means something.

own.label: Ask what she’d sing if nobody was listening
own.player: What would you sing if nobody was listening?
own.reply: Something cheerful. A really stupid pop song. Don’t tell anyone. It would ruin the whole thing I’ve got going.

own.label: Ask who looks after her
own.player: Who looks after you?
own.reply: My aunt Miranda. She’s a police officer and pays for my room above the hall and pretends she doesn’t. I pretend not to know. It works for both of us.

own.label: Ask about her mother
own.player: What was your mom like?
own.reply: Carmen. The beautiful one, everyone says. She died when I was six. The file says overdose. I sing because she did.

calls.label: Ask what the circle wants from her
calls.player: Has anyone asked you to sing somewhere strange?
calls.reply: Victoria wants me as the circle’s voice. I said nothing, and she took that as yes. There’s an invitation with my name on it in the hall’s letterbox. I haven’t opened it.
calls.note: Raven Solis has been invited by Victoria Blackwood to sing at the rite.

calls.label: Ask about the old hymn
calls.player: What’s the old hymn you learned?
calls.reply: Priya found it in the old books and asked the altos to try it. I can sing it. It’s the same round that’s on the circle’s tape. I might be the only person in Sunfall who knows both sides’ music.
calls.note: Raven Solis says the old hymn in St. Brigid’s books is the same round the circle uses.

life.news: Told a band their fee tonight. They thought I was the merch girl. The drummer went white.
life.more: They wanted double because they’d been on the radio once. I said the radio doesn’t pay my electric. They took the fee. Then they bought a T-shirt off me, because they still thought I might be the merch girl. Both are true.

life.news: The old ladies at choir gave me another black scarf. That’s nine.
life.more: They were scared of me for a month when I turned up in black lipstick. Now they knit me scarves. Black ones, specially. Mrs. Duarte says black is hard to knit because you can’t see your mistakes. I said that’s why I like it.

life.news: Someone sent me a letter with no name on it. I haven’t opened it.
life.more: It’s on the shelf by my bed. I keep looking at it. I’m not mysterious, I just don’t know what to do most of the time, so I do nothing, and people decide it means something. That’s what’s happening with the letter.

life.news: Argued with my boyfriend. He thinks everything dark is cool. It’s not cool. It’s just dark.
life.more: He likes the idea of the Old Quarter more than the Old Quarter. He wants me to be the girl in the songs. I’m a girl who does the door and sings alto and eats cereal for dinner. I don’t know if he’s met her.

gossip.says: Teresa Bellamy stands next to me in the choir and sings harmony so quietly you have to lean in. She told me black lipstick is fine in church as long as I mean the words.
gossip.note: Raven Solis says Teresa Bellamy, a Sister of Mercy, told her black lipstick is fine in church.
gossip.ask: Raven says you told her black lipstick is fine in church, as long as she means the words.
gossip.answer: I did, and I meant it. God isn’t looking at her lipstick. He’s listening to that alto, which is the best thing in the choir. I’m so glad she has someone to tell things to. She doesn’t talk much, but she sings like she does.

gossip.says: Jessica Rivera sings alto next to me too. She works at the pharmacy and hums the hymns while she counts pills. Customers think the place is haunted.
gossip.note: Raven Solis says Jessica Rivera hums hymns at the pharmacy.
gossip.ask: Raven says you hum hymns at the pharmacy and people think it’s haunted.
gossip.answer: Oh no. Do they? I don’t notice I’m doing it. Counting needs a rhythm. I’ll try to hum something less spooky. Raven’s lovely, you know. She looks scary and then she lends you her scarf.

gossip.says: Zadie Foster gave me five stars once, in the paper. I’d never played a proper gig. I’ve never been able to play like that since.
gossip.note: Raven Solis says Zadie Foster once gave her five stars.
gossip.ask: Raven says you gave her five stars for her first gig.
gossip.answer: The girl with the broken guitar? That was Raven? Of course it was. She played the back room of the Lucky Cactus like it held thousands. Tell her she doesn’t need to play like that again. She needs to play like that once more, and then like someone new.

women.name: Ophelia Byrne
women.look: Sun-kissed fair skin, chestnut high ponytail, gold hoop earrings, black mesh top and tartan skirt

women.name: Nyx Calder
women.look: Pale skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, tortoiseshell glasses, black mesh top and tartan skirt

women.name: Selene Ward
women.look: Pale skin, a sleek low bun, long lashes and a sleepy gaze, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Billie Wraith
women.look: Warm brown skin, blunt black bob, sharp winged eyeliner, plum corset dress

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I run the goth night at the casino lounge out on the state road. Velvet, a smoke machine, slot machines in the next room. It shouldn’t work. It works.

own.label: Ask if Wraith is her real name
own.player: Is Wraith your real name?
own.reply: It’s the one I chose. The one I was born with belongs to a man on the radio. You’d know his voice. Everybody does. That’s the problem with it.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: An apartment near the casino, paid for by the lounge’s fee. It’s more than any goth night has ever paid. I haven’t asked why. I’m good at not asking.

own.label: Ask what she’s reading
own.player: What are you reading?
own.reply: One page a week, with six friends, from a photocopy of an old book Victoria made before the museum took the original. It’s a book club. It’s also the circle’s catechism class. We’re six pages in.
own.note: Billie Wraith runs a book club for the circle that reads Victoria’s photocopy of the founders’ book, one page a week.

own.label: Ask if she’s close to her family
own.player: Are you close to your family?
own.reply: My mother left when I was twelve, for a Bluebird’s second husband’s brother. I’ve said that sentence out loud once before. Now twice.

calls.label: Ask how she got the casino booking
calls.player: How did you get the casino booking?
calls.reply: My father’s paycheck comes from the casino, so a goth girl got a casino booking at nineteen. I signed something. I’ve read it since. On paper, every invitation that goes out through the Black Lace shop is a casino promotion, and my name is on the paper.
calls.note: Billie Wraith signed the casino lounge contract at nineteen; on paper every invitation through the Black Lace shop is a casino promotion with her name on it.

calls.label: Ask if she’s seeing anyone
calls.player: Are you seeing anyone?
calls.reply: Sloane Mercer, on the nights she’s sober enough to find me. She makes me laugh, and when I laugh I say things I shouldn’t. I told her something in bed I’ve never told anyone. I haven’t asked myself why. I think I know.

life.news: Full house at the lounge tonight. A man lost his rent on the slots and danced it off to a dirge. Beautiful.
life.more: He came through from the casino side looking like the end of the world, stood at the back for one song, then danced until we closed. Black tie, no partner, eyes shut. Some people need a funeral for their money. We provide.

life.news: Somebody booked a bachelorette party at the lounge and asked for black roses on every table. I didn’t ask.
life.more: Black roses, black candles, a cake shaped like a coffin. The bride wanted it. Or her mother did. Morrigan Hale did the place cards in silver ink. We looked at them and laughed until we had to sit down. Weddings are getting very goth.

life.news: My father said my name on the radio tonight. Wished me luck with the lounge. Live. I turned it off.
life.more: The name I was born with. On Sunfall FM, in that voice everyone in town knows. He thinks it’s a kindness. It’s a leash. I sat in the car outside the casino until the next song was over, then went in and did my eyeliner again.

life.news: Sloane turned up sober and on time. Twice this week. I don’t know what to do with myself.
life.more: She brought coffee and remembered how I take it. We sat on the fire escape and watched the casino lights come on, and I laughed at something she said so hard I said something I meant. Careful, Billie.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler runs the Furnace and leaves the back door open for anyone who needs to get out of something. She’s the only venue manager who scares me.
gossip.note: Billie Wraith says Nixie Adler leaves the Furnace’s back door open for people who need to get out.
gossip.ask: Billie Wraith says you leave the Furnace’s back door open for anyone who needs it.
gossip.answer: Always. Old foundry rule. Heat needs somewhere to go, and so do people. Billie came in through the front once, years ago, and I’ve been waiting for her to use the back. She will. People always do.

gossip.says: Morrigan Hale does the calligraphy on my envelopes and makes tiny silver coffins that brides buy for their bridesmaids. Weddings are getting very goth.
gossip.note: Billie Wraith says Morrigan Hale does the calligraphy on her lounge’s envelopes.
gossip.ask: Billie says brides buy your little silver coffins for their bridesmaids now.
gossip.answer: They do. Death is in this season. I tell them the coffins mean a love that outlasts everything, which is true if you squint. Billie sends me envelopes to letter. Some of them I letter very slowly, and think about who they’re going to.

women.name: Indigo Crossley
women.look: Rosy fair skin, long red curls, tortoiseshell glasses, plum corset dress

women.name: Moth Delaney
women.look: Porcelain skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, a beauty mark above her lip, silver-buckled platform boots and black jeans

women.name: Ivy Sable
women.look: Warm brown skin, honey-blonde beach waves, a silver ear cuff, black lace corset top

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Gothic jewelry at the Canal Bench. Rings, cuffs, little silver things for people who like their sadness wearable. After the bench closes I throw pots.

own.label: Ask where she fires her pots
own.player: Where do you fire your pots?
own.reply: In the Sisters’ kiln, in the garden at St. Brigid’s, one evening a week. The nuns let anyone with clay use it. They think I’m the quiet potter. I am.

own.label: Ask what she did before jewelry
own.player: What did you do before jewelry?
own.reply: At twenty I was a lady’s maid in one of the old founding houses. I dressed the daughter for her first party. When the family threw her out, I helped her pack her trunk, and they dismissed me for it. Best thing I ever did.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do you have family?
own.reply: A brother. Dale. Works at the police station, married, two boys. We don’t talk as much as we should. I keep meaning to fix that.

own.label: Ask what she’s making at the kiln
own.player: What are you making at the kiln these days?
own.reply: Cups. Thirteen of them, black glaze, a little mark pressed into the base. A commission for some friends. The nuns admire the glaze and never turn them over.
own.note: Ivy Sable makes thirteen black cups with a mark pressed into the base, fired in the Sisters’ kiln at St. Brigid’s.

calls.label: Ask if she keeps any secrets
calls.player: Got any secrets?
calls.reply: One. I burned a book in the Sisters’ kiln. A photocopy some friends were reading together, one page a week. They hadn’t finished. I had. I kept the ashes in a jar. I don’t know why I kept them.
calls.note: Ivy Sable burned the circle’s photocopied book in the Sisters’ kiln before the book club had finished it, and kept the ashes in a jar.

calls.label: Ask about her brother
calls.player: How’s your brother?
calls.reply: Dale hasn’t come home. The men at the station say he ran off with a woman. Dale couldn’t run off with a woman if she carried him. Carla won’t say it, so I will. Something has happened to my brother.
calls.note: Ivy Sable is Dale Pruett’s sister and doesn’t believe the station’s story that he ran off with a woman.

life.news: A woman bought a ring for her own funeral today. She wanted to be sure it would suit her. It does.
life.more: Black onyx, a little skull on the shoulder of the band. She tried it on, turned her hand in the light and said she’d be the best-dressed corpse in the county. I gave her a discount for taste. We’re having coffee next week.

life.news: Opened the kiln this evening and one of my pots had cracked into the shape of a face. Not a nice face.
life.more: Long, sad, mouth open like it was halfway through a word. One of the Sisters came over, looked at it, and crossed herself very calmly. Then she asked if she could have it for the pantry window. I said yes. It’s watching the street now.

life.news: Burned my hand on the soldering iron. Nothing serious. Swore in four languages.
life.more: Silver work makes you careless when you’ve done it for ten years. I held my hand under the canal pump until it stopped stinging, and an old man passing by told me I’d done it wrong. He was right. I hate that he was right.

life.news: Sold a whole tray of earrings to a bachelorette party. Black lace and silver bats, eleven matching pairs.
life.more: The bride wanted everyone in black, which her mother apparently hated. They put the earrings on at the bench, shrieked at themselves in my little mirror, and left singing. The mother came back an hour later and bought a pair for herself.

gossip.says: Sister Agnes Castillo lets anyone with clay use the kiln in the garden. She’s never asked what I make. I think she knows more than she lets on, and she lets on exactly nothing.
gossip.note: Ivy Sable says Agnes Castillo lets anyone with clay use the Sisters’ kiln.
gossip.ask: Ivy says you never ask what anyone makes in your kiln.
gossip.answer: Why would I? Clay is honest. Whatever goes in comes out what it is. Ivy works quietly and cleans up after herself, which is more than I can say for the novices. If she ever wants to tell me what she makes, I’ll listen. I’ve heard everything at least once.

gossip.says: Billie Wraith runs the goth night at the casino lounge and keeps losing the rings I make her. I think she gives them away. I’ve stopped minding.
gossip.note: Ivy Sable says Billie Wraith keeps losing the rings Ivy makes her.
gossip.ask: Ivy says you keep losing her rings.
gossip.answer: I don’t lose them. I give them to girls at the lounge who look like they need something heavy to hold on to. Tell Ivy her rings are all over the Old Quarter, on the right hands. She’ll pretend not to care. She cares.

women.name: Astrid Sorrow
women.look: Freckled fair skin, glossy black ponytail, a silver ear cuff, fishnet sleeves under a band tee

women.name: Salem Bell
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, dirty-blonde ponytail, a small nose stud, velvet choker and black slip dress

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Gothic jewelry at the Canal Bench. I’m the senior one after Juno, which means I get the commissions nobody else wants and make the coffee nobody else makes. Old Quarter women hand my pieces down. I like knowing I’ll outlive myself.

own.label: Ask about the telescope
own.player: Is that a telescope on your roof?
own.reply: Bought at a charity auction. I outbid a man who wanted it for his boat. Some nights I drive it out past the canyon with a friend from the other side of town. We look at the stars. We don’t say what else we look at.

own.label: Ask about her name
own.player: Is Salem your real name?
own.reply: It is now. I picked it the night I moved to the Old Quarter. The woman I was before had a different name and a house key. I still have the key. That’s all you get for free.

own.label: Ask why her walls are bare
own.player: Why is there nothing on your walls?
own.reply: Every photograph from before I was eighteen has the same house in the background. I’d rather look at a blank wall and decide what goes there. Nothing has yet. I’m picky.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do you have family?
own.reply: A younger sister. We didn’t speak for ten years. Then one night she rang me out of nowhere and asked me something only I could answer. Now we’re close the way two knives in a drawer are close.

own.label: Ask about Victoria’s circle
own.player: Are you part of Victoria’s circle?
own.reply: I’m the one who says no. There are thirteen of us, and she lets exactly one person decide anything. I’ve said no twice. The first time I lost, and I don’t talk about where that ended up. The second time is still going.
own.note: Salem Bell is in Victoria Blackwood’s circle of thirteen and is the only one allowed to tell her no. She has done it twice.

calls.label: Ask if her father left her anything
calls.player: Did your father leave you anything?
calls.reply: A blue ribbon. It was tied on his stone in the cemetery. I took it the week I left home, and it’s on my bedpost now. Men in this town who marry into the wrong families get a ribbon, and nobody asks why they all died young. I ask.
calls.note: Salem Bell took a blue ribbon from her father’s stone. She says men who marry into the wrong families get one, and die young.

calls.label: Ask what she knows
calls.player: You know more than you say, don’t you?
calls.reply: I know the whole shape of it. What the old families did, why the bell rang, and why my sister thinks she can undo it. She found it out from a trunk. She found it out wrong. Ask me again when it’s over.
calls.note: Salem Bell says she knows what the old families’ rite was for, and that Victoria learned it from a trunk and got it wrong.

life.news: Finished a mourning ring for a woman who’s worn her mother’s for forty years. She wanted her own, finally.
life.more: Jet and silver, a plain band, her mother’s initials inside where only she’ll see them. She put it on, took the old one off and held both in her palm for a long time. Then she paid in cash and left without a word. Best kind of customer.

life.news: A crow landed on the bench’s windowsill this morning and watched me solder for an hour.
life.more: It didn’t blink, and it didn’t touch the crumbs Juno put out. It just watched my hands. When I finished the piece it tapped the glass once and left. Juno says it was critiquing. I say it was approving. We’ll never know.

life.news: Up on the roof all night with the telescope, and the clouds never moved. Not one star.
life.more: My friend drove out past the canyon anyway, and we sat on separate car hoods for three hours looking at nothing and not talking about it. Then the sun came up and we both pretended it had been worth it. It was, a little.

life.news: Taught the new apprentice to mark her work today. She cried. I pretended not to see.
life.more: Your mark is the only thing about a piece that’s entirely yours. Mine is a bell with no clapper. I didn’t tell her why. She’ll make up her own reasons, and they’ll be better than mine.

gossip.says: Lenore Vale marks her silver because I taught her to. She’s better at it than I am now, and she still checks my face before she shows anyone.
gossip.note: Salem Bell says she taught Lenore Vale to mark her silver.
gossip.ask: Salem says she taught you to mark your work.
gossip.answer: She did. She held my hand on the punch the first time so I wouldn’t ruin the ring. Salem doesn’t teach anyone anything she doesn’t want them to keep forever. I still check her face. I always will.

gossip.says: Victoria Blackwood listens to nobody. Nearly nobody. Ask her who gets to tell her no.
gossip.note: Salem Bell says almost nobody can tell Victoria Blackwood no.
gossip.ask: Salem says almost nobody gets to tell you no.
gossip.answer: Salem says a great deal for a woman who only speaks in hints. Yes. One person. She’s used it twice, I let her, and I’m still deciding whether I’ll let her again.

women.name: Coraline Dusk
women.look: Freckled fair skin, jet-black waist-length hair, a gap-toothed smile, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Juno Varley
women.look: Fair skin, sleek middle-parted dark hair, a gap-toothed smile, long black velvet coat

women.name: Lilith Kestrel
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, dark brown messy bun, gray-green eyes, silver-buckled platform boots and black jeans

women.name: Ezraine Quinn
women.look: Rosy fair skin, a sleek low bun, rosy cheeks, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Eris Moon
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, platinum pixie cut, thin wire-rimmed glasses, plum corset dress

women.name: Marlowe Poe
women.look: Pale skin, glossy black ponytail, a small nose stud, long black velvet coat

women.name: Wren Black
women.look: Pale skin, copper waist-length waves, strong dark brows, studded leather jacket

women.name: Milena Kovac
women.look: Rosy fair skin, short silver-dyed crop, a wide bright smile, black mesh top and tartan skirt

women.name: Vesper Lane
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, long red curls, strong dark brows, plum corset dress

women.name: Hex Morrow
women.look: Olive skin, chestnut high ponytail, amber eyes, long black velvet coat

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I’m the newest at the Canal Bench. I make the small things. Charms, clasps, whatever the others are too bored to cast. I’m very good at small things.

own.label: Ask where she lives
own.player: Where do you live?
own.reply: A room above the Furnace. Nixie found it for me. The music comes up through the floor every night and I sleep like a stone. Nixie regrets it. I can tell.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: I bake for a book club. Elaborate cakes. They collapse. Billie serves them in bowls and nobody complains to my face.

own.label: Ask what she wants out of life
own.player: What do you want out of life?
own.reply: To be chosen. And I have been. Someone very important told me I’m the future. I believe her. Do you know what that feels like, to be picked?

own.label: Ask about the most reckless thing she’s done
own.player: What’s the most reckless thing you’ve done?
own.reply: I opened a letter that came to the Furnace for a girl called Maren. An invitation to dinner at the lodge. I answered it. As her. It sounded like an adventure. Now they think Maren Caldwell is coming to dinner, and I’m going instead.
own.note: Hex Morrow answered a lodge dinner invitation addressed to Maren Caldwell, as Maren, and plans to go in her place.

calls.label: Ask what she’s proudest of
calls.player: What are you proudest of?
calls.reply: I made a mold. You pour chalk in, it sets in a perfect shape, and you can draw the same mark on a door in two seconds, exactly the same every time. Clever, right? I’m not allowed to say what it’s for.
calls.note: Hex Morrow casts chalk in a mold so the same mark can be drawn on doors in seconds.

calls.label: Ask about her old school friends
calls.player: Do you keep in touch with school friends?
calls.reply: Arielle. We sat two desks apart. She’s at the paper now, very serious. She asked me why I wanted a box of clippings lost. I said because someone asked. That was the whole reason. It still is.
calls.note: Hex Morrow asked Arielle Brooks to lose a box of clippings because someone in the circle told her to.

life.news: The band at the Furnace played my request three times tonight. I danced on a table. Nixie pretended not to see.
life.more: Velvet coat, boots, a table that was definitely not built for dancing. Somebody filmed it. I look like a storm in a coat. Nixie made me sweep the floor afterward, which I did, still dancing.

life.news: Cake collapsed again. Lemon this time. It folded in half like it was ashamed of me.
life.more: I’d followed the recipe exactly, which never helps. Billie looked at it for a long moment and got out the bowls without a word. Everyone ate it. Nobody looked me in the eye. I cried in the alley for a minute and then I was fine.

life.news: My parents called and asked if I’m eating. Then asked if I’m dating anyone. Then asked about the weather.
life.more: In that order, in the same tone. I said yes, no and hot. My mother said good to all three. I don’t think she was listening. I don’t think she wanted to be.

life.news: Cast forty silver bats in one afternoon. Juno says it’s a bench record. I’m insufferable now.
life.more: Little ones, wings out, for earrings. My fingers are black and I burned my thumb twice and I’ve never been happier. Juno bought me a soda as a prize. I keep the can on my windowsill.

gossip.says: Nixie Adler found me my room above the Furnace and has been regretting it ever since. She pretends not to watch me dance on the tables. She watches.
gossip.note: Hex Morrow says Nixie Adler found her a room above the Furnace.
gossip.ask: Hex says you found her a room and regret it.
gossip.answer: I regret the tables. Not the girl. Hex is a storm in a velvet coat and storms need somewhere to break. Better above my bar than somewhere worse. I leave the back door open for her. She hasn’t needed it yet.

gossip.says: Arielle Brooks sat two desks from me at school. Now she works at the paper and looks at me like I’m a story she hasn’t decided to write.
gossip.note: Hex Morrow says Arielle Brooks, her old school friend, works at the paper.
gossip.ask: Hex says you look at her like a story you haven’t written yet.
gossip.answer: I do, and I hate that I do. She was the funniest girl in our year, and now she says things like she’s been chosen. I keep waiting for her to call me. I think one day she will, and I think I won’t like what she says.

women.name: Dahlia Grieve
women.look: Porcelain skin, short silver-dyed crop, gray-green eyes, velvet choker and black slip dress

women.name: Sorrel Vane
women.look: Deep brown skin, wavy dark hair with a deep side part, tortoiseshell glasses, black lace corset top

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: Jewelry. Canal Bench. I don’t talk much.

own.label: Ask what she does in the mornings
own.player: What do you do in the mornings?
own.reply: Birdwatching on the dry river, before breakfast. Two other women watch upstream. None of us has ever spoken. It’s perfect.

own.label: Ask why she wears sunglasses indoors
own.player: Why the sunglasses indoors?
own.reply: So nobody looks at me. So I don’t look at them. Someone told me once that I’d said too much. I haven’t said much since.

own.label: Ask if she paints
own.player: Do you paint?
own.reply: The underpass mural. The night sky part. I paint it from memory. I’ve stood under that sky on nights with no moon, holding a candle. You remember the stars properly when it’s that dark.

own.label: Ask if she has siblings
own.player: Do you have any siblings?
own.reply: A brother, Ben. He takes photographs for the Night Wire. He deleted one of me once. He thinks I don’t know. I know.

calls.label: Ask why she seems nervous
calls.player: You seem nervous. What happened?
calls.reply: I left a key on Rowan Pike’s counter. Old iron, heavy. I was told the youngest holds it. I couldn’t throw it in the reservoir and I couldn’t keep it. So I gave it to the one person who wouldn’t ask.
calls.note: Sorrel Vane left an old iron key on Rowan Pike’s counter because she wants out; she was told the youngest holds it.

calls.label: Ask what she wants to say
calls.player: There’s something you want to say.
calls.reply: I collected thirteen pendants. Handed every one over. I know every name. I was told I’d said too much, once, so I stopped saying anything. I’m saying this.
calls.note: Sorrel Vane collected the thirteen pendants and knows every name they went to.

life.news: Saw a vermilion flycatcher on the dry river. First one this year. I didn’t tell anyone. Now I’m telling you.
life.more: Red like a struck match, sitting on a dead branch. The woman upstream saw it too. We looked at each other across a hundred yards and nodded. That’s the most I’ve said to anyone all week.

life.news: Someone left a pair of sunglasses on my bench. Exactly like mine. No note.
life.more: Same frames, same tint. I put them on. They were my prescription. I don’t know anyone who knows my prescription except the optician, and he’s eighty and never leaves his shop. I’m wearing them now. I don’t know why.

life.news: My brother came by the bench and didn’t say anything for twenty minutes. Neither did I. Then he left.
life.more: Ben stood by the window with his camera bag and looked at me like he wanted to take a picture and couldn’t. I kept working. When he left he touched the top of my head the way he used to. I had to stop working after that.

life.news: Painted a new constellation on the underpass. I made it up. Nobody has noticed it isn’t real.
life.more: Seven stars in the shape of a heron. I gave it a name in my head that I won’t say out loud. People point at it on their way past. A woman told her friend it was the bird that watches the river. She’s right.

gossip.says: Rowan Pike runs the shop on the corner and never asks why you’re there. That’s the whole reason I go in.
gossip.note: Sorrel Vane says Rowan Pike never asks customers why they’re there.
gossip.ask: Sorrel says you never ask why anyone’s in your shop.
gossip.answer: Because mostly I already know. Sorrel comes in, buys nothing, stands by the window, leaves. Once she left something behind. I put it somewhere safe. I didn’t ask. If she ever wants it back, it’s exactly where she thinks it is.

gossip.says: Sienna Navarro runs the underpass mural and lets me paint the night sky without talking. She does all the talking. It works.
gossip.note: Sorrel Vane says Sienna Navarro runs the underpass mural.
gossip.ask: Sorrel says you do all the talking at the mural.
gossip.answer: Somebody has to! Sorrel paints like she’s praying and I narrate like a nature documentary. A while back she added something to the sky that I didn’t plan. I left it. It looked like it belonged there. I didn’t ask, and she didn’t tell.

women.name: Kayla Mendoza
women.look: Dark skin, blunt black bob, gray-green eyes, floral blouse and jeans

own.label: Ask about decorating people’s homes
own.player: What’s it like decorating people’s homes?
own.reply: Everyone wants a calm neutral palette and then cries when they see it. I tell them gray is a mood, not a personality.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: What do you show at your film night?
own.reply: Romcoms, unapologetically. The neighbors bring wine and shout at the screen when he runs to the airport. We know he’ll make it. We need him to.

own.label: Ask about her worst impulse buy
own.player: What’s your worst impulse buy?
own.reply: A velvet sofa the color of a flamingo. It doesn’t fit through my door. It lives in my sister’s garage. I visit it.

own.label: Ask what her own home is like
own.player: What’s your own home like?
own.reply: Unfinished. I do everyone else’s and never mine. I think I’m waiting until there’s someone to choose the curtains with.

own.label: Ask about her daughter
own.player: Do you have children?
own.reply: Nikki, nineteen. I had her at sixteen and my family were horrified for about a year, then adored her. She works nights at the pharmacy and is sharper than me.

own.label: Ask about her film night
own.player: Who comes to your film nights?
own.reply: The neighbors, with wine. We watch romcoms and shout at the airport scene. We know he makes it. We need him to.

calls.label: Ask about the job she can’t photograph
calls.player: Have you ever done a job you couldn’t show anyone?
calls.reply: The lodge’s dining room, through the jeweler, cash, no photographs. The table seats nine. The ninth chair, at the end, has a blue ribbon on it, and the client asked me to match the fabric to the ribbon.
calls.note: Kayla Mendoza decorated the lodge’s dining room: a table for nine, with a blue ribbon on the ninth chair.

life.news: A client asked for a calm neutral palette. I gave her one. She cried. I said, gray is a mood, not a personality.
life.more: Everyone wants calm and neutral and then they see it and realize they’ve painted their life the color of a filing cabinet. I brought her a yellow cushion. She held it like a puppy. We’re repainting the kitchen.

life.news: Film night with the neighbors. When he ran through the airport, all eleven of us screamed.
life.more: Romcoms every other week in my front room. People bring wine and opinions. Tonight Mrs. Okafor threw a cushion at the screen when she nearly missed the plane. Everyone shouted GO. It’s the best night in the street.

life.news: Visited my flamingo sofa at my sister’s. It still doesn’t fit through my door. I sat on it for an hour.
life.more: A velvet sofa the color of a flamingo. I bought it in a fit of joy and it doesn’t fit through my front door. It lives in my sister’s garage and I go and visit it like a horse at a stable. One day I’ll have a door wide enough.

life.news: Finished three people’s homes this month. Mine still has no curtains.
life.more: I do everyone else’s and never mine. My daughter says I’m waiting for someone to choose them with. She’s nineteen and sharper than me. She’s right. I’ve had the fabric samples on the table for a year. Pick one for me? I’m joking. Mostly.

gossip.says: Olivia Reid hires me to stage the houses she sells. She describes them like film genres and I have to make them look like the film. I once made a damp apartment look like a romcom. It sold in a day.
gossip.note: Kayla Mendoza says she stages the houses Olivia Reid sells.
gossip.ask: Kayla says she once made a damp apartment look like a romcom for you.
gossip.answer: She did. Fairy lights, a stack of books, two mugs on the windowsill. Nobody noticed the damp because they were busy imagining being kissed in the kitchen. That’s Kayla. She doesn’t sell houses. She sells the next chapter.

gossip.says: Daniela Cruz makes dresses that last ten years. I asked her to make me curtains once. She said she doesn’t do curtains. Then she made them anyway. They’re perfect. I still haven’t hung them.
gossip.note: Kayla Mendoza says Daniela Cruz made her curtains she hasn’t hung.
gossip.ask: Kayla says you made her perfect curtains and she still hasn’t hung them.
gossip.answer: A year! They’re folded on her table like a wedding dress waiting for a wedding. Well-made things get better with time, but they do need hanging. I’ve offered to come around with a ladder. She says she’s waiting for the right person to hold it.

women.name: Brittany Hale
women.look: Light-brown skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, sharp winged eyeliner, turquoise peasant top

own.label: Ask about her souvenirs
own.player: What do you collect?
own.reply: Roadside souvenirs! A snow globe of a cactus, a spoon from a motel that burned down, a fridge magnet of the bear. I need help.

own.label: Ask about being a florist
own.player: What’s the best part of being a florist?
own.reply: Weddings. The worst part is weddings. Brides cry, mothers cry, I cry, the flowers wilt.

own.label: Ask what’s confusing her
own.player: Is something confusing you?
own.reply: Two people told me completely different stories about the same night of the gala. One of them is lying, and they both bought peonies.

own.label: Ask what flowers say that people can’t
own.player: What do flowers say that people can’t?
own.reply: Sorry, mostly. I sell more sorry than love. Men walk in looking at the floor and point at the roses.

own.label: Ask where she finds her souvenirs
own.player: Where do you find your souvenirs?
own.reply: The same market on Sundays. There’s a whole gang of us who buy spoons and snow globes and never once talk about anything but spoons. It’s very restful.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: What’s your sister like?
own.reply: Beatrice runs on a bad knee and good coffee. She told me a man at the club once called me a lovely sister. It wasn’t a compliment. She bought me a door chain.

calls.label: Ask about the two peony buyers
calls.player: Who were the two customers with different stories?
calls.reply: Eloise Rainer said she was at the kitchen door laughing with a man who left through it. Simone Ellery swore nobody left by the kitchen and Eloise wasn’t even there. Both bought peonies for the same table. One of them is lying. I write down what customers tell me, for the cards. Mr. Kell came in twice for peonies too.
calls.note: Brittany Hale heard Eloise Rainer and Simone Ellery give opposite accounts of the club’s kitchen door on gala night.

life.news: Bought a snow globe of a motel that burned down. My shelf now has a theme: places that no longer exist.
life.more: A snow globe of a cactus, a spoon from a motel that burned down, a fridge magnet of the bear. I need help. There’s a market where women like me fight over the same stall. I lost a gas station globe last month and I’m still not over it.

life.news: Did the flowers for a wedding where everyone cried, including the flowers. They wilted by the speeches.
life.more: Weddings in the desert. Everyone cries and the flowers wilt. The groom’s dad said the roses looked how he felt. I gave him one for his buttonhole. He wore it all night, completely flat. Best photo of the day.

life.news: Sold more sorry than love today. Six men. Six bunches. Six apologies.
life.more: Men walk in on the way home after doing something stupid. I can tell what they did from what they buy. Roses, he forgot something. Lilies, he’s in real trouble. Today one man bought both. I gave him a card and a pen and a stern look.

life.news: Beatrice came into the shop and rated my flowers like a coffee. She gave the tulips an eight. Highest she’s ever given anything.
life.more: My big sister rates everything out of ten. Coffee, people, my life choices. Eight for tulips is basically a medal. I made her a little bunch to take to the office. She said it was a seven out of ten bunch. She kept it on her desk all week.

gossip.says: My sister Beatrice Hale rates every coffee in Sunfall out of ten. She once rated our mom’s Christmas dinner a six. Mom hasn’t forgiven her. It was a six.
gossip.note: Brittany Hale says her sister Beatrice Hale once rated their mom’s Christmas dinner a six.
gossip.ask: Brittany says you rated your mom’s Christmas dinner a six out of ten.
gossip.answer: It was a six! The sprouts were a crime and I’m a journalist, I can’t lie in print or at the table. Brittany gave it a nine to make up for me and Mom gave her extra dessert. Sources are sacred. So is dessert.

gossip.says: Elena Vargas runs the other flower shop and we share a van. She’s much gentler than me. She knows what every flower means. I just know which ones say sorry.
gossip.note: Brittany Hale says she and Elena Vargas share a flower van.
gossip.ask: Brittany says you know what every flower means and she only knows which ones say sorry.
gossip.answer: Sorry is a very important meaning. Most people only buy flowers when something big happens: love, death, apology. Brittany handles the apologies, I do the rest. She makes people laugh while she wraps them. That’s worth more than knowing what a hyacinth means.

gossip.says: Marianne Keene from the Bluebirds beats me to the good stall at the junk market every month. She drove two hundred miles for a plastic flamingo once. She’s my hero and my enemy.
gossip.note: Brittany Hale says Marianne Keene beats her to the junk market stall every month.
gossip.ask: Brittany says you’re her hero and her enemy at the junk market.
gossip.answer: I’ll accept both titles. Junk with a memory beats diamonds without one. Brittany has a good eye and terrible timing. She arrives when the good things are gone and then buys something wonderful nobody else noticed. That’s a talent. I’ll never tell her.

women.name: Nina Petrov
women.look: Rosy fair skin, soft brown fringe and a low knot, thin wire-rimmed glasses, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about her bakery
own.player: How did a pastry chef end up in the desert?
own.reply: I followed a man here from St. Petersburg. The man left. The ovens stayed. I chose the ovens.

own.label: Ask about her painting
own.player: You paint watercolours?
own.reply: Desert landscapes. Watercolour is like this town: you can’t correct a mistake, only paint over it and hope.

own.label: Ask about the torn page
own.player: Why do you keep a torn notebook?
own.reply: A customer left a notebook at the counter with one page torn out. The next page shows the impression of the writing: a list of table numbers and a time I can’t read.
own.note: Nina Petrov has a notebook left at her counter; the page after a torn-out one shows an impression of table numbers.

own.label: Ask what she’d do over
own.player: If you could do one thing over, what would it be?
own.reply: I’d have said yes to a man who asked me to dance at a wedding in my twenties. I said I was tired. I wasn’t tired.

own.label: Ask what the bakery is known for
own.player: What should I order at your bakery?
own.reply: The rye, and the Napoleon. The club orders the Napoleon for its small dinners. The Sisters order rye for the volunteers. I prefer the Sisters.

own.label: Ask when she paints
own.player: When do you paint?
own.reply: At dawn, before the dough. Badly, which is the point. Watercolour is like this town: you can’t fix a mistake, only paint over it and hope.

calls.label: Ask about the notebook in her till
calls.player: What’s in the notebook you keep in the register?
calls.reply: A customer left it a week before the benefit. A page was torn out, but the next page holds the shape: Table 9, Table 4, Table 1, a time, and the word kitchen. The customer was Elena Cross. I’ve kept it with the takings.
calls.note: Nina Petrov has Elena Cross’s notebook; the page beneath a torn one shows Table 9, Table 4, Table 1, a time, and kitchen.

calls.label: Ask about the dinner she said no to
calls.player: Has anyone asked you out lately?
calls.reply: A widower from the casino’s board, Terence Ash. He wanted one honest meal before the club’s. I said I was tired. A lady from the club is planning to marry him, they say. I didn’t want to be the honest meal.
calls.note: Nina Petrov says the casino widower Terence Ash is expected to marry into the club.

life.news: Painted the desert at dawn before the dough. Made a mistake. Couldn’t fix it. Painted a cloud over it.
life.more: Watercolour is like this town: you can’t correct a mistake, only paint over it and hope. The cloud is now my favorite part. It looks like a dog. My actual dog looked at it and barked. High praise.

life.news: My mother rang from home and asked if I was eating. I said I make bread for a living. She said, that’s not eating.
life.more: She rings once a week and asks the same three things. Am I eating, am I married, am I coming home. No, no and no. Then she tells me about her neighbor’s cat. Ten years, the same call. I’d be lost without it.

life.news: Beat Julia at cards. Took her croissants. She said I cheat. I count. It’s different.
life.more: The pastry chefs in town have a card school. We’re rivals all week and friends for one evening. Julia plays very slowly and with feeling. I win. She pays in croissants. I eat them and tell her they’re too buttery. They’re perfect.

life.news: Danced alone in the bakery after closing. I said no to a dance once, when I was young. I think about it.
life.more: At a wedding, years ago, a man asked me to dance. I said I was tired. I wasn’t tired. I was scared it would matter. I followed a different man across the world instead and he left. The ovens stayed. Tonight I danced with the ovens.

gossip.says: Julia Mercer is my rival and she bakes like she’s in love with the dough. She has a secret name for her future café in a drawer. I know what it is. I’ll never tell her I know.
