gossip.note: Nina Petrov says she secretly knows the name Julia Mercer has chosen for her café.
gossip.ask: Nina says she knows the secret name for your café.
gossip.answer: She does NOT. Nobody knows. It’s in a drawer. Does she? How? Oh, the card night, I said it in my sleep on the sofa. Tell her if she steals it I’ll put salt in her sugar tin. Actually, tell her nothing. I’m changing the name.

gossip.says: Sophia Moretti from the Sisters bakes the parish bread with her family and her ovens are older than mine. She came to borrow flour once and stayed to pray for my sourdough starter. It’s never been better.
gossip.note: Nina Petrov says Sophia Moretti once prayed for her sourdough starter.
gossip.ask: Nina says you prayed for her sourdough starter and it’s never been better.
gossip.answer: Well, it looked so sad! God bless every living thing, and a starter is a living thing. It just needed some kindness and a warmer shelf. Nonna says all bread is a prayer. Nina says all bread is chemistry. We’re both right. The starter doesn’t mind.

women.name: Jessica Rivera
women.look: Olive skin, rose-gold bob, a beauty mark above her lip, striped T-shirt dress

own.label: Ask what the pharmacy is like
own.player: What’s it like working in a pharmacy?
own.reply: People tell me things they wouldn’t tell their doctor while I find their ointment. I know half of Sunfall’s secrets and all of its rashes.

own.label: Ask about her choir
own.player: You sing in a choir?
own.reply: Second soprano, hidden at the back. I mouth the high notes. Nobody has noticed in four years, or they’re too polite to say.

own.label: Ask if she’s shy or just careful
own.player: Are you shy, or just careful?
own.reply: Both. I rehearse phone calls in the shower. I once said you too to a waiter who told me to enjoy my meal. I still think about it.

own.label: Ask what she’d do if she weren’t scared
own.player: What would you do if you weren’t scared?
own.reply: Sing a solo. Just once. Loud, at the front, with everyone looking. Then probably faint.

own.label: Ask how she got the job
own.player: How did you end up at the pharmacy?
own.reply: My uncle’s a pharmacist and got me in. Dad fixes the museum’s lifts, Mom runs the parish school office. A very quiet family. I fit right in.

own.label: Ask about rehearsing calls
own.player: Do you really rehearse phone calls?
own.reply: In the shower, every time. I once said you too to a waiter who told me to enjoy my meal. I still think about it at night.

calls.label: Ask what the lodge’s van collects
calls.player: What does the van from the ridge pick up?
calls.reply: Every night with no moon: burn dressings, sutures, sedatives on a prescription from a doctor I’ve never seen. Once a veterinary tranquilizer we don’t stock, ordered in from a vet in the city. I copy the prescriptions. I’m quiet. I copy things.
calls.note: Jessica Rivera says the lodge’s van collects burn dressings, sutures, sedatives and once a veterinary tranquilizer on moonless nights.

life.news: A customer told me something they wouldn’t tell their doctor while I found their ointment. Again. It’s the counter.
life.more: People tell me things while I’m looking for their cream. I know half of Sunfall’s secrets and all of its rashes. I never tell. I just nod and say, aisle three. I think the shelves make people feel like they’re in confession.

life.news: Rehearsed a phone call in the shower for twenty minutes. Then the person didn’t answer.
life.more: I rehearse every call. What I’ll say, what they’ll say, the polite goodbye. I had it perfect. It went to voicemail and I panicked and said, you too. To a voicemail. I’m going to live under the counter now.

life.news: Sang the high note in choir today. Out loud. Nobody fainted.
life.more: Second soprano, hidden at the back, mouthing the high notes for four years. Today I forgot to mouth it and it just came out. Teresa turned around and looked so happy I nearly cried. I went straight back to mouthing. One note at a time.

life.news: Paige from the movie theater brought me popcorn at the end of her shift. I brought her bandages. Best trade in Sunfall.
life.more: The all-night pharmacy is next door to the movie theater. She burns her hands on the popcorn machine and I burn my brain on the night shift. We meet on the sidewalk at closing and swap supplies like spies. She tells me the endings of films. I never know the starts.

gossip.says: Paige Dalton works at the movie theater next door and knows how every film ends and how none of them start. She cries at endings of films she’s never seen. I think she’s the kindest person on the street.
gossip.note: Jessica Rivera says Paige Dalton at the movie theater cries at endings of films she hasn’t seen.
gossip.ask: Jessica says you cry at the endings of films you’ve never seen.
gossip.answer: I don’t need the start to know it matters! If someone’s running through an airport at the end, they made it, and I’m happy for them. Jessica’s the kind one. She gives me bandages and never asks how I burned myself. It’s always the popcorn machine.

gossip.says: Raven Solis sings alto in our choir in black lipstick. The old ladies were scared of her for a month. Now they knit her scarves. She has the most beautiful voice in the church.
gossip.note: Jessica Rivera says Raven Solis sings alto in black lipstick at St. Brigid’s.
gossip.ask: Jessica says you have the most beautiful voice in the church.
gossip.answer: Jessica has the most beautiful voice in the church. She just doesn’t use it. I hear her when she forgets to mouth. I don’t say anything, because I don’t know what to say. But I hear her. Tell her that.

gossip.says: Teresa Bellamy runs the choir roster and keeps threatening to put me down for a solo. The one about the lighthouse. I’d die. She knows I’d die. She keeps threatening anyway.
gossip.note: Jessica Rivera says Teresa Bellamy keeps threatening to give her a solo.
gossip.ask: Jessica says you keep threatening to give her the lighthouse solo.
gossip.answer: It isn’t a threat, it’s faith! She has a lovely voice and she hides it at the back like a secret. Hospitality is holy, and so is letting your light out from under the bushel. I won’t make her. I’ll just keep the lighthouse song warm for her.

women.name: Alana Brooks
women.look: Deep brown skin, honey-blonde beach waves, a silver ear cuff, mint polo shirt

own.label: Ask about the museum
own.player: What’s it like working at the museum?
own.reply: Quiet, cool and full of things people loved enough to keep. I tell school groups not to touch, and then I let the shy kids touch one thing.

own.label: Ask about her cookbooks
own.player: I hear you collect strange cookbooks?
own.reply: A church fundraiser book from the fifties with eleven recipes for jelly salad. Every family in it is listed by name. It’s the best history of Sunfall I own.

own.label: Ask what’s worrying her
own.player: Something on your mind?
own.reply: A woman who used to clean at the museum saw something on the gala night and told me. Now she tells everyone she was home all night. People don’t forget like that. They get frightened like that.
own.note: Alana Brooks says a museum cleaner who saw something on gala night now claims she was home all night.

own.label: Ask what she’d put in a museum of her life
own.player: What would go in a museum of your life?
own.reply: A burnt pan, a library card, and a letter I never sent. The letter would be the main exhibit.

own.label: Ask about her cookbook shelf
own.player: What’s on your cookbook shelf?
own.reply: A Victorian guide to feeding forty and a wartime pamphlet on cactus. Mom’s cookbooks went in the fire, so I’m rebuilding the shelf. It’s the only thing I have that keeps getting bigger.

own.label: Ask about her sisters
own.player: Are you the eldest Brooks?
own.reply: Eldest of four, plus two cousins. I do weekends at the diner and weekdays at the museum. I sign for every loan that comes through the museum door. Lately I wonder what I’m signing.

calls.label: Ask about the night of the fire
calls.player: What happened the night the diner burned?
calls.reply: The file says it started in the fryer. The fryer was off. I turned it off myself. And the private booking that night was for nine.
calls.note: Alana Brooks says the Lucky Cactus fire that killed her mother can’t have started in the fryer: she had turned it off, and the private booking that night was for nine.

life.news: Found a wartime cookbook at a market. Recipes for cake with no eggs, no butter and no hope. I’m making one tonight.
life.more: My mom’s cookbooks went in the fire. I’ve been rebuilding the shelf ever since: a hundred-year-old guide to feeding forty, a pamphlet about potatoes, and now this. The shelf is the only thing I’ve got that keeps getting bigger. The cake will be terrible. I’ll love it.

life.news: Signed for another crate at the museum front desk. Started reading what I sign. Nobody likes that.
life.more: I run the front desk. I sign for the loans. Lately I’ve been reading the forms all the way down, and the men who bring the crates look at their watches. I’m not suspicious. I’m thorough. It’s a different thing. Isn’t it?

life.news: Weekend shift at the Lucky Cactus. Nobody sat in Mom’s booth. Nobody ever does.
life.more: Four sisters run the diner in shifts since she died. Her booth is by the window and we keep it empty. Kimberly says sell it. I say no. I set a coffee on her table at the end of every shift and drink it myself. That’s my way of sitting with her.

life.news: A student from the university spent the whole evening in the museum’s quiet gallery and thanked me on the way out. Nobody thanks the front desk.
life.more: She comes most evenings. Very quiet, writes in a notebook, reads every label twice. Today she said, thank you for keeping it open. I nearly cried at a front desk. I’ve started leaving the gallery light on a little longer for her.

gossip.says: My sister Kimberly Brooks runs an office, does the diner’s accounts, rides a motorcycle and wants to sell our mom’s booth. She’s the one who keeps us all going. I’ll never let her sell the booth.
gossip.note: Alana Brooks says her sister Kimberly Brooks keeps the family going but wants to sell their mother’s booth.
gossip.ask: Alana says you keep the whole family going, but she’ll never let you sell the booth.
gossip.answer: I know she won’t. That’s why I keep saying it. Somebody has to say the thing out loud so the rest of us can keep it. Alana sets a coffee on that table every shift and drinks it herself. I’ve seen her. I’ll never sell the booth. Don’t tell her.

gossip.says: Bernadette Flores conserves paintings at the museum and she’s the only one there who looks at an object before she looks at its price. She brings me tea when the crates come in. She knows I don’t like the crates.
gossip.note: Alana Brooks says Bernadette Flores brings her tea when the museum crates come in.
gossip.ask: Alana says you bring her tea when the crates come in.
gossip.answer: She stands so still at the desk when the vans arrive. Someone should bring her tea. A mended thing has a story, and so does a crate, if you read the label properly. Alana reads every label. That’s rarer than people think.

gossip.says: Emma Frost from the university comes to the museum most evenings and sits in the quiet gallery with her notebook. She reads every label twice. She thanked me tonight for keeping it open.
gossip.note: Alana Brooks says Emma Frost studies in the museum’s quiet gallery most evenings.
gossip.ask: Alana says you read every label in the gallery twice.
gossip.answer: Labels lie sometimes, so you have to read them twice to catch them. History. I like the dead. They don’t text back, but they don’t ghost you either. Alana leaves the light on for me longer than she has to. I noticed. I wrote it down.

women.name: Samantha Price
women.look: Warm beige skin, strawberry-blonde braid crown, a tiny scar through one eyebrow, mint polo shirt

own.label: Ask about her work
own.player: What do you do?
own.reply: I sell houses on the reservoir side. Reservoir Residential, the good firm, not the other one. Big houses, big views, sad sellers. Ask me anything about square footage.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What do you do for fun?
own.reply: Ballroom, at the studio in the Sunfall Quarter. I started going to meet buyers. I’ve met four women who aren’t buying and one man with quarry hands who dances like a dream.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do you have family?
own.reply: Two sisters, Odette and Bethany. We have dinner once a week and I sell them absolutely nothing. I’m the middle one, which explains everything about me.

own.label: Ask about her neighbors
own.player: What are your neighbors like?
own.reply: One side’s a founding family, the other side’s another founding family, and the third side is a house whose lights never come on. Ever. Some nights there’s a car outside. Still no lights.

own.label: Ask who buys houses like hers
own.player: Who buys houses like that?
own.reply: Honestly? Every house I’ve sold on the reservoir side in five years came from a widow. Four of them went to the same trust under different names. I hadn’t thought of that as a sentence until my sister said it out loud.
own.note: Samantha Price says every reservoir-side house she has sold in five years came from a widow, and four went to the same trust under different names.

calls.label: Ask if she’s seeing anyone
calls.player: Are you seeing anyone?
calls.reply: A driver for the Foundation. Sweet, quiet, drives out to the junction a lot. I asked him once what’s out there. He changed the subject so fast he nearly hit a mailbox.

calls.label: Ask about the house with no lights
calls.player: Have you been inside the house with no lights?
calls.reply: Once, to check a leak. My firm keeps the key. It’s furnished for a dinner. Table set for nine, napkins folded. Nobody has ever eaten there. I fixed the leak and left really fast.
calls.note: Samantha Price’s firm holds the key to the empty house next to hers; inside, a dinner table is set for nine and never used.

life.news: Sold the big white house on the reservoir in one showing. Full asking price. I’m unbearable today.
life.more: The buyers walked in, saw the view, held hands. I said nothing for ten whole minutes, which for me is a medical event. Then I said the magic words, original hardwood. Done by lunch. I bought myself shoes I cannot walk in.

life.news: Ballroom tonight. I finally nailed the quickstep. My instructor cried. Or he had something in his eye.
life.more: Two years of stepping on everybody’s feet and suddenly I’m floating. The man with the quarry hands spun me so fast the whole studio went past like a carousel. The waltz class gave us a round of applause. I’m retiring at the top.

life.news: Showed a house to a couple who fought the entire time. In every single room. They put in an offer.
life.more: Kitchen, bathroom, garden, garage. A different fight in each one. At the end they kissed in the driveway and said it felt like home. Maybe it does. I went home and lay on my floor for a while.

life.news: A client paid my commission in cash. In a cookie tin.
life.more: A very old man, very polite, very clean bills. He said he doesn’t trust banks or cookies. I didn’t ask what that meant. My manager made me count it twice. It was all there, plus a ten-dollar bill with a phone number written on it.

gossip.says: Olivia Reid runs the other firm, the one that does the ridge. She smiles at me at every open house like she knows something about my listings. She doesn’t. Probably.
gossip.note: Samantha Price says Olivia Reid runs the rival real estate firm.
gossip.ask: Samantha says you smile at her like you know something.
gossip.answer: I smile at everyone, sweetheart, it’s the job. But yes, I know some things about the reservoir side that Samantha doesn’t, because she never reads past the price. She’s a lovely girl. Tell her to read past the price.

gossip.says: Bethany Price is my sister and the smart one. She reads things. She reads my contracts for fun. It’s deeply annoying and she’s always right.
gossip.note: Samantha Price says her sister Bethany Price reads her contracts for fun.
gossip.ask: Samantha says you read her contracts for fun.
gossip.answer: Somebody should! Sam signs things the way other people wave. She’s the most charming person in our family and the least curious, and I love her for it, mostly. Tell her I’m coming to dinner and I’m bringing questions.

women.name: Jade Carter
women.look: Waifish and slight, a slim small-busted figure, pale freckled skin, wide-set gray eyes with a sleepy sullen gaze, a gap-toothed smile, golden-brown ringlets, an oversized yellow sundress

women.name: Karina Flores
women.look: Slight and narrow-shouldered, pale freckled skin, wide-set heavy-lidded eyes, a strong nose, an ash-blonde lob, a sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask what tourists ask her
own.player: What do tourists ask you?
own.reply: Whether the cacti are real, whether the desert is always this hot and whether I’m single. Yes, yes, and it depends on the tip.

own.label: Ask what her book club reads
own.player: What does your book club read?
own.reply: Thrillers where the husband did it. Every time. We’re a very suspicious book club. Two members have since divorced.

own.label: Ask about Sunfall’s best-kept secret
own.player: What’s Sunfall’s best-kept secret?
own.reply: A hot spring past the old drive-in, behind a fence that says no entry. Nobody checks. I only take people there off the books.

own.label: Ask if she’d ever leave Sunfall
own.player: Would you ever leave Sunfall?
own.reply: I show people this town every day, so I know how small it is. Still, I keep finding new corners. Maybe I’m waiting for a reason to stay.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Have you got family in town?
own.reply: My sister Bernadette at the museum, my cousin Gina at the Daily. Dad built the museum’s display cases and married Mom at St. Brigid’s. We’re a family of people who look after old things.

own.label: Ask about her tour route
own.player: Where does the tour go?
own.reply: Casino, canyon, the Old Mission, the reservoir, the Cemetery Chapel. I wrote the script. There’s a second script in my head I don’t say out loud.

calls.label: Ask what the second script is
calls.player: What’s in the script you don’t say aloud?
calls.reply: At the Cemetery Chapel I tell the tourists the angels face the desert. In my head I’m counting the stones with blue ribbons and their dates. I’ve walked it forty times. I could recite them.
calls.note: Karina Flores knows every blue-ribboned grave at the Cemetery Chapel and its date.

life.news: Tourists asked the three questions again. Are the cacti real, is it always this hot, am I single.
life.more: Yes, yes, and it depends on the tip. Today a man asked all three in one breath. I said, yes, yes, and you’ve just lost your chance by asking in that order. His wife laughed so hard she gave me the tip herself.

life.news: Found a new corner of the old town nobody’s ever put on a tour. A courtyard with a fig tree. I’m keeping it.
life.more: I can’t stay in a room. I need new corners. This one has a fig tree older than the town and a cat who runs the place. I’m not putting it on the tour. Some things are for me. And maybe for one person I’d take there.

life.news: Book club met. We read a thriller where the husband did it. The husband always does it. We’re very suspicious.
life.more: Two members have divorced since we started. I’m not saying the books did it. I’m saying the books didn’t help. Tonight someone said, what if the wife did it? We all went silent. Then we reread the last chapter.

life.news: Took a busload of pensioners to the old cemetery. They told me better stories than I told them.
life.more: One woman pointed at a stone and said, he owed my father twelve dollars. Another said, she danced better than anyone in the county. I put my microphone down and let them do the tour. Best reviews I’ve ever had.

gossip.says: My sister Bernadette Flores works at the museum fixing paintings with a brush the width of an eyelash. I tell every tour group she’s the museum ghost. She waves at them very slowly. It’s the best part of the tour.
gossip.note: Karina Flores says she tells tour groups her sister Bernadette Flores is the museum ghost.
gossip.ask: Karina says you wave at her tour groups like a ghost.
gossip.answer: Slowly, so they’re not sure. A child screamed last time. Karina was delighted. I keep beautiful things from falling apart a little longer, and that includes my sister’s tours. She brings me a coffee after. That’s the fee.

gossip.says: Talia Farouk writes the travel column and sends people to the places nobody visits on purpose. Then they come on my tour and ask why I don’t go there. She’s my rival. I’ve never met her. I read every word.
gossip.note: Karina Flores says Talia Farouk the travel columnist is her rival.
gossip.ask: Karina says you’re her rival and she reads every word you write.
gossip.answer: Does she? Places nobody visits on purpose. Readers send me hate mail and then go there. If they’re joining her tour afterwards, I’m doing her advertising. Tell her I’d like to meet her. On a bus. Going nowhere. It’s the only place I talk.

women.name: Molly Sutton
women.look: Light olive skin, rose-gold bob, a small nose stud, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask what reception is like
own.player: What’s it like working on reception?
own.reply: I say good morning about three hundred times a day. I mean it every time, which I think scares people.

own.label: Ask about her cactus garden
own.player: How many cacti do you have?
own.reply: Forty-one. They all have names. Gerald is the big one. He’s had a hard year. We don’t talk about the incident with the cat.

own.label: Ask if she talks a lot
own.player: Do you always talk this much?
own.reply: Only when I’m nervous. And happy. And bored. Okay, yes. But I’m a very good listener too, I promise. Go on. Your turn.

own.label: Ask what she wishes people knew
own.player: What do you wish people knew about you?
own.reply: That I’m not as silly as I sound. I notice who’s having a bad day before they’ve said a word. I just say good morning extra nicely to them.

own.label: Ask about her sister
own.player: Who do you live with?
own.reply: My big sister Phoebe. She cooks, pays the bills and is asleep by ten. She ran our house from fourteen and ran me too. I talk enough for both of us.

own.label: Ask what she says on the phone
own.player: What do you say when you answer the phone?
own.reply: Blue Ribbon Foundation, Scholarship Drive office, how may I help. Three hundred times a day, and I mean it every time, which I think scares people.

calls.label: Ask about the visitors’ book
calls.player: Who visits the committee room?
calls.reply: I write everyone in a book, because Phoebe taught me to. A man in a lanyard goes up to the committee room without signing. He’s in my book eleven times, no surname. I call him the tall gentleman. Mr. Kell calls him Marchbanks.
calls.note: Molly Sutton’s visitors’ book has Marchbanks, the tall gentleman, going up to the committee room unsigned eleven times.

life.news: Said good morning three hundred and twelve times today. I meant every one. A man cried. Good cried.
life.more: I say good morning about three hundred times a day and I mean it every time, which I think scares people. Today a man came in looking like a raincloud, and I said it, and he stopped and said, thank you, nobody’s said that to me in a week. I gave him a mint.

life.news: I have forty-two cacti now. The new one is called Gerald the Second. After Gerald. Who had an incident.
life.more: We don’t talk about the incident with the cat. Gerald survived. He’s had a hard year. Gerald the Second is small and full of hope. I’ve put him next to Gerald so he can learn. Phoebe says I talk to them too much. They’ve never complained.

life.news: Phoebe made dinner and I talked for an hour and she said four words. Perfect sister evening.
life.more: She cooks, pays the bills and is asleep by ten. I talk enough for both of us. Her four words were: pass the salt, Molly. I counted. I’m not as silly as I sound. I notice who’s having a bad day before they do. Phoebe was having a good one.

life.news: Someone at work was having a bad day and wouldn’t say. I noticed before they did. I brought them a cactus.
life.more: I can always tell. It’s in how they hold their coffee. They said they were fine. I put a tiny cactus on their desk with a note saying, also fine. They kept it. Sometimes people don’t want to talk. They just want to know someone saw.

gossip.says: My big sister Phoebe Sutton runs the canyon before sunrise with no phone, cooks every dinner and is asleep by ten. She ran our whole house from fourteen. She’d never say it was hard. It was.
gossip.note: Molly Sutton says her sister Phoebe Sutton ran their household from the age of fourteen.
gossip.ask: Molly says you ran your whole house from fourteen and never said it was hard.
gossip.answer: Somebody had to. Dad was on the boats and Mom had gone. Molly talked enough for both of us and I did the bills. It wasn’t hard. Fine. It was hard. It’s easier now she’s grown up and only talks for one of us. Mostly.

gossip.says: Catherine Bell from the Bluebirds always stops at my desk and asks how my cacti are. By name. She remembers Gerald. Nobody else remembers Gerald.
gossip.note: Molly Sutton says Catherine Bell always asks after her cacti by name.
gossip.ask: Molly says you remember her cactus Gerald by name.
gossip.answer: Of course I remember Gerald. He had an incident. You don’t forget a cactus with a history. Molly’s desk is the only honest thing in that building. She notices who’s having a bad day before they do. She noticed mine twice. I owe her a cactus.

gossip.says: Anna Voss always hangs her coat on the same hook at the front desk and tells me a terrible joke. Every time. They’re very bad. I write them down.
gossip.note: Molly Sutton says Anna Voss tells her a terrible joke every time she hangs up her coat.
gossip.ask: Molly says you tell her a terrible joke every time you hang up your coat.
gossip.answer: Darling, they’re not terrible, they’re vintage. Molly laughs at every single one as if it’s the first joke ever told. Do you know how rare that is? At the club I’m furniture. At Molly’s desk I’m a comedian. I need that desk.

women.name: Christina Brooks
women.look: Lightly tanned fair skin, a sleek low bun, a wide bright smile, sporty tracksuit jacket

women.name: Daphne Laurent
women.look: Pale skin, short silver-dyed crop, freckles across her nose, floral blouse and jeans

women.name: Riley Dawson
women.look: Freckled fair skin, short silver-dyed crop, a small nose stud, yellow sundress

own.label: Ask about her business
own.player: What’s Dawson & Dawson?
own.reply: Me, mostly. My sister Faye is the second Dawson, and she bakes. The second Dawson is a joke. The van doesn’t know that, so we keep it.

own.label: Ask what she’s decorating at the moment
own.player: What are you working on at the moment?
own.reply: Heritage work. The old Rialto’s lobby, a shop downtown with its original tiles, and the Bluebird Club’s committee room. Old rooms tell you how to paint them if you’re patient.

own.label: Ask what she draws in her sketchbook
own.player: What do you draw in that sketchbook?
own.reply: Shopfronts, before they’re gone. I’ve drawn the old cobbler’s from the curb outside the laundromat. Funny thing: I’ve seen other women sketching the same cobbler’s from different curbs. We’ve never spoken. It’s like a club with no meetings.

own.label: Ask if there’s someone special
own.player: Is there someone in your life?
own.reply: A river man. Which in Sunfall means a boy who rents out boats on the reservoir. He smells of engine oil and sunscreen, and he’s the kindest person I know. Don’t tell him I said that.

own.label: Ask if decorating runs in the family
own.player: Is decorating a family thing?
own.reply: My dad did the Bluebird Club’s rooms for thirty years. He fell from a ladder in the lodge’s dining room when I was little. The club called it an accident and paid for everything. I could paint a straight line at eight. I took the firm.

own.label: Ask if anything strange happened at the club
own.player: Did anything strange happen while you worked at the club?
own.reply: They asked me to leave the committee room at a certain hour, and I did. Then I came back for my brushes, because I don’t leave tools. They were still in there. Nine of them around the table, and a woman in a creased linen suit holding an envelope. I told the club I’d left when asked. I told my sister the truth.
own.note: Riley Dawson went back to the Bluebird Club’s committee room for her brushes and saw nine people at the table and a woman in a creased linen suit holding an envelope.

calls.label: Ask about the pictures in the committee room
calls.player: What are the pictures on the committee room walls like?
calls.reply: Collages. I took them down to paint and put them back, twice. The second time I looked properly. I’ve got one made of receipts in my kitchen, by Daisy Chen, so I know a story when it’s glued. Those ones are stories. I just don’t know whose.

calls.label: Ask about her dad’s accident
calls.player: What happened after your dad’s accident?
calls.reply: The club paid my mom. Generously, everyone said. And she signed something. She keeps the paper in a cookie tin under her bed. She says nobody has ever asked her about it. I think she wants somebody to.
calls.note: Riley Dawson says the club paid her mother after her father’s fall in the lodge’s dining room, and her mother signed a paper she still keeps.

life.news: Painted a ceiling today without a single drip. Thirty feet up. Nobody saw. Tell me I’m amazing.
life.more: The Rialto lobby. Plaster roses all the way around and a sky in the middle that somebody painted in 1931. I matched the blue by eye. Faye says nobody looks at ceilings. That’s the point. You do it right for the one person who looks up.

life.news: Faye brought home a cake that failed. It looks like a hat. It tastes incredible.
life.more: She bakes for a group of pastry chefs who bet on each other’s cakes. When one collapses, it comes home to me. Tonight’s was meant to be a cathedral. It’s a hat. We ate half of it with spoons, standing at the counter.

life.news: Drove past the lodge today on a job. Didn’t go in. I never do.
life.more: My dad worked there for years. That’s where he fell. The club paid for everything and sent flowers. I’ll paint any room in Sunfall but that one. Faye says that’s not very professional. I say it’s the most professional thing I do.

life.news: Took the van to the reservoir after work and got rowed around by my favorite boat man. Sunset. Engine oil. Perfect.
life.more: He can’t row in a straight line to save his life, which is funny for a boat man. We went in circles for an hour and talked about nothing. I’d paint that sky if anyone would believe the colors.

gossip.says: Daisy Chen made a collage out of receipts and I bought it for my kitchen. Every time I look at it I find another story. One receipt is for a single birthday candle.
gossip.note: Riley Dawson says she bought one of Daisy Chen’s receipt collages for her kitchen.
gossip.ask: Riley says she has one of your receipt collages in her kitchen.
gossip.answer: She does. She argued me up on the price, which nobody does. That one has the receipt for a single birthday candle in it. Riley’s the only person who ever asked me who it was for. I said I don’t know. That’s the point.

gossip.says: A woman from the police records office sketches the same old cobbler’s that I do, from across the street. Cassidy Boone. We nod. We’ve never spoken. It’s perfect.
gossip.note: Riley Dawson says Cassidy Boone sketches the same old cobbler’s shop she does.
gossip.ask: Riley says you sketch the same cobbler’s she does, from across the street.
gossip.answer: The cobbler’s downtown, before they knock it down. I take the curb by the bus stop. She takes the laundromat side. We nod and never talk. It’s the best friendship I have. Don’t ruin it by introducing us.

women.name: Lacey Wilson
women.look: Deep brown skin, twist-out coils, a small nose stud, red gingham shirt

own.label: Ask about the flower shop
own.player: What’s it like running a flower shop?
own.reply: It’s my mom’s shop, Wilson’s Flowers on Brown Avenue. People only come in when something big happens. Love, a death, an apology. You see the whole town’s heart from behind the counter.

own.label: Ask what she does in the evenings
own.player: What do you do in the evenings?
own.reply: I go up on the roof and look at the stars. Other people drive out past the canyon to see them properly. I see them from the poor end of Brown Avenue. They’re the same stars.

own.label: Ask who her biggest customers are
own.player: Who are your biggest customers?
own.reply: The parish altar, the Cemetery Chapel’s chrysanthemums, and the Foundation’s committee room. The Foundation’s flowers are always white. Always. I’ve never been told why. I think I know.

own.label: Ask if she keeps a diary
own.player: Do you keep a diary?
own.reply: A journal of what I want. That’s new for me. I used to write down what other people wanted from me. Now it’s one line a night, for me. It’s harder than it sounds.

own.label: Ask if she’s ever been in love
own.player: Have you ever been in love?
own.reply: At nineteen. A Bluebird’s nephew. He dressed me, took me to the club, had a gown made, and proposed in St. Brigid’s with a ring from Whitmore’s. The committee didn’t approve. He was gone within a month. Someone else’s now.

own.label: Ask why the white flowers bother her
own.player: Why do the white flowers bother you?
own.reply: Because I know which stones they go to in the end. Twelve of them, at the Cemetery Chapel. I know whose. The twelfth one is his. I wrote in my journal what I’d say to the Foundation’s man about it. My mom tore the page out. She said the shop is the shop.
own.note: Lacey Wilson says the Foundation’s white flowers end up on twelve stones at the Cemetery Chapel, and the twelfth is her former fiancé’s.

calls.label: Ask how her mom is
calls.player: How’s your mom?
calls.reply: Ill, in a slow way. She still does the altar flowers when she can stand long enough. She taught me lilies at twelve, next to Elena Vargas. We were the two littlest florists in the parish.

calls.label: Ask if she still has the ring
calls.player: Do you still have the ring?
calls.reply: I kept it. Clara Whitmore from the jeweler’s has asked for it back twice. She says rings remember. I don’t know what she means. I don’t like how she says it.

life.news: Clear night. I counted shooting stars from the roof. Seven. I made the same wish seven times.
life.more: My dog sat with me and my cat sat on the dog. We stayed up until the canyon went dark. I wished the same thing every time, which is either very sensible or a waste of six wishes. I’m not telling you what it was. Yet.

life.news: Someone ordered a single white rose with no card, paid cash, and asked me to leave it on the shop step overnight. I did.
life.more: In the morning it was gone. No one saw who took it. My mom said not to ask. She says that a lot about the white orders. I wrote it in my journal anyway, under things I want to know.

life.news: My mom had a bad day. I did the altar flowers alone for the first time. My hands shook.
life.more: She’s been ill a long time, slowly. Today she couldn’t stand long enough. I did the lilies the way she taught me, and nobody at the parish noticed it wasn’t her. That was the worst part. And the best part. I cried in the van after.

life.news: Wrote something new in my journal tonight. Something I want. First time I didn’t cross it out.
life.more: One line. It’s small, but it’s mine, and it isn’t about the shop or my mom or anybody else. I read it back three times. I’m stronger when I’m pushed. I just never used to push myself.

gossip.says: Elena Vargas and I learned the altar lilies side by side when we were twelve. We still help each other out when one shop runs short.
gossip.note: Lacey Wilson learned altar flowers alongside Elena Vargas as a girl.
gossip.ask: Lacey Wilson says you two learned the altar lilies side by side at twelve.
gossip.answer: We did, under Agnes Castillo’s eye. Lacey was the neat one. I was the one who talked to the flowers. We still swap chrysanthemums when one of us runs out. She always gives me more than I ask for.

gossip.says: Daniela Cruz made me a gown once, for the club. The most beautiful thing I’ve ever worn. I wore it one time.
gossip.note: Lacey Wilson says Daniela Cruz made her a gown for the club that she wore once.
gossip.ask: Lacey says you made her a gown for the club and she only wore it once.
gossip.answer: Once. I remember it. Ivory, a low back, pockets because she asked. Every dress I make should outlast the evening it was made for. That one didn’t get the chance. I’d make her another tomorrow.

women.name: Giselle Ford
women.look: Dark skin, ash-blonde lob, a gap-toothed smile, sporty tracksuit jacket

own.label: Ask about the front desk
own.player: What’s it like working the hospital’s front desk?
own.reply: Twelve years. Everyone’s worst night starts with me. I’m cheerful about it. That’s the job. If I looked worried, they’d really panic.

own.label: Ask what she does for fun
own.player: What are you into outside work?
own.reply: Old records. Singers who made one album and vanished. I buy them at a stall downtown and play them for the night porters. They pretend to hate it. One of them hums along now.

own.label: Ask about her family
own.player: Do you have family in Sunfall?
own.reply: My sister Katrina. She’s the quiet one with the camera, and I’m the loud one with the desk. Our dad was a signalman. He taught us both to listen down the line for the train. She listens. I talk over it.

own.label: Ask about the visitor book
own.player: Do you really write down everyone who comes in?
own.reply: Everyone. Real names, fake names, the ones who sign with an X. Twelve years of it. I’ve never once read it like a story. My sister did once. She went quiet, and Katrina’s always quiet, so that’s saying something.

own.label: Ask her something serious
own.player: Can I ask you something serious?
own.reply: Ugh. Fine. One serious thing, and then you have to tell me something stupid. Those are the rules at my desk.

calls.label: Ask if everyone comes in the front
calls.player: Does everyone come in through the front?
calls.reply: Mostly. A porter told me some men come in through the ambulance bay instead, so they never pass my desk. I asked if a receptionist is allowed to write the back door in the front desk’s book. Nobody’s said no yet.
calls.note: Giselle Ford says some men come into the hospital through the ambulance bay so they never pass the front desk.

calls.label: Ask if there’s someone special
calls.player: Is there someone special at the hospital?
calls.reply: A night porter. Sometimes. He hums along to my records and pretends he isn’t. That’s about as serious as I get, so don’t push it.

life.news: Found a record at the stall today by a woman who sang one perfect album and then just stopped. I’m obsessed.
life.more: Nineteen seventy-four, one album, nine songs, and then nothing. No comeback, no explanation. I played it at the desk all night. A man waiting for his wife asked who it was. I said nobody knows. He said that was the saddest thing he’d ever heard, then asked me to write down the name.

life.news: Someone checked in tonight as John Doe the Third. I wrote it down. I write everyone down.
life.more: He had a burned thumb and a very bad mustache. I said, Mr. Doe, please take a seat, your family has been expecting you. He laughed so hard he forgot it hurt. That’s my whole medical training right there.

life.news: Long night. Somebody’s kid. I smiled the whole time. Now my face won’t stop.
life.more: That’s the part nobody tells you. You smile so the family doesn’t fall apart in the lobby, and then you get home and your face still won’t come down. I put a record on and lay on the floor until it was light out.

life.news: Dinner with my sister. We talked about absolutely nothing for two hours. Perfect.
life.more: Katrina and I have a rule: no hospital, no cameras, nothing heavy. We talk about shoes and our dad’s terrible jokes. She laughed once, out loud. I’m counting it as a win for the whole year.

gossip.says: Maya Serrano runs the emergency department like a bar at closing time. Nobody fights on her shift. I think they’re scared of her snacks running out.
gossip.note: Giselle Ford says nobody fights on Maya Serrano’s shift in the emergency department.
gossip.ask: Giselle says nobody dares start anything on your shift.
gossip.answer: Because I feed them. A man can’t throw a punch with a granola bar in his hand. Giselle sends them to me smiling and I meet them with a snack. Between us we’ve calmed down half of Sunfall.

gossip.says: Veda Thorn’s mom works the night ward. Veda comes in at the end of the shift with coffee for her mom and black lipstick for everyone else. The porters are terrified and delighted.
gossip.note: Giselle Ford says Veda Thorn’s mother works the night ward at the hospital.
gossip.ask: Giselle says you bring your mom coffee at the end of her night shift.
gossip.answer: Every time. She’s worked nights since before I was born. Giselle always waves me through like I’m famous. The porters look at me like I’m about to curse the building. I might.

gossip.says: Emily Fairchild stitches faster than anyone in the hospital and apologizes the whole time. Sorry, sorry, nearly done. Patients love her. The doctors find it exhausting.
gossip.note: Giselle Ford says Emily Fairchild is the fastest stitcher at the hospital.
gossip.ask: Giselle says you apologize the whole time you’re stitching someone up.
gossip.answer: I do not. Well. Maybe a little. If someone’s bleeding, saying sorry feels like the least I can do. Giselle says hello to people having a heart attack. We all cope differently.
